5.  I have made a critical edition of the
	    Kṣaṇabhaṅgasiddhi-Anvayātmikā on the basis of three previous
	    editions and the manuscript from the Nepal National
	    Library. I have also improved its some parts with the Pathna
	    manuscript, Jñānaśrīmitra’s Kṣaṇabhaṅgādhyāya and other
	    Naiyāika’s works, such as the Nyāyabhūṣaṇa and the
	    Tātparyaṭīkā.  However, I have made the database of other
	    works without a thorough investigation of them.  I have
	    intended to use it as a reference for reading the
	    Anvayātmikā.  Thus, I must admit that there are lots of
	    errors and misspellings in this version.  I would appreciate
	    it if the user would point out any mistake in this database
	    so that I can improve it.

Woo, Jeson 
	  Penn and Hiroshima U.

Explanatory Remarks

	  1.  This is a database of Ratnakīrti’s works.  It
	    includes the whole work in the
	    Ratnakīrtinibandhāvaliḥ.

	    2.  The list of the works is as follows:
	    1) Sarvajñasiddhiḥ
	      2) Īśvarasādhanadūṣaṇam
	      3) Apohasiddhiḥ
	      4) Kṣaṇabhaṅgasiddhiḥ-Anvayātmikā
	      5) Kṣaṇabhaṅgasiddhiḥ-Vyatirekātmikā
	      6) Pramāṇāntarbhāvaprakaraṇam
	      7) Vyāptinirṇayaḥ
	      8) Sthirasiddhidūṣaṇam
	      9) Citrādvaitaprakāśavādaḥ
	      10) Santānāntaradūṣaṇam

	    3.  The texts used for this database are as follows:
	    1), 2), 3), 4), 6), 7), 9) and 10): Ratnakīrtinibandhāvaliḥ, ed. A. Thakur, 
              Patna: Kashi Prasad Jayaswal Research Institute, 2nd ed. 1975.
	    5): An Eleventh-Century Buddhist Logic of Exists, A. C. Senape Mcdermott, 
              Dordrecht-Holland: D. Reidel Publishing Company, 1967.
	    8): La Refutation Bouddhique de la Permanence des Choses
	    (Sthirasiddhidūṣaṇa) et la Preuve de la Momentanite des
	    Choses (Kṣaṇabhaṅgasiddhi), K. Mimaki, Paris: Instititut de
	    Civilization Indienne, 1976.

	    4.  I give the page and the line numbers in two different ways.
	    4.1 The numbers in each individual database but 5)
	      and 8) correspond to the page and the line numbers in
	      Thakur’s second edition.  For instance, [30.10] indicates
	      the page 30 and the line 10 in the edition.  The numbers
	      in 5) and 8) respectively correspond to those which appear
	      in Macdermott’s and Mimaki’s editions.  Therefore, their
	      numbers indicate the page and the line numbers in Thakur’s
	      first edition.
	      4.2 The whole number in the database of
	      Ratnakīrtinibandhāvaliḥ corresponds to the page and the
	      line numbers in Thakur’s second edition.

	    5.  I have made a critical edition of the
	    Kṣaṇabhaṅgasiddhi-Anvayātmikā on the basis of three previous
	    editions and the manuscript from the Nepal National
	    Library. I have also improved its some parts with the Pathna
	    manuscript, Jñānaśrīmitra’s Kṣaṇabhaṅgādhyāya and other
	    Naiyāika’s works, such as the Nyāyabhūṣaṇa and the
	    Tātparyaṭīkā.  However, I have made the database of other

	    intended to use it as a reference for reading the
	    Anvayātmikā.  Thus, I must admit that there are lots of

children.text: Sarvajñasiddhiḥ
children.translated_text: Proof of the Omniscient One (<s>Sarvajñasiddhi</s>)

children.text: namas tārāyai
children.translated_text: Homage to <s>Tārā</s>.

children.text: yasminn avajñā narakaprasūtir bhaktiś ca sarvābhimatapradāyinī |
children.translated_text: He in whom disregard gives rise to hell, and devotion bestows all that is desired,

children.text: avyāhataṃ yo jagadekabandhuḥ sa jñāyate sarvavid atra nirmalam ||
children.translated_text: whose [knowledge] is unimpeded, who is the sole kinsman of the world — he is known as the omniscient one, the pure one.

children.text: iha hi dharmajñād aparam anavaśeṣajñam anicchann api
kumārilo
children.translated_text: <s>Kumārila</s>

children.text:
dharmajña eva kevale pratiṣiddhe
	vedam upādeyam abhimanyamānaḥ paṭhati
children.translated_text: thinking that the knower of <s>dharma</s> alone, when everything else is excluded, should accept the <s>Veda</s> as authoritative, states:
Here indeed, even one unwilling [to accept] someone other than a knower of <s>dharma</s> as a knower of everything without remainder —

children.text: dharmajñatvaniṣedhas tu kevalo 'tropayujyate |
children.translated_text: "But only the denial of the knowledge of <s>dharma</s> is relevant here;

children.text: sarvam anyad vijānaṃs tu puruṣaḥ kena vāryate || iti |
children.translated_text: a person who knows everything else — by what is he prevented?" Thus.

children.text: tad ayam ācāryo 'pi sarvasarvajñacaraṇareṇusanāthaṃ yāvad ākāśaṃ jagadicchann api tribhuvanacūḍāmaṇībhūtasaparikaraheyopādeyatattvajñapuruṣapuṇḍarīka-prasādhanād apy apramāṇakajaḍavaidikaśabdarāśipramukhasakaladurmatipravādapratihatir ity antarnayann āha –
children.translated_text: Therefore this master too, while desiring the world extending up to the sky, accompanied by the dust of the feet of the all-knowing omniscient one, and wishing to establish the supreme person who knows the truth of what is to be rejected and accepted, together with his retinue — who are the crest-jewels of the three worlds — yet incorporating [the point that] refutation of all the assemblages of false doctrines headed by the inert mass of unauthoritative <s>Vedic</s> words of the dull-witted is [also achieved thereby], says:

children.text: heyopādeyatattvasya sābhyupāyasya vedakaḥ |
children.translated_text: "He who knows the truth of what is to be rejected and accepted, together with the means [thereto],

children.text: yaḥ pramāṇam asāviṣṭo na tu sarvasya vedakaḥ ||
PV

children.translated_text: is the authority — such a one is sought, not one who knows everything."

children.text:
ityādi || tad idānīm upayuktasarvajñam eva tāvat prasādhayāmaḥ |
	  paryante tu sarvasarvajñadohadam apy apaneṣyāmaḥ | svāsthyam
	  āsthīyatām |
children.translated_text: And so forth. Therefore, let us now first establish the omniscient one who is relevant [to our purpose]. At the end, we shall also dispel the longing for an omniscient one who knows absolutely everything. Let there be composure.

children.text: yo yaḥ sādaranirantaradīrghakālābhyāsasahitacetoguṇaḥ sa sarvaḥ sphuṭībhāvayogyaḥ |
children.translated_text: Whatever mental quality is accompanied by practice that is respectful, uninterrupted, and of long duration — all such [qualities] are capable of becoming vivid;

children.text:
yathā yuvatyākāraḥ kāminaḥ puruṣasya | yathoktābhyāsasahitacetoguṇāś
	  cāmī caturāryasatyaviṣayā ākārā iti svabhāvo hetuḥ |
children.translated_text: just as the form of a young woman [becomes vivid] for a man filled with desire. And these mental qualities, accompanied by such practice as described, which have the four noble truths as their object, are forms [of cognition] — this is the reason based on essential nature (<s>svabhāva-hetu</s>).

children.text:
tatra na tāvād
	āśrayadvāreṇa hetudvāreṇa vāsiddhisambhāvanā |
	saṃkalparūḍhānāṃ caturāryasatyākārāṇām
cetoguṇa
children.translated_text: being merely a mental quality,

children.text:
mātrasya ca hetoḥ
	pratyātmavedyatvāt | nāpi
	sādaranirantaradīrghakālābhyāsalakṣaṇaṃ hetuviśeṣaṇam
	asambhāvanīyam | tathā hi saṃsārasvabhāvaṃ duḥkhātiśayam
	apanetum iyaṃ saṃkalpārūḍhā caturāryasatyākārabhāvanā
	prārabdhā | asyāś cāsambhāvanā nāma kiṃ (1) bhāvyasya
	saṃkalpārūḍhatvāsambhavāt (2) anarthitvāt (3)
	heyarūpāniścayāt (4) heyasya nityatvāt (5) tasyāhetutvāt
	(6) taddhetor nityatvāt (7) heyahetvaparijñānāt (8)
	tadbādhakābhāvāt (9) bādhakāparijñānāt (10) cittasya
	doṣātmakatvāt (11) tasya vyavasthitaguṇatvāt (12)
	bhavāntarābhāvāt (13) dhvastadoṣapunarudbhavād veti
	trayodaśa vikalpāḥ ||
children.translated_text: and the reason [itself] are known through personal experience. Nor is the qualifier of the reason — namely, practice characterized as respectful, uninterrupted, and of long duration — to be deemed impossible. For this contemplation of the four noble truth-forms, having risen to deliberate resolve, has been undertaken in order to remove the extreme of suffering, which is the nature of <s>saṃsāra</s>. And the impossibility of this [contemplation] — is it due to (1) the impossibility of the object of contemplation having risen to deliberate resolve, (2) the absence of motivation, (3) uncertainty about the nature of what is to be rejected, (4) the permanence of what is to be rejected, (5) its being uncaused, (6) the permanence of its cause, (7) non-comprehension of the cause of what is to be rejected, (8) the absence of an antidote, (9) non-comprehension of the antidote, (10) the mind being inherently defiled, (11) its having fixed qualities, (12) the non-existence of future lives, or (13) the re-arising of destroyed defilements? — these are the thirteen alternatives.
In this regard, there is no suspicion of unestablishedness either through the substratum or through the reason. For the four noble truth-forms that have risen to the level of deliberate resolve,

children.text:
tatra na tāvad ādyaḥ pakṣaḥ |
	saparikaraheyopādeyātmakasya caturādyasatyākārasya bhāvyasya
	vikalpārūḍhasya pratyātmavedyatvāt ||
children.translated_text: Of these, the first alternative is not [valid], because the object of contemplation — the four primary truth-forms, whose nature includes what is to be rejected and accepted together with [their] retinue — having risen to the level of conceptual determination, is known through personal experience.

children.text:
nāpi dvitīyaḥ |
	duḥkhamātrasyāpi parityāgārthitvena vyāpteḥ
	sarvajanānubhavasiddhatvāt ||
children.translated_text: Nor is the second [valid], because it is established through the experience of all people that even suffering alone is pervaded by the desire for its relinquishment.

children.text:
nāpi tṛtīyaḥ | saṃsārātmano
	duḥkhasvarūpasya pratīteḥ | katham asya duḥkhātmakatvam iti cet |
	saṃkṣepataḥ kathitaṃ
children.translated_text: Nor is the third [valid], because <s>saṃsāra</s> in its essential nature is experienced as having the nature of suffering. If it be asked: how is it of the nature of suffering? It has been stated in brief:

children.text: sākṣād duḥkhaprakṛti narakaṃ pretatiryakkharūpaṃ martye śama kvacana tad api grastam evāsukhena |
children.translated_text: "Hell is suffering by its very nature; the realms of hungry ghosts and animals are [likewise]; in the human realm there is peace in some measure, but even that is consumed by unhappiness;

children.text: devānāṃ ca kṣayam upagate puṇyapātheyapiṇḍe caṇḍajvālāvyatikaramuco hanta bhogāsta eva ||
children.translated_text: and for the gods, when the provisions of merit are exhausted, alas — those very enjoyments become [flames] emitting fierce blazing fire."

children.text: iti ||
children.translated_text: Thus.

children.text: na ca caturthaḥ | vārtamānikapañcaskandhātmakasya duḥkhasyotpādadarśanāt ||
children.translated_text: Nor is the fourth [valid], because the arising of suffering, whose nature is the present five <s>skandhas</s> (aggregates), is observed.

children.text: na ca pañcamaḥ | duḥkhasya kādācitkatvāt ||
children.translated_text: Nor is the fifth [valid], because suffering is occasional [and therefore not permanent].

children.text: nāpi ṣaṣṭhaḥ | kāryakādācitkatvasya anityahetukatvena vyāptatvāt ||
children.translated_text: Nor is the sixth [valid], because the occasional nature of an effect is pervaded by [the fact of] having a non-permanent cause.

children.text: nāpi saptamaḥ | duḥkhe viparyāsatṛṣṇāpravṛttiśaktikarmabhiḥ sahitasyātmadṛṣṭilakṣaṇasya hetoḥ sāṃsārikapañcaskandhalakṣaṇakāryānyathānupapattito niścayāt | yad āhuḥ
children.translated_text: Nor is the seventh [valid], because there is certainty, from the impossibility of the effect being otherwise, that suffering has as its cause the view of a self (<s>ātma-dṛṣṭi</s>) — accompanied by error, craving, the power of activity, and <s>karma</s> — and the effect is the <s>saṃsāric</s> five aggregates. As they say:

children.text: ahaṃkāras tāvat tadanu mamakāras tadubhayaprasūto rāgādis tadahitamater dveṣadahanaḥ |
children.translated_text: "First ego-consciousness, then the sense of 'mine'; from those two arises attachment and the rest; from hostility of mind toward the disagreeable comes the fire of hatred;

children.text: tataḥ śeṣaḥ kleśas tata udayinaḥ karmavisarādvisārī saṃsāraḥ śaraṇarahito dāruṇataraḥ ||
children.translated_text: then the remaining afflictions (<s>kleśas</s>); from those arise actions; from the spreading of actions, <s>saṃsāra</s> spreads forth — shelterless, most terrible."

children.text: tasmāt tṛṣṇāviparyāsāv ātmadṛṣṭipuraḥsarau |
children.translated_text: "Therefore, craving and error, preceded by the view of self,

children.text: aṃsāriskandhajanakau nirṇītau kāryahetutaḥ ||
children.translated_text: are ascertained, from the effect, to be the producers of the <s>saṃsāric</s> aggregates."

children.text:
ātmadarśanasya
	cāvidyātvam ātmapratikṣepato draṣṭavyam | tadabhāve 'pi
	kṣaṇabhaṅgaprastāve paralokādikam anākulam avasthāpitam ||
children.translated_text: And that the seeing of a self is a form of <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance) is to be understood from the refutation of the self. Even in its absence [i.e., even without the self-view], in the context of momentariness, the next world and so forth have been established without confusion.

children.text: na cāṣṭamaḥ | ātmadṛṣṭirūpāyā avidyāyāḥ pratipakṣabhūtasya nairātmyadarśanasya sambhavāt ||
children.translated_text: Nor is the eighth [valid], because the seeing of selflessness (<s>nairātmya-darśana</s>), which is the antidote to <s>avidyā</s> in the form of the self-view, is possible.

children.text: nāpi navamaḥ | nairātmyadarśanasya mārgaśabdavācyasya pramāṇato niścitatvāt ||
children.translated_text: Nor is the ninth [valid], because the seeing of selflessness, designated by the word 'path' (<s>mārga</s>), has been ascertained through valid means of knowledge (<s>pramāṇa</s>).

children.text: daśamo 'py asambhavī | doṣāvasthāyāṃ cittasya saṃskārāpekṣatvāt | yo hi yatsvabhāvas tasmin svabhāve vyavasthito na saṃskāram apekṣate | yathā doṣam apanīya tapanīyam akṣayadaśāyām avasthitam | apekṣate ca cittam avidyāvasthāyāṃ saṃskāram iti vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhiḥ | pratiṣedhyasya tatsvabhāvatvasya yadvyāpakaṃ saṃskāranirapekṣatvaṃ tadviruddhaṃ tadapekṣatvam iti cittasya doṣātmakatvakṣatiḥ ||
children.translated_text: The tenth too is impossible, because the mind in its defiled state is dependent on conditioning (<s>saṃskāra</s>). For that which has a certain nature, when established in that nature, does not depend on conditioning — just as gold, once its impurities are removed, is established in its imperishable state. But the mind in its state of <s>avidyā</s> does depend on conditioning — this constitutes the apprehension of what is contradictory to the pervader (<s>vyāpaka-viruddha-upalabdhi</s>). That is: the pervader of the property to be negated (being of the nature of defilement) is independence from conditioning, and what contradicts that is dependence on conditioning — thus the thesis that the mind is inherently defiled is undermined.

children.text: ekādaśo 'py ayuktaḥ | cetasas tattatsamskārātiśaye prajñātiśayadarśanāt ||
children.translated_text: The eleventh too is unjustified, because in the mind, when there is a superabundance of particular conditionings, a superabundance of wisdom is observed.

children.text: na ca dvādaśaḥ | paralokaprasādhanāt | tathā hi, yac cittaṃ tat cittāntaraṃ pratisandhatte | yathedānīntanaṃ cittam | cittaṃ ca maraṇakālabhāvīti svabhāvahetuḥ |
children.translated_text: Nor is the twelfth [valid], because of the establishment of the next world. Namely: whatever is a mind gives rise to another mind — just as the present mind does. And the mind exists at the time of death — this is a reason based on essential nature (<s>svabhāva-hetu</s>).

children.text: na cārhaccaramacittena vyabhicāraḥ | tasyāgamamātrataḥ pratītatvāt | niḥkleśacittāntarajananād vā | hetor vā kleśe satīti viśeṣaṇād ity anāgatabhavasiddhiḥ | evaṃ yac cittaṃ tac cittāntarapūrvakaṃ yathedānīntanaṃ cittaṃ | cittaṃ ca janmasamayabhāvīty arthataḥ kāryahetur ity atītabhavasiddhiḥ ||
children.translated_text: Nor is there deviation [from the thesis] on account of the final mind of an <s>Arhat</s>, because that [i.e., its cessation] is known only from scripture. Or because it generates a mind-moment free from afflictions. Or because the reason is qualified by 'when affliction is present' — thus future existence is established. Similarly, whatever is a mind is preceded by another mind, just as the present mind is. And the mind exists at the time of birth — this is essentially a reason from effect (<s>kārya-hetu</s>) — thus past existence is established.

children.text: na ca trayodaśaḥ | doṣakāraṇasyātmadarśanasya yadviruddhaṃ nairātmyadarśanaṃ tasya nirupadravatvāt | bhūtārthatvāt | svabhāvatvāc ca | sarvadāvasthiteḥ | tan nāyaṃ viśeṣaṇāsiddho 'pi hetuḥ | tathāpīdṛśo 'bhyāso na kasyacid dṛśyata iti cet | na dṛśyatām | sambhāvanā tāvad aśakyapratiṣedhā | idānīntanajanapravṛttiś cāvyāhateti nāparaṃ gamyate | ata evedaṃ sambhāvanānumānam ucyate ||
children.translated_text: Nor is the thirteenth [valid], because the seeing of selflessness, which contradicts the self-view that is the cause of defilement, is without adversity, because it apprehends reality, because it is [the mind's] essential nature, and because it is always present. Therefore this reason is not unestablished even in its qualifier. If it be objected: 'But such practice is never seen in anyone' — let it not be seen; at least the possibility [of it] cannot be denied. And the activity of present-day people remains unimpeded — thus nothing further follows. For this very reason, this is called an inference establishing possibility.

children.text:
na caiṣa viruddho hetuḥ | sapakṣe
	kāminy ākāre sambhavāt |
children.translated_text: Nor is this a contradictory reason (<s>viruddha-hetu</s>), because it obtains in the homologous instance (<s>sapakṣa</s>) — in the case of the form of a young woman for a lover.

children.text:
na cānaikāntikaḥ | abhyāsasahitacetoguṇasphuṭapratibhāsayoḥ
	kāryakāraṇayor ghaṭakumbhakārayor iva sarvopasaṃhāreṇa
	pratyakṣānupalambhataḥ kāryakāraṇabhāvasiddhāv
	abhyāsasahitacetoguṇatvasya sādhanasya sphuṭapratibhāsakaraṇayogyatayā
	vyāptisiddheḥ | tathā hi vyāptyadhikaraṇe kāmātur avartini yuvatyākāre
	sādaranirantaradīrghakālābhyāsasahitacetoguṇāt pūrvaṃ anupalabdhiḥ
	sphuṭābhasya | paścād abhyāsasaṃvedanaṃ sphuṭābhasaṃvedanam iti |
	trividhapratyakṣānupalambhasādhyaḥ kāryakāraṇabhāvaḥ
	sphuṭapratibhāsābhyāsasacivacittākārayor iyam upapannā
	sarvopasaṃhāravatī vyāptiḥ | ato 'naikāntikatāpy asambhavinīty
	anavadyo hetuḥ ||
children.translated_text: Nor is it inconclusive (<s>anaikāntika</s>), because the causal relation between the two — the mental quality accompanied by practice and vivid appearance — which are [related as] effect and cause like a pot and a potter, is established through threefold perceptual non-apprehension with complete induction. Namely, in the domain of the pervasion, in the case of the form of a young woman for a passionate lover: prior to the mental quality accompanied by respectful, uninterrupted, long-duration practice, there is non-apprehension of vivid appearance; subsequently, there is the apprehension of practice along with the apprehension of vivid appearance. This causal relation between vivid appearance and the mental form accompanied by practice — established through threefold perceptual non-apprehension — constitutes a pervasion with complete induction. Therefore inconclusiveness too is impossible — hence the reason is faultless.

children.text:
nanu katham anumānataḥ
	sarvajñasiddhipratyāśā | tasya parokṣatvena
	tatpratibaddhaliṅgāniścayāt | kiṃ ca sarvajñasattāsādhane sarvo hetur
	na trayīṃ doṣajātim atipatati | sarvajñe hi dharmiṇy asiddhatvam |
	asarvajñe hi viruddhatvam | ubhayātmake 'py anaikāntikatvam iti ||
children.translated_text: Objection: How can there be the expectation of proving omniscience through inference? Since [the omniscient one] is imperceptible, there can be no certainty of a logical mark connected with him. Moreover, any reason adduced to prove the existence of an omniscient being cannot escape the threefold fault: with respect to the omniscient subject, there is unestablishedness; with respect to the non-omniscient, there is contradiction; and with respect to what partakes of both natures, there is inconclusiveness.

children.text:
api ca abhyāsāt kāraṇāt kāryasya
	sphuṭābhasya pratītau nāvaśyaṃ kāraṇāni kāryavanti bhavantīty
	anaikāntikatā | atha sphuṭībhāvayogyatānumīyate | sāpi śaktir ucyate |
	sā ca kārye 'nantarā sāntarā vā | atrādyā kāryasamadhigamyā | na
	cādhigatakāryasya tayā kaścid upayogaḥ | dvitīyā tu kāryāvasāyam
	aikāntikaṃ na sādhayet ||
children.translated_text: Furthermore, even if the production of vivid appearance (the effect) from practice (the cause) is established, not all causes necessarily have their effects — hence inconclusiveness. If, however, what is inferred is the capacity for becoming vivid: that too is called a power (<s>śakti</s>). And that is either immediately followed by its effect or separated from it. In the first case, it is known together with the knowledge of the effect, and there is no use for one who has already ascertained the effect. In the second case, it would not conclusively establish the determination of the effect.

children.text: na ca kāryāpratītau yogyatāniścayaḥ sambhavī | nāpi yogyatāmātrasādhane kṛtārthaḥ sādhanavādī | sarvajñajñāne kārye vivādasya tādavasthyād | bhavatu sphuṭībhāvasya siddhiḥ | tathāpi kaḥ prastāvaḥ sarvajñavivāde sādhanam ārabdhavataḥ sphuṭatvaṃ cetasaḥ sādhayitum ||
children.translated_text: Nor is the ascertainment of capacity possible when the effect has not been apprehended. Nor is the proponent of the proof satisfied with merely proving capacity, since the dispute concerns the effect — namely, omniscient knowledge — and remains as before. Granted that vividness is established; even so, what occasion is there, for one who has undertaken the proof in the dispute about omniscience, to prove the vividness of the mind?

children.text: kiṃ ca prasiddhānumāne bhūtalasya dharmiṇi kumbhakāraghaṭayor api dharmayoḥ pratītatvāt kāryakāraṇabhāvo grahītuṃ śakyata eva | prastute tu kāmātur asantānavartino yuvatyākārasya dharmiṇas tatpragatābhyāsasphuṭatvayor api dharmayoḥ parokṣatvāt | kathaṃ kāryakāraṇagṛhītiḥ | yathā ca naiyāyikaṃ prati yuṣmābhir ucyate pratyakṣato na kāryamātraṃ puruṣavyāptaṃ sidhyati | kiṃ tv avāntaram eva ghaṭajātīyaṃ kāryam iti tathā nākāramātram abhyāsapūrvakaṃ sidhyati | kiṃ tv avāntaram eva yuvatyākārasāmānyam iti vyaktam eva | na cābhyāsakāryaḥ sphuṭībhāvaḥ | tadabhāve 'pi svapne darśanāt ||
children.translated_text: Moreover, in a well-known inference, because both properties — the potter and the pot — are perceived in the substratum (the ground), the causal relation can indeed be grasped. But in the present case, since both properties — the practice pertaining to the form of a young woman for a passionate lover (the subject) and the vividness arising from it — are imperceptible, how can the causal relation be grasped? And just as it is said by you against the <s>Naiyāyikas</s>: 'From perception, it is not mere effect-hood that is established as pervaded by a person, but only a particular subclass of effects, namely those of the pot-type' — similarly, it is clear that it is not mere mental form that is established as preceded by practice, but only a particular subclass, namely, that belonging to the class of the form of a young woman. Nor is vividness an effect of practice, since it is seen even in dreams in its absence.

children.text: kiṃ ca sarvavido 'pi yadi caturāryasatyaparijñānataḥ sarvajñatāsthitiḥ, tarhi ghaṭādikatipayavastujñāne 'pi sarvajñeti sādhvī śuddhiḥ | api ca
children.translated_text: Moreover, even for one who knows everything, if omniscience consists in the comprehension of the four noble truths, then even in the knowledge of a few things such as a pot, one would be omniscient — an excellent purification indeed! Furthermore,

children.text: jñānavān mṛgyate kaścit taduktapratipattaye |
children.translated_text: "A knowledgeable person is sought in order to understand what he has stated,

children.text: ajñopadeśakaraṇe vipralambhanaśaṅkibhiḥ ||
(PV II 30)

children.translated_text: by those who suspect deception in the instruction of an ignorant person."

children.text:
iti yuṣmābhir evocyate | na ca sarvajñānavān viśeṣaniṣṭhatayādhigantuṃ
	  śakyate | na cāsya sattāmātrasiddhau kaścid upayogaḥ, pravṛtter
	  anaṅgatvād iti sarvam asamañjasam ||
children.translated_text: Thus it is stated by you yourselves. And an omniscient knower cannot be ascertained as committed to a particular [teaching]. Nor is there any use in merely establishing his existence, since it would not serve as a ground for action — thus everything is incoherent.

children.text:
atrocyate | na vayaṃ
	sākṣātsarvajñasattāpratijñāyāṃ hetuvyāpāram anumanyāmahe |
	bhūdharādhīnavahnisattāvat | kiṃ tu caturāryasatyākārasvarūpe dharmiṇi
	sphuṭābhatvasya sādhyasyāyogavyavacchedārthaṃ parvate
	'gnimātrāyogavyavacchedavat | sphuṭābhatvaṃ tu kāminy ākārādidṛṣṭānte
	dṛṣṭam eva | tac ca parvatīyāgnivat | pakṣadharmatābalataḥ
	satyacatuṣṭayādhikaraṇaṃ sidhyat sarvajñatām ācakṣmahe | yathoktam
children.translated_text: To this we reply: We do not approve of the reason functioning to directly prove the existence of an omniscient being — like the existence of fire depending on a mountain. Rather, [we use the reason] for the purpose of excluding the impossibility of vividness as the property to be proved, in the subject that consists of the four noble truth-forms — just as excluding the mere impossibility of fire on a mountain. And vividness is indeed seen in the example of the form of a young woman for a lover. And that [vividness], like fire on a mountain, being established through the force of the property-of-the-subject, when established in the substratum of the four truths, we call omniscience. As it has been said:

children.text: ityabhyāsabalāt parisphuṭadaśākoṭiḥ sphurat sambhavī heyādeyatadaṅgalakṣaṇaguṇaḥ sarvajñatā saiva naḥ ||
children.translated_text: "Thus, through the force of practice, the culmination of the state of vividness, which is possible, is an attribute characterized as what is to be rejected, what is to be adopted, and their respective means — that is what we mean by omniscience."

children.text: iti |
children.translated_text: Thus.

children.text:
tad
	atrābhyāsasahitacaturāryasatyākāraḥ samagro dharmī sāmagryam
	abhyāsaviśiṣṭacetoguṇatvamātraṃ hetuḥ sphuṭībhāvayogyatāsādhyam |
	yathā sāgnitvānagnitvasandehe parvatātmā pramāṇapratīto dharmī |
	tathātrāpi sarvajñatvāsarvajñatvavivāde 'pi pratyātmaviditaḥ
	satyacatuṣṭayākāro dharmī | tasmāt sphuṭābhatvena sādhyena dṛṣṭānte
	vyāptisiddher asty eva tatpratibaddhaliṅganiścayaḥ | sādhyasandehe
	'pi dharmiṇaś caturāryasatyākārasya siddher na trividhadoṣajāter
	avasaraḥ | yogyatāyāḥ prasādhanena ca kāraṇāt kāryapratītāv
	anaikāntikatvam ity apy anabhyupagamapratihatam | yogyatā ca
	sāntaraiva sādhyate | iyaṃ ca na gamayatu nāmaikāntataḥ kāryasattvam |
	anupapadyamānaṃ punar asya sambhavam ākṣipaty eva | tadā bhāvini kārye
	sandehe 'pi kāraṇayogyatā niścīyata eva | brīhyādau bhāviphalāniścaye
	'pi yogyatāniścayena pravṛtteḥ | anyathā śilāśakalāder apy
	upādānaprasaṅgaḥ |
children.translated_text: Therefore, here the entire subject (<s>dharmin</s>) is the form of the four noble truths (<s>caturāryasatya</s>) accompanied by practice (<s>abhyāsa</s>); the reason (<s>hetu</s>) is merely the property of being a mental quality endowed with practice; and the provable property (<s>sādhya</s>) is the capacity for becoming vivid (<s>sphuṭībhāva</s>). Just as a mountain, established by a means of valid cognition (<s>pramāṇa</s>), is the subject in the case of doubt about whether it possesses or lacks fire, so too here, even in the dispute about whether [the Buddha] is omniscient or not, the subject is the form of the four truths known to one's own experience. Therefore, since the invariable concomitance (<s>vyāpti</s>) is established in the example through the provable property of not-yet-being-vivid, there certainly exists the ascertainment of the logical mark (<s>liṅga</s>) that is bound to that [property]. Since the subject's form of the four noble truths is established even when there is doubt about the provable property, there is no occasion for the threefold class of faults. And the objection that there is the fault of inconclusiveness (<s>anaikāntikatva</s>) because one cognizes the effect from the cause by establishing [mere] capacity — that is refuted by the fact that it is not accepted [by us]. Moreover, capacity is established together with an intermediate [link]. And even if this [capacity] does not invariably establish the existence of the effect, it nevertheless necessarily implies its possibility. Then, even when there is doubt about the [future] effect, the causal capacity is ascertained with certainty — just as in the case of rice and the like, where one engages [in planting] through the ascertainment of capacity even when there is uncertainty about the future fruit. Otherwise, there would be the absurd consequence that even stone fragments and the like would be adopted [as seeds].

children.text: tajjātīyasya śarāvasthapaṅkoptasya sāmarthyam upalabdham iti cet | atrāpi kāminy ākāre bhāvanājātīyasya sphuṭībhāvakaraṇayogyatā dṛṣṭeti samānam |
children.translated_text: If it is objected that the capacity of a [seed] of that same class, [namely] a lump of clay placed on a kiln-shelf, has been observed — here too it is the same: the capacity for producing vividness of a [mental state] of the same class as meditation (<s>bhāvanā</s>) on the form of the beloved has been observed.

children.text:
evaṃ yogyatāmātrasādhanenaiva
	kṛtārthaḥ sādhanavādī | sarvajñakāraṇabhāvāt tadabhāvavādināṃ
	nirdalanāt | kāryasya ca traikālikasya sambhāvanāprasādhanāt |
	muttkyarthināṃ ca pravṛtter avirodhāt | vādino 'pi
	tanmātrasādhanasyābhipretatvāt | ata eva kaḥ prastāvaḥ
	sarvajñasattāvivāde sphuṭībhāvasādhanasyetyādy apy anavakāśam |
	sarvajñaśabdena sphuṭībhāvayogyatāyā vivakṣitatvāt | tathā
	kāryakāraṇapratītir api sambhavaty eva | tathā hi kāminy
	abhyāsasantatisahacāri sambhramkāryavacodarśanam eva kāminy ākārasya
	tadbhāvanāyāś ca darśanam | tathābhūtakāyavaco 'darśanam eva bhāvanāyā
	adarśanam | evaṃ
	sphuṭapratibhāsasantatisahacāriviśiṣṭakāyavacodarśanaṃ
	sphuṭapratibhāsadarśanam | tathāvasthitakāyavaco 'darśanam eva
	sphuṭapratibhāsādarśanam ity asaty eva prastute 'pi
	pratyakṣānupalambhataḥ kāryakāraṇabhāvapratītiḥ |

iyaṃ ca
	tathāvasthakāmātur aśarīravacanagrahaṇe
	tadekadeśabhūtayuvatyākārābhyāsasphuṭapratibhāsagrahaṇavyavasthā
	vyāvahārikeṇāvaśyaṃ svīkartavyā | anyathā
children.translated_text: And this determination — that when one grasps the bodiless speech of one in such a state of desire, one [thereby] grasps the vivid appearance [produced by] the practice of the form of the young woman that constitutes a part of that [state] — must necessarily be accepted by the pragmatist (<s>vyāvahārika</s>). Otherwise,

children.text: citta
children.translated_text: the mental (<s>citta</s>) —

children.text:
caityarūparasagandhasparśaparamāṇupuñjādyātmakasya
	kumbhakāraghaṭapradeśāder api rūpaikadeśagrāhakaṃ cakṣuḥpratyakṣaṃ na
	samudāyavyavasthāpakam iti sarvavyāvahārikapramāṇocchedaprasaṅgaḥ |
	tathā bāhyaghaṭakām ityādīnāṃ śaktikṛtasya mahato jātibhedasya
	sambhavād anyajātīyavyāptigrahe 'nyajātīyād buddhimadanumānam
	ayuktam | saṃkalpārūḍhānāṃ tu jalajvalanayuvatyākārādīnāṃ
	bāhyatvenādhyastānām api vijñānaikasvarūpatayaikajātīyatvam astīti
	bhāvanāsahitākāramātreṇaiva vaiśadyavyāptir astu ||
children.translated_text: [if one argues that] even in the case of the pot-maker's pot-location and the like, which consists of an aggregate of atoms of form, taste, smell, and touch constituting the <s>caitya</s> (mind-object), the visual perception that grasps only a portion of form does not establish the aggregate — then there would follow the absurd consequence of the destruction of all pragmatic means of valid cognition (<s>pramāṇa</s>). Furthermore, since there exist great differences of class (<s>jāti</s>) produced by capacity (<s>śakti</s>) among external things such as pots and the like, inference from another class to a different class by intelligent beings would be improper. But for things of the class of water, fire, the form of a young woman, and the like, which are superimposed as external though they are in reality of the nature of consciousness alone — since they are of a single class by virtue of having consciousness as their sole nature — let the invariable concomitance with vividness be established merely through the form accompanied by meditation.

Thus, the proponent of the proof has accomplished his purpose merely by establishing [the existence of] capacity. Because the state of being a cause of omniscience [is established], the position of those who deny its existence is demolished. Because the possibility of the effect — whether past, present, or future — is thereby established. Because the activity of those who seek liberation is not contradicted. And because the proponent himself intends to prove merely that much. Therefore, the objection 'What is the occasion for proving vividness in the dispute about the existence of the omniscient?' and the like is also without scope, since 'omniscient' is used to mean 'possessing the capacity for vividness.' Likewise, the cognition of the cause-effect relation is indeed possible. For the perception of bodily and verbal behavior (<s>kāyavacas</s>) — the effect of agitation — accompanying a continuous stream of practice on the form of the beloved is itself the perception of that form and of the meditation upon it. And the non-perception of such bodily and verbal behavior is itself the non-perception of the meditation. Similarly, the perception of distinctive bodily and verbal behavior accompanying a continuous stream of vivid appearances is the perception of vivid appearance. And the non-perception of bodily and verbal behavior in such a state is itself the non-perception of vivid appearance — thus, even when the subject is not directly at hand, the cognition of the cause-effect relation [is established] through perceptual non-apprehension (<s>pratyakṣānupalambha</s>).

children.text:
na ca svapne sphuṭatāvyabhicāraḥ |
	bhāvanāsiddhalakṣaṇayor hetvor jātibhede tatkāryayor ekatvābhimāne 'pi
	jātibhedasyāvaśyaṃ svīkartavyatvāt | dṛśyate hi siddhasādhyā
	vaiśadyajātir anapekṣya viparītabhāvanāṃ nidrāvicchede vicchidyamānā |
	bhāvanābhāvinī tu na vinā vipakṣābhyāsaṃ jāgrato 'pi | yad āhuḥ
children.translated_text: Nor is there a deviation [of the rule] regarding vividness in dreams. Because even when there is the assumption of identity between the effects of two causes — [namely] the cause characterized by meditation (<s>bhāvanā</s>) and the cause characterized by the accomplished [dream-state] — the difference of class must necessarily be accepted. For one observes that the vividness of the class that is accomplished [in dreams] ceases when sleep is interrupted, without depending on contrary meditation. But the [vividness] that is to be produced by meditation does not [cease] for one who is awake, even without the practice of the opposite. As they say:

children.text:
svapne 'pi sphuṭatā tathaiva na tathāpy ekatvam evānayor na
	  prākārasamatvam eva samatāṃ jāteḥ samāmaṅgati |
children.translated_text: Even in dreams there is vividness, yet there is no identity between the two; the mere similarity of mode does not entail identity of class.

children.text:
anyanniddhanirodhabādhyam itaradbādhyaṃ pratyatnaiḥ punar vaiśadyaṃ
	  viparītabhāvanabalān nairghṛṇyabhede yathā ||
children.translated_text: One [dream-vividness] is obstructed by the cessation of sleep; the other is obstructed by efforts [of contrary practice]. Vividness [produced] by the force of contrary meditation [illustrates] a difference in mercilessness [i.e., obstinacy].

children.text: iti ||
children.translated_text: Thus.

children.text: yad api ghaṭādikatipayajñāne 'pi sarvajñaḥ syād ity uktam | tatrāpi
children.translated_text: As for the objection that 'one would be omniscient even through the knowledge of a few things like pots and the like' — in response to that too:

children.text: ghaṭādiprakṛtāśeṣavedane 'pi bhayaṃ bhavād dheyata yadi ko doṣaḥ so 'pi sarvajñatāṃ vrajet |
children.translated_text: 'Even if one knows all things beginning with pots and the like, if you maintain that there is [still] cause for fear, what is the fault? He too would attain omniscience.

children.text: saṃsāraduḥkhamokṣāya spṛhayanto vayaṃ punar bhajema tadupāyajñaṃ sthātuṃ tadgītavartamani ||
children.translated_text: We, however, who long for liberation from the suffering of <s>saṃsāra</s>, would resort to one who knows the means to that [liberation], and would abide on the path sung by him.'

children.text: ity uttaraṃ draṣṭavyam | tathā sattāmātre vipratipannān prati sattaiva kevalā prasādhitā | viśeṣajijñāsāyāṃ tu pramāṇopapannakṣaṇikanairātmyavādina eva sugatasya bhagavataḥ sarvajñatā | ata etad api nirastaṃ yad āha Bhaṭṭaḥ
children.translated_text: This answer should be considered. Likewise, for those who dispute [the Buddha's] mere existence, only his mere existence has been established. But when there is a desire to know the specifics, the omniscience belongs to the Blessed <s>Sugata</s> (the Buddha) alone, who propounds the doctrines of momentariness (<s>kṣaṇika</s>) and non-self (<s>nairātmya</s>) that are supported by valid means of cognition. Therefore, the following objection raised by <s>Bhaṭṭa</s> is also refuted:

children.text: sugato yadi sarvajñaḥ kapilo neti kā pramā |
children.translated_text: 'If the <s>Sugata</s> (Buddha) is omniscient, what is the proof that <s>Kapila</s> is not?

children.text: athobhāv api sarvajñau matabhedaḥ kathaṃ tayoḥ || iti |
children.translated_text: And if both are omniscient, how is there a difference of doctrine between them?'

children.text: tasmāt
children.translated_text: Therefore:

children.text: uktakrameṇa munirājanaye pramāyāḥ śaktir vyanakti gatim apramitāṃ kṛpāṃ ca |
children.translated_text: 'By the method stated, [this argument] reveals the capacity of the means of valid cognition for the lineage of the King of Sages (<s>Munirāja</s>, the Buddha), as well as [His] immeasurable compassion.

children.text: anyatra tu dvayam udastam ado 'stamāne tenaika eva śaraṇaṃ sa nirātmavādī ||
children.translated_text: Elsewhere, however, both [capacity and compassion] are extinguished, being set [like the sun]. Therefore, He alone — the proponent of non-self (<s>nirātmavādin</s>) — is the [sole] refuge.'

children.text: iti viśeṣasiddhir apy anavadeyeti sarvam anākulam ākulādhayaḥ pare na pratipadyante | sādhane 'sminn avadye 'pi durnītidahanadagdhabuddhayaḥ punar apy etad ācakaṣate | bādhakapramāṇasadbhāvāt sarvajñasyāsadvyavahāro yuktaḥ sadvyavahārapratiṣedho vā prasādhakapramāṇābhāvād veti ||
children.translated_text: Thus, the establishment of the specific [claim] is also unobjectionable — everything is clear. Those whose minds are troubled do not understand. Even though this proof is faultless, those whose intellects are burned by the fire of bad reasoning still raise this objection: 'Since a defeating means of valid cognition (<s>bādhaka-pramāṇa</s>) exists, it is proper that the omniscient one's existence be negated; or, the affirmation of his existence [should be rejected] due to the absence of an establishing means of valid cognition.'

children.text: atra vicāryate kiṃ punar asya bhagavato bādhakaṃ pramāṇaṃ pratyakṣam anumānaṃ śabdādikaṃ veti vikalpāḥ ||
children.translated_text: Here we examine: what, then, is the defeating means of valid cognition against this Blessed One? Perception (<s>pratyakṣa</s>)? Inference (<s>anumāna</s>)? Verbal testimony (<s>śabda</s>) and the like? — these are the alternatives.

children.text: na tāvat pratyakṣaṃ | pratyakṣaṃ hi kevalapradeśādau pravartamānaṃ svapravṛttiyogyam eva tatra vastu pratiṣedhati | na vastumātram | na ca sarvajñasya pratyakṣapravṛttiyogyatāsti | svabhāvaviprakṛṣṭatvāt tasya ||
children.translated_text: First, not perception. For perception, operating upon mere particular locations and the like, negates only that entity which is fit for its own operation in that domain — not entity as such. And the omniscient one does not possess fitness for the operation of perception, because he is remote from the [ordinary] nature [of perceptible things].

children.text: syād etat | na vayaṃ pratyakṣaṃ pravartamānam abhāvaṃ sādhayatīti brūmaḥ | kiṃ tarhi | nivartamānam | tathā hi yatra vastuni pratyakṣasya nivṛttis tasyāsadbhāvaḥ | yathā śaśaviṣāṇādeḥ | yatra tu pratyakṣasya pravṛttis tasya sadbhāvo yathā ghaṭādeḥ | asti ca sarvajñe pratyakṣanivṛttiḥ | tad asyāpy abhāvaḥ kena nivāryata iti ||
children.translated_text: One might object: 'We do not say that perception, while operating, establishes absence. Rather, [we say it does so] while ceasing to operate. For when perception ceases with respect to a certain entity, that entity's non-existence [is established] — just as with the horn of a hare and the like. But where perception does operate, the entity exists — just as with a pot and the like. And in the case of the omniscient one, perception does cease. Therefore, what prevents his non-existence from [being established]?'

children.text: ucyate | nivartamānaṃ pratyakṣam abhāvaṃ sādhyatīti ko 'rthaḥ | kiṃ pratyakṣasya yā nivṛttis tato 'bhāvasiddhiḥ, nivṛttisahitād vā pratyakṣāt, nivṛttād vā pratyakṣād iti |
children.translated_text: We reply: What is the meaning of 'perception, while ceasing to operate, establishes absence'? Does the absence follow from the very cessation of perception? Or from perception accompanied by cessation? Or from perception that has [already] ceased?

children.text: nādyaḥ pakṣaḥ | saty api vastuni pratyakṣanivṛtter upalabhyamānāyā vastvabhāvaniyatatvāsiddheḥ ||
children.translated_text: Not the first alternative. Because, even when the entity exists, the cessation of perception is observed to occur, and its being invariably connected with the non-existence of the entity is not established.

children.text: nāpi dvitīyaḥ | svābhāvena saha kasyacit sāhityānupapatteḥ | anyathā tannivṛttatvānupapatteḥ ||
children.translated_text: Nor the second. Because it is impossible for anything to coexist with its own absence. Otherwise, it could not have ceased.

children.text: na ca tṛtīyaḥ | tathā hi nivṛttāt pratyakṣād abhāvasiddhir ity asataḥ pratyakṣād ity uktaṃ bhavati | na cāsato hetubhāvaḥ sambhavati | sarvasamarthyavirahalakṣaṇtvāt tasya | na hi tac ca nāsti tena ca pratipattir iti nyāyam | ato na tāvat pratyakṣaṃ sarvajñabādhakam ||
children.translated_text: Nor the third. For 'absence is established from perception that has ceased' amounts to saying 'from a non-existent perception' — and a non-existent thing cannot function as a cause, since it is characterized by the absence of all capacity. For it is not logical that something both does not exist and yet produces cognition. Therefore, perception is not a defeater of the omniscient one.

children.text: nāpy anumānam | tad dhi trividhaliṅgajatvena trividham | tatra kāryasvabhāvayor vidhisādhanatvāt, pratiṣedhe sādhye 'navasaraḥ | na ca dṛśyānupalambhaḥ tatprabhedo vā kāryānupalabdhyādir yogyānupalambho vā parābhimato 'tra pramāṇam | sarvajñatāyāḥ svabhāvaviprakṛṣṭatvenādṛśyatvāt ||
children.translated_text: Nor is inference [a defeater]. For inference, being produced by three types of logical marks (<s>liṅga</s>), is threefold. Of these, since the [marks of] effect (<s>kārya</s>) and essential nature (<s>svabhāva</s>) serve to establish positive [facts], they have no scope when the provable property is a negation. Nor is the non-apprehension of the perceptible (<s>dṛśyānupalambha</s>), or its subdivision — non-apprehension of the effect (<s>kāryānupalabdhi</s>) and the like — nor the non-apprehension of the fit (<s>yogyānupalambha</s>) accepted by the opponent, a [valid] means of cognition here — because omniscience, being remote from [ordinary] nature, is imperceptible.

children.text: nanu kāraṇānupalambhād eva sarvajñatāpratiṣedhaḥ sidhyati | tathā hi tatkāraṇam indriyavijñānaṃ vā mānasaṃ vā bhāvanābalajaṃ vā | bhāvanābalajam api cākṣuṣaṃ vā, mānasaṃ veti vikalpāḥ |
children.translated_text: One objects: 'The negation of omniscience is established precisely from the non-apprehension of its cause (<s>kāraṇānupalambha</s>). For its cause is either sense-cognition (<s>indriya-vijñāna</s>), or mental cognition (<s>mānasa</s>), or cognition born from the power of meditation (<s>bhāvanā-balaja</s>). And [cognition] born from the power of meditation is either visual (<s>cākṣuṣa</s>) or mental' — these are the alternatives.

children.text: tatra na tāvac cakṣurindriyavijñānam aśeṣārthagrāhi | tasya pratiniyatārthaviṣayatvāt | deśāntare kālāntare ca tathaiva pratiniyamaḥ | anyathā hetuphalabhāvābhāvaprasaṅgāt | anekendriyavaiyarthyaprasaṅgāc ca | tathā ca kārikā
children.translated_text: Of these, first, visual sense-cognition does not apprehend all objects without remainder, because it has a specifically delimited object-domain. And in different places and different times, there is the same delimitation. Otherwise, there would follow the absurd consequence of the absence of the cause-effect relationship [between sense and object]. And there would follow the absurd consequence of the uselessness of the other sense-faculties. And the verse (<s>kārikā</s>):

children.text: ekendriyapramāṇena sarvajño yena kalpyate |
children.translated_text: 'One who posits that [a person] is omniscient through a single sense-faculty as the means of valid cognition —

children.text: nūnaṃ sa cakṣuṣā sarvān rasādīn pratipadyate ||
children.translated_text: surely he apprehends all tastes and the like through the eye alone!'

children.text: yajjātīyaiḥ pramāṇaiś ca yajjātīyārthadarśanam |
children.translated_text: 'Through whichever class of means of valid cognition, whichever class of objects is perceived —

children.text: bhaved idānīṃ lokasya tathā kālāntare 'py abhūt || iti |
children.translated_text: that [holds] for the world now, and it was so in other times as well.'

children.text: tataś caivaṃ prayogaḥ kartavyaḥ | buddhacakṣurnātītādiviṣayam | cakṣustvāt | asmadādicakṣurvat | acakṣur vā |
children.translated_text: Therefore, the following argument should be formulated: 'The eye of the Buddha does not have past [and future] objects as its domain, because it is an eye — like our own eye and the like.' Or: '[It is] not an eye at all,

children.text: atītādiviṣayatvāt | śabdavat | iti sarvam etat śrotrādāv api draṣṭavyam | na cakṣurādiprakarṣaḥ svārtham atikramya dṛṣṭaḥ |
Kārikā
children.translated_text: The verse (<s>kārikā</s>):

because it has past [and future] objects as its domain — like sound.' And all this should be applied to the ear and the other [sense-faculties] as well. Nor is any enhancement of the eye and the like observed to transcend its own proper object.

children.text: yatrāpy atiśayo dṛṣṭaḥ sa svārthānatilaṅghanāt |
children.translated_text: 'Even where enhancement is observed, it would operate [only] in the domain of distant, subtle, and the like [objects] —

children.text: dūrasūkṣmādivṛttau syān na rūpe śrotravṛttitaḥ ||
(ŚV II 114)

children.translated_text: because it does not transcend its own proper object; not in [apprehending] form through the operation of the ear.'

children.text: Bṛhaṭṭīkā
children.translated_text: The <s>Bṛhaṭṭīkā</s> (Great Sub-commentary)

children.text: ca
children.translated_text: also [states]:

children.text: śrotragamyeṣu śabdeṣu dūrasūkṣmopalabdhitaḥ |
children.translated_text: 'With respect to sounds, which are accessible to the ear, an enhancement of the person is observed

children.text: puruṣātiśayo dṛṣṭo na rūpādyupalambhanāt ||
children.translated_text: through the apprehension of distant and subtle [sounds] — not through the apprehension of form and the like.'

children.text: cakṣuṣāpi ca dūrasthasūkṣmarūpopalambhanam |
children.translated_text: 'And even by the eye, the apprehension of distant and subtle forms

children.text: kriyate 'tiśayaprāptyā na tu śabdādidarśanam ||
children.translated_text: is accomplished through the attainment of enhancement — but not the perception of sound and the like.'

children.text: na caitad vaktavyam | yadi nāmaikaikenendriyeṇa tajjñānena vā sarvasyāgrhaṇaṃ tathāpi pañcabhir indriyais tajjñānair vā svasvaviṣayapravṛttair evātiśayaprāptair bhaviṣyatīti | ekaikasyāpi niḥśeṣasvaviṣayagrahaṇādarśanāt | paracittādyatīndriyāṇāṃ grahaṇābhāvāc ca | tad evam indriyavijñānaṃ vā nāśeṣagrāhīti na prathamaḥ pakṣaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Nor should one say: 'Even if each individual sense-faculty or its cognition does not apprehend everything, nevertheless, the five sense-faculties or their cognitions, each operating upon its own proper object, having attained enhancement, will [collectively do so].' Because the exhaustive apprehension of even its own object-domain is not observed for each individual [sense-faculty]. And because there is no apprehension of supersensible things such as others' minds and the like. Thus, since sense-cognition does not apprehend everything without remainder, the first alternative is [refuted].

children.text: nāpi dvitīyaḥ | tathā hi yady api tanmānasaṃ sarvārthaviṣayaṃ tathāpi na tasya svātantryeṇārthagrahaṇe vyāpāro 'sti | manaso bahirasvātantryāt | anyathāndhavadhirādyabhāvaprasaṅgaḥ | teṣām api manaso bhāvāt | pāratantrye cetndriyajñānaparigṛhītārthaviṣayatvād atītānāgatadūrasūkṣmavyavahitaparacittāder arthasyendriyaparijñānāgocarasya manasā paricchedo na prāpnotīti kathaṃ sarvajñatā ||
children.translated_text: Nor the second. For even if that mental [cognition] has all objects as its domain, nevertheless, it has no independent operation in apprehending objects, because the mind lacks independence with respect to external [objects]. Otherwise, there would follow the absurd consequence of the non-existence of the blind, the deaf, and the like, since they too possess minds. And if [the mind is] dependent, then, because it has as its object-domain only the objects grasped by sense-cognition, it cannot determine objects such as past, future, distant, subtle, concealed, and others' minds — which are beyond the scope of sense-apprehension. How then could there be omniscience?

children.text: na ca bhāvanābalajaṃ sarvārthagrāhīti tṛtīyaḥ pakṣaḥ | tathā hi tadbhāvanābalajam api yadīndriyāśritam iti caturthaḥ pakṣaḥ, tadā so 'saṅgataḥ | indriyasya tajjñānasya ca niyataviṣayaviṣayatvapratipādanāt ||
children.translated_text: Nor is [cognition] born from the power of meditation all-apprehending — [refuting] the third alternative. For if that [cognition] born from the power of meditation is sense-dependent — the fourth alternative — then that [alternative] is incoherent, because it has been demonstrated that sense-faculties and their cognitions have delimited object-domains.

children.text: atha bhāvanābalena tathāvidham utpannaṃ manovijñānaṃ sarvārthagrāhīti pañcamaḥ pakṣaḥ | tadānvarthatvāt pratyakṣaśabdasya tasya ca bhāvanābalāvalambino 'py anakṣajatvāt nārthasākṣātkāritvam astīti pratipādanīyam | kiṃ ca svaviṣayasīmānam anatipatyaiva prakarṣo 'pi dṛśyate | na tu sarvaviṣayatveneti | kathaṃ tenāpi sakalārthajātādivedanam | yato na kasyacid abhyāse 'py atīndriyārthadarśitvam upalabdham ||
children.translated_text: Now the fifth thesis: that mental consciousness (<s>manovijñāna</s>) produced through the power of meditation (<s>bhāvanā</s>) and of such a nature grasps all objects. Since the word '<s>pratyakṣa</s>' (perception) applies to it according to its [etymological] meaning, and since, although dependent on the power of meditation, it is not born from the sense-organs (<s>akṣa</s>), it must be demonstrated that it does not have the capacity for direct apprehension of objects. Moreover, excellence is observed only without transgressing the boundaries of one's own domain of objects, not by way of apprehending all objects. How then can even that [meditation-born consciousness] cognize the entire range of objects? For no one, even through practice, has been observed to perceive supersensory objects.

children.text: Bṛhaṭṭīkā
children.translated_text: <s>Bṛhaṭṭīkā</s> [Great Commentary]:

children.text: ye 'pi sātiśayā dṛṣṭāḥ prajñāmedhābalair narāḥ |
children.translated_text: Even those men who are seen to possess excellent powers of intelligence and memory,

children.text: stokastokāntaratvena na te 'tīndriyadarśanāḥ ||
children.translated_text: with only slight differences in degree, do not perceive supersensory objects.

children.text: prājño 'pi ca naraḥ sūkṣmān athān draṣṭuṃ kṣamo 'pi san |
children.translated_text: Even an intelligent man, though capable of seeing subtle objects,

children.text: sajātīr anatikrāman nātiśete parān api ||
children.translated_text: does not surpass others without transgressing the bounds of his own kind.

children.text: ekāvavarakasthasya pratyakṣaṃ yat pravartate |
children.translated_text: The perception that operates for one standing in a single room

children.text: śaktis tatraiva tasya syān naivāvavarakāntare ||
children.translated_text: has its capacity only there, and not in another room.

children.text: ye cārthā dūravicchinnā deśaparvatasāgaraiḥ |
children.translated_text: And those objects that are separated by far distances — by regions, mountains, and oceans,

children.text: varṣadvīpāntarair ye ca kas tān paśyed ihaiva san ||
children.translated_text: and those in other continents and lands — who can see them while being right here?

children.text: atra varṣaḥ kālaviśeṣaḥ |
children.translated_text: Here, '<s>varṣa</s>' means a particular period of time.

children.text: evaṃ śāstravicāreṣu dṛśyate 'tiśayo mahān |
children.translated_text: Thus, in the investigation of the sciences, great excellence is observed,

children.text: na tu śāstrāntarajñānaṃ tanmātreṇaiva sidhyati ||
children.translated_text: but knowledge of another science is not accomplished by that [excellence] alone.

children.text: jñātvā vyākaraṇaṃ dūraṃ buddhiḥ śabdāpaśabdayoḥ |
children.translated_text: Having learned grammar, the intellect [can discriminate] between correct and incorrect words from afar,

children.text: ākṛṣyate na nakṣatratithigrahaṇanirṇaye ||
children.translated_text: but it is not drawn to the determination of constellations, lunar days, and eclipses.

children.text: jyotirvic ca prakṛṣṭo 'pi candrārkagrahaṇādiṣu |
children.translated_text: And even an excellent astronomer, [skilled] in the eclipses of the moon, sun, and so forth,

children.text: na bhavatyādiśabdānāṃ sādhutvaṃ jñātum arhati ||
children.translated_text: is not able to know the correctness of words beginning with '<s>ā</s>' and similar forms.

children.text: tathā vedetihāsādijñānātiśayavān api |
children.translated_text: Likewise, even one possessing excellent knowledge of the <s>Vedas</s>, <s>Itihāsas</s>, and so forth

children.text: na svargadevatāpūrvapratyakṣīkaraṇe kṣamaḥ ||
children.translated_text: is not capable of directly perceiving heaven, deities, or <s>apūrva</s> (unseen merit).

children.text: daśahastāntaraṃ vyomno ye nāmotplutya gacchati |
children.translated_text: One who leaps up into the sky to a distance of ten arm-lengths —

children.text: na yojanam asau gantuṃ śakto 'bhyāsaśatair api |
children.translated_text: even with hundreds of practices, he is not able to traverse a <s>yojana</s>.

children.text: tasmād atiśayajñānair atidūragatair api |
children.translated_text: Therefore, even by cognitions of great excellence, reaching very far,

children.text: kiñcid evādhikaṃ jñātuṃ śakyate na tv atīndriyam || iti |
children.translated_text: only something slightly more can be known, but not the supersensory. Thus [ends the quotation].

children.text: pratyakṣasūtre tu kāśikākāraḥ paramatam āśaṅkyāha, tan na, avagataviṣayatvād bhāvanāyāḥ | na cākasmād avagater utpattiḥ sambhavati | sarvotpattimatāṃ kāraṇavattvāt | atha pramāṇāntarāvagataṃ bhāvyate | kiṃ bhāvanayā | tata eva tatsiddheḥ | kiṃ ca tatpramāṇam | na tāvad anumānaṃ dharmādharmayoḥ pūrvam agrahaṇena tadvyāptaliṅgasaṃvedanāsambhavāt | jagadvaividhyārthāpatter api hi kim api kāraṇam astīti etāvad unnīyate | na tu kaścid viśeṣaḥ | na cānirdiṣṭaviśeṣaviṣayā bhāvanā bhavati | yogaśāstreṣv api hi viśeṣā eva dhyeyatayopadiśyante |
children.translated_text: In the <s>Pratyakṣasūtra</s>, however, the author of the <s>Kāśikā</s>, having raised the opponent's view, says: That is not so, because meditation (<s>bhāvanā</s>) has [only] previously apprehended objects as its domain. For the arising of apprehension cannot occur suddenly from nowhere. Because all things that arise have causes. Now if what is meditated upon was apprehended through another means of valid cognition (<s>pramāṇa</s>), what is the use of meditation? Since [the object] is already established through that [other pramāṇa] itself. Moreover, what is that [other] means of valid cognition? It is certainly not inference (<s>anumāna</s>), because, since <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s> (merit and demerit) were not apprehended previously, the apprehension of a logical mark (<s>liṅga</s>) pervaded by them is impossible. Even from the inference of the twofold nature of the world, only this much is derived: that some cause exists — but no specific detail. And meditation cannot have as its object something whose specific nature is unspecified. For even in the treatises on <s>yoga</s>, only specific objects are taught as fit for meditation,

children.text: dhyeya ātmā prabhuryo 'sau hṛdi dīpa iva sthitaḥ | (Maitrī Up. 6,30)
children.translated_text: 'The Self to be meditated upon is the Lord, who is established in the heart like a lamp' (<s>Maitrī Upaniṣad</s> 6.30),

children.text: ityādibhiḥ | āgamamānāt tarhi avagataṃ bhāvayiṣyate | yadi pramāṇāt tadā tata evāvagateḥ | kiṃ bhāvanayā | hānopādānārthaṃ hi vastu jijñāsyate | te ca tata eva siddhe iti vyarthā bhāvanā | kāruṇiko 'pi hi dharmāgamān eva śiṣyebhyo vyācakṣīta | na bhāvanābhedam anubhavet |
children.translated_text: and so forth. If then one will meditate on what is apprehended from scripture (<s>āgama</s>) — if [it is apprehended] from a valid means of knowledge, then it is already apprehended through that itself; what is the use of meditation? For a thing is investigated for the purpose of adopting and rejecting [it], and since those [purposes] are already accomplished through that [pramāṇa] itself, meditation is pointless. Even a compassionate [teacher] would simply expound the scriptures on <s>dharma</s> to his disciples; he would not experience the distinction [gained through] meditation.

children.text: atha vipralambhabhūyiṣṭhatvād āgāmānāṃ pramāṇam āgamo na veti vicikitsamāno bhāvanayā jijñāsate | tan na | tato 'pi tadasiddheḥ | bhāvanābalapriniṣpannam api jñānam anāśvsanīyārtham eva | abhūtasyāpi bhāvyamānasyāparokṣārthavat prakāśanāt | yathā hi tair evoktam
children.translated_text: Now if, because scriptures are mostly deceptive, one who doubts whether scripture is or is not a valid means of knowledge seeks to ascertain [the truth] through meditation — that is not so, because even thereby [the truth] is not established. For even knowledge produced through the power of meditation has unreliable content, since even what is unreal, when meditated upon, appears as if directly present. As indeed they themselves have said:

children.text: tasmād bhūtam abhūtaṃ vā yad yad evābhibhāvyate |
children.translated_text: Therefore, whether something is real or unreal, whatever is intensely meditated upon,

children.text: bhāvanāpariniṣpattau tat sphuṭā kalpadhīḥ phalam ||
children.translated_text: when the meditation reaches its culmination, the result is a vivid conceptual cognition.

children.text: PV III 285; PVin I 30.

api ca bhāvanābalajam apramāṇam | gṛhītagrahaṇāt | yāvad eva hi gṛhītaṃ tāvad eva bhāvanayā viṣayīkriyate | mātrayāpy adhikaṃ na bhāvanā gocarayati | yogābhyāsāhitasaṃskārapāṭavanimittā hi smṛtir eva bhāvaneti gīyate | sā ca pramāṇam iti sthitam eva | na ca taduttarakālaṃ sākṣātkārijñānam udetīti pramāṇam asti | indriyasannikarṣam antareṇārthasākṣātkārasya kvacid adarśanāt | yogināṃ dharmādharmayor aparokṣapratibhāsaṃ jñānaṃ nāsti, indriyasannikarṣābhāvād asmadādivat ||
children.translated_text: Furthermore, what is born from the power of meditation is not a valid means of knowledge (<s>pramāṇa</s>), because it apprehends [only] what has [already] been apprehended. For meditation makes its object only that which has already been apprehended — it does not bring even a fraction more into its scope. For what is celebrated as meditation is nothing but memory (<s>smṛti</s>), caused by the refinement of latent impressions (<s>saṃskāra</s>) produced through the practice of <s>yoga</s>. And it is established that memory is [itself] a valid means of knowledge. But there is no evidence that a directly apprehending cognition arises subsequent to it, since direct apprehension of an object has never been observed anywhere without sense-organ contact (<s>indriyasannikarṣa</s>). <s>Yogins</s> do not possess a cognition in which <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s> appear directly, because of the absence of sense-organ contact, just as in our own case.

children.text: Vācapatis tu Kaṇikāyām āha | satyaṃ śrutānumānagocaracāriṇī bhāvanā viśadābhajñānahetur iti nāvajānīmahe | kin tu yadviṣayajātaṃ tad eva viśadapratipattigocaraḥ | na jātu rūpabhāvanāprakarṣo rasaviṣayavijñānavaiśadyāya kalpate |
children.translated_text: <s>Vācaspati</s>, however, says in the <s>Kāṇikā</s>: It is true that we do not disparage meditation that operates within the domain of what is accessible to scripture and inference as a cause of vivid cognition. However, whatever class of objects [it operates upon], that alone is the domain of its vivid apprehension. The excellence of the meditation on form can never serve to produce vividness of cognition regarding taste.

children.text: nanu na viṣayāntaravaiśadyahetubhāvaṃ bhāvanāyāḥ saṅgirāmahe | kintu śrutānumānaviṣayavaiśadyahetutām eva | tadviṣayaś ca samastavastunairātmyam iti tadbhāvanāprakarṣaḥ samastavastunairātmyaṃ viśadayan samastavastuviśadatām antareṇa tadupapatteḥ samastavastuvaiśadyam āvahatīty uktam |
children.translated_text: We do not concede that meditation causes vividness regarding other objects. Rather, [we maintain] only that it causes vividness regarding the objects of scripture and inference. And the object of these is the selflessness (<s>nairātmya</s>) of all things. Therefore, the excellence of the meditation on that, by making vivid the selflessness of all things — since that cannot be established without the vividness of all things — brings about the vividness of all things. Thus it has been stated.

children.text:
satyam uktam | ayuktaṃ tu tat |
	tathā hi nāgamānumānagocaratvaṃ nirātmanāṃ vastubhedānāṃ
	paramārthasatām | na hi te eteṣām anyanivṛttimātrāvagāhinī
	paramārthasatsvalakṣaṇaṃ gocarayitum arhataḥ | nāpi tadviṣayā bhāvanā | tadagrāhyam api svalakṣaṇaṃ tadadhyavaseyatayā tadviṣaya iti
	tadyonir api bhāvanā tadviṣayeti tatprakarṣas tadvaiśadyahetur iti cet | na | tadadhyavaseyasyāpi paramārthasattvābhāvāt | tathā hi yad
	anumānena gṛhyate yac cādhyavasīyate te dve apy anyanivṛttī, na
	vastunī |
Cf. also

svalakṣaṇāvagāhitve
	'bhilāpasaṃsargayogyapratibhāsānupapatteḥ ||
children.translated_text: [This follows from the principle:] If [cognition] were to apprehend the <s>svalakṣaṇa</s> (particular), the appearance of something fit for association with verbal expression would be impossible.

True, it has been stated. But it is incorrect. For thus: the selflessness is not the object of scripture and inference insofar as the real distinctions among things are ultimately real (<s>paramārthasat</s>). For these [scripture and inference], which apprehend only the exclusion of what is other (<s>anyanivṛtti</s>), are not able to bring into their scope the <s>svalakṣaṇa</s> (particular) that is ultimately real. Nor does meditation on them [have that particular as its object]. [Objection:] Although the <s>svalakṣaṇa</s> is not grasped by them, still, insofar as it is determined (<s>adhyavasīyate</s>) through them, [scripture and inference] have it as their object; therefore meditation born from them also has it as its object, and its excellence is the cause of vividness regarding it. [Reply:] No, because even what is determined [through them] is not ultimately real. For thus: what is grasped by inference and what is determined — both of these are merely the exclusion of what is other (<s>anyanivṛtti</s>), not real entities.

children.text:
mā bhūt tayoḥ svalakṣaṇaṃ viṣayaḥ |
	tatprabhavabhāvanāprakarṣaparyantajanmanas tu viśadābhasya cetaso
	bhaviṣyati | kāmīnīvikalpaprabhavabhāvanāprakarṣād iva kāmātur asya
	kāminīsvalakṣaṇasākṣātkāraḥ | karikumbhakaṭhorakucakalaśahāriṇi
	hariṇaśāvalolalocane campakadalāvadātagātralate lāvaṇyasarasi
	nirantaralagnalalitadoḥkandalīmūlamāliṅganam aṅgane preyasitare
	prayaccha | sañjīvaya jīviteṣvari, patito 'smi tava caraṇanalinayor
	iti vacanakāyaceṣṭayor upalabdheḥ | asti ca vikalpāvikalpayoḥ
	kathañcit samānaviṣayateti nātiprasaṅga iti cet | satyam | sambhavaty
	ayam anubhavo na punar asyārthe prāmāṇyasambhavaḥ | atadutpatter
	atadātmanas tadavyabhicāraniyamāyogāt | atādātmyaṃ cārthasya vijñānād
	atirekāt | anatireke 'pi ca vijñānānām anyonyasya bhedād atādātmyāt |
	ekasya vijñānasyetaravijñānavedanānupapatteḥ |
	vijñānasvalakṣaṇaikatvābhyupagame ca tannityam ekam advitīyaṃ
	brahmābhyasanīyam iti kṣaṇikanairātmyābhyāsābhyupagamo dattajalāñjaliḥ
	prasajyeta | tan na tādātmyāt tasyāvyabhicāraḥ | nāpi tatkāryatvāt |
	bhāvanāprakarṣakāryaṃ khalv evan na viṣayakāryam | yady ucyeta
	pāramparyeṇa tatkāryam anumānavat | yathā hi vahnisvalakṣaṇād
	dhūmasvalakṣaṇam | tato dhūmānubhavas tato dahanavikalpaḥ, tataś
	cānumānam utpannam iti pāramparyeṇa vahnipratibandhāt prāpakaṃ ca
	vahner dāhapākakāriṇaḥ tathedam api
	anumānajanitabhāvanāprakarṣaparyantajaṃ pāramparyeṇārthaprasūtatayā
	tadavyabhicāraniyamāt tatra pramāṇam iti | tat kim anumānena vahniṃ
	vyavasthāpya bhāvayato yad vahniviṣayamativiśadavijñānaṃ tat pramāṇam
	iti | om iti brubāṇasya parvatanitambārohaṇe
	satīndriyasannikarṣajanmano dahanavijñānasya
	bhāvanādhipatyaviśadābhavijñānena saha saṃvādaniyamaprasaṅgaḥ |
	visaṃvādaś ca bahulam upalabhyate | lakṣaṇayogini ca
	vyabhicārasambhave tallakṣaṇam eva bādhitam iti viśadābham api
	prātibham iva saṃśayākrāntam apramāṇam | tadbhāvanāyā bhūtārthatvaṃ na
	tajjaviśadābhavijñānaprāmāṇyahetuḥ, vyabhicārāt | etañ ca
	prāsarpakasyeva saktukarkarīprāptimūlalābhamanorathaparamparāhito
	draviṇasambhārasākṣātkāras tathāgatasya
	nirātmakasamastavastusākṣātkāra ity āpatitam |
	sarvārthavastubhāvanāparikarmitacittasantānavartivijñānaṃ
	pratyālambanapratyayatvam arthamātrasya |
children.translated_text: Let it be that the <s>svalakṣaṇa</s> is not the object of those two [inference and scripture]. But for the vivid consciousness born at the culmination of meditation arising from them, there will be [direct apprehension of the particular] — just as one tormented by desire, through the excellence of meditation born from conceptual imagination regarding a woman, directly apprehends the <s>svalakṣaṇa</s> (particular) of the woman: 'O beloved more dear [than all], whose pitcher-like breasts rival the hardness of an elephant's frontal globe, whose eyes are as tremulous as those of a fawn, whose body is a vine as fair as the petals of a <s>campaka</s> flower, who is a lake of beauty — bestow the embrace at the root of your graceful creeper-like arms, perpetually clinging! Revive me, O mistress of my life, for I have fallen at your lotus-feet!' — because such speech and bodily gestures are observed. And there is somehow a shared object between conceptual and non-conceptual cognition, so there is no overextension [of the argument]. [Reply:] True, this experience is possible, but there is no possibility of its being a valid cognition regarding [external] objects. For, since [the cognition] does not arise from that [object], and since it is not of the nature of that [object], a necessary invariable relation with that [object] is impossible. And the object is not identical with cognition, because [the object] is different from cognition. Even if [they were] not different, since cognitions are mutually different and thus not identical [with one another], one cognition cannot be cognized by another cognition. And if the unity of all cognitions as <s>svalakṣaṇa</s> were accepted, then that [cognition] would be eternal, one, and non-dual — the <s>Brahman</s> to be meditated upon — and the acceptance of the practice of momentariness and selflessness would be abandoned. Therefore, there is no invariable relation [between cognition and object] on account of identity. Nor on account of being its effect. For [vivid cognition] is indeed the effect of the excellence of meditation, not the effect of the object. If it be said that it is indirectly the effect of that [object], like inference — just as from the <s>svalakṣaṇa</s> of fire arises the <s>svalakṣaṇa</s> of smoke, from that the experience of smoke, from that the conceptual cognition of fire, and from that arises inference, so that, indirectly, because of being dependent on fire, [inference] is a means of apprehending fire that burns and cooks; similarly, this [vivid cognition] too, born at the culmination of the excellence of meditation generated by inference, being indirectly produced from the object, and because of its necessary invariable relation with that [object], is a valid means of knowledge regarding it — [we reply:] Does the vivid cognition that arises when one ascertains fire through inference and then meditates upon it constitute a valid means of knowledge? Yes, one might say. But then, even when climbing a mountainside, the cognition of fire born from sense-organ contact would have to be in necessary agreement with the vivid cognition born from the predominance of meditation, which is absurd. And disagreement [between them] is frequently observed. When there is the possibility of deviation in what possesses the defining characteristic, that very defining characteristic is undermined. Therefore, even a vivid [cognition], like an intuitive flash, being invaded by doubt, is not a valid means of knowledge. That the meditation is about a real object does not serve as a ground for the validity of the vivid cognition born from it, because of deviation. And thus, the <s>Tathāgata's</s> direct apprehension of the selflessness of all things turns out to be like the direct apprehension of wealth by a traveler whose chain of wishful thoughts is rooted in obtaining a pot of barley flour. [Objection:] The consciousness occurring in the mental continuum that has been refined by meditation on the totality of objects — its <s>ālambanapratyaya</s> (object-condition) is simply the object itself.

children.text: tathā ca tadutpatteḥ tadavyabhicāraniyama iti cet | na | arthasya hy ālambanapratyayatvavijñānaṃ pratīndriyāpekṣatvena vyāptam | tac cāsmāt svaviruddhopalabdhyā vyāvartamānam ālambanapratyayatām apy arthasya nivartayati | na khalv indhanaviśeṣo dhūmahetur iti vināpi dahanaṃ sastreṇāpi saṃskārair dhūmam ādhatte | tadādhāne vā samastakāryahetvanumānocchedaprasaṅgaḥ | bhāvanāyāś ca bhūtārthāyā arthānapekṣāyā eva viśadavijñānajananasāmarthyam upalabdhaṃ kāmāturādivartinyā iti bhūtārthāpi tannirapekṣaiva samartheti nārthasyālambanapratyayatvaṃ śakyāvagamam | api ca ālambanapratyayāpi ta evāsya kṣaṇā yujyante, ye tasya purastāt tanā avyavadhānās tathā ca ta evāsya grāhyā na punaḥ pūrvatarāḥ | tatkālā anāgatāś ceti na sarvaviṣayatā | atha dṛśyamānā dhātutrayaparyāpannāḥ prāṇabhṛto janmāntaraparivartopāttātītānāgataskandhakadambakopādānopādeyātmāna iti taddarśanaṃ dṛśyamānatādātmyena tadviśeṣaṇatayātītānāgatam api gocarayati | na cāsmadādidarśanasyāpi tathātvaprasaṅgaḥ, rāgādimalāvṛtatvāt | tasya ca bhagavato nirmṛṣṭanikhilakleśopakleśamalaṃ vijñānamanāvaraṇaṃ paritaḥ pradyotamānam ālambanapratyayaṃ sarvākāraṃ gocarayet | tasya ca sākṣāt paramparayā ca kathañcit sarveṇa sambandhād deśakālaviprakīrṇavastumātraviśiṣṭasvabhāvatayā tathaiva gocarayet | na caitat sarvagrahaṇam antareṇeti sarvaviṣayam asya vijñānam anāvaraṇaṃ siddham |
children.translated_text: And therefore, because it arises from that [object], there is an invariable relation with it. [Reply:] No, because the cognition that an object is an <s>ālambanapratyaya</s> (object-condition) is pervaded by dependence on the sense-organs. And that [sense-dependence], being excluded from this [meditation-born cognition] by the apprehension of what contradicts it, removes also the object's status as <s>ālambanapratyaya</s>. For a particular type of fuel is not the cause of smoke in such a way that even without fire, mere material modifications (<s>saṃskāras</s>) could produce smoke; and if they could, the consequence would be the destruction of all causal inference. And the capacity of meditation — even when about a real object but independent of [external] objects — to generate vivid cognition has been observed, as in the case of one tormented by desire and similar [cases]. Therefore, even when about a real object, [meditation] is independent of that [object] in its capacity, so the object's status as <s>ālambanapratyaya</s> cannot be established. Moreover, only those moments that are immediately prior and uninterrupted are suitable as <s>ālambanapratyaya</s> for it, and thus only those are its objects, not those more remote; and those [moments] that are contemporaneous and those that are future — therefore there is no apprehension of all objects. [Objection:] But the living beings seen [by the omniscient one], comprised within the three realms (<s>dhātus</s>), possess a nature that includes the aggregates (<s>skandhas</s>) of past and future acquired through the cycle of births in other lifetimes, and so seeing them — by virtue of identity with what is seen, as their qualification — also brings within its scope the past and future. And there is no such consequence for our perception, because it is veiled by the stains of passion (<s>rāga</s>) and other [afflictions]. But the cognition of that Blessed One, having cleansed all the stains of afflictions (<s>kleśa</s>) and secondary afflictions (<s>upakleśa</s>), is unveiled, shining forth on all sides, and would bring within its scope the <s>ālambanapratyaya</s> in all its aspects. And since everything is somehow connected to it, directly or indirectly, by virtue of its nature being qualified by the totality of objects scattered across space and time, it would bring [everything] within its scope in just that way. And this [apprehension] is impossible without grasping everything — therefore his cognition, being unveiled, is established as having all objects as its domain.

children.text: tad anupapannam | vicārāsahatvāt | tathā hīyam ālambanapratyayasya sarvaviśiṣṭātmatā bhāvikī na vā | bhāvikī cet | na tāvat sarvasminn ālambanapratyaye caikā sambhavati | ekasyānekavṛttitvānupapatteḥ | nānā cet | ālambanapratyayāś ca sarve ceti tattvam | tathā ca na sambandha iti na tadgrahaṇe sarvagrahaṇam | vikalpāropitatayā tv avikalpakaṃ samastavastuviṣayaṃ sarvatra pratīyata iti subhāṣitam | svālambanapratyayamātragocaram evāvikalpakaṃ samastavastuviśiṣṭālambanādhyavasāyajananam tenādhyavasāyānugatavyāpāram avikalpakam api samastavastuviṣayaṃ bhavati | yad āha
children.translated_text: That is untenable — because it cannot withstand scrutiny. For this universal-particular nature of the object-condition (<s>ālambanapratyaya</s>) — is it intrinsic or not? If intrinsic: it is not possible for one [single universal nature] to exist in every object-condition, since it is impossible for one thing to function in multiple instances. If [it is] multiple: then the truth is that the object-conditions are all [distinct]. And thus there is no relation [between them], so the apprehension of one does not entail the apprehension of all. However, [the Buddhist position is] well stated: the non-conceptual cognition (<s>avikalpaka</s>) is experienced everywhere as having all things as its object through the superimposition of conceptual construction (<s>vikalpa</s>). The non-conceptual cognition, which has only its own object-condition as its scope, produces the determination (<s>adhyavasāya</s>) of an object qualified by all things; therefore, even the non-conceptual cognition, having its operation accompanied by determination, has all things as its object. As it is said:

children.text: vyavasyantīkṣaṇād eva sarvākārān mahādhiyaḥ |
(PV III 107)

children.translated_text: 'The great intellects determine all aspects from the very moment [of perception].'

children.text: iti cet | atha katipayavastvālambanānubhavasya kutastya eṣa mahimā yataḥ samastavastvavasāya iti | rāgādyāvaraṇavigamād iti cet | tarhi yathāvad vastūni paśyet | na punar asmād apārthatvam asyeti | tad ayuktaṃ vikalpanirmāṇakauśalam asya yujyeta | tattvāvarakatā hi sulabhamalānāṃ kleṣādīnāṃ na punarvikalpanirmāṇapratibandhatā | tasmād bhāvanāprakarṣamātrajatvāt, arthāvyabhicāraniyamābhāvāt, viśadābham api saṃśayākrāntatvād apramāṇam apratyakṣaṃ ceti sāmpratam ||
children.translated_text: If [one objects]: whence comes this power to the experience whose object-condition is only some particular things, such that it determines all things? If [one replies]: from the removal of the obscurations of desire (<s>rāga</s>) and so forth — then [the cognition] would perceive things as they truly are. And it should not [produce] falsity from this. That is untenable — skill in the fabrication of conceptual construction would apply to it. For the obscuration of reality is easy for defilements (<s>kleśa</s>) and the like, being impurities; but they are not hindrances to the fabrication of conceptual construction. Therefore, because [such cognition] arises merely from the culmination of meditation (<s>bhāvanā</s>), because there is no fixed rule of non-deviation from the object, and because even while having vivid appearance it is beset by doubt — it is neither a valid means of knowledge (<s>pramāṇa</s>) nor direct perception (<s>pratyakṣa</s>). This is established.

children.text:
yad api sadarthaprakāśanaṃ buddheḥ
	svabhāvo 'sadarthatvaṃ cāgantukam iti, asati bādhake sadarthatvam
	eveti, tad ayuktam |
	anumitabhāvitavahniviṣayaviśadābhajñānaprāmāṇyaprasaṅgāt tadvidhasya
	kvacid bādhadarśanād aprāmāṇyam ihāpi samānam | anyatrābhiniveśāt |
	tad iha yadi viśadābhavijñānahetutvaṃ bhāvanāyā viśeṣaṇatrayayogena
	sādhyate, tataḥ siddhasādhanam | bhavatu tathāgatas
	tathābhūtavijñānavān | na tv etad vijñānam asya pratyakṣam
	apramāṇatvāt | tathā cāpakṣadharmatayā hetor asiddhatā |
	prasiddhadharmaṇo dharmiṇo 'jijñāsitaviśeṣatayā anumeyatvābhāvāt |
	atha pratyakṣavijñānahetutā bhāvanāyāḥ paraṃ pratyasiddhā sādhyate,
	tathā ca sati sādhyaviparyayavyāpter viruddhatā hetoḥ,
	viśeṣaṇatrayavatyāpi bhāvanāyā viśadābhabhrāntavijñānajanakatvāt |
	dṛṣṭāntasya ca sādhyahīnatvāt | yadā ca bhūtārthabhāvanājanitatve 'pi
	nāsya prāmāṇyam abhūtārthatvāt, tadā yad ucyate,
