children.translated_text: As for the [claim] that 'the nature of cognition is to reveal real objects, and the apprehension of unreal objects is adventitious; in the absence of invalidation, its apprehension of real objects [stands]' — that is untenable. Because there would be the unwanted consequence that the vivid cognition regarding fire, which is the object of something inferred and then meditated upon, would also be valid. Since invalidation is seen in some cases for cognitions of that type, invalidity applies here equally — due to attachment to other [objects]. If, then, the capacity of meditation to produce vivid cognition is to be established with the conjunction of three qualifications, then it is <s>siddhasādhana</s> (proving what is already established). Granted that the <s>Tathāgata</s> possesses such cognition — but this cognition of his is not direct perception, since it is not a valid means of knowledge. And thus the logical reason fails to be a property of the thesis-subject (<s>pakṣadharmatā</s>). Because there is no inferability of a thesis-subject whose property is already established, regarding an undesired specification. If, on the other hand, what is being proved is the capacity of meditation to produce perceptual cognition, which is unestablished for the opponent — then, the logical reason is contradictory (<s>viruddha</s>), since it is pervaded by the opposite of what is to be proved: even meditation possessing the three qualifications produces vivid but erroneous cognition. And the example lacks the property to be proved. And when, even though [the cognition] is born of meditation on a real object, it has no validity because its object is unreal — then as to what is said:

children.text: nirupadravabhūtārthasvabhāvasya viparyayaiḥ |
children.translated_text: 'For a cognition whose nature is an unimpaired real object, by contrary [cognitions]'

children.text: na bādhā yatnavattve 'pi buddhes tatpakṣapātataḥ ||
children.translated_text: 'there is no invalidation, even with effort — because of the cognition's partiality toward that [real object].'

children.text: iti | tad anupapannam | bhūtārthatve 'pi hi buddheḥ tatpakṣapātitā bhūtārthaiḥ pratipakṣair bādho na bhavet | abhūtārthā tv iyaṃ sātmībhāvam āpannāpy ātmātmīyadṛṣṭir iva sambhavadbādhā | tasmāt pratipakṣavivṛddhimātram | na tv ātyantikī vivṛddhiḥ sambhavati | yayā samūlakāṣaṃ kaṣitā doṣā na punar udbhaviṣyanti | ata evāsthirāśrayatve 'pi apunaryatnāpekṣatve 'pi asya nātyantikī niṣṭhā sambhavati | ātmātmīyadṛśa iva virodhipratyayasambhavāt | tatsambhavaś cābhūtārthatvāt | śrutānumitaviṣayaṃ tu pratyakṣaṃ na sambhavaty eva | tayoḥ parokṣarūpāvagāhitvāt | pratyakṣasya ca tadviparītatvāt | tadgatabhūtābhūtārthānuvidhāyitvena svaviṣaye śrutānumānajñānāpekṣayā prāmāṇyānupapatteś ca ||
children.translated_text: That is untenable. For even if the cognition apprehends a real object, its 'partiality toward that' means that invalidation by real counter-cognitions would not occur. But this [cognition] has an unreal object — even though it has become identified with the self, like the view of self and 'mine' (<s>ātmātmīyadṛṣṭi</s>), it is susceptible to invalidation. Therefore, [what occurs] is merely the growth of the counter-cognition — but absolute growth is not possible, by which the defilements, extracted root and all, would never arise again. For this very reason, even though it does not depend on a stable basis or renewed effort, an absolute conclusion is not possible for it — because contrary cognitions may arise, just as with the view of self and 'mine.' And that possibility [of contrary cognitions arising] is due to [the cognition's] having an unreal object. But direct perception regarding what is heard or inferred is simply impossible — because those [hearing and inference] apprehend objects of a hidden nature, while direct perception is the opposite of that; and because the validity [of perception] is impossible regarding its own object when it follows the real or unreal nature of those [hearing and inference], in dependence on the cognitions of hearing and inference regarding its own object.

children.text: tat siddham etat bhūtārthabhāvanāprakarṣaparyantajavijñānam apratyakṣam arthe 'prāmāṇyāt | yad apramāṇaṃ tad apratyakṣam arthe | yathā kāmātur asya kāminīvijñānam | apramāṇaṃ ca tat | nitāntaviśadābhatve sati bhāvanāprakarṣajatvāt | yan nitāntaviśadābhatve sati bhāvanāprakarṣajaṃ vijñānaṃ tad apramāṇam |
children.translated_text: Thus it is established: the cognition born at the culmination of meditation on a real object is not direct perception, because it is not a valid means of knowledge regarding the object. What is not a valid means of knowledge is not direct perception regarding the object — just as the cognition of a woman by a man afflicted with desire. And that [cognition arising from meditation] is not a valid means of knowledge. Because, while being extremely vivid in appearance, it arises from the culmination of meditation. Whatever cognition is extremely vivid in appearance and arises from the culmination of meditation — that is not a valid means of knowledge.

children.text: yathānumitabhāvitavahniviśadavijñānam iti | samānahetujatvaṃ samānarūpatayā vyāptam | yad āha
children.translated_text: Just like the vivid cognition of fire that has been inferred and [then] meditated upon. The sameness of cause entails sameness of form. As it is said:

children.text: tadatadrūpiṇo bhāvās tadatadrūpahetujāḥ
(PV III 251ab)

children.translated_text: 'Entities that are of such-and-such a form or not are born from causes of such-and-such a form or not.'

children.text: iti | tad asya prāmāṇyaṃ nivartamānaṃ tulyahetujatvam api nivartayati | na caiṣa bhūtārthabhāvanāprakarṣaparyantajo 'nindriyasannikṛṣṭānumitabhāvitavahnivaiśadye ca nirātmakasamastavastuvaiśadye ca viśiṣyate | na ca rāgādyāvaraṇaviraho viśeṣaḥ | na khalv ete kambalādivad āvarakā vijñānasya | kiṃ tu tadākṣiptamanā vividhaviṣayabhedatṛṣṇādiparipluto na śaknoti bhāvayitum iti bhāvanādaramātra eva tadvirahopayogaḥ | asti cehāpi śiśirabharasambhṛtajaḍimamantharatarakāyakāṇḍasyānumitavahnibhāvanābhiyoga iti na hetubhedataḥ pratibandhasiddhiḥ | na caikapārthivāṇusamavāyikāraṇajanmabhir abhinnauṣṇyāpekṣaikavahnisaṃyogāsamavāyikāraṇair gandharasarūpasparśair nānāsvabhāvair vyabhicāraḥ | sāmarthyavaicitryād ekatve 'pi pārthivasya paramāṇoḥ | tadvaicitryaṃ ca kāryavaicitryopalambhāt | tac ca nityasamavetaṃ nityam, kāraṇasāmarthyaprakrameṇa ca pārthivāvayavini kārye jāyata iti avadātam | pariśiṣṭaṃ tu granthavyākhyānasamaye vyākhyāsyāmaḥ | tadāstāṃ tāvat ||
children.translated_text: Therefore, [the negation of] its validity also negates its arising from the same kind of cause. And this [cognition] born at the culmination of meditation on a real object is not distinguished — neither in the vividness regarding fire that is not in contact with the senses and has been inferred and meditated upon, nor in the vividness regarding all selfless things. Nor is the absence of the obscuration of desire (<s>rāga</s>) and the like a distinguishing factor. For these do not obscure cognition like a blanket and so forth. Rather, one whose mind is seized by them, inundated with craving for various object-distinctions, is unable to meditate — so the usefulness of their absence is merely for the effort of meditation. And here too there is the engagement in meditation on inferred fire by one whose body is sluggish and slow, stiffened by the mass of cold — so the hindrance is not established from the difference in cause. Nor is there deviation through the diverse natures — smell, taste, color, and touch — which, though of different natures, arise from the same material atoms as co-inherent causes, depending on a single fire as co-occurring cause with undifferentiated heat. [This is] because of the diversity of potency even in a single material atom. And that diversity [is known] from the observation of diversity in effects. And that [diversity] is eternally co-inherent and eternal, and arises in the material composite effect through the progression of causal potency — this is well established. The remainder we shall explain at the time of commenting on the text. Let that be set aside for now.

children.text: trilocanas
children.translated_text: <s>Trilocana</s>,

children.text: tu
children.translated_text: however,

children.text: nyāyaprakīrṇake
children.translated_text: in the <s>Nyāyaprakīrṇaka</s>,

children.text: prāha | iha kila duḥkhasamudayanirodhamārgākhyānyāryāṇāṃ satyāni catvāri | teṣām satyānāṃ svarūpasākṣātkārijñānaṃ yogipratyakṣaṃ | tatra duḥkhaṃ phalabhūtāḥ pañcopādānaskandhāḥ | tac ca svarūpato jñātavyam | ta eva hetubhūtāḥ samudayaḥ | sa ca prahātavyaḥ | niḥkleśāvasthā cittasya nirodhaḥ | sa ca sākṣātkartavayaḥ | tadavasthāprāptihetur nairātmyakṣaṇikatvādyākāraś cittaviśeṣo mārgaḥ | sa ca bhāvayitavya iti saugatamatam |
children.translated_text: states: Here indeed, the <s>Āryas</s> (Noble Ones) hold four truths, called suffering (<s>duḥkha</s>), origination (<s>samudaya</s>), cessation (<s>nirodha</s>), and the path (<s>mārga</s>). The cognition that directly realizes the nature of those truths is yogic perception (<s>yogipratyakṣa</s>). Among these, suffering consists of the five aggregates of clinging (<s>pañcopādānaskandha</s>), which are the effects — and that is to be known in its own nature. Those same [aggregates], as causes, are origination — and that is to be abandoned. The state of the mind free from defilements (<s>kleśa</s>) is cessation — and that is to be directly realized. The special state of mind characterized by selflessness (<s>nairātmya</s>), momentariness (<s>kṣaṇikatva</s>), and so forth, which is the cause of attaining that state, is the path — and that is to be cultivated. Such is the Buddhist doctrine.

children.text: atrocyate | mārgas tāvat pramāṇapariśuddho na bhavatīty uktaṃ prāk | ato 'bhūtaviṣayasya vikalpasyābhyāsād asatyārthavijñānaṃ syān na saṃvādi | api ca pramāṇapariśuddhamārgavādī śākyaḥ pramāṇaṃ pṛṣṭaḥ san sattvākhyaliṅgajaṃ vikalpaṃ brūyāt | tato yāvad vikalpena darśitarūpaṃ tat sarvam asat | śabdasaṃsṛṣṭatvāt | tasmiṃs ca bhāvyamāne sattve bhāvakasya vikalpakasya bhāvanopahite viśadābhatve śabdasamsṛṣṭagrāhyanimittaṃ vikalpakatvaṃ nivartate | tadvyāvṛttau grāhyam api śabdasaṃsṛṣṭaṃ nivartate | ato nirvikalpakam api yogijñānaṃ nirviṣayaṃ prasaktam | yat tu pāramārthikaṃ vastvātmakaṃ na tatpramāṇapariśuddham | śuddhau vā bhāvanayā | bhāvyasya sākṣādvijñātatvāt | na cānyasmin śabdasaṃsṛṣṭe bhāvyamāne sphuṭam anyad rūpaṃ bhavati | śokātur asyāpi niruddhendriyavyāpārasya tanayabhāvanāyāṃ mitrādipratibhāsaprasaṅgāt |
children.translated_text: To this we reply: the path, to begin with, is not purified by valid means of knowledge — as was stated earlier. Therefore, from the repeated practice (<s>abhyāsa</s>) of a conceptual construction that has an unreal object, there would be a cognition of an unreal object — not a concordant [valid] one. Moreover, the follower of the <s>Śākya</s> (Buddha) who maintains that the path is purified by valid means of knowledge, when asked about the valid means, would point to the conceptual construction (<s>vikalpa</s>) born from the inferential sign called 'being' (<s>sattva</s>). From that, whatever form is shown by conceptual construction — all of it is unreal, because it is mixed with words (<s>śabdasaṃsṛṣṭa</s>). And when that 'being' is meditated upon, and the conceptual cognition of the meditator reaches vividness affected by meditation, the conceptuality — which has as its cause the apprehended object mixed with words — ceases. With the cessation of that, the apprehended object mixed with words also ceases. Therefore, even the non-conceptual yogic cognition (<s>nirvikalpaka yogijñāna</s>) is consequentially objectless. As for what is ultimately real and of the nature of a real entity — that is not purified by valid means of knowledge; or if purified, [it is so] through meditation. Because the object of meditation is known directly. But when something else, mixed with words, is meditated upon, a vivid [cognition of] another form does not arise — for [if it did], there would be the unwanted consequence that even one grieving, whose sense-faculties are restrained, would, while meditating on his son, experience the appearance of a friend and so forth.

children.text: kṣaṇikatve bhāvye samāropite vāstavaṃ kṣaṇikatvam eva yogivijñānapratibhāsīti cet | na | satyāsatyayor ekatvābhāvātmake hi bhede 'satyabhāvane 'pi yadi satyapratibhāsaḥ, tarhi satyatanayābhyāse 'pi śabdasāmyād abhedinas tanayasaṃjñakasya kasyacid aparasya svarūpapratibhāsaprasaṅgaḥ | tasmād abhūtaviṣayābhyāsaṃ nirvikalpakam api saṃvādān na pramāṇam iti na sarvajñasiddhiḥ |
children.translated_text: If [one objects]: when momentariness is the object of meditation, being superimposed, the actual momentariness itself appears in the yogin's cognition — no, [that does not follow]. For in a difference that is of the nature of non-identity between real and unreal: if, even while meditating on the unreal, there is the appearance of the real, then even in the practice regarding a real son, due to the similarity of the word, there would be the unwanted consequence that the appearance of the own-nature of some other [being] bearing the designation 'son' who is non-different [in name] would arise. Therefore, [practice] with an unreal object, even [when] non-conceptual, is not a valid means of knowledge due to [lack of] concordance — hence the establishment of omniscience (<s>sarvajña</s>) fails.

children.text: api ca bhāvyasya vastunaḥ punaḥ punaś cetasi niveśanam abhyāsaḥ | sa ca brahmacaryeṇa tapasā sādaraṃ dīrghakālaṃ nirantaramāsevito dṛḍhabhūmir asphuṭākārasya vikalpasya sphuṭābhatvajanana iṣṭaḥ | sa kṣaṇikatvanairātmyavādinā draḍhayitum aśakyaḥ | tathā hi bhāvyagrāhī yādṛśo vikalpa utpannas tādṛśa eva niranvayaṃ nirudhyate | tasmiṃś ca niruddhe punaḥ punar utpadyamānaḥ pratyayas tādṛśa evāpūrva utpadyate | tad anena paryāyeṇa kalpasahasre 'py apūrvotpatter aviśeṣān na tajjanyaḥ saṃskāro 'bhyāsa utpadyate | etena viśiṣṭavijñānotpādo 'bhyāso vyākhyātaḥ | niranvayaniruddhaṃ hi pūrvapūrvavijñānaṃ katham uttarāvasthāntaraṃ viśiṣtaṃ janayet | sarvathā kramabhāvibhiḥ pratyayair avasthitam eva rūpaṃ śakyaṃ saṃskartum | anavasthitaṃ tu svotpādavyayayogimātram ity aviśiṣṭaṃ syāt | tasmāt pratyāvṛttibhāvyavastupratyayajaḥ saṃskāro vyutthānapratyayasaṃskāravirodhī yasyāsti tasyaivātmanaḥ prakṛṣṭo 'pi bhāvyasākṣātkāripratyayahetur iti yuktaṃ paśyāmaḥ | kiṃ ca cittam ekāgraṃ vyavasthāpayituṃ vikṣepatyāgārtham abhyāso 'nuṣṭhīyate | na ca kṣaṇikavādināṃ vikṣiptaṃ cittam asti | pratyarthaniyatatayā sarvasya vittaikāgratvāt | tathā hi yadi sākāraṃ vikalpavijñānaṃ svapratibhāsaniyatatvāt ekāgram eva tat kathaṃ vikṣipyate | atha nirākāraṃ tathāpi vikalpakaṃ prati vikalpyaṃ bhinnam eva | na tu sarvavikalpānāṃ vikalpyam asti | tato nirākāram api vijñānaṃ niyatālambanatvād ekāgram eva, na vikṣiptam | sarvathā nāsti kṣaṇikavādinām ekam anekārtham avasthitaṃ cittaṃ yad ekāgraṃ kartum iṣyate | tad evam abhyāsānupapatter asarvajñavatyāṃ cittasantatau na ca vijñānaviśeṣaḥ sarvajñaḥ sidhyatīti ||
children.translated_text: Moreover, meditation (<s>abhyāsa</s>) is the repeated presentation of the object to be meditated upon in the mind. When it is practiced with celibacy (<s>brahmacarya</s>), austerity (<s>tapas</s>), care, for a long time, and without interruption, it is accepted [by Buddhists] as having a firm foundation and as generating vividness from what was indistinct in conceptual form. [But] it cannot be solidified by one who holds the doctrine of momentariness and selflessness. For the conceptual cognition that apprehends the object of meditation, of whatever kind it arises, ceases without residue in exactly the same form. And when that has ceased, the cognition that arises again and again arises as an entirely new one of exactly the same kind. Therefore, by this succession, even in a thousand <s>kalpas</s> (cosmic ages), because there is no difference from new arising, no conditioning (<s>saṃskāra</s>) born from it — [i.e.,] meditation — arises. By this, the [Buddhist account of] meditation as the production of a distinguished cognition is refuted. For how could cognition that has ceased without residue generate a subsequent, more distinguished state? In every respect, only a form that persists through successive cognitions can be conditioned. What does not persist, being merely subject to its own arising and perishing, would be undistinguished. Therefore, it is the conditioning born from the cognition of the object repeatedly meditated upon, which opposes the conditioning of the dispersed cognition — only he who possesses a self for which [this conditioning exists] can have the cause of even the most advanced cognition that directly realizes the object of meditation. This is what we consider reasonable. Furthermore, meditation is undertaken for the purpose of abandoning distraction, in order to establish one-pointedness of mind. But for proponents of momentariness, there is no distracted mind — because all cognition is one-pointed, being fixed on each respective object. For if the conceptual cognition that has form [i.e., is representational] is one-pointed by being fixed on its own appearance, how is it distracted? And if it is formless [i.e., non-representational], even then the object of conceptualization is distinct from the conceptual [cognition] — but not all conceptual cognitions have an object of conceptualization. Therefore, even formless cognition, being of fixed object, is one-pointed, not distracted. In no way do proponents of momentariness have one persistent mind with multiple objects that one wishes to make one-pointed. Thus, since meditation is impossible, in a mental continuum that does not possess omniscience, no special cognition that is omniscient can be established.

children.text: nyāyabhūṣaṇakāras tv āha | sarvajñānānāṃ nirālambanatve saṃvedamātratve ca yogītarapratyayayoḥ ko viśeṣaḥ | śuddhāśuddhatvam iti cet | bhavatu nāmaivam | tathāpi caturāryasatyādiviṣayatvam ayuktam | na hi svātmamātravedanena caturāryasatyādikam sākṣātkṛtam iti yuktam, atiprasaṅgāt.
children.translated_text: The author of the <s>Nyāyabhūṣaṇa</s> (<s>Bhāsarvajña</s>), however, says: If all cognitions of the omniscient [being] are objectless and are mere self-awareness (<s>saṃvedamātra</s>), what is the difference between yogic cognition and the cognition of other [ordinary persons]? If [the difference is] purity versus impurity: let it be so. Even then, having the Four Noble Truths and so forth as objects is untenable. For it is not reasonable that the Four Noble Truths and so forth are directly realized through mere self-awareness alone — because of the unwanted over-extension.

children.text: tadākāratvena tadviṣayatvam iti cet, tat kim idānīṃ sautrāntikamatam abhyupagataṃ satyam | tathāpy atītānāgataviṣayatvaṃ katham | na hy asataḥ kaścid ākāro 'sti | dṛṣṭaśrutānumitākāraś ca yadi bhāvanābalataḥ spaṣṭa evāvabhāti, tathā ca sati bhrāntam eva yogipratyakṣaṃ syāt | avidyamānasya vidyamānākāratayā pratibhāsanāt, svapnavat | tathā 'visaṃvāditvān na bhrāntam | na | anumānajñānasya bhrāntatve 'pi avisaṃvāditvābhyupagamāt |
children.translated_text: If it be said that having it as its form constitutes having it as its object — then is the <s>Sautrāntika</s> view now accepted as true? Even so, how can there be objecthood with respect to past and future [things]? For a non-existent has no form whatsoever. And if a form [previously] seen, heard, or inferred appears vividly through the force of meditation, then <s>yogic</s> perception (<s>yogi-pratyakṣa</s>) would be nothing but erroneous, since what does not exist appears in the form of what does exist — like a dream. [If it be said:] 'Because it is non-discordant, it is not erroneous' — no, because even inferential cognition is accepted as non-discordant despite being erroneous.

children.text: atha bhrāntasyāpi saṃvāditvena prāmāṇyam | tathāpi pratyakṣalakṣaṇasyābhrāntatvaviśeṣaṇaṃ virudhyate | na cāvisaṃvāditvam api tvanmate yuktam | yataḥ prāpyārthadarśakatvaṃ vā, pravṛttiviṣayopadarśakatvaṃ vā, avabhātād arthakriyāniṣpattir vā bhavatām avisaṃvāditvam abhipretam | na caitad atītādyarthajñāne sambhavati | vartamānārthajñānasyāpi kṣaṇikatvapakṣe nopapadyata eva | tasmāt saugatānāṃ yogipratyakṣopavarṇanam ayuktam eveti ||
children.translated_text: If even an erroneous [cognition] has validity through being concordant — even so, the qualifier 'non-erroneous' in the definition of perception (<s>pratyakṣa</s>) is contradicted. Nor is non-discordance (<s>avisaṃvāditva</s>) justified on your view. For your intended meaning of non-discordance is either: (i) the capacity to show an object to be attained, (ii) the capacity to show the object upon which activity is directed, or (iii) the accomplishment of purposeful action (<s>arthakriyā</s>) from the appearance [of an object]. But none of these is possible in the cognition of past and other [non-present] objects. And even for the cognition of a present object, it is not tenable on the theory of momentariness (<s>kṣaṇikatva</s>). Therefore, the description of <s>yogic</s> perception by the Buddhists is indeed unjustified.

children.text: kiṃ cedam api vaktum ucitam | yady anumānapūrvakam artheṣu bhāvanābalajajñānam āśvāsabhājanaṃ, tadāstāṃ tāvad anumānapauruṣapratyāśā | pratyakṣeṇāpi cakṣurdahanādikaṃ gṛhītvā bhāvanāprakarṣaparyante jātaṃ sthirataraṃ tadākāravijñānaṃ syāt, yāvan na viparītabhāvanābhiyogaparyantaḥ | astaṃ gataś ca tadviṣayo 'vasthānataraprāpto veti kathaṃ pramāṇopanītavastugocaratve 'pi saṃvādāśvāsaḥ | api ca yadā hālika eva havyāśanam anumāya bhāvanayā sphuṭayet, tadā na tadyogijñānaṃ paramārthaviṣayābhāvād iti pratyakṣāntaraprasaṅgaḥ |
children.translated_text: Furthermore, is it even appropriate to say this? If knowledge born from the power of meditation upon objects — preceded by inference — is worthy of confidence, then set aside for now the expectation of what inference can accomplish. For even through perception, having grasped [something] such as fire by the eye, the cognition of that form arising at the culmination of intensive meditation would be more stable [than the original perception], lasting until the undertaking of contrary meditation. But the object [of that original perception] has set and has reached another state — so how can there be confidence in concordance even when it has as its object a thing presented by a valid means of cognition? Moreover, when a farmer, having inferred fire, makes it vivid through meditation — then that yogic cognition would not [be valid], because there is no ultimate-reality object [of fire in the field] — and so there would follow the absurd consequence of yet another kind of perception.

children.text: kiṃ ca tadyogijñānam indriyajñānād bhinnam abhinnaṃ vā | abhedapakṣe na yogijñānaṃ nāma pratyakṣeṇa bhinnam indriyajñānenaiva saṅgrahāt | na ca bhāvanopaskṛtasantānasya tathodayād bhedavyavasthā | rasāyanādisaṃskārāpekṣayāpi pratyakṣāntaravyavasthāprasaṅgāt | bhedapakṣe ca bhāvanāsambhavaṃ jñānaṃ kṣaṇikasākṣātkāri | indriyajñānaṃ ca syairyagrāhīti sādhvī siddhiḥ | indriyajñānasyāpi tadavasthāyām asthairyagrhaṇe kṛtaṃ yogijñānena | na ca tasyākasmikaḥ kṣaṇikatvāvabodhaḥ | bhāvanodbhūtavaiśadyasya hi tadbodhaḥ | na cendriyajñānasya bhāvanā | api tu manovijñāne | tām antareṇāpi sākṣāt kriyālābhe ca bhāvanāvaiyarthyam iti kāraṇābhāvād eva sarvajñapratihatiḥ ||
children.translated_text: Furthermore, is that yogic cognition different from or identical with sense-cognition? On the thesis of non-difference, there is no separate yogic cognition, since it is subsumed under sense-cognition itself. Nor can a distinction be maintained merely because it arises thus in a mental continuum that has been refined by meditation — for there would follow the absurd consequence of establishing yet another kind of perception for [a continuum] refined by elixirs and the like. On the thesis of difference, the cognition born without meditation would directly apprehend momentary [things], and sense-cognition would grasp stable [things] — an excellent establishment indeed! But if even sense-cognition in that state does not grasp stability, then what use is yogic cognition? Nor is its cognition of momentariness uncaused — for that cognition belongs to the clarity born from meditation. But meditation does not belong to sense-cognition; rather, it belongs to mental cognition (<s>mano-vijñāna</s>). And if direct realization is obtained even without meditation, then meditation would be useless — therefore, the very refutation of the omniscient [is established] from the absence of a cause.

children.text:
atrābhidhīyate | yat tāvat sarvapadārthasaṃvedanasya kāraṇaṃ
	kim indriyajñānam ityādi valgitaṃ tatra bhāvanābalajaṃ manovijñānam
	eva sarvapadārthagrāhīti pañcama evāsmākaṃ pakṣaḥ | ataḥ
	pakṣāntarabhāvino doṣā anubhyupagamapratihatāḥ | yac cāsmadabhyupagate
	pañcame pakṣe dūṣaṇam uktam, anarthatvāt pratyakṣaśabdasya, tasya ca
	bhāvanābalāvalambino 'py anakṣajatvān nārthasākṣātkāritvam astīti, tad
	asaṅgatam | tathā hi pratyakṣaśabdasya tāvad akṣāśritatvaṃ
	vyutpattinimittam arthasākṣātkāritvaṃ tu pravṛttinimittam iti
	pratipāditam | na ca bhāvanābalāvalambino manovijñānasyānakṣāśritatve
	'py arthasākṣārkaraṇe kaścid asti śaktipratighātaḥ | yathā hi
	cakṣurindriyaṃ svasāmarthyān atikrameṇa yogyadeśastham artham apekṣya
	svavijñānajanane pravartate, tathā
	sarvāvidyāparipanthibhūtārthabhāvanāsahitaṃ mana indriyam api
	yogyadeśastham arthaṃ prāpya svavijñānajanane pravartiṣyate |
	aprāpyakāritāyā ubhayoḥ sādhāraṇatvāt | arthavattāyāś ca manaso 'pi
	tadānīm iṣṭatvāt | pṛthagjanasya tu na tādṛśī śaktiḥ, yato
	netraśrotravanmano 'pi tādṛṅmaryādayā yogyadeśastham arthasahakāriṇam
	āsādya vedanam utpādayet, sarvāvidyonmūlakasya bhāvanāviśeṣasya
	sahakāriṇo 'bhāvād iti nātiprasaṅgaḥ | tadavasthāyāṃ tu śrutinayanayor
	iva manaso 'pi kiyaddūreṇa viṣayasannidhivyavasthitika eva pramātuṃ
	kṣamaḥ | kevalam etāvad ucyate | yāvat tena śakyam adhigantuṃ
	svākārārpaṇasamarthaṃ sahakāri vastu tāvad itarajanāsādhāraṇaṃ
	truṭyadrūpatayā tasya gocarībhavatīti | ata evārthākāro vastuto na
	bhāvanāmātrajanita iti na visaṃvādaśaṅkāpi | bhāvanayā punas
	tadīyasantāne netra ivāñjanaviśeṣeṇa śaktir atiśayavatī kācid arpitā
	yatparajanāsādhāraṇadarśanam asya | tasmād anakṣajatve 'pi
	amnovijñānasyārthasākṣātkāritvaṃ sambhavati |
children.translated_text: To this we reply: As for the bluster 'What is the cause of the cognition of all objects — is it sense-cognition?' and so forth — our position is precisely the fifth alternative: that mental cognition born from the power of meditation alone is the apprehender of all objects. Therefore, the faults pertaining to the other alternatives are refuted by not being accepted [by us]. And as for the objection raised against our accepted fifth alternative — namely, that the word <s>pratyakṣa</s> (perception) would be meaningless, since, although dependent on the force of meditation, because it is not born from sense-faculties (<s>akṣa</s>), it has no direct realization of objects — that is incoherent. For the derivational basis (<s>vyutpatti-nimitta</s>) of the word <s>pratyakṣa</s> is dependence on sense-faculties, but its functional basis (<s>pravṛtti-nimitta</s>) is the direct realization of objects — this has been demonstrated. And there is no impediment to the power of mental cognition dependent on the force of meditation to directly realize objects, even though it is not dependent on sense-faculties. For just as the visual sense-faculty, transcending its own capacity, operates to produce its own cognition in dependence upon an object situated in a suitable location, so too the mind as a sense-faculty (<s>manas-indriya</s>), accompanied by the meditation on the reality that is the antidote to all <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance), having reached an object situated in a suitable location, will operate to produce its own cognition. Because the property of operating without physical contact (<s>aprāpyakāritā</s>) is common to both. And because the mind too at that time is accepted as having objects [as its domain]. For an ordinary person, however, there is no such capacity — hence the mind does not produce cognition by reaching an object functioning as a cooperating condition within the same range as the eye or ear and the like, because the specific cooperating condition — namely, the distinctive meditation that uproots all <s>avidyā</s> — is absent for the blind and the like. Hence there is no over-extension. In that state, just as hearing and sight [operate within] a certain distance to establish proximity of objects, so too the mind is capable of cognizing only [objects] within a certain range of proximity. It is merely stated this much: whatever cooperating reality, capable of imparting its own form [to cognition], can be apprehended by it — to that extent, it comes within its range as something not shared by ordinary persons, in a mode of dissolving forms. For this very reason, the form of the object is not in reality produced by meditation alone — so there is not even the suspicion of discordance. By meditation, however, a capacity of superabundant power is imparted to that [yogin's] mental continuum — just as a special collyrium [imparts power] to the eye — by which he has a vision not shared by ordinary persons. Therefore, even though not born from sense-faculties, the direct realization of objects by mental cognition is possible.

children.text: nanu manaso bahirasvātantryam | anyathāndhabadhirādyabhāvaprasaṅgāt | uktaṃ ca yogināṃ dharmādharmayor aparokṣapratibhāsaṃ jñānaṃ nāsti | indriyasannikarṣābhāvād asmadādivad iti |
children.translated_text: Objection: The mind has no independence with respect to external [objects]. Otherwise, there would follow the absurd consequence of the non-existence of the blind, the deaf, and the like. And it has been stated: 'Yogins have no cognition that directly apprehends <s>dharma</s> (merit) and <s>adharma</s> (demerit), because of the absence of sense-contact — just like ourselves.'

children.text: api ca arthasya hy ālambanapratyayatvam indriyāpekṣatvena vyāptam | tac cāsmāt svaviruddhopalabdhyā vyāvartamanam ālambanapratyayatām api tasya nivartayati | na khalv indhanaviśeṣo dhūmahetur iti vināpi dahanaṃ sahasreṇāpi saṃskārair dhūmam ādhatte | tadādhāne samastakāryahetukānumānocchedaprasaṅgaḥ | na ca bhāvanābalena kasyacid atīndriyadarśitvaṃ sarvajñatvaṃ vā dṛṣṭam iti cet |
children.translated_text: Moreover, the status of an object as a supporting condition (<s>ālambana-pratyaya</s>) is pervaded by dependence on a sense-faculty. And that [pervading property], being excluded from the present [case] by the apprehension of what contradicts the pervader (<s>sva-viruddha-upalabdhi</s>), also excludes its being a supporting condition. Surely, a particular kind of fuel is not a cause of smoke such that, even without fire, it produces smoke through a thousand conditionings. [If it did,] there would follow the absurd consequence of the destruction of all inferences based on aggregate-cause-effect [reasoning]. And [if it be said:] 'No one has been observed to have supersensory vision or omniscience through the power of meditation' —

children.text: atrocyate | manaḥśabdena tāvad asmākam anakṣajaṃ vijñānam evābhipretam | na cāsminn andhabadhirādyabhāvaprasaṅgaḥ | sarvāvidyāpratipakṣabhūtārthabhāvanālakṣaṇasya sahakāriviśeṣasyāndhādīnām abhāvāt | indriyasannikarṣābhāvād iti tv arthasākṣātkāritvamātrāpekṣayā sandigdhavyatirekitve anaikāntikī kāraṇānupalabdhiḥ | asmadvidhārthasākṣātkāritvāpekṣayā punaḥ siddhasādhanam ||
children.translated_text: To this we reply: By the word 'mind' (<s>manas</s>), we intend precisely cognition not born from sense-faculties. And in this [position], there is no absurd consequence of the non-existence of the blind, the deaf, and the like — because the specific cooperating condition, namely meditation on reality that is the antidote to all <s>avidyā</s>, is absent for the blind and the like. As for '[there is no yogic perception] because of the absence of sense-contact' — with respect to merely having the direct realization of objects, this is an inconclusive (<s>anaikāntika</s>) causal non-apprehension, because the negative concomitance is doubtful. With respect to the direct realization of objects for people like us, however, it proves what is already established (<s>siddha-sādhana</s>).

children.text: asmadādiviśeṣaṇaśūnyasyārthasākṣātkāritvamātrasyaivendriyādhīnatva-darśanād anaikāntikatvam asambhavīti cet | yady evam arthasākṣātkāritvamātrasyendiryavadālokādhīnatvam upalabdham iti na santamase paśyeyur ulūkādayaḥ | atha vyabhicāradarśanād ālokasyāvyāpakatvam, vyabhicāraśaṅkayā tarhīndriyasyāpy avyāpakatvam | vyāptyā śaṅkā khaṇḍyata iti cet | śaṅkāsambhavād vyāptir evāsambhavinī yadi prathamata eva vyāptiḥ, vyabhicāro 'pi na dṛśyeta |
children.translated_text: If it be objected: 'Inconclussiveness is impossible, because dependence on sense-faculties is observed for the mere direct realization of objects, without the qualifier "for people like us"' — if so, then since dependence on light has been observed for the mere direct realization of objects just as dependence on sense-faculties has, owls and the like should not see in total darkness. If, however, the non-pervasiveness of light [is established] from the observation of deviation — then, by the suspicion of deviation, the non-pervasiveness of sense-faculties too [should follow]. If it be said: 'The suspicion is dispelled by the pervasion' — if the pervasion were [established] in the first instance, the deviation too would not be observed, and therefore the very pervasion, because the suspicion would be impossible, would itself be impossible.

children.text: tasmād vyabhicāradarśanaṃ vyāptiśaithilyād eva | sati ca vyāptiśaithilye śaṅkāpi nyāyād āpatantī kena pratihanyate | ulūkādīnāṃ bhinnajātīyatvād ālokābhāve 'py arthasākṣātkāritvam astv iti cet | tarhi bhagavato 'pi bhūtārthabhāvanāprakarṣaparyantamahāpralayavāyunā nirastānādyāvipakṣasya saṃsārakūpapatitebhyaḥ prāṇibhyo 'sty evādbhūtavaijātyam iti yuktam asyāvidyāpratipakṣabhāvanātiśayasahitātmakāntarapratyayād ālambanapratyayāc ca sākṣādutpannasyendriyam antareṇārthasākṣātkāritvam | ataḥ kāraṇānupalabdhiḥ kāśikākārasya vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhiś ca vācaspateḥ sandigdhavyatirekitvād anaikāntikī | sandigdhavyatirekitvaṃ tu dūṣaṇam asmadīśvaradūṣaṇe prasādhitam ||
children.translated_text: Therefore, the observation of deviation is due precisely to the loosening of the pervasion. And when the pervasion is loose, even the suspicion that naturally arises — by what is it repelled? If it be said: 'Because owls and the like are of a different species, they can have direct realization of objects even in the absence of light' — then for the Blessed One too, whose beginningless contrariety [of defilement] has been blown away by the great storm at the culmination of meditation on reality, there is indeed a wondrous difference of species from the beings who have fallen into the well of <s>saṃsāra</s>. Therefore, it is proper that his [cognition], directly produced from both the mental supporting condition (<s>ālambana-pratyaya</s>) possessing a superabundance of the meditation that is the antidote to <s>avidyā</s>, and the object-condition, has direct realization of objects even without a sense-faculty. Therefore, the causal non-apprehension of the author of the <s>Kāśikā</s>, and the apprehension of what contradicts the pervader by <s>Vācaspati</s>, are inconclusive (<s>anaikāntika</s>) due to doubtful negative concomitance. And the doubtful negative concomitance has been demonstrated as a fault in our refutation of <s>Īśvara</s>.

children.text: tasmāt sādhāraṇakarmanirjātānām asmadādīnām arthasākṣātkāritvam indiryāpekṣatvena vyāptam iti siddhasādhanam | prasiddhānumānasya ca na kṣatir dṛśyatvopādher dhūmādeḥ pratyakṣānupalambhato vyāptigrahaṇāvirodhāt | sāṃsārikāgocarārthasākṣātkāritvamātrāpekṣayā tu sandigdhavyatirekitvam | adṛśyasya pratyakṣānupalambhābhyāṃ kenacid vyāptigrahaṇāyogāt | viparyaye bādhakapramāṇasya cāsambhavād iti | na cātīndriyadarśitvaṃ sarvajñatvaṃ vādarśane 'pi niṣeddhuṃ śakyate, adṛśyānupalambhato niṣedhāyogāt | kāraṇānupalambatas tanniśedha iti cet | kāraṇābhāvo 'pi adarśanamātrato na sidhyatīti tadavasthaḥ paribhavaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Therefore, [the claim that] the direct realization of objects by people like us, who are produced by ordinary <s>karma</s>, is pervaded by dependence on sense-faculties — this proves what is already established (<s>siddha-sādhana</s>). And there is no damage to the well-known inference [of fire from smoke], because there is no contradiction in grasping the pervasion through perceptual non-apprehension of the perceptible logical mark, namely smoke. But with respect to the mere direct realization of objects not within the scope of <s>saṃsāric</s> beings, there is doubtful negative concomitance — because no one can grasp the pervasion through perceptual non-apprehension of what is imperceptible. And because a defeating means of valid cognition to the contrary is impossible. And [the existence of] supersensory vision or omniscience cannot be negated even when it is not observed — because negation from the non-apprehension of the imperceptible is impossible. If it be said: 'Their negation follows from the non-apprehension of a cause' — the absence of a cause too is not established from mere non-observation, so the objection remains in the same condition.

children.text: yad api kāśikākāreṇābhihitam, atha pramāṇāntarāvagataṃ bhāvyate, kiṃ bhāvanayā, tata eva tatsiddher iti | tad apy asaṅgataṃ | pramāṇāntaraṃ hy anumānam | na ca caturāryasatyasvarūpe vastutattve niścite sākṣātkāram antareṇa kleśajñeyāvaraṇakṣatir iti svārtham api tāvad bhāvanā yuktimatī | tattvasākṣātkāriṇi ca cittasantāne sati śakyasākṣātkriyam idam ity anye 'pi niścayānantaraṃ sākṣātkriyāyai pravartyante, tadupadiṣṭasvargasādhanaṃ cārthabhāvanayānusarantīti svargāpavargalakṣaṇaparārthasiddhaye ca bhāvanā saphaleti | anyathā tattvāsākṣātkāriṇo lokānatikrāntasya vacanam anādeyam eva syād iti kva parārthavārtāpi | yac ca kiṃ ca tatpramāṇam ityādy ārambhya tasmād bhūtam abhūtaṃ vety etatparyantena dharmādharmayor anumānāpravartanam uktam, tatra dharmādharmaśabdena kim abhipretam | yadi kṣaṇikanirātmakavastu tattvam, tadā tasya pratyakṣeṇāniścaye 'pi yathā viparyaye bādhakapramāṇabalena vyāptisaṃvedanaṃ tathā kṣaṇabhaṅgasādhanāvasare vyavasthāpitam | atha vastūnāṃ svargādisādhanatvam abhipretam, tadā tadviṣayaparijñānāprasādhane 'pi nāsmākaṃ kācit kṣatiḥ | saparikarasaṃsāranirvāṇaparijñānenaivopayuktasarvajñaprasādhanāt | yad āhuḥ: heyopadeyatattvasyetyādi (PV I 217a) |
children.translated_text: As for what the author of the <s>Kāśikā</s> has said — 'If what is contemplated has been ascertained through another means of valid cognition, what is the use of meditation, since its establishment [follows] from that [other means] alone?' — that too is incoherent. For the 'other means of valid cognition' is inference. And without direct realization, even when the reality of the four noble truths has been ascertained, the destruction of the obstructions of affliction (<s>kleśāvaraṇa</s>) and knowledge (<s>jñeyāvaraṇa</s>) does not occur — thus meditation is justified even for one's own purpose. And when there exists a mental continuum that directly realizes reality, others too, having ascertained 'this can be directly realized,' are prompted toward direct realization after that determination — and they follow through meditation on the object the means to heaven that he has taught — thus meditation is fruitful for the accomplishment of the purpose of others too, characterized as heaven and liberation. Otherwise, the word of one who has not directly realized reality and who has not transcended the world would be unacceptable — so where would there even be talk of benefiting others? And as for what has been said beginning with 'What is its means of valid cognition?' and ending with 'Therefore, whether real or unreal' — namely, that inference does not operate with respect to <s>dharma</s> (merit) and <s>adharma</s> (demerit) — what is intended by the words <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s> there? If the reality of momentary and selfless things is meant, then even though it cannot be ascertained through perception, the apprehension of pervasion through the force of a defeating means of valid cognition when there is a contrary [thesis] has been established — just as in the occasion of proving momentariness. But if the capacity of things to be means to heaven and the like is meant, then even if the comprehension of that is not established, there is no loss for us — because the useful omniscient [being] is established merely through the comprehension of <s>saṃsāra</s> and <s>nirvāṇa</s> together with their accessories. As they say: 'Of what is to be rejected and adopted, the truth...' and so forth (PV I 217a).

children.text: yad api, api ca bhāvanābalajaṃ gṛhītagrahaṇād apramāṇam ity uktam, tatra gṛhītaṃ nāma pratyakṣeṇānumānena vā | pramāṇāntarasyābhāvāt | na tāvat pratyakṣaṃ kṣaṇikatvādāv arvācīnasya kasyacid asti | anumānena caikavyāvṛttiviśiṣṭe vastutattve 'vasite 'pi sarvātmanā spaṣṭavastutattvasākṣātkāri pratyakṣaṃ na gṛhītagrāhi, anumānena vastutattvāsparśanāt | na ca taduttarakālam ityādi tu kāraṇānupalabdhidūṣaṇaprastāve prativyūḍham iti |
children.translated_text: As for the objection that 'cognition born from the power of meditation is not a valid means of cognition because it apprehends what has [already] been apprehended' — in that case, 'already apprehended' [means apprehended] either by perception or by inference, since there is no other means of valid cognition. First, no recent person's perception exists with regard to momentariness and the like. And even when the real nature of things qualified by a single exclusion (<s>ekavyāvṛtti</s>) has been ascertained by inference, the perception that directly realizes the clear real nature of things in its entirety does not apprehend what has [already] been apprehended, because inference does not touch the real nature of things. The objection that '[this happens] at a subsequent time' and the like has already been countered in the context of the refutation [based on] non-apprehension of the cause.

children.text: yad api
vācaspatinā
children.translated_text: by <s>Vācaspati</s> —

children.text: satyam ityādinā punaḥ punar uttarottaram āśaṅkya tat kim anumānena vahniṃ vyavasthāpyetyādinā bhāvanābalajasyānumānapūrvakatve visaṃvādam upadarśyopasaṃhṛtam, tan na bhāvanāyā bhūtārthatvaṃ tajjaviśadavijñānaprāmāṇyahetuḥ, vyabhicārād iti | tad asaṅgatam | tathā hy ayaṃ vahniviṣaye 'numānapūrvakabhāvanābalataḥ spaṣṭavahnipratyayaḥ kiṃ vahner apy utpannaḥ, tathābhūtabhāvanāmātrād eva vā |
children.translated_text: beginning with 'True...' and repeatedly raising further and further objections, concluding by demonstrating inconsistency in the thesis that [cognition] born from the power of meditation is preceded by inference, with [the argument] 'Is fire then to be established by inference?' and so on — [namely,] 'the factual truth of meditation is not the ground for the validity of the vivid cognition born from it, because of deviation (<s>vyabhicāra</s>)' — that is incoherent. For this vivid cognition of fire arising from the power of meditation preceded by inference regarding fire — does it arise from the fire itself, or merely from the meditation in such a form?
As for the objection

children.text: parathampakṣe visaṃvādaś ca bahulam upalabhyate iti yad uktaṃ tad durbhāṣitam | sākṣād arthād utpannasyāpi visaṃvādasambhave 'nyasyāpi pratyakṣasya hastakatyāgaprasaṅgāt |
children.translated_text: In the first alternative, the statement that 'inconsistency is frequently observed' is poorly formulated, because even for [cognition] arisen directly from the object, if inconsistency were possible, then other [types of] perception too would have to be abandoned.

children.text: dvitīyapakṣe tu bhāvanāprakarṣamātrajasyārthād anutpannasya bahulaṃ visaṃvādopalambhe 'pi bhāvanārthābhyāṃ sākṣād utpannasya yogipratyakṣasyāpi visaṃvādasambhava iti sthavīyasī bhrāntiḥ |
children.translated_text: In the second alternative, the claim that since [cognition] born merely from the excellence of meditation — not arisen from the object — is frequently observed to be inconsistent, therefore even <s>yogipratyakṣa</s> (yogic perception), which arises directly from both meditation and the object, must also be subject to inconsistency — this is a grosser delusion.

children.text: nanu yadīndriyaṃ vināpi bhāvanārthābhyāṃ yogijñānam utpadyate, tarhi parvate bhāvanāvahnibhyāṃ vahnijñānam utpadyatām avisaṃvādi | visaṃvādaś ca bahulam upalabhyata iti cet | na | sākṣād vahner utpāde sati visaṃvādābhāvāt | kevalam utpāda eva durāpaḥ | na hi vayaṃ pramāṇadṛṣṭavastubhāvanāsahitaṃ mana indiryam arthasvarūpagrāhijñānaṃ janayatīti brūmaḥ, api tv asaddṛṣṭilakṣaṇāvidyāparipanthikṣaṇikanairātmyalakṣaṇasarvavastutattvabhāvanāsahitam | na ca vahnitvaṃ sarvavastutattvam, kiṃ tu kṣaṇikanairātmyam eveti kṣaṇabhaṅgaprasādhanataḥ pratipāditam iti | kiṃ ca svamanīṣāparikalpitaḥ khalv ayam anumitabhāvitavahniviṣayaviśadaḥ pratyayaḥ | na punar asya loke sambhavaḥ | tathā hi niṣprayojanam anunmatto na kaścid bhāvayati | prayojanaṃ ca śiśirabharamanthakāyakāṇḍasyāpi dāhādimātram eva, tac cānumitenaiva vahninā taddeśopasarpaṇāt sidhyati | anupasarpaṇe bhāvānāvaiyarthyam | purastāt tu bhāvite parisphurati tadathāpekṣayā bhrāntiḥ prāsarpakasyevetyādy upahāsyam apy asya kṣatātmano durnītipūtigavībhakṣaṇādhmātajaradgomāyor udgāra iva satām asahyaḥ |
children.translated_text: If one objects: 'If yogic cognition arises from meditation and the object even without a sense-faculty, then let non-discordant cognition of fire on a mountain arise from meditation and fire [alone]! And inconsistency is frequently observed' — [we reply:] No. When fire is directly produced [i.e., present],

children.text: yad api tato 'nantaramāśaṅkyārthasyālambanapratyayatvam indriyāpekṣitvena vyāptam iti prasādhitam, tatpūrvam eva pratyuktam | tathā bhāvanayās cetyādyāśaṅkyārthasyālambanapratyayatvam aśakyāvagamam iti yad uktaṃ tad apy asambaddham |
children.translated_text: As for the objection raised immediately after that — that 'the object's being an objective condition (<s>ālambanapratyaya</s>) is pervaded by dependence on a sense-faculty' — that was already answered before. And the further objection that begins with 'And of meditation...' — that 'the object's being an objective condition cannot be ascertained' —

children.text: cakṣurindriyasyāpy artham antareṇa dvicandrakeśoṇḍukādau viśadabhrāntajñanajananasāmarthyam upalabdham ity arthasahitam api kevalam eva samartham | ato ghaṭāder apy ālambanapratyayatvam aśakyāvagamam iti indriyapratyakṣam api pratihataṃ syād iti | tathāpi cālambanapratyayāpi ta eva yujyanta ityādir na punar vikalpanirmāṇapratibandhateti paryanto vyarthaḥ | asmābhir evaṃvidhasya prastute 'nabhyupagatatvāt | ata eva tasmād bhāvanāprakarśamātrajatvāt, arthāvyabhicāraniyamābhāvāt, viśadābham api saṃśayākrāntatvāt, apramāṇam apratyakṣaṃ ceti sāmpratam ity upasaṃhāro 'pi dhikkāraḥ | sarveṣām eva hetūnām asiddhatvāt | bhāvanābalajasyārthād apy utpatter indriyapratyakṣavat | sadarthaprakāśanaṃ buddheḥ svabhāva ityādy asmākam api manoharam | bhāvanāyāś ca sāmānyena sphuṭābhajñānahetutvaṃ sādhyate | pramāṇopannacaturāryasatyaviṣayaniṣṭhāyāṃ tu sāmarthyāt pratyakṣapramāṇahetutāpi sādhyate | ata eva kāminīpratibhāsasyāpramāṇatve 'py apratyakṣatve 'pi sphuṭābhatvasya sādhyadharmasāmānyasya sambhavāt na viruddho hetuḥ | nāpi dṛṣṭāntasya sādhyaśūnyateti | na ca nairātmyadṛṣṭiḥ sambhavadbādhā, arthād utpatter abhūtārthatvābhāvāt |
children.translated_text: even the visual sense-faculty, without an [external] object, is observed to have the capacity to produce vivid erroneous cognitions such as the double moon, floaters, and the like. Being capable even in conjunction with the object, it is also capable [of producing cognition] by itself alone. Therefore, even the status of pots and the like as objective conditions cannot be ascertained.

children.text: śrutānumitaviṣayaṃ pratyakṣaṃ na sambhavatīty apy ayuktam | āgamānumānayor dvividho viṣayaḥ grāhyo 'dhyavaseyaś ca | tatra grāhyaḥ svākāraḥ, adhyavaseyas tu pāramārthikavastusvalakṣaṇātmā | asya ca parokṣatve 'numānasāmagrīsambhave 'numānaviṣayatvam, pratyakṣasāmagrīsambhave ca krameṇa pratyakṣaviṣayatvaṃ dṛṣṭam eva | tat siddham ityādyupasaṃhāro 'pi paryākula eva | apramāṇatvād iti hetuś ca prathamo 'siddhaḥ | bhāvanābalajasyārthād apy utpatteḥ, pramāṇaśaktisambhavāt, indriyapratyakṣavat | bhāvanābalajatvād iti dvitīyas tu sandighavyatirekitvād anaikāntikaḥ | tathā yathānumitabhāvitavahniviṣayaviśadajñānam iti dṛṣṭānto 'py asambhavīti pratipāditam | bhavatu vā, tathāpi yogijñānasya tena saha tulyahetutvam asiddham | tad dhi pramāṇadṛṣṭavastubhāvanāmātrajam | yogijñānaṃ tv avidyāpratipakṣasarvavastutattvabhāvanāviṣayābhyām utpannam iti mahāntam api viśeṣam asau durmatiprapātapatito nāvagāhata ity upekṣaṇīyaḥ ||
children.translated_text: The claim that 'perception regarding objects that are heard or inferred is impossible' is also unjustified. For scripture (<s>āgama</s>) and inference have two types of objects: the apprehended (<s>grāhya</s>) and the determined (<s>adhyaveseya</s>). Of these, the apprehended is their own form (<s>svākāra</s>), and the determined is the unique particular (<s>svalakṣaṇa</s>) that is the ultimately real entity. And the latter —

children.text: nyāyaprakīrṇe tu mārgas tāvat pramāṇapariśuddho na bhavatīty uktaṃ yat, tat tatprasādhakapramāṇenaiva prayuktam |
children.translated_text: As for the statement in the <s>Nyāyaprakīrṇa</s> that 'the path, for the present, is not purified by a means of valid cognition' — that was formulated precisely with the means of valid cognition that establishes it.

children.text: yac cāpi cetyādy ārabhya yogijñānaṃ nirviṣayaṃ prasaktam ity uktam tatra keyaṃ nirviṣayatā nāma | kiṃ vikalpākāranivṛttau nirākāratā, arthākārād visadṛśākāratā, atha tadākāratve 'pi tadvastusaṃsparśitā |
children.translated_text: And as for the criticism beginning with 'and...' up to 'yogic cognition is established to be without an object' — what is this so-called 'objectlessness'? Does it mean: (1) absence of form upon the cessation of the form of conceptual construction (<s>vikalpa</s>)? Or (2) having a form dissimilar to the form of the object? Or (3) even while having that [object's] form, lacking contact with that real thing?

children.text: na tāvat prathamaḥ pakṣaḥ kṣamaḥ | jñānasya nirākāratānupapatteḥ |
children.translated_text: The first alternative is not tenable, because it is impossible for cognition to be without form (<s>nirākāra</s>).

children.text: nāpi dvitīyaḥ | kāminyādibhāvanāyās tadākārasyaiva viśadasya darśanāt |
children.translated_text: Nor the second, because in the meditation on a beloved woman and the like, the vivid [form] that appears is observed to be precisely that [object's] form.

children.text: na ca tṛtīyaḥ | arthasamarpitākārasaṃsparśam apāsyānyasyārthasaṃsparsasyāyogāt |
children.translated_text: Nor the third, because having rejected contact with the form bestowed by the object, it is impossible for there to be contact with an object in any other way.

children.text: tathā coktam:
children.translated_text: And it has been said:

children.text: arthena ghaṭayatyenām |
children.translated_text: '[Meditation] connects this [cognition] with the object' —

children.text: (PV III 305a)
ityādi
children.translated_text: and so on.

children.text: tayoś caikatvenādhyavasāyād bāhya eva pravṛttinivṛttī, vyāvahārikasya sphuṭībhāvo 'pi bahirabhimatasya paryante vikalpopādeyakṣaṇasyaiva sphuṭasyodayaḥ | tāvataiva sa viṣayas tena sākṣātkṛta iti vyavahāraḥ kevalam arthād apy utpattau | anyathā vyabhicārād aprāmāṇyam | na ca vikalpopadarśitam api rūpam avastu jñānātmakatvāt | anātmakatve prakāśāyogāt | tadbhāvanaiva cārthabhāvanā, tatsphuṭībhāva eva bāhyasphuṭībhāvaḥ, prakārāntareṇa bāhyasparśāyogāt | etena yat pāramārthikam ityādi na sarvajñasiddhir itiparyantaṃ prayuktam |
children.translated_text: And because both [the internal image and the external object] are determined as one, activity and cessation are directed to the external [object] alone. Even the pragmatic vividness [of cognition] — the clear arising of the particular moment that is to be apprehended by the conceptual construction imputed as external — [occurs] in the final analysis with respect to what is considered external. By just that much, that [external thing] is directly realized by it — such is the determination.

children.text: yac cāpi cetyādi na yuktaṃ paśyāma itiparyantena dūṣaṇam uktam, tad apy asaṅgatam | tathā hi yādṛśa eva bhāvyagrāhī pratyayaḥ prathamo niranvayo niruddhas tādṛśa evāpara utpadyata iti niyamaniścayakāraṇaṃ na kiñcid asti caṇḍadevatāsparśād anyat, kṣaṇikatvād iti cet | nanu kṣaṇikatvaṃ sthāyitayā virudhyate na visadṛśotpādena, tad dhi prācīnaṃ niranvayanirodhe yathā sadṛśakṣaṇāntaram ārabhate tathā svahetugatasāmarthyayogāt kāryotpādānumeyād yadi viśeṣaleśaviśiṣṭaṃ kṣaṇāntaram utpādayati, tadā na kācit kṣatiḥ | na hi bhavata iva bhāvasyāpi kṣaṇikatāyāṃ pradveṣo nāma | tasmān na kṣaṇikatvottaraviśiṣṭakṣaṇajanakatvayor virodha iti nāpārthako 'bhyāsaḥ |
children.translated_text: And as for the criticism beginning with 'and...' up to 'we do not see it to be justified' — that too is incoherent. For whatever kind of cognition first apprehends the object of meditation and ceases without remainder — another of exactly that kind arises. The ground for the certainty of this rule —

children.text: yac cedaṃ kiñcetyādinā kṣaṇikatve cittam avikṣiptam āveditam, tad apy asādhu | nairātmyāditattvaparāṅmukhasya sarvasyaiva vikṣiptatvāt | bhāvanābalena tattvasākṣātkāriṇaḥ samāhitatvāt | atha ca tattvasākṣātkriyālābhāt grāhakākārāvagrahasambhavāt ca vyāvahārikam api vikṣiptam asti cittam | yato mamaiva doṣakṣayo bhāvīti mārgāmyāsapravṛttir abhyāhateti | paramārthataḥ prāpyādīnām abhāve 'pi tatsaṃkalpasyaivānādyavidyāprabhāvitasya sarvatra pravartakatvāt | ata eva mārgasatyābhyāsāt siddhaḥ sarvajñaḥ |
children.translated_text: And the statement that 'the mind is shown to be undistracted with regard to momentariness' beginning with 'whatever...' — that too is unsound. Because everyone who is turned away from the reality of non-self (<s>nairātmya</s>) and the like is distracted in every respect. Because one who directly realizes reality through the power of meditation is concentrated (<s>samāhita</s>). And yet, [regarding] reality —

children.text: nyāyabhūṣaṇasyāpi yogācārāpekṣayā dūṣaṇam aprastutam | bahirarthābhyupagamenaiva sādhanaprakramāt | yac coktam tathāpy atītānāgataviṣayatvaṃ katham, na hy asataḥ kaścid ākāro 'stīti, tad etat prastāvān avagāhanaphalam | upayuktasarvajñādhikāreṇa hi sarvakṣaṇikanirātmakavastubhāvanopakṣepaḥ, na sarvasarvajñāpekṣayā | tato 'tītānāgatam apratīyamānam api na bādhakam | tāvataiva duḥkhanirodhasiddheḥ | parasmai ca kṣaṇikatvādiniṣṭhakasya deśanāvatārāt | na ca sarvasarvajñahastakatyāgaḥ | tathā hi caturāryasatyasākṣātkāraprāptau nirāvaraṇāntaḥkaraṇasya kāruṇyātiśayāt sarvākāraparārthaparatayā sakalagocaracāriṇi cetasi ciravirūḍhotsāhasya tādṛgupāyaviśeṣādhigamo bhavaṣyati, yam anutiṣṭhatas tadutpattim antareṇāpi devatādhipatyāt satyasvapnavat | pratiparamāṇusarvaviṣayaṃ yathā deśakālākārapratyavasthānukāri sphuṭataraṃ jñānam udiyāt, tadā na tāvad vastuvyabhicārakṛtaṃ visaṃvāditvam, vastūnām eva pratibhāsanāt | utpattisārūpyābhyāṃ vedyasthitir iti tu pṛthagjanāpekṣayā | yoginas tu sārūpyamātreṇaiva grahaṇam iti nyāyaḥ |
children.translated_text: The criticism directed at the <s>Nyāyabhūṣaṇa</s> from the standpoint of the <s>Yogācāra</s> is irrelevant, because the proof is formulated precisely on the basis of the acceptance of external objects (<s>bahirarthābhyupagama</s>). And as for the objection 'Even so, how can past and future [objects] be the domain? For a non-existent [thing] has no form' — that pertains to the occasion —

children.text: yad Vārttikam
children.translated_text: The <s>Vārttika</s> [says]:

children.text: aviśuddhadhiyaḥ prati |
children.translated_text: 'For those of impure intellect,

children.text: grāhyagrāhakacinteyam acintyā yogināṃ gatiḥ || iti |
(PV III 532)

children.translated_text: this investigation of the apprehended and the apprehender [is intended]; the course of the <s>yogins</s> is inconceivable.'

children.text: tad evaṃ bhāvibhūtayor ajanakayor api yogijñāne sphuraṇam abādhyam | bhāvibhūtayos tarhi yadi svarūpasya sphuraṇam, vartamānataiva syāt | atha svarūpam asannihitaṃ jñānam eva tadākāram iti nirālambanaṃ niyamena | tad api nāsti | yasmād asannihite 'py arthe bhāvanābalāt taddeśakālākārānukāri vijñānaṃ katham anālambanam | tathātvenādhyavasāyāc ca, adhyavasitakālaviśiṣṭasyaiva satyasvapnavat tasya prāpteḥ |
children.translated_text: Thus, the appearance of future and past [objects] — which are not [present] causes — in yogic cognition is uncontradicted. [Objection:] If it is the intrinsic nature (<s>svarūpa</s>) of past and future [objects] that appears, then they would have to be present. [Reply:] Alternatively, [if one says that] the intrinsic nature is not proximate, and that cognition itself assumes that form, then it is necessarily without an object-support (<s>nirālambana</s>) — that too is not the case. For how can a cognition that, through the power of meditation (<s>bhāvanā</s>), conforms to the spatial, temporal, and formal characteristics of the object — even when the object is not proximate — be without an object-support? And because of determination (<s>adhyavasāya</s>) as being of that nature, the [cognition] pertains to [the object] as qualified by the determined time, like [experience in] dream and waking.

children.text: yad
Bhāṣyam
children.translated_text: the <s>Bhāṣya</s> (Commentary):
As stated in

children.text: yathā sa dṛṣṭaḥ śaradādikālayuktas tathā tasya na bādhitatvam |
children.translated_text: 'Just as he was seen conjoined with the autumn and other seasons, so there is no contradiction of that [cognition].

children.text: tatkālayuktas tu na tena dṛṣṭas tathāpratītāv api nāsti doṣaḥ ||
(PVA II 615)

children.translated_text: But as conjoined with that [present] time he was not seen by him — even in the absence of such [present] apprehension, there is no fault.'

children.text: jñānamātrasya tu tattvataḥ sphuraṇāc ca na vartamānatāprasaṅgaḥ saṅgataḥ | tathā kṣaṇikatvapakṣe 'pi ekatvādhyāropasāmarthyān na vyavahārikaṃ prati pramāṇasya kācit kṣatir iti śāstre prapañcitam |
children.translated_text: And because in reality it is mere cognition (<s>jñānamātra</s>) that manifests, there is no valid objection that [past and future objects] would have to be present. Similarly, even in the thesis of momentariness (<s>kṣaṇikatva</s>), owing to the capacity to superimpose unity, no harm is done to valid cognition with respect to conventional reality — as has been elaborated in the treatises.

children.text: yad api kiñ cedam api vaktum ucitam ityādy ārabhya bhāvanābalajasyānumānapūrvakatve 'pi pratyakṣapūrvakatve 'pi vyabhicārābhidhānam, tadarthād api bhāvanābalajasya sākṣādutpattisvīkārād apahastitam | yathendriyajasyāpi dvicandrādijñānasyārthād anutpatter aprāmāṇyam, arthendriyābhyām utpattau tu prāmāṇyam evaṃ pramāṇapūrvakasyāpi bhāvanāmātrād utpannasyāprāmāṇyam, bhāvanārthābhyām utpannasya tu prāmāṇyam |
children.translated_text: As for the statement of deviation [of meditation-born cognition], beginning with 'Is it also appropriate to say this...' and so forth, regarding both cases where meditation-born [cognition] is preceded by inference and where it is preceded by perception — that too is removed by the acceptance of the direct arising of meditation-born [cognition] from the object itself. Just as sense-born cognition of two moons and the like is not a valid means of knowledge because it does not arise from the [actual] object, but is a valid means of knowledge when it arises from both the object and the sense-organ; so too, cognition preceded by a valid means of knowledge, when produced merely from meditation, is not a valid means of knowledge, but when produced from both meditation and the object, it is a valid means of knowledge.

children.text: yadi yogijñānasyārthād utpattiḥ, pramāṇapūrvakatvāpekṣayā na kiñcit prayojanam iti cet | na | deśakālavastuviśeṣam apāsya sāmāneyana sarvadikkālavartivastumātraṃ kṣaṇikanirātmakam ity aniścaye mahāprayāsasādhyapuruṣāyuṣavyāpinyāṃ bhāvanāyām eva pravṛtter abhāvāt | na ca hāliko havyāśanam anumāya sphuṭīkaroti yena pratyakṣāntaratvaprasaṅgaḥ | asāmarthyavaiyarthyābhyāṃ tadasambhavapratipādanāt |
children.translated_text: [Objection:] If yogic cognition arises from the object, there is no purpose in it being preceded by a valid means of knowledge. [Reply:] No, because without the ascertainment — through a general cognition that sets aside particular details of place, time, and objects — that 'the totality of things existing in all directions and times is momentary and selfless,' there would be no engagement in meditation, which requires great effort extending over one's entire life. Nor does a plowman, having inferred fire, make it vivid [through meditation], so that the objection of [yogic cognition] becoming another kind of perception would arise — since its impossibility has been demonstrated on the grounds of incapacity and purposelessness.

children.text: yad apy uktaṃ yogino jñānam indriyajñanād abhinnaṃ bhinnaṃ vā | tatra prathamapakṣe tāvan na vastudoṣaḥ | tādṛkpuruṣaviśeṣasya siddhatvāt | vyavasthādūṣaṇam api nāsti | sādhyatayaiva tādṛgdaśāviśeṣasya lokātikrāntātiśayasya paramapuruṣārtharūpasya sādhanaviśeṣapratipādanāya pṛthagjanasādhāraṇendriyajñānād bhedena nirdeśāt | paramapuruṣārthaviṣayatvābhāvād eva ca rasāyanādisaṃskārajasyāpi jñānasya na pratyakṣāntaratā | bhedapakṣe 'pi na tāvat sthairyetarasphuraṇakṛtopālambhasambhavaḥ | indriyajñānenāpi vastu sarvātmanā gṛhṇatā truṭyadrūpasyaiva grahaṇāt | adhyavasāyo hi pūrvaṃ durllabhaḥ idānīṃ tu bhāvanābalanirdalitāvidye cittasantāne so 'pīndriyajñānena janyata iti viśeṣaḥ |
children.translated_text: As for the objection that yogic cognition is either identical with or different from sense-cognition: in the first alternative, there is no defect in the thing itself, since the existence of such an extraordinary person is established. Nor is there a fault in the [apparent] inconsistency of classification, because it is distinguished from the sense-cognition common to ordinary persons precisely for the purpose of demonstrating the special means of attainment, since [yogic cognition] is a particular stage that transcends the ordinary and constitutes the supreme goal of human existence (<s>paramapuruṣārtha</s>). And precisely because it does not pertain to the supreme goal of human existence, cognition born from the refinement [of sense-organs] through elixirs (<s>rasāyana</s>) and the like is also not a separate kind of perception. In the alternative of difference, too, there is no possibility of the objection based on the appearance of stability or otherwise, since even sense-cognition, when grasping the object in its entirety, grasps only what is momentary in form. The determination (<s>adhyavasāya</s>) [of objects] is indeed difficult to achieve previously, but now, in a mental continuum whose ignorance (<s>avidyā</s>) has been shattered by the power of meditation, even that [determination] is produced by sense-cognition — this is the [only] difference.

children.text: nanu yogino manovijñānendriyajñānābhyāṃ paśyata ākāradvayasphuraṇaprasaṅga iti cet | satyam | satyajñānākāras tāvad vastuno na bhinnadeśo 'nyatarabhrāntiprasaṅgāt | atas tāv ākārāv apratimau kayā gatyā sphurata iti ko nirṇetuṃ kṣamaḥ | yad āha: acintyā yogināṃ gatir iti |
(PV III 530d)

children.translated_text: [Objection:] For the yogin who perceives through both mental cognition (<s>manovijñāna</s>) and sense-cognition, there would be the absurd consequence of two cognitive aspects appearing simultaneously. [Reply:] True. But the aspect of a true cognition is not in a different location from the object — otherwise there would be the absurd consequence that one of them is erroneous. Therefore, by what means those two aspects — which are incomparable — manifest, who is capable of determining? As it is said: 'The ways of <s>yogins</s> are inconceivable.'

children.text: sarvathā tu na yogijñānasya kṣatir iti siddham | tad evaṃ kāraṇānupalambhād api na sarvajñatābhāvaḥ |
children.translated_text: In every respect, therefore, no harm comes to yogic cognition — this is established. Thus, even from the non-apprehension of a [valid] counter-reason, the non-existence of omniscience (<s>sarvajñatā</s>) does not follow.

children.text: nanu yadi nāma yuṣmadabhimatasyānumānasya na bādhakam, tathāpy asaty evānumānaṃ bādhakam | tathā hi śakyam idam abhidhātum
children.translated_text: [Objection:] Even if there is no defeater for the inference you accept, nevertheless, an inference that it [omniscience] does not exist would be a defeater. For the following can be stated:

children.text: sugato 'sarvajñaḥ | jñeyatvāt, prameyatvāt, sattvāt, puruṣatvāt, vakṛtvāt, idriyādimattvād ityādi | rathyāpuruṣavat |
children.translated_text: The <s>Sugata</s> (Buddha) is not omniscient, because of being an object of knowledge (<s>jñeya</s>), because of being provable (<s>prameya</s>), because of existing (<s>sat</s>), because of being a person (<s>puruṣa</s>), because of being a speaker (<s>vaktṛ</s>), because of possessing sense-organs and the like — like a man in the street.

children.text: tathā ca Bṛhaṭṭīkā
children.translated_text: And so the <s>Bṛhaṭṭīkā</s> [states]:

children.text: yasya jñeyaprameyatvavastusattvādilakṣaṇāḥ |
children.translated_text: He for whom logical reasons such as being an object of knowledge, being provable, being an entity, existing, and the like

children.text: nihantuṃ hetavaḥ śaktāḥ ko nu taṃ kalpayiṣyati ||
children.translated_text: are capable of defeating [his omniscience] — who would postulate such a one [as omniscient]?

children.text: Kārikāpi
children.translated_text: The <s>Kārikā</s> (Verse) also [states]:

children.text: pratyakṣādyavisaṃvādi prameyatvādi yasya ca |
children.translated_text: He whose attributes such as being provable, which are not contradicted by perception and the like,

children.text: sadbhāvavāraṇe śaktaṃ ko nu taṃ kalpayiṣyati |
(ŚV II 132)

children.translated_text: are capable of preventing his existence [as omniscient] — who would postulate such a one?

children.text: atrocyate | kim ete jñeyatvādayaḥ sarvajñatvena sākṣād viruddhāḥ paramparayā vā | aviruddhavidhāne pratiṣedhāyogāt | sa ca sākṣād virodhaḥ parasparaparihārasthitilakṣaṇo vā, bhāvābhāvavat, sahānavasthānalakṣaṇo vā, dahanatuhinavad iti |
children.translated_text: To this we reply: Are these properties such as being an object of knowledge and the like directly contradictory to omniscience, or indirectly? For there is no logical basis for negation when there is no contradiction. And that direct contradiction is either defined as consisting in mutual exclusion of existence, like being and non-being, or defined as the impossibility of co-existence, like fire and frost.

children.text: na tāvad ādyaḥ pakṣaḥ | yad vyavacchedanāntarīyako yasya paricchedas tayor eva parasparaparihārasthitilakṣaṇo virodhaḥ | na ca jñeyatvādi sarvajñatvavyavacchedena sthitam | kiṃ tarhi | ajñeyatvādivyacacchedena | tathā sarvajñatvam asarvajñatvavyavacchedena, na tu jñeyatvavyavacchedena |
children.translated_text: The first alternative does not hold. For mutual exclusion of existence is the contradiction between that whose determination is inseparable from the exclusion of the other. But being an object of knowledge and the like are not established through the exclusion of omniscience; rather, they are established through the exclusion of not being an object of knowledge and so forth. Similarly, omniscience is established through the exclusion of non-omniscience, not through the exclusion of being an object of knowledge.

children.text: nāpi dvitīyo virodhaḥ | yasya hy avikalakāraṇasya bhavato yat sannidhānād abhāvas tayor eva sahānavasthānalakṣaṇo virodhaḥ | na ca sarvajñatvaṃ prāk pravṛttam avikalakāraṇaṃ dṛṣṭaṃ yena paścāj jñeyatvādisadbhāve nirvartata iti syāt | tathātve sati deśādiniṣedha eva bhaven na tu sarvathoccheda iti |
children.translated_text: Nor does the second type of contradiction [hold]. For the impossibility of co-existence is the contradiction between something that, having its complete set of causes, ceases to exist in the presence of another. But omniscience, previously operative and with complete causes, has never been observed [to cease] such that, upon the subsequent presence of the property of being an object of knowledge and so forth, it would cease. And even if that were the case, it would only amount to a negation with respect to a particular place and time, not to absolute annihilation.

children.text: na ca paramparayā virodhaḥ | sa hi bhavan niṣedhyasya sarvajñatvasya vyāpakaviruddhatvāt, kāraṇaviruddhatvāt, kāryaviruddhatvāt, svabhāvaviruddhakāryatvāt, vyāpakaviruddhakāryatvāt, kāraṇaviruddhakāryatvāt, kāryaviruddhakāryatvāt, svabhāvaviruddhavyāptatvāt, vyāpakaviruddhavyāptatvāt, kāraṇaviruddhavyāptatvāt, kāryaviruddhavyāptatvād vā bhavet | tatra sarvajñatvasyāsattvāt, vyāpakakāraṇakāryāṇām asiddhes tadviruddhakāryavyāpyābhāvāt na prameyatvādayaḥ sarvajñatvena paramparayāpi viruddhāḥ |
children.translated_text: Nor is there indirect contradiction. For such [indirect contradiction] with respect to the omniscience to be negated would have to be either through being contradictory to its pervader (<s>vyāpaka</s>), contradictory to its cause (<s>kāraṇa</s>), contradictory to its effect (<s>kārya</s>), being an effect of what is contradictory to its nature (<s>svabhāva</s>), being an effect of what is contradictory to its pervader, being an effect of what is contradictory to its cause, being an effect of what is contradictory to its effect, being pervaded by what is contradictory to its nature, being pervaded by what is contradictory to its pervader, being pervaded by what is contradictory to its cause, or being pervaded by what is contradictory to its effect. In this case, since the pervader, cause, and effect of omniscience are themselves unestablished — and since the effects pervaded by what contradicts them are also absent — properties such as being provable are not even indirectly contradictory to omniscience.

children.text: nanu vaktṛtvaṃ virudhyata eva sarvaviṣayanirvikalpajñānaviruddhavikalpakāryatvād vaktṛtvasya | naitad yuktam | savikalpāvikalpayor yugapadavṛtter vikalpatvena sarvajñasyāvirodhāt |
children.translated_text: [Objection:] But being a speaker (<s>vaktṛtva</s>) is indeed contradictory [to omniscience], because being a speaker is an effect of conceptual thought (<s>vikalpa</s>), which is contradictory to non-conceptual cognition of all objects. [Reply:] This is not correct, because conceptual and non-conceptual [cognitions] do not occur simultaneously, and being a conceptualizer does not contradict the omniscient one.

children.text: kas tarhi pṛthagjanād asya bheda iti cet | ucyate | yathā māyākāro nirmitāśvādiviṣayaṃ vijñānaṃ nirviṣayatvena niścinvannabhrāntaḥ, tadanyasmāc ca śreṣṭhaḥ, tathā bhagavān api śuddhalaukikavikalpasammukhībhāve 'pi na bhrānto nāpi pṛthagjanasamāna iti | tataś ca nirvikalpakasarvajñajñānavikalpayor virodhābhāvād vaktṛtvaṃ sarvajñatvena sahāviruddham eva ||
children.translated_text: [Objection:] Then what is his difference from an ordinary person? [Reply:] We say: Just as a magician, while ascertaining that his cognition of conjured horses and the like has no real object, is not deluded and is superior to others [who are deceived], so too the Blessed One, even when confronted by pure worldly conceptual thought (<s>śuddhalaukikavikalpa</s>), is neither deluded nor equal to ordinary persons. Therefore, since there is no contradiction between non-conceptual omniscient cognition and conceptual thought, being a speaker is entirely non-contradictory with omniscience.

children.text: etenaid api nirastam yad āha kāśikākāraḥ, samādher vyutthāyopadekṣyata iti cet | na | vyutthitasya hy abhilāpinī pratītir bhrāntabhāṣitam apramāṇaṃ bhaved iti ||
children.translated_text: By this, the following statement of the author of the <s>Kāśikā</s> is also refuted: 'If [one says that] he will teach after arising from <s>samādhi</s> (meditative absorption) — no, because for one who has arisen [from samādhi], the verbal cognition would be erroneous speech, not a valid means of knowledge.'

children.text: yad apy uktaṃ Bṛhaṭṭīkāyām
children.translated_text: As for what is stated in the <s>Bṛhaṭṭīkā</s>:

children.text: yadā copadiśedekaṃ kiñcit sāmānyavaktṛvat |
children.translated_text: 'When he would teach one particular thing, like any ordinary speaker,

children.text: ekadeśajñagītaṃ tan na syāt sarvajñabhāṣitam ||
children.translated_text: that would be the utterance of one who knows only a part, not the speech of an omniscient one' —

children.text: tad api nirastam, vikalpenaikasya kasyacid āmukhīkṛtvopadeśe 'pi nirvikalpena sarvam avabudhyamānasya vacanānāṃ sarvajñabhāṣitatvād eva ||
children.translated_text: that too is refuted, because even when he brings forward and teaches one particular thing through conceptual thought, since he comprehends everything through non-conceptual [cognition], his words are indeed the speech of an omniscient one.

children.text: yat punaḥ Kārikāyām uktam
children.translated_text: Furthermore, what is stated in the <s>Kārikā</s>:

children.text: sānnidhyamātratas tasya puṃsaś cintāmaṇer iva |
children.translated_text: 'By his mere presence, like a wish-fulfilling gem,

children.text: niścaranti yathākāmāṃ kuḍyādibhyo 'pi deśanāḥ ||
children.translated_text: teachings issue forth at will, even from walls and the like' —

children.text: evam ādyucyamānaṃ hi śraddadhānasya śobhate |
children.translated_text: what is thus stated is pleasing to one who has faith;

children.text: kuḍyādiniḥsṛtatvāt tu nāśvāso deśanāsu naḥ ||
children.translated_text: but because [the teachings] issue from walls and the like, we have no confidence in [those] teachings.

children.text: kin nu buddhapraṇītāḥ syuḥ kiṃ vā kaiścid durātmabhiḥ |
children.translated_text: Are they perhaps composed by the <s>Buddha</s>, or rather uttered by some evil beings,

children.text: adṛśyair vipralambhārthaṃ piśācādibhir īritāḥ ||
children.translated_text: invisible ones such as <s>piśācas</s> (ghouls) and the like, for the purpose of deception?

children.text: Bṛhaṭṭīkāyām api
children.translated_text: In the <s>Bṛhaṭṭīkā</s> also:

children.text: tasmin dhyānasamādhisthe cintāratnavadāsthite |
children.translated_text: 'When he abides in meditative absorption (<s>dhyānasamādhi</s>), established like a wish-fulfilling gem,

children.text: niścaranti yathākāmaṃ kuḍyādibhyo 'pi deśanāḥ ||
children.translated_text: teachings issue forth at will, even from walls and the like.

children.text: tābhir jijñāsitān arthān sarvān jānanti mānavāḥ |
children.translated_text: Through those [teachings], people come to know all the matters they wished to inquire about,

children.text: hitāni ca yathāyogaṃ kṣipramāsādayanti te ||
children.translated_text: and they quickly obtain beneficial things as appropriate.'

children.text: ityādi kīrtamānaṃ tu śraddadhānasya śobhate |
children.translated_text: What is thus proclaimed is pleasing to one who has faith;

children.text: vayam aśraddadhānās tu ye yuktīr arthayāmahe ||
children.translated_text: but we who lack faith seek rational arguments.

children.text: kuḍyādiniḥsṛtānāṃ ca na syād āptopadiṣṭatā |
children.translated_text: And those [teachings] that issue from walls and the like would not have the status of being taught by a trustworthy person (<s>āpta</s>),

children.text: viśvāsaś ca na tāsu syāt kenaitāḥ kīrtitā iti ||
children.translated_text: and there would be no confidence in them — by whom were they uttered?

children.text: kin nu buddhapraṇītāḥ syuḥ kiṃ vā brāhmaṇavañcakaiḥ |
children.translated_text: Are they perhaps composed by the <s>Buddha</s>, or taught by <s>Brāhmaṇa</s>-deceivers

children.text: krīḍadbhir upadiṣṭāḥ syur dūrasthapratiśabdakaiḥ ||
children.translated_text: playing [tricks], or by those who produce echoes from a distance?

children.text: kiṃ vā kṣudrapiśācādyair adṛṣṭaiḥ parikalpitāḥ |
children.translated_text: Or perhaps fabricated by petty ghosts (<s>piśācas</s>) and the like, who are invisible?

children.text: tasamān na tāsu viśvāsaḥ kartavyaḥ prājñamānibhiḥ ||
children.translated_text: Therefore, those who consider themselves wise should place no confidence in them.

children.text: etad apy anabhyupagamenaiva nirastam | śuddhalaukikavikalpasaṃmukhībhāvenaiva tasya deśakatvābhyupagamād iti ||
children.translated_text: This too is refuted simply by not accepting [that premise], since we accept that his teaching occurs precisely through the confrontation with pure worldly conceptual thought.

children.text: atha vā yathā cakrasyoparate 'pi daṇḍapreraṇāvyāpāre pūrvāvegavaśād bhramaṇam | evaṃ bhagavati pratyastamitasamastavikalpajāle 'pi sthite yadi pūrvapraṇidhānāhitasatatānābhogavāhinī deśanā syāt tadā ko virodhaḥ | vivakṣābhāve kathaṃ vacanapravṛttir iti na vaktavyam | tadabhāve 'pi nidrāṇasya tattatpravyaktavacanasandarśanāt | vacanamātrasya vivakṣayā vyāpter abhāvāt | tasmād yathā pūrvābhyāsato jhaṭiti prabodhitasyāriṇā prahārādidānenānurūpa eva prakramaḥ śastroddharaṇādikaḥ, tathā sarvavedino 'pi sakalāḥ kalāḥ ity anākulam |
children.translated_text: Alternatively, just as a wheel, even after the activity of being propelled by the stick has ceased, continues to revolve due to its prior momentum — so too, even when the Blessed One abides with the entire net of conceptual thought having subsided, if there is a spontaneously flowing teaching (<s>deśanā</s>), effortless and continuous, deposited by his prior resolve (<s>praṇidhāna</s>), what contradiction is there? One should not object that 'without the intention to speak, how can speech occur?' — because even in the case of a sleeping person, clearly articulated words of various kinds are observed, and speech as such is not pervaded by [the requirement of] an intention to speak. Therefore, just as one who has been suddenly awakened by an enemy, through prior practice, immediately engages in the appropriate procedure of drawing weapons and the like for delivering blows, so too, even for the all-knowing one, all skills [proceed] — without confusion.

children.text: yad āhālaṅkāraḥ
children.translated_text: As the <s>Alaṅkāra</s> [treatise] states:

children.text: śatrusānnidhyamātreṇa pravartante 'vikalpataḥ |
children.translated_text: 'By the mere proximity of an enemy, there arise without conceptual thought

children.text: prāg eva tannirākāriprakramāḥ kopanirmitāḥ ||
(PVA III 275)

children.translated_text: the procedures for repelling him, fashioned by [prior] anger.'

children.text: yat punar uktam: piśācādikṛtaśaṅkayā nātrāśvāsaḥ satāṃ yukta iti |
children.translated_text: As for the further objection: 'Due to the suspicion of [teachings being produced by] ghosts (<s>piśācas</s>) and the like, confidence in them would not be appropriate for good people' —

children.text: tad asaṅgatam, yataḥ
