children.translated_text: 'Because they are effects.'

children.text: yad yat kāryaṃ tat tad upādānādyabhijñakartṛkam | yathā prāsādādi |
children.translated_text: 'Whatever is an effect has a maker who knows the material cause and the rest — like a palace and the like.'

children.text: tathā ca vivādādhyāsitās tanvādayaḥ |
children.translated_text: 'And bodies and the like, which are the subject of dispute, are such.'

children.text: tasmāt tatheti |
children.translated_text: 'Therefore they are thus.'

children.text: evaṃ sthitvā sthitvā pravṛttidharmakatvāt, sanniveśavattvāt, arthakriyākāritvād ityādayo hetavaḥ kathitapañcāvayavakrameṇa boddhavyā iti |
children.translated_text: Having taken this position, [other] reasons too — such as 'because of possessing the property of being at rest and then being active,' 'because of possessing arrangement,' 'because of producing purposeful action' — are stated in the stated five-membered syllogistic format.

children.text: tad etad durmativispanditaṃ jagadandhīkaraṇaṃ na satām upekṣitum ucitam iti kiñcid ucyate | iha khalu buddhimatkāryamātrayoḥ sādhyasādhanayoḥ sarvopasaṃhāravatī vyāptis tāvad avaśyaṃ grahītavyā | anyathā gamyagamakabhāvāyogāt | sā ca gṛhyamāṇā kiṃ kāraṇakāryamātrayor iva viparyayabā

dhakapramāṇabalāt grāhyā | yad vā 'gnidhūmayor iva viśiṣṭānvayavyatirekagrahaṇapravaṇaviśiṣṭapratyakṣānupalambhābhyāṃ boddhavyā | uta svavyavasthayā sapakṣāsapakṣayor bhūyor darśanādarśanābhyāṃ pratyetavyā | āhosvit sapakṣāsapakṣayoḥ sakṛddarśanābhyāṃ jñātavyeti catvāro vikalpāḥ |
children.translated_text: [the pervasion between] intelligence and [effect-hood can be grasped].

This display of bad reasoning, which blinds the world, is not fitting for the wise to ignore — therefore something is said. Here indeed, [in the argument from] effect-hood in general to an intelligent [maker], the pervasion is to be grasped either through the force of a defeating means of valid cognition. Or, just as between fire and smoke, through perceptual non-apprehension conducive to grasping the specific positive and negative concomitance,

children.text: na tāvad ādyaḥ pakṣaḥ, sādhyaviparyaye buddhimadabhāve kāryatvasāmānyasya sādhanasya bādhakapramāṇābhāvāt. nanu bādhakapramāṇā
bhāvo 'siddhaḥ
children.translated_text: is unestablished.

children.text: . tathā hīdaṃ kāryatvaṃ yathā buddhimatā vyāptam iṣyate tathā deśakālasvabhāvaniyatatvenāpi, kadācikakāraṇasannidhimattayāpi, sāmagrīkāryatvenāpi vyāptam upalabdham | sa ca deśādiniyamaḥ kādācitkakāraṇasanndhiḥ sāmagrī vā buddhimatpūrvikā siddhā | yadi punar acetanāni cetanānadhiṣṭhatāni kāryaṃ kuryuḥ tato yatra kvacanāvasthitāni janayeyur iti na deśakālasvabhāvaniyataprasavaṃ kāryam upalabhyeta |
children.translated_text: For this effect-hood, just as it is accepted as pervaded by an intelligent [being], so too it is [pervaded] by being determined by place, time, and nature; and mere proximity to occasional causes

The first alternative is not [valid], because there is no defeating means of valid cognition (badhaka-pramana) for the reason 'effect-hood in general' when the provable property is contradicted — i.e., in the absence of an intelligent [being]. Objection: The absence of a defeating means of valid cognition

children.text: hetusamavadhānajanmatayā na kāryaṃ pratyekaṃ kāraṇair janyata iti cet | samavadhānam eva tu kāraṇānāṃ kutaḥ | kādācitkaparipākādadṛṣṭaviśeṣād iti cet | nanv ayam acetanaḥ kathaṃ yathāvat kāraṇāni sannidhāpayet | no khalu kvacid avasthitāni daṇḍādīni vinā kumbhakāraprayatnam adṛṣṭaviśeṣavaśād eva parasparaṃ sannidhīyante | sannihitāni vā kāryāya prabhavantīti buddhimatā deśakālasvabhāvaniyamasya kādācitkakāraṇasannidheḥ sāmagryāś ca vyāptisiddhiḥ | buddhimadabhāve caiṣāṃ vyāpakānāṃ nivṛttau nivartamānaṃ kāryatvaṃ buddhimatpūrvakatvena vyāpyata iti pratibandhasiddhaye vyāpakā
nupalambhatrayam upanyastam |
children.translated_text: a threefold non-apprehension has been presented.

children.text: tathā na
children.translated_text: Likewise, it is not

children.text: kāryaṃ buddhimatparityāgād ahetukam eva bhavatīti sambhāvyam, deśakālasvabhavaniyamābhāvaprasaṅgāt | nāpi buddhimato 'nyasmād eva bhavatīti śaṅkanīyam, sakṛd apy utpādābhāvaprasaṅgāt | na cānyasmād asmād api bhavatīti sambhāvyam, aniyatahetutve 'hetutvaprasaṅgāt | tathā buddhimantam antareṇāce
children.translated_text: to be supposed that the effect, upon the abandonment of an intelligent [being], would be simply causeless — because there would follow the absurd consequence of the absence of determination by place, time, and nature. Nor is [it to be supposed that] from another [cause] other than an intelligent [being]

children.text: tanena karaṇe sarvadā kriyāyā avirāmaprasaṅgaś cety api viparyayabādhakam atiprasaṅgacatuṣṭayaṃ vyāptiprasādhakam iti | kāryatvasya hetupūrvakatvam iva buddhimatpūrvakatvam apy avāryam iti cet |
children.translated_text: Therefore, with respect to the instrument [of production], there would also be the absurd consequence of the ceaseless continuity of activity at all times — thus, these four overextensions as counter-proofs and the three proofs of pervasion [are presented]. [Objection:] Just as being an effect is necessarily preceded by a cause, so too being preceded by an intelligent [agent] cannot be prevented.

[is sufficient]. If it be said: 'An effect is not produced by each cause individually, because [it requires] an assemblage of causes' — then whence comes the assemblage of causes itself? From the fact of being occasional,

children.text: atrocyate | sidhyaty evedaṃ manorājyaṃ yadi deśakālasvabhāvaniyamasya kādācitkakāraṇasannidheḥ samagryāś ca buddhimatpūrvakatvena vyāptiḥ sidhyati | kevalam etad eva durāpam | buddhimadabhāve 'pi hi svahetubalasamutpannasannidheḥ pratiniyatadeśakālaśaktinācetanenāpi sāmagrīlakṣaṇakāraṇaviśeṣeṇa kriyamāṇāni deśakālasvabhāvaniyamakādcitkakāraṇasannidhisāmagrīkāryatvāni yujyanta iti sandigdhāsiddhā vyāpakānupalabdhayaḥ ||
children.translated_text: To this we reply: This castle in the air would succeed if the pervasion were established, namely that the restriction of place, time, and nature, occasional causal proximity, and the aggregate [of conditions] are pervaded by being preceded by an intelligent [agent]. But this alone is difficult to achieve. For even in the absence of an intelligent [agent], a proximity that has arisen through the force of its own causes, through a non-sentient entity possessing specific powers restricted to particular places and times, also as a particular causal aggregate, can produce the properties of restriction of place, time, and nature, occasional causal proximity, and aggregation — therefore, the [three] non-apprehensions of the pervader are of doubtful establishment (<s>sandigdhāsiddha</s>).

children.text: buddhimadabhāve samavadhānam eva kuta iti cet | tad api cetanānadhiṣṭhitayathoktācetanasāmagrīviśeṣād eva | so 'pi tādṛśād ity anādyacetanasāmagrīparamparāto 'pi deśādiniyamasambhāvanāyāṃ nāvaśyaṃ buddhimadapekṣā | ghaṭāder deśakālasvabhāvaniyamaḥ kādācitkakāraṇasannidhiś ca, sāmagrī ca buddhimatpūrvikā dṛṣṭā ity aparopi deśakālasvabhāvaniyamādis tathaiveti cet | yady evaṃ ghaṭādikam api kāryaṃ bahuśo buddhimatpūrvakam upalabdham iti sarvam eva kāryaṃ tathāstu, kim anena vyāpakānupalambhopanyāsadurvyasanena | ghaṭāder bahuśo buddhimatpūrvakatvadarśane 'pi na sarvatra kāryamātrasya tathābhāvaniścayaś cet | deśādiniyamādīnām apīdaṃ samānam iti katham atrāpi śaṅkāvyudāsaḥ ||
children.translated_text: [Objection:] In the absence of an intelligent being, whence does the coordination [of causal factors] come? [Reply:] That too [comes] from just such a particular non-sentient aggregate as described, not governed by a conscious being. And that too [comes] from such [a non-sentient aggregate], and so, given the conceivability of the restriction of place and the like even from a beginningless succession of non-sentient aggregates, dependence on an intelligent being is not necessary. [Objection:] The restriction of place, time, and nature of pots and the like, their occasional causal proximity, and their aggregate are observed to be preceded by an intelligent being; therefore, other instances of restriction of place, time, and nature are likewise. [Reply:] If so, pots and the like, being observed as effects preceded by an intelligent being in many cases, let all effects be so — what need is there for this perverse insistence on presenting the non-apprehension of the pervader? And if, even when being preceded by an intelligent being is observed in many cases for pots and the like, there is no certainty that all effects are so, then the same applies to restriction of place and the like — so how is the doubt dispelled in this case either?

children.text: astu tadā pratyakṣam eva sarvatra vyāptigrāhakam iti cet | na tarhi viparyayabādhakapramāṇabalād vyāptigrahanirvāhaḥ | pratyakṣaṃ ca tatrāśaktam iti dvitīyavikalpāvasare nivedayiṣyate |
tathāsiddhe
children.translated_text: When it [the pervasion] is thus unestablished,

children.text: kāryakāraṇabhāve dhūmasyāhetukotpattāv anyasmād evotpattāv anyasmād apy utpattau sambhāvyamānāyāṃ
children.translated_text: with respect to the causal relation of smoke [and fire], when causeless origination of smoke, or origination from something else, or [the possibility of] origination from yet another [factor] is entertained,

children.text: deśādiniyamābhāvasakṛdutpādābhāvāhetutvaprasaṅgāḥ
children.translated_text: the absurd consequences of absence of restriction of place and the like, absence of single occurrence, and causelessness

children.text: saṅgacchante | prastute tu buddhimatkāryamātrayoḥ kāryakāraṇabhāvo nādyāpi siddhaḥ | sādhayituṃ vā śakyaḥ | na cācetanasya kartṛtve kriyāyā
children.translated_text: follow. But in the present case, the causal relation between an intelligent being and mere effecthood has not yet been established, nor can it be established. Nor does the absurd consequence of ceaseless activity

children.text: avirāmaprasaṅgaḥ saṅgataḥ | na hy acetanam ity eva sarvadā sāmarthyayogi, tasyāpi svahetuparamparāpratibaddhasāmarthyatvād ity acetanakāraṇaviśeṣaparamparāsambhāvanāyāṃ nāvaśyaṃ buddhimadākṣepa iti svamatavyālopaviklavavikrośitamātram evedaṃ na punar atra nyāyagandho 'pi |
children.translated_text: follow in the case of a non-sentient agent. For it is not the case that simply because something is non-sentient it always possesses the capacity [to produce]; since even that [non-sentient entity's] capacity is dependent on its own chain of causes. Therefore, given the conceivability of a succession of specific non-sentient causes, dependence on an intelligent being is not necessary — and so this is merely the panicked outcry of one who sees his own position undermined, not even a trace of valid reasoning.

[Objection:] Then let perception alone be the means of ascertaining pervasion everywhere. [Reply:] In that case, there is no establishing of pervasion through the force of counter-proof reasoning. And perception is incapable of doing so — this will be explained at the occasion of the second alternative.

children.text: tad evaṃ vyāptisādhanārtham upanyastaṃ vyāpakānupalambhatrayaṃ sandigdhāsiddham atiprasaṅgatucaṣṭayaṃ ca buddhimatkāryamātrayor vyāptyasiddhāv asaṅgatam | ataḥ kāryatvaṃ sādhanaṃ sandigdhavipakṣavyāvṛttikatvād anaikāntikam ||
children.translated_text: Thus, the three non-apprehensions of the pervader presented for the purpose of establishing pervasion are of doubtful establishment, and the four overextensions are inconclusive when the pervasion between an intelligent being and mere effecthood is unestablished. Therefore, the proof — effecthood (<s>kāryatva</s>) — is inconclusive (<s>anaikāntika</s>), because its exclusion from the counter-positive is doubtful.

children.text: atra Vācaspatiḥ prāha: sandigdhavipakṣavyāvṛttikatvaṃ nāma hetudoṣa eva na bhavati | tat kathaṃ nirasyate | tathā hi ya eva vipakṣe dṛṣṭo hetuḥ sa eva prameyatvādivad abhimataṃ na sādhyet | yas tu mahatāpi prayatnena mṛgyamāṇo 'sapakṣe nopalakṣitaḥ sa kathaṃ sādhyaṃ na sādhayet |
avaśyaṃ śaṅkayā bhāvyaṃ niyāmakam apaśyatām |
children.translated_text: 'Doubt is necessary for those who do not see a determining factor' —

children.text: iti tu dattāvakāśā laukikam aryādātikrameṇa saṃśayapiśācī labdhaprasarā na kvacin nāstīti nāyaṃ kvacit pravarte
children.translated_text: but the demoness of doubt, having been given scope, transgressing the path of noble ones regarding worldly [matters], having gained free play, does not stop anywhere — so one would never

children.text: ta | sarvasyaivārthasya kathañcic chaṅkāspada
children.translated_text: engage [in any action]. Because everything can be seen as somehow a ground for doubt.

children.text: tvadarśanāt
children.translated_text: [This follows from the observation that everything is potentially doubtful.]

children.text: | anarthaśaṅkāyāś ca prekṣāvatāṃ nivṛttyaṅgatvāt | antataḥ snigdhānnapānopayoge 'pi maraṇadarśanāt | tasmāt prāmāṇikalokayātrām anupālayatā yathādarśanaṃ śaṅkanīyam, na tv adṛṣṭam api | viśeṣasmṛtyapekṣo hi saṃśayo nāsmṛter bhavati | na ca smṛtir ananubhūtacare bhavati |
children.translated_text: And because apprehension of harm is a factor in the cessation of activity for discerning persons. Ultimately, even in the consumption of rich food and drink, death has been observed. Therefore, one who upholds the worldly conduct [sanctioned] by valid cognition should doubt only in accordance with what has been observed, not even what has never been seen. For doubt depends on the recollection of a specific [contrary instance] and does not arise from non-recollection. And recollection does not operate in the domain of what has never been experienced.

Here <s>Vācaspati</s> says: Doubtful exclusion from the counter-positive is simply not a defect of the logical reason. So how is it refuted? For thus: a logical reason that has been observed in the counter-positive would indeed fail to prove [the thesis], like 'being provable' and the like. But one that, despite being sought with the greatest effort, is not observed in the counter-positive — how could it fail to prove the thesis?

children.text: tad uktaṃ mīmāṃsāvārttikakṛ
tā adhyuṣṭasahasrikāyām:
children.translated_text: in the <s>Adhyuṣṭasāhasrikā</s>:

children.text: nāśaṅkā niḥpramāṇiketi |
children.translated_text: 'There is no doubt without a basis in valid cognition.'

children.text: (ŚV II 60cd)

children.translated_text: As is stated by the author of the <s>Mīmāṃsāvārttika</s>

children.text: tathā tenaiva Bṛhaṭṭīkāyām:
children.translated_text: Similarly, by the same [author] in the <s>Bṛhaṭṭīkā</s>:

children.text: utprekṣeta hi yo mohād ajātam api bādhakam |
children.translated_text: 'He who, out of delusion, would imagine a defeater that has never arisen,

children.text: sa sarvavyavahāreṣu saṃśayātmā kṣayaṃ vrajet || iti |
(=TS

children.translated_text: that one, whose nature is [consumed by] doubt in all transactions, would be ruined.'

children.text: tad etat pralāpamātram | na hi mahatāpi prayatnena vipakṣe mṛgyamāṇasya hetor adarśanamātreṇa vyatirekaḥ sidhyati | tathā hi vipakṣe hetur nopalabhyata ity anena tadupalambhakapramāṇanivṛttir ucyate |

pramāṇaṃ ca prameyasya kāryam, nākāraṇaṃ viṣaya iti nyāyāt | na ca kāryanivṛttau kāraṇanivṛttir upalabdhā, nirdhūmasyāpi vahner upalambhāt | yadi punaḥ pramāṇasattayā prameyasattā vyāptā syāt, tadā yuktam etat | kevalam iyam eva vyāptir asambhavinī, sarvasya sarvadarśitvaprasaṅgāt | tan nādarśanamātreṇa vyatirekasiddhiḥ | yathoktam:
children.translated_text: And a means of valid cognition is an effect of the provable object, and an object that is not a cause [of cognition cannot be known] — according to this principle. And the cessation of an effect does not entail the observed cessation of its cause, since fire is apprehended even without smoke. If, however, the existence of the provable were pervaded by the existence of the means of valid cognition, then this would be correct. But this very pervasion is impossible, because it would lead to the absurd consequence that everyone would see everything. Therefore, there is no establishing of exclusion [from the counter-positive] merely through non-observation. As stated:

children.text: sarvādṛṣṭiś ca sandigdhā svādṛṣṭir vyabhicāriṇī |
children.translated_text: 'Non-observation by everyone is doubtful; non-observation by oneself is subject to deviation,

children.text: vindhyādrirandhradūrvāder adṛṣṭāv api sattvataḥ || iti
children.translated_text: because of the existence [of things] even when unobserved, such as <s>dūrvā</s> grass in the caves of the <s>Vindhya</s> mountains.'

children.text: sakalavipakṣasyārvācīnaṃ praty adṛśyatvāt ||
children.translated_text: Because the entire counter-positive is imperceptible to an ordinary person.

All this is mere prattle. For the exclusion [of the logical reason] from the counter-positive is not established merely by the non-observation of the reason in the counter-positive, even with the greatest effort. For thus: by [the statement] 'the logical reason is not observed in the counter-positive,' what is expressed is the cessation of the means of valid cognition (<s>pramāṇa</s>) that would apprehend it.

children.text: yac coktam: saṃśayapiśācī labdhaprasarā na kvacin nāstīti na kvacit pravarteteti | tad asaṅgatam | arthasaṃśayasyāpi prekṣāvatāṃ pravṛttyaṅgatvāt pravṛttir avirodhiny eva | anarthasandehaḥ sarvatra kartuṃ śakyate | antataḥ snigdhānnapānopayoge 'pi maraṇadarśanād apravṛttir iti cet | durjñānam etat | tathā hy arthasandeho 'narthasandeho veti nāyaṃ ṣaṣṭhīsamāsaḥ | kin tv arthonmukhaḥ sandeho 'rthasandehaḥ, anarthonmukhaḥ sandeho 'narthasandeha iti śākapārthivādivanmadhyapadalopī samāsaḥ | evaṃ sati snigdhānnapānādāv arthasandeha eva, tajjātīyasya svapara
santāne dṛṣṭipuṣṭyādyarthasya koṭiśaḥ karaṇadarśanāt, maraṇāder anarthsya kvacit kadācid darśanāt |
children.translated_text: [Thus] harm such as death [is observed] somewhere and occasionally.

children.text: etadviparīto
children.translated_text: The opposite of this

children.text: 'narthasandeho draṣṭavyaḥ | tasmāt pramāṇādivārthasaṃśayād api prekṣāvatāṃ tatra tatra pravṛttir durvāraiva ||
children.translated_text: is to be regarded as doubt about harm. Therefore, even from doubt about benefit — like [doubt arising from] valid cognition and the like — the engagement of discerning persons in various matters is utterly irresistible.

As for the statement that 'the demoness of doubt, having gained free play, does not stop anywhere, so one would never engage [in action]' — that is unfounded. Because doubt about [possible] benefit is indeed a factor in the engagement of discerning persons, engagement [in action] is entirely non-contradictory. [Objection:] Doubt about harm can be raised everywhere; ultimately, even in the consumption of rich food and drink, death has been observed, so [one should] not engage [at all]. [Reply:] This is poorly reasoned. For thus: 'doubt about benefit' and 'doubt about harm' — this is not a genitive compound [meaning 'doubt of benefit/harm']; rather, 'a doubt oriented toward benefit is doubt about benefit; a doubt oriented toward harm is doubt about harm' — it is a compound with elision of the middle term, like '<s>śākapārthiva</s>' and the like. This being so, in the case of rich food, drink, and the like, there is indeed doubt about benefit, because things of that kind are observed millions of times to produce effects such as nourishment for oneself and others, while harm such as death is observed [only] somewhere and occasionally.

children.text: yad apīdaṃ lapitaṃ yathādarśanaṃ śaṅkanīyaṃ nādṛṣṭapūrvam api viśeṣasmṛtyapekṣo hi saṃśaya ityādi | tad asambaddhaṃ | sādhakabādhakapramāṇābhāvād eva paryudāsavṛttyā
vastvantara
children.translated_text: from the form of another

children.text: rūpāt sarvatra saṃśayotpatteḥ | kiṃ ca viśeṣasmṛtyapekṣa evāyaṃ saṃśayaḥ | tathā hi lakṣaṇayogitvāyogitvābhyām eva tajjātīyātajjātīye vaktavye | anyathā lakṣaṇapraṇayanam anarthakaṃ syāt | evaṃ ca sati tādātmyatadutpattilakṣaṇapratibandhaviyogitvena sādhāraṇena dharmeṇa prameyatvadhūmatvakārya
children.translated_text: entity. Moreover, this very doubt depends on the recollection of a specific [instance]. For thus: what is of the same kind and what is not of the same kind must be determined by the possession or non-possession of the defining characteristic. Otherwise, the formulation of defining characteristics would be purposeless. This being so, since, in your view, provability, smoke-hood, effecthood, and the like are of the same kind as the common property of being devoid of the connection defined as identity (<s>tādātmya</s>) and origination (<s>tadutpatti</s>), the observation of the deviation of provability itself gives rise to the doubt — and thus this [doubt] is raised precisely in accordance with what has been observed.

children.text: tvādīnāṃ tvanmatena sajātīyatvāt prameyatvavyabhicāradarśanam eva śaṅkām upasthāpayatīti yathādarśanam evedam āśaṅkitam |
children.translated_text: [Thus the doubt about the deviation of effecthood is established from observation.]

As for this chatter: 'One should doubt only in accordance with what has been observed, not something never seen before, because doubt depends on the recollection of a specific [contrary instance],' and so forth — that is incoherent. Because doubt arises everywhere, by way of exclusion (<s>paryudāsa</s>), precisely from the absence of establishing and defeating means of valid cognition,

children.text: yaś ca Kumārilasya sākṣitvenopanyāsaḥ sa khalu
dadhibhāṇḍe viḍālaḥ sākṣīti
children.translated_text: does not escape the proverb 'a cat as witness at the milk-pot' —

children.text: pravādaṃ nātipatatīti kim atra vaktavyam | tad evaṃ vipakṣe 'darśanamātreṇa hetor vyatirekāsiddheḥ sandigdhavipakṣavyāvṛttikatvaṃ nāma hetudūṣaṇaṃ durvāram eva | ata evā
children.translated_text: so what more need be said? Thus, since the exclusion of the logical reason from the counter-positive is not established merely through non-observation in the counter-positive, the [alleged] defect of doubtful exclusion from the counter-positive is indeed unavoidable. And therefore,

children.text: syopanyāso 'doṣodbhāvanaṃ nāma nigrahasthānam iti yad anenāveditaṃ tad api sāvadyam | pratyutāsmin heto
children.translated_text: the announcement by him [Vācaspati] that 'the presentation of this [objection] constitutes the fallacious debate-point (<s>nigrahasthāna</s>) of raising a non-existent defect' — that too is faulty. On the contrary, when there is a genuine defect in this logical reason that should be addressed, [for him to say] 'this is not a defect of the reason, therefore it need not be addressed, and its presentation constitutes the fallacious debate-point of raising a non-existent defect' — this wretched one himself

children.text: ḥ saddūṣaṇe parihartavye nāyaṃ hetudoṣo 'to na parihartavyo 'sya copanyāso 'doṣodbhāvanaṃ nāma nigrahasthānam iti bruvann ayam eva tapasvī svamatena niranuyojyānuyogalakṣaṇena nigrahasthānena nigṛhyata iti kṛpām arhati | tad evaṃ viparyayabādhakapramāṇābhāvād avyāpter asiddheḥ sandigdhavipakṣavyāvṛttikatvād anaikāntikaḥ kāryatvalakṣaṇo hetuḥ ||
children.translated_text: is caught by the debate-point (<s>nigrahasthāna</s>) defined, according to his own system, as objecting to what is not objectionable — and so he deserves our compassion. Thus, since the pervasion is unestablished due to the absence of counter-proof reasoning, and due to [the reason's] doubtful exclusion from the counter-positive, the logical reason characterized as effecthood (<s>kāryatva</s>) is inconclusive (<s>anaikāntika</s>).
And the citation of <s>Kumārila</s> as a witness — that indeed

children.text: athāgnidhūmayor iva viśiṣṭānvayavyatirekagrahaṇapravaṇaviśiṣṭapratyakṣānupalambhābhyāṃ vyaptir niścīyata iti dvitīyaḥ pakṣaḥ | atrocyate | kiṃ dṛśyaśarīropādhinā buddhimanmātreṇa vyāptigṛhyate, āhosvit dṛśyaśarīropādhividhureṇa dṛśyādṛśyasādhāraṇeneti vikalpau | yady ādyaḥ pakṣah, tadā tathābhūtasādhyam antareṇāpy utpadyamāne viṭapādau kāryatvadarśanāt prameyatvādivat sādhāraṇānaikāntiko hetuḥ |
children.translated_text: Now the second alternative: pervasion is ascertained through particular perception and non-apprehension, which are apt for grasping particular positive and negative concomitance, as in the case of fire and smoke. To this we reply: Is pervasion grasped with respect to an intelligent being merely as qualified by a visible body, or with respect to one not qualified by a visible body, [i.e.,] common to both visible and invisible [intelligent beings]? If the first alternative, then, since effecthood is observed even in sprouts and the like that arise without such [a visible-bodied intelligent being], the logical reason is inconclusive as a common [reason], like provability and the like.

children.text: nanu vṛkṣādayaḥ pakṣīkṛtāḥ | kathaṃ tair vyabhicāraḥ | trividho hi bhāvarāśiḥ | sandigdhakartṛko yathā vṛkṣādiḥ | prasiddhakartṛko yathā ghaṭādiḥ | akartṛko yathā ākāśādiḥ | tatra prasiddhakartṛke ghaṭādau pratyakṣānupalambhābhyāṃ vyāptim ādāya sandehapade kṣmāruhādau kāryatvam upasaṃhṛtya buddhimān anumīyate | na punar asu vyabhicāraviṣayo bhavitum arhati |
children.translated_text: [Objection:] But trees and the like have been included in the thesis [as things to be proved]. How then can they constitute a deviation? For the class of entities is threefold: (1) of doubtful authorship, such as trees and the like; (2) of known authorship, such as pots and the like; (3) without an author, such as space and the like. Among these, having established the pervasion through perception and non-apprehension with respect to pots and the like which are of known authorship, one applies effecthood to trees and the like — which are the locus of doubt — and infers an intelligent [author]. They [trees] should not become the locus of deviation.

children.text: yad āha: na sādhyenaiva vyabhicāra iti | ayuktam etat | na hi vyabhicāraviṣaya eva pakṣe bhavitum arhati:
children.translated_text: As stated: 'There is no deviation by the very thing to be proved.' This is incorrect. For the locus of deviation should not be in the thesis itself:

children.text: sandigdhe hetuvacanād vyasto hetor anāśrayaḥ
(PV IV 91)

children.translated_text: 'When there is doubt, the statement of the reason is reversed — the reason has no locus'

children.text:
iti nyāyāt | vyabhicāraviṣayatā ca dṛśyaśarīropādher
		buddhimanmātrasya tṛṇādyutpattau dṛśyānupalambhena pratikṣiptatvāt |
		tataś ca kṣmādharādir eva sandigdhakartṛkaḥ pakṣīkartum ucitaḥ
		kṣmāruhādis tv acetanakartṛka iti caturtho bhavarāśir neṣṭavyaḥ | atha
		vyabhicāracamat
kārāttri
children.translated_text: [the argument continues in the next section]...

children.text:
vidhabhāvarāśivyavasthāpanārthaṃ ca viṭapādau
		pratyakṣāpratikṣiptena dṛśyādṛśyasādhāraṇena buddhimanmātreṇa vyāptir
		avagamyata iti dvitīyaḥ saṅkalpaḥ | tadā viṭapādau buddhimanmātrasya
		sambhāvyamānatvād na sādhāraṇānaikāntikatāṃ brūmaḥ | kiṃ tarhi
		vyāptigrahaṇakāle dṛśyādṛśyasādhāraṇasya buddhimanmātrasya
		sādhyasyādṛśyatayā dṛśyānupalambhena vyatirekāsiddher vyāpter abhāvat
		sandigdhavyāvṛttikatvam ācakṣmahe | tathā hi | yadā kumbhakāravyāpārāt
		pūrvaṃ kumbhasya vyatirekaḥ pratyetavyas tadā na sādhyābhāvakṛto
		ghaṭavyatirekaḥ pratyetuṃ śakyaḥ | yathā hi viṭapādijanmasamaye
		buddhimanmātrāsyādṛśyatvena niṣeddhum aśakyatvāt sattāsambhāvanā tathā
		ghaṭādāv api vyatirekaniścayakāle buddhimanmātrasyādṛśyatvāt
		sattvasambhāvanāyāṃ sādhyābhāvaprayuktasya sādhanābhāvasyāsiddhatvena
		vyāpter abhāvāt kathaṃ na sandigdhavyatireko hetuḥ |
children.translated_text: And for the purpose of establishing the arrangement of positive and negative instances, in the case of tree-branches and the like, the invariable concomitance is understood with a mere intelligent being — which is common to the visible and the invisible — that is not refuted by perception. This is the second conception. Then, since a mere intelligent being is conceivable in the case of tree-branches and the like, we do not assert the fault of being a common inconclusive reason (<s>sādhāraṇānaikāntika</s>). Rather, we state that at the time of grasping the invariable concomitance, since the provable — namely, a mere intelligent being that is common to the visible and the invisible — is invisible, the counter-concomitance (<s>vyatireka</s>) cannot be established through the non-apprehension of the visible, and therefore, due to the absence of the invariable concomitance, [the reason] has a doubtful exclusion. For when the counter-concomitance of the pot must be ascertained prior to the potter's activity, the absence of the pot cannot be ascertained as caused by the absence of the provable. For just as at the time of the birth of tree-branches and the like, the existence [of an intelligent being] is conceivable because a mere intelligent being cannot be negated due to its invisibility, so too in the case of pots and the like, at the time of ascertaining the counter-concomitance, since a mere intelligent being is invisible, the absence of the means of proof [supposedly] caused by the absence of the provable is not established — and therefore, since the invariable concomitance is absent, how is the reason not one of doubtful exclusion?

— according to this principle. And being a locus of deviation [is established] because an intelligent being merely qualified by a visible body has been excluded in the origination of grass and the like through the non-apprehension of a visible [agent]. Therefore, only the earth and the like, whose authorship is doubtful, are appropriate to include in the thesis; trees and the like, however, have a non-sentient author — and so this fourth class of entities should not be denied. Now, [even] from the astonishment at the deviation

children.text: yaccokta
children.translated_text: And the following was stated:

children.text: yathā kāryaṃ ca syān nirupādānāṃ ceti nāśaṅkanīyam, tathā kāryaṃ ca bhaved akartṛkaṃ ceti nāśaṅkanīyam iti, tatrāpi kāryaṃ ca syān nirupādānaṃ ca bhaved iti na vaktavyam iti kenaivaṃ pratārito 'si | yadi hy atra pratyakṣānupalambhābhyāṃ vyāptir gṛhyate tadā katham upādānapūrvakaṃ kāryamātraṃ sidhyati | vyāptigrahaṇaprakārāntaraṃ ca tvayāpi nopanyastam | dṛśyādṛśyasādhāraṇayor upādānakāryamātrayor dṛśyaviṣayābhyāṃ pratyakṣānupalambhābhyāṃ vyāpter
children.translated_text: 'Just as one should not doubt that something might be an effect and yet lack a material cause, likewise one should not doubt that something might be an effect and yet lack a maker' — in that case too, the claim 'it should not be said that it might be an effect and yet lack a material cause' — who has deceived you thus? For if the invariable concomitance is grasped here through perception and non-apprehension, then how is the thesis established that all effects are preceded by a material cause? And you too have not presented any alternative method of grasping the invariable concomitance — because the invariable concomitance of material cause and effect in general, which are common to the visible and the invisible, cannot be

children.text: abhyūhitum
children.translated_text: inferred

children.text: aśakyatvāt | svamatavyālopaprasaṅgas tu pramāṇacintāvasare 'prāptāvakāśaḥ | viparyayabādhakapramāṇabalād vātra vyāptisiddhiḥ | tathā hi yathāṅkurādikaṃ kāryaṃ niyatadeśakālasvabhāvatvena vyāptaṃ tathā śālitvādināpi jātibhedena vyāptam upalabdham | tataś cānupādānapūrvakatvād vipakṣātmanaḥ śālitvādijātibhedasya vyāpakasya nivṛttau nivartamānaṃ kāryatvam upādānapūrvakatve viśrāmyat tena vyāptaṃ sidhyati | na cānupādānenāpi kriyamāṇaḥ śālitvādijātibhedo yujyate, upādānaṃ vinā
children.translated_text: through perception and non-apprehension, which have only visible objects. The absurd consequence of undermining one's own position, however, has no scope at the time of investigating the means of valid cognition. Or else, the establishment of the invariable concomitance here is by the force of a defeating means of valid cognition for the contrary. For just as an effect such as a sprout and the like is pervaded by having a determinate spatial, temporal, and essential nature, so too it is observed to be pervaded by a specific class such as 'rice-ness' and the like. Therefore, since the class-distinction of 'rice-ness' and the like — which constitutes the negative example — is excluded when [something is] not preceded by a material cause, the property of being an effect, which subsists in being preceded by a material cause, is established as pervaded by it. Nor can a class-distinction of 'rice-ness' and the like be produced even without a material cause, because without a material cause,

children.text: kṛtād anu
children.translated_text: from the created, following the

children.text: pādānād eva kevalād ekajātīyakāraṇāt tadatajjātīyakāryotpattau kāryabhedasyāhetukatvaprasaṅgāt | tad uktam:
children.translated_text: material cause alone — a single-class cause — if effects of both that class and other classes were produced, then the class-distinction of effects would be without a cause. As has been stated:

children.text: tadatadrūpiṇo bhāvās tadatadrūpahetujāḥ ||
children.translated_text: 'Entities of that and other forms are born from causes of that and other forms.'

children.text: iti |
children.translated_text: Thus.

children.text: (PV III 251ab)

anyathānupādānād eva kṣityāder aṅkurādikam utpadyetety aṅkurārthino bījaṃ nānusareyuḥ | tasmād viparyayabādhakapramāṇabalād eva kāryatvasya hetumātrapūrvakatvenevopādānapūrvakatvenāpi vyāptisiddhir iti nyāyaḥ | na caivaṃ kāryamātrakartṛtvamātrayor api vyāptiprasādhakaṃ viparyaye bādhakaṃ pramāṇam asti, pūrvoktasya vyāpakānupalambhatrayasyātiprasaṅgacatuṣṭayasya ca prāg eva pratyākhyātatvāt | tasmāt kāryaṃ ca syāt na ca dhīmatkartṛpūrvakam iti śaṅkāṃ kurvāṇaḥ prativādī vinā caraṇamardanādinā niṣeddhum aśakyaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Otherwise, sprouts and the like would be produced from earth alone without a material cause, and those who desire sprouts would not pursue seeds. Therefore, the rule is that the invariable concomitance of the property of being an effect with being preceded by a material cause is established precisely by the force of the defeating means of valid cognition for the contrary — just as [it is established] with being preceded by a cause in general. But there is no such defeating means of valid cognition for the contrary that establishes the invariable concomitance of mere 'being an effect' with mere 'having a maker' — because the threefold non-apprehension of the pervader and the fourfold overextension [objections] stated earlier have already been refuted. Therefore, the opponent who raises the doubt 'it might be an effect and yet not be preceded by an intelligent maker' cannot be stopped without [figuratively] trampling his feet.

children.text: nanu yadi dṛśyāgnidhūmasāmānyayor iva
dṛśyā
children.translated_text: the invariable concomitance is [grasped] through perception and non-apprehension only of visible

children.text: eva kāryakāraṇasāmānyayoḥ pratyakṣānupalambhato vyāptis tadā paracittānumānakṣatiḥ | svaparasantānasādhāra
children.translated_text: cause-and-effect universals, then [there would be] damage to the inference of others' minds. Because [the mind], which is common to one's own and others' mental continua and is invisible,

children.text: ṇenādṛśyena
children.translated_text: being invisible —

children.text: cinmātreṇa pratyakṣato dṛśyaviṣayād
children.translated_text: mere consciousness (<s>cinmātra</s>), from perception that has a visible object,

children.text: vyāptigrahaṇāyogād ity api na vācyam | bāhyārthasthitau hi svaparasantānasādhāraṇasya cinmātrasya svarūpeṇādṛśyatve 'pi dṛśyaśarīreṇa sahaikasāmagrīpratibandhād avinirbhāgavartitvam asty eva | tato yathā ghaṭaviṣayaṃ pratyakṣaṃ rūpaikadeśapravṛttam apy avyabhicārāt samudāyopasthāpakam tathā dehagrāhakam eva pratyakṣaṃ dehāvinirbhāgavarti svaparasantānasādhāraṇaṃ cinmātraṃ kampāder vyāpakam adhigacchanti | tad evaṃ dṛśyātmano dṛśyāvinirbhāgavartino vā padārthasya
children.translated_text: cannot be the basis for grasping the invariable concomitance' — this too should not be said. For, given the existence of external objects, even though mere consciousness, which is common to one's own and others' continua, is invisible in its own nature, it is invariably present (<s>avinirbhāgavarti</s>) together with the visible body by being bound in a single causal complex. Therefore, just as perception directed at a pot, though operating upon only a portion of form, establishes the aggregate due to non-deviation, so too perception that grasps the body ascertains mere consciousness — which is present inseparably from the body and common to one's own and others' continua — as the pervader of trembling and the like. Thus, the establishment and grasping of the invariable concomitance of an entity that is either visible in nature or inseparably present with the visible is

children.text: vyāvahārikapaṭupratyakṣataḥ siddhir vyāptigrahaś ca, na tu tathātvavinākṛtādṛśyasādhāraṇacinmātrasyeti santānāntarānumānam ucitam | tasmād yadi pratyakṣānupalabhābhyāṃ vyāptigrahas tadā dṛśyenaiva dṛśyasyeti nyāyaḥ |
children.translated_text: through pragmatically acute perception, but not of mere consciousness that is common [to all] and invisible without being of such a nature [i.e., without being inseparable from the visible] — therefore the inference of another's mental continuum is justified. Hence, if the invariable concomitance is grasped through perception and non-apprehension, then the rule is: only of the visible by the visible.

children.text: tad ayaṃ saṃkṣepārthaḥ:
children.translated_text: This is the summary of the argument:
One objects: 'If, just as with the universals of visible fire and smoke,

children.text: kāryatvasya vipakṣavṛttihataye sambhāvyate 'tīndriyaḥ kartā ced vyatirekasiddhividhurā vyāptiḥ kathaṃ sidhyati |
children.translated_text: 'If a supersensible maker is posited to eliminate the presence of the property of being an effect in the negative example, then how can the invariable concomitance, which is bereft of the establishment of the counter-concomitance, be established?

children.text: dṛśyo 'tha vyatirekasiddhimanasā kartā samāśrīyate tattyāge 'pi tadā tṛṇādikam iti vyaktaṃ vipakṣe kṣaṇam ||
children.translated_text: If, on the other hand, a visible maker is relied upon for the establishment of the counter-concomitance by the mind, then even upon his absence, grass and the like clearly [exhibit] the [property of being an effect] in the negative example for a moment.'

children.text: ato na pratyakṣānupalmbhābhyām api vyāptisiddhiḥ ||
children.translated_text: Therefore, the invariable concomitance is not established even through perception and non-apprehension.

children.text: nanu bhūyodarśanādarśanābhyāṃ pratibandhaḥ pratīyata iti tṛtīya evāsamākaṃ pakṣaḥ | kevalaṃ sa pratibandho na tadutpattilakṣaṇo grahītavyaḥ | kin tu svābhāvikaḥ | sa eva darśanādarśanābhyāṃ pratīyate | tathā caitam evārthaṃ Vācaspatiḥ prāha:
The following collects material from
#nvtṭ-nsū_1-1.5
na sapakṣāsapakṣayor
children.translated_text: 'Not by observation and non-observation

children.text: darśanādarśanābhyāṃ
children.translated_text: in the positive and negative examples

children.text: kāryatvasya gamakatvam api tu svābhāvikapratibandhabalād iti brūmaḥ | sa eva tu sapakṣāsapakṣayor darśanādarśanābhyāṃ vakṣyamāṇena krameṇa pratīyata iti tadupakṣepo 'pi yuktaḥ |
children.translated_text: is the indicative capacity of the property of being an effect [established], but rather by the force of the natural necessary connection' — so we maintain. 'And that [natural connection] is cognized through observation and non-observation in the positive and negative examples by the method to be explained' — so its mention [of observation] is also justified.

children.text: tena yasyāsau
children.translated_text: Therefore, for whomever that

children.text: svābhāvikaḥ
children.translated_text: natural

children.text: pratibandho niyataḥ siddhaḥ sa eva gamako gamyaś cetaraḥ sambandhīti yujyate | tathā hi dhūmādīnāṃ vahnyādibhiḥ saha sambandhaḥ svābhāviko na tu vahnyādīnāṃ dhūmādibhiḥ | te hi vinā dhūmādibhir upalambhyante | yadā tv
children.translated_text: necessary connection is ascertained as fixed — he alone is the indicator, and the other is the indicated correlate. This is fitting. For the connection of smoke and the like with fire and the like is natural, but not that of fire and the like with smoke and the like. For [fire and the like] are observed without smoke and the like. But when

children.text: ārdrendhanādisambandham
children.translated_text: they come into contact with wet fuel and the like,

children.text: anubhavanti tadā dhūmādibhiḥ sambadhyante | tasmād vahnyādīnām ārdredhanādyupādhikṛtaḥ sambandho na tu svābhāvikas tato na niyataḥ | svābhāvikas tu dhūmādīnāṃ vahnyādibhiḥ sambandhaḥ, tadupādher anupalabhyamānatvāt | kvacid vyabhicārasyādarśanāt | anupalabhyamānasyāpi kalpanānupapatteḥ | na cānupalabhyamāno darśanānarhatayā sādhakabādhakapramāṇābhāvena sandihyamāna upādhiḥ sambandhasya svābhāvikatvaṃ pratibadhnātīti yuktam | yathoktaṃ prāk seyaṃ saṃśayapiśācītyādi | tasmād upādhiṃ prayatnenānviṣyanto 'nupalabhyamānā nāstīty avagamya svābhāvikatvaṃ niścinumaḥ ||
children.translated_text: then they are connected with smoke and the like. Therefore, the connection of fire and the like is conditioned by the auxiliary condition (<s>upādhi</s>) of wet fuel and the like — it is not natural, and hence not invariable. But the connection of smoke and the like with fire and the like is natural, because no conditioning factor (<s>upādhi</s>) for it is apprehended, because no deviation is observed anywhere, and because even of an unapprehended [upādhi], the supposition is untenable. Nor is it proper that a conditioning factor that is unapprehended — and hence doubtful due to the absence of both establishing and defeating means of valid cognition, as it is unfit for observation — should obstruct the naturalness of the connection. As was stated earlier: 'This is the phantom of doubt...' and so on. Therefore, having searched for the conditioning factor with effort and not apprehending it, we determine [the connection] to be natural, understanding [the upādhi] to be non-existent.

One objects: 'The necessary connection (<s>pratibandha</s>) is cognized through repeated observation and non-observation — that is indeed our third position. However, that necessary connection should not be understood as characterized by production from [the cause]. Rather, it is natural (<s>svābhāvika</s>). And that very [natural connection] is cognized through observation and non-observation.' And <s>Vācaspati</s> too states this very meaning:

children.text: syād etat | anyasyānyena sahakāraṇena cet svābhāvikaḥ sambandho bhavet, sarvaṃ sarveṇa sambadhyeta | tathā ca sarvaṃ sarvasmād gamyeta | athānyac ced anyasya kāryaṃ kasmāt sarvaṃ sarvasmān na bhavati, anyatvāviśeṣāt | tataś ca sa evātiprasaṅgaḥ | yady ucyeta svabhāvā na paryanuyojyāḥ | tasmād anyatvāviśeṣe 'pi kiñcid eva kāraṇaṃ kāryaṃ ca kiñcid iti | nanv eṣa svabhāvānanuyogo 'kāryakāraṇabhūtānām api svabhāvapratibandhe tulya eva | tasmād yat kiñcid etad api ||
children.translated_text: One might object: 'If one thing's natural connection with another were [established merely] through co-occurrence, then everything would be connected with everything. And thus everything would be inferable from everything. Or, if something else is the effect of something else, why does not everything arise from everything — since there is no distinction in their being different? And so the same overextension [applies]. If one says "Natural properties are not to be questioned" — therefore, even though there is no distinction in being different, only some things are causes and only some are effects — then this appeal to the unquestionable nature of natural properties is equally applicable to the natural necessary connection between things that are not in a cause-effect relation. Therefore, all this [amounts to nothing].'

children.text: kim asya sambandhasya vyāptigrāhakaṃ pramāṇam iti cet | ucyate
children.translated_text: If one asks: What is the means of valid cognition that grasps the invariable concomitance of this connection? — we reply:

children.text: bhūyodarśanagamyā hi vyāptiḥ sāmānyadharmayoḥ |
(ŚV, anumāna, 12)

children.translated_text: 'The invariable concomitance of general properties is known through repeated observation' —

children.text: iti prasiddham eva | asyāyam arthaḥ kāśikākāreṇa vyākhyātaḥ—prācīnānekadarśanajanitasaṃskārasahāye carame
cetasi
children.translated_text: in the mind

children.text: cakāsti dhūmasyāgniniyatasvabhāvatvam, ratnatattvam iva parīkṣakasya, śabdatattvam iva vyākaraṇasmṛtisaṃskṛtasya, brāhmaṇatvam iva mātāpitṛsambandhasmaraṇasacivasyetyādi | na hy etat sarvam āpātato na pratibhātam iti purastād api pratibhāsamānam anyathā bhavatīti ||

children.translated_text: 'Through repeated observation — that is, by the mind assisted by repeated observation — the connection of things of that class is grasped. Therefore, smoke does not deviate from fire. Even in [a case of apparent] deviation, it would transgress the connection that is free from conditioning factors. The means of valid cognition that removes the suspicion of the reason's occurrence in the negative example is perception itself, called non-apprehension, which is the ground for the certainty of the absence of a conditioning factor whose apprehension-conditions are met. Therefore, the natural connection is established' — and 'so too here' — thus his own position has been established.

children.text: Vācaspatināpīdam uktam – abhijātamaṇibhedatattvavad bhūyodarśanajanitasaṃskārasahāyam indriyam eva dhūmādīnāṃ vahnyādibhiḥ svābhāvikasambandhagrāhīti yuktam iti ||
children.translated_text: <s>Vācaspati</s> too has stated: 'Just as with the true nature of the classification of fine gems, it is proper that the sense-faculty itself, assisted by latent impressions generated by repeated observation, grasps the natural connection of smoke and the like with fire and the like.'

children.text: sati tadutpatter anyaḥ svābhāvikaḥ sambandhaḥ śabdāsphālanamātram evedam | na khalu nirūpyamāṇaḥ prāpyate | tathā hi svābhāvikas tu dhūmādīnāṃ vahnyādibhiḥ sambandhaḥ tadupādher anupalabhyamānatvāt | kvacid vyabhicārasyādarśanād iti tvayaivāsya lakṣaṇam uktam | etac cāsiddham | yataḥ, upādhiśabdena svato 'rthāntaram evāpekṣaṇīyam abhidhātavyam | na cārthāntaraṃ dṛśyatāniyatam, adṛśyasyāpi deśakālasvabhāvaviprakṛṣṭasya sambhavāt | tataś ca dhūmasyāpi hutāśena saha sambandhe syād upādhiḥ, na copalakṣyata iti katham adarśanān nāsty eva yataḥ svābhāvikasambandhasiddhiḥ ||
children.translated_text: since production from that [cause exists], the other [so-called] "natural connection" is a mere verbal flourish — it cannot in fact be ascertained upon examination. For: "the connection of smoke and the like with fire and the like is natural because no conditioning factor for it is apprehended, and because no deviation is observed anywhere" — this is the definition you yourself have stated. But this is not established. Because: by the word 'conditioning factor' (<s>upādhi</s>), something other [than the cause] must indeed be meant. And that other thing is not restricted to the visible, since even an invisible [factor], remote in space, time, or nature, is possible. Therefore, even in the connection of smoke with fire, there might be a conditioning factor that is not perceived. How then, from its non-observation, [can one conclude] that it certainly does not exist, and [thereby establish] the natural connection?
To that, we reply:

children.text: atha

If the production from that [cause] is not accepted, then even with thousands of observations, [the question remains:] must fire necessarily exist wherever smoke exists, or not?

children.text: kadācid arthāntaram upādhim apekṣya dhūmo 'pi syān nāgnir iti kim atra niṣṭaṅkakāraṇam | tadupādher anupalabhyamānatvāt | kvacid vyabhicārasyādarśanād iti tu yad uktaṃ tat pratyuktam eva | adṛśyasyāpy upādheḥ sambhāvyamānatvāt | vyabhicārasya ca pratyayāntaravaikalyenāhatyādarśane 'pi niṣeddham aśakyatvāt | ata eva tayor bādhakābhāve 'pi sādhakabādhakapramāṇābhāvāt śaṅkā sambhavaty eva | na punas tavāmunā viklavavikrośitamātreṇa vyāvartate | na caitavatā prāmāṇikalokayātrātikramaḥ | prāmāṇikair eva sādhakabādhakapramāṇābhāve nyāyaprāptasya saṃśayasya vihitatvāt | na ca sarvatrāpravṛttiprasaṅgaḥ, pamāṇād arthasaṃśayāc ca pravṛtter upapatteḥ | na cānarthasandehaḥ sarvatra kartuṃ śakyate, kvacid arthonmukhatāyā eva darśanāt ||
children.translated_text: Sometime, depending on some other conditioning factor, there might be smoke but no fire — what ground for certainty exists here? The statement that 'because no conditioning factor for it is apprehended, and because no deviation is observed anywhere' has already been answered: because even an invisible conditioning factor is conceivable, and because even when deviation is not observed due to the deficiency of some other condition, it cannot be negated. For precisely this reason, even in the absence of defeating [evidence] for those two [criteria], doubt is possible due to the absence of both establishing and defeating means of valid cognition. Nor is [this doubt] averted merely by your panicked outcry. Nor does this overstep the practice of those who rely on valid means of cognition, because doubt — which is logically warranted in the absence of establishing and defeating means of valid cognition — has been sanctioned by the authoritative logicians themselves. Nor is there the absurd consequence of inactivity everywhere, because activity is justified both from a means of valid cognition and from doubt about [obtaining] a desired object. Nor can doubt about harm be produced everywhere, because a tendency toward a [desired] object is observed in some cases.
But

children.text: yac cānyatvāviśeṣe 'pi kiñcid eva kāraṇaṃ kāryaṃ ca kiñcid iti svabhāvo yathā na paryanuyojyas tathaiṣa svabhāvānanuyogo 'kāryakāraṇabhūtā

karaṇam atilāghavam āviskaroti vācaspateḥ | tathā hi vastutvāviśeṣe 'py agnir dahati nākāśam ity atra yathā nātiprasaṅgaḥ saṅgataḥ pramāṇasiddhatvād asyārthasya, tathā bhedāviśeṣe 'pi kiñcid eva kasyacit kāraṇaṃ kāryaṃ ca kiñcid ity atrāpi nātiprasaṅgāvatāraḥ | bhede sati tadanvayavyatirekānuvidhānalakṣaṇasya kāryakāraṇabhāvasya pramāṇasiddhatvād eva | na caivaṃ svābhāvikasambandhaśabdavācyo 'rthaḥ pramāṇasiddhaḥ kaścid asti, tallakṣaṇasyāsiddhatvād uktatvāt | na ca pratijñāsiddhe vastuny atiprasaṅgo nābhaidhātavyaḥ, sarveṣāṃ sarvatra tadrūpābhyupagamamātreṇa vijetṛtvaprasaṅgāt | yad āhālaṅkārakāraḥ:
children.translated_text: performance reveals the extreme levity of <s>Vācaspati</s>. For just as, despite there being no difference in 'thing-ness,' fire burns and not space — here there is no over-extension, because this fact is established by valid means of knowledge — similarly, despite there being no difference in otherness, only something specific is the cause of something, and only something specific is the effect — here too there is no entering of over-extension, precisely because the cause-effect relation, characterized by conformity with the co-presence and co-absence of that [cause], is established by valid means of knowledge. But no such fact expressed by the term 'intrinsic connection' (<s>svābhāvikasambandha</s>) is established by valid means of knowledge — because, as was stated, its defining characteristic is unestablished. And one should not say that over-extension does not apply to something established merely by assertion — because everyone would become a victor everywhere merely by accepting a form [that suits them]. As the rhetorician says:

And as for the [claim] that despite there being no difference in otherness, only something specific is a cause and only something specific is an effect — this is a natural fact (<s>svabhāva</s>) not subject to further inquiry — similarly, this non-inquirability of the natural fact applies equally to the intrinsic connection (<s>svabhāvapratibandha</s>) even between things that are not cause and effect —

children.text: kiṃ ca svābhāvikasambandha iti ko 'rthaḥ | kiṃ svato bhūtaḥ svahetuto bhūto 'hetuko veti trayaḥ pakṣāh | na tāvad ādyaḥ pakṣaḥ, svātmani kāritravirodhāt | dvitīyapakṣe tu tadutpattir eva sambandho mukhāntareṇa svīkṛta iti na kaścid vivādaḥ |ahetukatve tu deśakālasvabhāvaniyamābhāvaprasaṅgād ity asaṅgataḥ svābhāvikaḥ sambandhaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Furthermore, what is the meaning of 'intrinsic connection' (<s>svābhāvikasambandha</s>)? Is it self-produced, produced from its own cause, or causeless? — these are three alternatives. The first alternative is untenable — because of the contradiction of an entity acting upon itself. In the second alternative, the production itself is the connection, accepted under another name — so there is no dispute. But if it is causeless, then the consequence would be the absence of restriction by place, time, and nature — and so the 'intrinsic' connection is incoherent.

By this, the following statement is [also refuted]: 'It is not through observation and non-observation in the positive and negative examples that the indicative capacity of being an effect [is established], but rather by the force of the intrinsic connection — and that [intrinsic connection] is itself apprehended through observation and non-observation in the positive and negative examples, in the manner that will be described.' This should be understood as merely disclosing one's own desired conclusion. For the defining characteristic of the intrinsic connection has been stated as [possessing] unconditional invariability without dependence on extraneous conditions (<s>upādhi</s>). And when that [intrinsic connection] is unestablished by the aforementioned reasoning, [the claim] that such invariability shines forth in the final cognition aided by the conditioning produced by repeated observation —

children.text: yac ca śabdatattvam iva brāhmaṇatvam iveti dṛṣṭāntīkṛtaṃ tad dvayam apy asmān pratyasiddham iti dṛṣṭāntayitum anucitam | abhijātamaṇibhedatattvaṃ tu parisphuratīti yuktam | tasya hy upadeśaparamparāto māṇikyavattenāpi kaṣṭenendradhanurākārajyotirādikaṃ lakṣaṇaṃ niścitam | na caivaṃ svābhāvikasambandhalakṣaṇaṃ tvayā svakapolaracitam api pramāṇena niścitam | yenāsyāpi tādṛśī vyavasthā syād iti yat kiñcid etat ||
children.translated_text: And as for the two things adduced as illustrations — like the nature of words (<s>śabdatattva</s>) and like Brāhmaṇa-hood (<s>brāhmaṇatva</s>) — both of these are unestablished for us, and so they are inappropriate as illustrations. But the nature of gem classification does shine forth [as a legitimate example]. For that [classification] is ascertained with difficulty even by one possessing gems, through the successive tradition of instruction, by [observing] characteristics such as the rainbow-like luster and so forth. But in the case of the defining characteristic of 'intrinsic connection,' even though it is fabricated by your own imagination, it is not ascertained by a valid means of knowledge — so that there could be a similar established practice for it. This [argument] is therefore inconsequential.

children.text: kiṃ ca bhavatu tāvad ayam anavadhāritarūpaḥ svābhāvikaḥ sambandhaḥ, tathāpi darśanādarśanābhyām asya grahaṇam atidurlabham | tathā hi yadi prācīnānekadarśanajanitasaṃskārasahāyena caramacetasā dhūmasyāgniniyatatvaṃ grāhyaṃ tadā sapakṣāsapakṣayoḥ koṭiśaḥ pravṛttadarśanādarśanajanitasaṃskārasahāyena caramacetasā pārthivatvasyāpi lohalekhyatvaniyatatvaṃ gṛhyata iti pārthivatvād api lohalekhyatvasiddhir astu | atha pārthivatvasya lohalekhyatvaniyatatvam eva nāsti vajre vyabhicāradarśanāt | tat kathaṃ pratyakṣeṇa niyatatvagrahaḥ | tarhi dhūmasya vahniniyatatvam eva nāsti, vyabhicārābhāvasya darśayitum aśakyatvāt | tat kathaṃ caramacittena niyamagraha ity apy tulyam |
children.translated_text: Furthermore, even granting this intrinsic connection whose nature is undetermined, still, its apprehension through observation and non-observation is extremely difficult. For if the invariable concomitance of smoke with fire is to be grasped by the final cognition aided by the conditioning produced by numerous prior observations, then by the final cognition aided by the conditioning produced by thousands of observations and non-observations in the positive and negative examples, the invariable concomitance of earthiness (<s>pārthivatva</s>) with inscribability-on-metal (<s>lohalekhyatva</s>) would also be grasped — and so, from earthiness too, inscribability-on-metal should be established. [Objection:] But earthiness does not have invariable concomitance with inscribability-on-metal — because deviation is observed in diamond. So how can invariable concomitance be grasped by perception [in that case]? [Reply:] Then smoke too does not have invariable concomitance with fire — because the absence of deviation cannot be demonstrated. So how can invariable concomitance be grasped by the final cognition? — the [objection] applies equally.

children.text: lakṣaṇaprāptatvābhāvāt | tasmāt saty api vyabhicāre tadupalambhasāmagryabhāvād vyabhicārānupalambhaḥ | prakārāntareṇa vā tadutpattilakṣaṇenāvyabhicāre vyabhicārānupalambha ity ubhayathāpi vyabhicāropalambhanivṛttir astu | tvayā tu yad avyabhicārapratipattinibandhanaṃ darśanādarśanam upavarṇitaṃ tatpārthivatvādau vyabhicārād dhūme 'pi nāvyabhicāranibandhanam iti dhūmo 'pi tvanmate nāśvāsabhājam iti prasaktam |
children.translated_text: not attain the status of being fit to be observed (<s>dṛśya</s>). Therefore, even when deviation exists, from the absence of the conditions for its apprehension, there is non-apprehension of deviation. Or alternatively, when there is non-deviation characterized by production from that [cause], there is non-apprehension of deviation — in either case, the cessation of the apprehension of deviation is [possible even when deviation exists]. But as for the observation-and-non-observation that you have described as the basis for ascertaining non-deviation — since it [leads to a] deviation [fallacy] in the case of earthiness and the like, it is not a basis for non-deviation even in the case of smoke — so even smoke, in your system, does not deserve confidence. This is the consequence.

[Objection:] Non-deviation [is established] from the non-observation of deviation. [Reply:] But what is the meaning of 'non-deviation from the non-observation of deviation'? Is it: non-deviation from the non-observation of deviation, or [non-deviation] from the absence of deviation? In the first alternative: let there be deviation or not — 'from the non-observation of deviation alone there is non-deviation' — this is consummate pedantry! But if the second alternative: then whence is the absence of deviation known? [Objection:] From non-observation. [Reply:] Then is that mere non-observation, or non-observation of what is fit to be observed (<s>dṛśya</s>)? The first is incapable [of proving absence]. For even in cases of non-observation, one cannot state that deviation does not exist — just as the deviation of a Brāhmaṇī woman [from chastity] that was destroyed long ago [remains unknown]. And even in cases of accumulated non-observation, deviation is [sometimes] observed after an extremely long interval. And the second is impossible — because when the conditions for observing deviation are present at some place, at some time, by some [observer], deviation is [still sometimes] observed. But when the conditions

children.text: asmanmate tu pratyakṣānupalambhābhyām ekatra kāryakāraṇabhāvasiddhau na vyabhicāraśaṅkāsambhavaḥ | tadabhāve tu: hetumattāṃ vilaṅghayed
(PV I 34d)
iti nyāyāt na saṃśayapiśācāvasaraḥ | tad evaṃ bhūyodarśanādarśanābhyām api na vyāptisiddhiḥ |
children.translated_text: by this principle, there is no occasion for the demon of doubt. Thus, even through repeated observation and non-observation, the establishment of pervasion (<s>vyāpti</s>) is not achieved [in your system].

In our system, however, once the cause-effect relation is established in a single instance through perception and non-apprehension, there is no possibility of doubt about deviation. And in the absence of that [doubt]: 'It would transgress the law of having a cause' —

children.text: tarhi sakṛt sapakṣāsapakṣayor darśanādarśanābhyām vyāpter niścaya iti caturtha eva pakṣo 'stu | tathā hi kāryatvasya buddhimanmātrapūrvakatvenānvayo ghaṭādau dṛṣtaḥ, ākāśādau buddhimatkāraṇanivṛttau kāryatvasya vyatirekaḥ | tataś ca sakṛdanvayavyatirekasiddhau vyāpteḥ siddhatvāt kuto 'naikāntikatā |
children.translated_text: [Objection:] Then let the fourth alternative be [accepted]: certainty of pervasion through a single observation and non-observation in the positive and negative examples. For the positive concomitance of being an effect (<s>kāryatva</s>) with being preceded merely by an intelligent [being] is observed in pots and the like; and in space and the like, the negative concomitance — the absence of being an effect when the intelligent cause is absent — [is also observed]. Therefore, once the positive and negative concomitance is established in a single instance, the pervasion is established — so whence comes inconclusiveness (<s>anaikāntikatā</s>)?

children.text: atrābhidhīyate | yadi buddhimatkāraṇakāryatvayor ekatra pratibandhaḥ pramāṇapratītaḥ syāt tadākāśādau buddhimannnivṛttau kāryatvasya nivṛttir iti yuktam | sa ca pratibandhaḥ tādātmyaṃ tadutpattiḥ svābhāviko 'nyo vā na sidhyati sādhakapramāṇābhāvād ity anantaram evāveditam | tataś cākāśādau buddhimannivṛttir api syāt | na ca kāryatvasya nivṛttir iti sandigdhavipakṣavyāvṛttikatvād anaikāntikaṃ kāryatvam |
children.translated_text: To this we reply: If the invariable connection between being an intelligent cause and being an effect were apprehended by valid means of knowledge in a single instance, then it would be justified [to say] that in space and the like, when the intelligent [cause] is absent, being an effect is absent. But that invariable connection — whether [conceived as] identity (<s>tādātmya</s>), production from that (<s>tadutpatti</s>), intrinsic connection, or some other [relation] — is not established, due to the absence of a valid means of knowledge to prove it — as was just stated. Therefore, even the absence of an intelligent being in space and the like may obtain, without the absence of being an effect. Because the exclusion from the negative example is doubtful (<s>sandigdhavipakṣavyāvṛttikatva</s>), being an effect is inconclusive (<s>anaikāntika</s>).

children.text: nanv ākāśasyāsamanmate nityatvaṃ tvanmate cāsattvam | tat katham ataḥ kāryatvavyatirekaḥ sandigdha iti cet | ucyate | na hy ākāśe
kāryatvavyā

children.text: vṛttimātraṃ vyatirekaḥ | kin tu sādhyābhāvaprayuktaḥ sādhanābhāvo vyatirekaḥ | sa cākāśe grahītum aśakyaḥ | yathā tatra buddhimatkāraṇanivṛttis tathā

And that cannot be grasped with respect to space. For just as the absence of an intelligent cause is [present] there, so too is the absence

children.text: 'cetanasyāpi kāraṇasya nivṛttiḥ |
children.translated_text: of a sentient cause of any kind.

[Objection:] But in your view, space is non-existent (<s>asat</s>), while in our view it is eternal. Then how is the negative concomitance of being an effect doubtful with respect to it? [Reply:] It is said: the negative concomitance with respect to space is not

children.text: tadutpattisiddhāv anvayavyatirekau sidhyataḥ ||
children.translated_text: when the production [relation] between them is established, positive and negative concomitance are [thereby] established.

[Objection:] True enough — just as in space there is the absence of an intelligent cause, so too there is the absence of any cause whatsoever, and so the invariable concomitance of being an effect with the intelligent cause cannot be ascertained. Nevertheless, the positive concomitance of being an effect with an intelligent being is observed in pots and the like; and in space too, the absence of being an effect necessitated by the absence of an intelligent being is apprehended — so how is the negative concomitance unestablished? [Reply:] Well then, in pots and the like too, the positive concomitance is not the mere co-existence of being an effect [with anything]. Rather, the positive concomitance is the co-existence of the proof (<s>sādhana</s>) necessitated by the co-existence of the provable (<s>sādhya</s>). And that cannot be grasped with respect to pots either. For just as the existence of an intelligent being is [present] there, so too is the existence of a mat, a wall, and so forth. Then who is to know whether being an effect exists because of the existence of an intelligent being, or because of the existence of a mat, a wall, and so forth? Therefore, in this matter, one should follow perception and non-apprehension of the specific [relation between] what is observable —

children.text: na ca pratibandhasādhakaṃ pramāṇaṃ svapne 'py astīti caturtho 'pi pakṣaḥ kṣataḥ |
children.translated_text: And there is no valid means of knowledge to establish the invariable connection — not even in a dream — so the fourth alternative too is refuted.

children.translated_text: And as for the illustration shown — that from the property-of-the-subject status of activity-in-general, a specific instrument characterized as the eye is established — that too is no different from the provable (<s>sādhya</s>). For there, it is merely a naming of a cause already established through the impossibility of otherwise accounting for the cognition of color, as 'the sense-organ called the eye.' Because no specific [property] characterized as 'being the eye' beyond [the capacity of] producing the cognition of color is established. [Objection:] If 'being the eye' means precisely the capacity to produce the cognition of color — let it be so; what is the fault? [Reply:] This is precisely what we call 'some other cause.' Similarly, if you too merely give the name 'special person' (<s>puruṣaviśeṣa</s>) to whatever is merely the substratum of intelligent-being-in-general, then we have no disagreement. What we dispute is that, in actuality, a special [property] such as omniscience and the like is established in the substratum of intelligent-being-in-general — just as the specific [property] of being the eye and the like [is established in each sense-organ]. Because neither the illustration nor the thing illustrated possesses the capacity to prove the specific [property].

children.translated_text: just as drying, breaking, and the like [are natural effects of non-sentient causes], inference of an intelligent [maker] would also follow [for them]. The negative example (<s>vaidharmyadṛṣṭānta</s>) of space and the like has already been refuted, because just as being preceded by an intelligent being [is possible there], so too being preceded by merely a cause is possible there — hence the basis for the absence of effecthood is not understood.

Now the nature of the proof (<s>sādhana</s>) is examined. This [property of] mere being-an-effect, which is common to <s>Meru</s>, <s>Mandara</s>, the earth, pots, cloth, and the like — that has been presented as the proof. But as long as its positive and negative concomitance with an intelligent [being] is not ascertained in even a single instance, its indicative capacity is unjustified. And that [concomitance] cannot be ascertained even in a dream. For let the effect characterized as a pot be apprehended [as arising] from a lump of clay when the potter's activity is present. But the negative concomitance — the absence of mere being-an-effect — before the [potter's] activity cannot be apprehended, because even in the absence of the potter, effects characterized as drying, breaking, and the like are observed in the lump of clay. And it is not [the case] that whatever is observed existing without something is an effect of that — because of over-extension. [Objection:] Let mere being-an-effect in the form of drying, breaking, and the like of the lump of clay, like grass and the like, also be made the subject. [Reply:] Let there be a negative concomitance of mere being-an-effect in the absence of an intelligent being — but demonstrate it even in a single instance, so that in the establishment of pervasion

By this, what was stated — 'There is no observation of deviation; by setting aside the specific individualities [of effects], we identify some other specific feature in pots and the like that consists in their coming into being after not existing, and on the basis of that we establish their being preceded by a person' — that too is rebutted. Because, even in the absence of a potter and the like, effects such as drying and breaking are observed in a lump of clay and the like, and therefore

children.text: nanu yadi kāryatvamātrasya na buddhimatā pratyakṣato vyāptigrahaḥ vyatirekābhāvāt, tvayāpi tarhi kathaṃ kṛtakatvasyānityatvena vyāptir avadhārayta iti cet | anapekṣālakṣaṇaviparyayabādhakapramāṇabalād iti brūmaḥ | tac cātadrūpaparāvṛttasyaiva kṛtakatvasya vipakṣād vyatirekaṃ sādhayati | na ca tvayā viparyayabādhakapramāṇam abhidhātuṃ śakyata iti prāg eva pratipāditam | sandigdhavipakṣavyāvṛttikatvād anaikāntikam idaṃ kāryatvamātram ||
children.translated_text: [Objection:] If the pervasion of mere effecthood with an intelligent [maker] is not grasped perceptually due to the absence of negative concomitance (<s>vyatireka</s>), then how do you too ascertain the pervasion of being produced (<s>kṛtakatva</s>) with impermanence (<s>anityatva</s>)? [Reply:] We say: through the force of counter-proof reasoning (<s>viparyayabādhaka</s>) whose defining characteristic is the absence of any further requirement. And that [reasoning] establishes the exclusion from the counter-positive of produced-ness, which is defined by the exclusion of what is not of that nature. But you are unable to state a counter-proof reasoning — as has already been demonstrated. Since its exclusion from the counter-positive is doubtful, this mere effecthood is an inconclusive (<s>anaikāntika</s>) [reason].

children.text: etena yad etat naiyāyikānām ākṣepaparihāraviḍambanam | iha khalu dve kāryatve | kāryamātram | viśiṣṭaṃ ca | tatrādyasya pratibandhāsiddher anaikāntikatvam | viśiṣṭasya bhūdharādiṣv asambhavād asiddhatvam iti | tad asaṅgatam | kāryatvamātrasyaiva pratibandhopapādanāt ||
children.translated_text: By this, the following display of objection-and-response by the <s>Naiyāyikas</s> [is also addressed]: 'Here indeed there are two kinds of effecthood: mere effecthood and qualified [effecthood]. Of the first, the invariable connection (<s>pratibandha</s>) is unestablished, hence it is inconclusive. The qualified [effecthood] is unestablished (<s>asiddha</s>) in mountains and the like because it does not apply there.' That is unfounded, because the invariable connection of mere effecthood itself is demonstrated.

children.text: yac coktaṃ viśiṣṭaṃ kāryatvam iti | kīdṛśaṃ punas tad iti vaktavyam | atha yat kāryaṃ puruṣānvayavyatirekānuvidhāyitayā tatpūrvakam upalabdham | yaddṛṣṭer akriyādarśino 'pi kṛtabuddhir utpadyate tat kāryaṃ sakalaprāsādādyanugataṃ bhūdharādivyāvṛttaṃ viśiṣṭam ity abhidhīyate | tad asundaram | vikalpānupapatteḥ ||
children.translated_text: As for what was stated about 'qualified effecthood' — what exactly is its nature? It must be specified. [They say:] That effect which is observed to be preceded by a person through conforming to the positive and negative concomitance of an intelligent [maker], and upon whose sight the conviction of [its being] made arises even in one who has not seen its manufacture — that effect, common to all palaces and the like but excluded from mountains and the like, is called 'qualified.' But that is inelegant, because of the impossibility of [logical] alternatives.

children.text: tathā cāha śaṅkaraḥ—kṛtabuddhiḥ kiṃ sādhyabuddhiḥ kiṃ vā sādhanabuddhiḥ | sādhyabuddhir api yadi gṛhītavyāptikasya, sā bhavaty eva | athāgṛhītavyāptikasya, kim anyatrāpi sā bhavantī dṛṣṭā | atha sādhanabuddhiḥ | tarhi svopagamavirodhaḥ, sarvasya bhāvasya kṛtakatvopagamād iti ||
children.translated_text: And so <s>Śaṅkara</s> [i.e., Śaṅkarasvāmin] says: Is this 'conviction of being made' (<s>kṛtabuddhi</s>) a cognition of the thesis (<s>sādhyabuddhi</s>), or a cognition of the reason (<s>sādhanabuddhi</s>)? If a cognition of the thesis: for one who has grasped the pervasion, it arises naturally; and for one who has not grasped the pervasion, has it been observed arising elsewhere too [i.e., in non-manufactured things]? If a cognition of the reason: then there is a contradiction with your own position, since you accept that all entities are effects.

payatu bhavān kiṃ buddhimadanvayavyatirekānuvidhānaṃ viśeṣaḥ | āhosvit tad darśanaṃ yat parvatādiṣu nastīty abhidhīyate | yadi pūrvakaḥ kalpaḥ, sa buddhimaddhetukatvaṃ tanubhuvanādīnām ātiṣṭhamānair abhyupeyata eva | na hi kāraṇaṃ kāryānanuvihitabhāvābhāvam anyo vaktyahrīkāt | atha taddarśanam iti caramaḥ kalpaḥ | na tarhi akriyā
children.translated_text: your honor examine this more carefully: Is the qualification the conformity to the positive and negative concomitance of an intelligent being? Or is it the observation [of that conformity], which is said to be absent in mountains and the like? If the first alternative, then those who maintain this must accept that bodies, worlds, and the like are indeed caused by an intelligent being. For no one except a shameless person would say that a cause does not conform in its existence and absence to its effect. If the last alternative — that it is the observation [of conformity] — then the arising of a conviction of being made in one who has not observed the making is impossible.

[Reply:] Well then! Since pots and the like that have come into existence are observed to conform to the positive and negative concomitance of an intelligent being, other things too — bodies, worlds, and the like — being of the same kind, cannot be pushed aside by a stick.',

children.text: upapannaiveti | kim asmākam adhikacintayety aṅgīkṛtyāpy u
children.translated_text: is well-founded. 'What need have we of further deliberation?' — [and] even though the qualified effecthood was accepted for the sake of argument,

children.text: ktaṃ viśiṣṭakāryatvam | tad eva tu nāstīti punar vistareṇa pratipāditam iti tad api sarvam anavadheyam eva | tathā hi kāryatvamātrasya tāvad uktena krameṇa vyāpter asiddhatvād anaikāntikatvam anirvāyam | yac ca viśiṣṭakāryatvaṃ vikalpya dūṣitaṃ tasyāsmābhir anabhyupagatatvāt taddūṣaṇāya prabandhaḥ prayāsaikaphalaḥ |  na hi kāryatvaṃ dvividham abhimatam | ekaṃ sarvakāryānugatam, aparaṃ parvatādivyāvṛttaṃ ghaṭapaṭaprāsādādyanuyāyīti | kiṃ tu kāryam anekajātīyakam | tatra yadi nāma paṭasya prāsādādibhiḥ saha vastutvasaṃsthānaviśeṣayogitvakāryatvādibhir dharmaiḥ sajātīyatvam asti tathāpi na tān dharmān buddhimatpūrvakānadhigacchati
children.translated_text: it has been demonstrated at length that it does not exist — so all of that too should be disregarded. For thus: the inconclusiveness of mere effecthood, whose pervasion is unestablished in the manner stated, is unavoidable. And as for the qualified effecthood that was examined and refuted — since we ourselves do not accept it, the effort spent refuting it has been fruitless. For effecthood is not accepted as being of two kinds — one common to all effects, and another excluded from mountains and the like and restricted to pots, cloths, palaces, and the like. Rather, effects are of many kinds. Among those, even if a cloth may be of the same kind as palaces and the like through properties such as substantiality, specific configuration, effecthood, and the like, nevertheless, conventional perception does not apprehend those properties as pervaded by an intelligent maker,

children.text: vyāvahārikaṃ pratyakṣaṃ, kāryatvādīnāṃ buddhimadvyatirekānuvidhānābhāvāt | tat kathaṃ prāsādaparvatādiṣu kāryatvādidarśanād buddhimadanumānam astu | kiṃ tu yasyaiva ghaṭajātīyakāryacakrasya vyatirekasiddhis tasya buddhimadvyāptatvaṃ pratyakṣataḥ sidhyatīty uktam | tena deśakālāntare ghaṭajātīyād eva buddhimadanumānam | yadā tu prāsādajātīyakam api buddhimaddhetukam ekatra pṛthag avadhāryate tadā tajjātīyād api buddhimatsiddhiḥ | evaṃ tattajjātīyasarāvodañcanaśakaṭapaṭakeyūraprabhṛtteḥ kāryacakrād buddhimatpūrvakatvena pṛthak pṛthag avadhāritād buddhimadanumānam anavadyam |
children.translated_text: because effecthood and the like do not conform to the negative concomitance of an intelligent being. How then can the observation of effecthood and the like in palaces, mountains, and so forth lead to the inference of an intelligent being? Rather, only the pervasion of the circle of effects of the pot-kind — for which negative concomitance is established — is established perceptually as pervaded by an intelligent being. Hence, inference of an intelligent being is possible only from the pot-kind in other places and times. And when the pervasion of the palace-kind too is separately ascertained as caused by an intelligent being in a particular instance, then inference of an intelligent being from that kind is also possible. Thus, from each separately ascertained circle of effects of various kinds — irrigation channels, carts, cloths, bracelets, and so forth — inference of an intelligent maker, separately established, is unobjectionable.

The gist of the matter here is as follows: To begin with, mere effecthood itself, through the invariable connection established in the manner described, when observed in mountains and the like, enables the inference of a [sentient] person — this being the establishment of our desired thesis

children.text: amum evārtham abhisandhāyācāryapādair abhihitam:
children.translated_text: It is with precisely this meaning in mind that the revered teacher (<s>Ācārya</s>) has stated:

children.text: siddhaṃ yādṛg adhiṣṭhātṛbhāvābhāvānuvṛttimat |
children.translated_text: 'That which is established as having a specific type of configuration and the like, conforming to the presence and absence of a superintendent —

children.text: sanniveśādi tad yuktaṃ tasmād yad anumīyate ||
(PV II 11)

children.translated_text: it is proper that inference be made from that.'

children.text: iti | evaṃ ghaṭapaṭaparvatadīnāṃ kāryatvavastutvādibhir dharmaiḥ sajātīyatve 'py avāntaraṃ ghaṭapaṭaparvatatvādijātibhedam ādāya lokasya vyāptigrāhakaṃ pratyakṣaṃ pravartata iti darśayituṃ saṃvyavahārapragalbhapuruṣabuddhyapekṣayā yaddarśanād akriyādarśino 'pi kṛtabuddhir bhavatīty uktam | na tu śāstraparavaśabuddhipuruṣāpekṣayā | tathā hi śāstrasaṃskārarahitasya vyavahārapragalbhasya puruṣasya devakulajātīyakaṃ puruṣapūrvakatayāvadhāritavato nagarād vanaṃ praviṣṭasya parvatadevakulayor darśane tayor dvayor apy akriyādarśino 'pi devakule kṛtabuddhir bhavati na parvate | tad anayor devakulaparvatayoḥ kāryatvādinā ekajātitve 'pi kṛtabuddhibhāvābhāvau na tayoḥ parvatadevakulatvalakṣaṇāvāntarajātibhedam anavasthāpya sthātuṃ prabhavataḥ | jātibhede ca siddhe devakulajātīye vyāpter grahaṇāt na parvatajātīyasya, na ca prāsādajātīyasya vyāptisiddhir iti na tato buddhimadanumānam | yadā tu prāsādasyāpi pṛthag vyāptigrahaḥ tadā tajjātīyād api buddhimadanumānam astu | na kṣitidharādijātīyasya svapne 'pi vyāptigrahaḥ | krīḍāparvatāder nāmamātrā
bhede 'pi parvatādibhir ekāntato bhinnasvarūpatvāt |
children.translated_text: are absolutely different in nature from [real] mountains and the like.
