children.translated_text: the first objection among the three <s>vikalpa</s>s has also been refuted through the resolution of the <s>āśrayāsiddhi</s> (unestablished substratum) defect.

children.text: dvitīyaṃ cāsaṅgatam, vikalpajñānena vyatirekasya pratītatvāt | na hy abhāvaḥ kaścidvigrahavān yaḥ sākṣātkartavyaḥ, api tu vikalpād eva vyavahartavyaḥ | na hy abhāvasya vikalpād anyā pratipattir apratipattir vā sarvathā | ubhayathāpi tadvyavahārahāniprasaṅgāt | evaṃ vaidharmyadṛṣṭāntasya hetuvyatirekasya ca vikalpād eva pratipattiḥ |
children.translated_text: And the second [objection] is also irrelevant, because the negative concomitance (<s>vyatireka</s>) is apprehended through conceptual cognition (<s>vikalpajñāna</s>). For absence is not some embodied thing that must be directly perceived; rather, it is to be dealt with through <s>vikalpa</s> alone. For a non-entity, there is no apprehension or non-apprehension other than through <s>vikalpa</s> at all — since in either case there would be the undesirable consequence of the loss of practical usage regarding it. Similarly, the apprehension of the dissimilar example (<s>vaidharmyadṛṣṭānta</s>) and of the negative concomitance of the <s>hetu</s> is through <s>vikalpa</s> alone.

children.text: tṛtīyam api dūṣaṇam asaṅgatam | vyāpakānupalambhena nirdoṣeṇa sattvasya kṣaṇikatvena vyāpter avyāhatatvāt |
children.translated_text: The third objection is also irrelevant, because the <s>vyāpti</s> (pervasion) of existence (<s>sattva</s>) with momentariness (<s>kṣaṇikatva</s>) remains unimpaired, [as established] through the faultless non-apprehension of the pervader (<s>vyāpakānupalambha</s>).

children.text: tad ayaṃ vyāpakānupalambho 'kṣaṇikasyāsattvam sattvasya tato vyatirekaṃ kṣaṇikatvena vyāptiṃ ca sādhayaty ekavyāpārātmakatvād iti sthitam ||
children.translated_text: Thus, this non-apprehension of the pervader establishes the non-existence of the <s>akṣaṇika</s>, the exclusion of existence (<s>sattva</s>) from it, and the pervasion [of existence] by momentariness — since these constitute a single operation. This is established.

children.text: nanu vyāpakānupalabdhir iti yady anupalabdhimātraṃ tadā na tasya sādhyabuddhijanakatvam avastutvāt | na cānyopalabdhir vyāpakānupalabdhir abhidhātuṃ śakyā bhūtalādivad anyasya kasyacid anupalabdher iti cet |
children.translated_text: [Objection:] If the non-apprehension of the pervader (<s>vyāpakānupalabdhi</s>) is merely non-apprehension, then it cannot generate the cognition of what is to be proved (<s>sādhya</s>), because it is a non-entity. Nor can it be said that the apprehension of something else constitutes the non-apprehension of the pervader, because — like the ground (<s>bhūtala</s>) and so forth — no other thing's apprehension [simply constitutes] non-apprehension [of the pervader].

children.text:
tad asaṅgatam | dharmyupalabdher
	  evānyatrānupalbdhitayā vyavasthāpanāt | yathā hi neha śiṃśapā
	  vṛkṣābhāvād ity atra vṛkṣāpekṣayā kevalapradeśasya dharmiṇa upalabdhir
	  vṛkṣānupalabdhiḥ | śiśapāpekṣayā ca kevalapradeśasya dharmiṇa
	  upalabdhir eva śiṃśapāyā abhāvopalabdhir iti
	  svabhāvahetuparyavasāyivyāpāro vyāpakānupalambhaḥ | tathā nityasya
	  dharmiṇo vikalpabuddhyavasitasya kramikāritvākramikāritvāpekṣayā
	  kevalagrahaṇād eva kramikāritvākramikāritvānupalambhaḥ |
	  arthakriyāpekṣayā ca kevalapratītir evārthakriyāyogapratītir iti
	  vyāpakānupalambhāntarād asya na kaścid viśeṣaḥ ||
children.translated_text: That is irrelevant. Because the apprehension of the <s>dharmin</s> (subject) itself is established as the non-apprehension of the other. Just as in 'there is no <s>śiṃśapā</s> tree here, because of the absence of a tree' — the apprehension of the bare location as the <s>dharmin</s> with respect to 'tree' constitutes the non-apprehension of tree, while the apprehension of the bare location as <s>dharmin</s> with respect to <s>śiṃśapā</s> constitutes the apprehension of the absence of <s>śiṃśapā</s> — thus the non-apprehension of the pervader has an operation that culminates in a <s>svabhāvahetu</s> (essential reason). Similarly, the mere apprehension of the permanent <s>dharmin</s>, as determined by conceptual cognition, with respect to sequential and simultaneous causal efficacy constitutes the non-apprehension of sequential and simultaneous causal efficacy. And the mere apprehension with respect to causal efficacy (<s>arthakriyā</s>) constitutes the apprehension of the impossibility of causal efficacy. Thus, this [argument] has no difference from other instances of the non-apprehension of the pervader.
Salutation to <s>Tārā</s>.

children.text:
adhyavasāyāpekṣayā ca bāhye 'kṣaṇike
	vastuni vyāpakābhāvād vyāpyābhāvasiddhivyavahāraḥ | adhyavasāyaś ca
	samanantarapratyayabalāyātākāraviśeṣayogād agṛhīte 'pi
	pravartanaśaktir boddhavyaḥ | īdṛśaś cādhyavasāyo
	'smaccitrādvaitasiddhau nirvāhitaḥ | sa cāvisaṃvādī vyavahāraḥ
	parihartum aśakyaḥ | yad vyāpakaśūnyaṃ tadvyāpyaśūnyam iti |
	etasyaivārthasyānenāpi krameṇa pratipādanāt | ayaṃ ca nyāyo yathā
	vastubhūte dharmiṇi tathāvastubhūte 'pīti ko viśeṣaḥ |
children.translated_text: And with respect to the external non-momentary entity (<s>vastu</s>), the practical usage establishing the absence of the pervaded follows from the absence of the pervader, through the operation of determinate cognition (<s>adhyavasāya</s>). And <s>adhyavasāya</s> should be understood as possessing the power of directing [action] even toward what is not [directly] apprehended, due to its connection with a specific form brought about by the force of the immediately preceding condition (<s>samanantarapratyaya</s>). And such <s>adhyavasāya</s> has been explained in our <s>Citrādvaitasiddhi</s> (Establishment of Variegated Non-duality). And that non-discordant practical usage cannot be avoided: 'whatever is devoid of the pervader is devoid of the pervaded' — since this very meaning is demonstrated through this procedure as well. And this principle applies equally whether the <s>dharmin</s> is a real entity or a non-entity — what difference is there?

children.text: tathā hy ekajñānasaṃsargy atra vikalpya eva | yathā ca hariṇaśirasi tenaikajñānasaṃsargi śṛṅgam upalabdhaṃ śaśaśirasy api tena sahaikajñānasaṃsargitvasambhāvanayaiva śṛṅgaṃ niṣidhyate, tathā nīlādāv apariniṣṭhitanityānityabhāve kramākramau svadharmiṇā sārdham ekajñānasaṃsargiṇau dṛṣṭau, yadi nitye bhavataḥ, nityagrāhijñāne svadharmiṇā nityena sahaiva gṛhye yātām iti sambhāvanayā ekajñānasaṃsargadvārakam eva pratiṣidhyate | kathaṃ punar etasminn ity ajñāne kramākramayor asphuraṇam iti yāvatā kramākramakroḍīkṛtam eva nityaṃ vikalpayām iti cet | ata eva bādhakāvatāro viparītāropam antareṇa tasya vaiyarthyāt |

kālāntare 'py ekarūpatayā nityatvam | kramākramau ca kṣaṇadvaye bhinnarūpatayā | tato nityatvasya kramākramikāryaśakteś ca parasparaparihārasthitilakṣaṇatayā durvāro virodha iti kathaṃ nitye kramākramayor antarbhāvaḥ | anantarbhāvāc ca śuddhanityavikalpena dūrīkṛtakramākramasamāropeṇa katham ullekhaḥ | tataś ca pratiyogini nitye 'pi vikalpyamāna ekajñānasaṃsargilakṣaṇaprāpte nityopalabdhir eva nityaviruddhasyānupalabhyamānasya kramākramasyānupalabdhiḥ | tata eva cārthakriyāśakter anupalabdhiḥ | tasmād vyāpakavivekidharmyupalabdhitayā na vyāpakānupalambhāntarād asya viśeṣaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Eternality means having a single form even at another time. And sequence and non-sequence [mean having] different forms even at two moments. Therefore, since eternality and the capacity for effects in sequence and non-sequence have the defining characteristic of mutually exclusive co-existence, the contradiction is irrefutable — so how can sequence and non-sequence be included in the eternal? And since they cannot be included, how can they be delineated by a pure eternality-concept from which the superimposition of sequence and non-sequence has been removed? Therefore, even when the counter-correlate — the eternal — is being conceptualized, attaining the status of being associated in a single cognition, the apprehension of the eternal is itself the non-apprehension of sequence and non-sequence, which, though contradicted by the eternal, is [simply] not apprehended. And from that very [non-apprehension], there is the non-apprehension of the capacity for causal efficacy (<s>arthakriyāśakti</s>). Therefore, since this is [in effect] an apprehension of the subject that discriminates the pervader, there is no difference between it and [any] other non-apprehension of the pervader.

children.text: na tv etad avastu dharmitvopayogivastvadhiṣṭhānatvāt pramāṇavyavasthāyā iti cet | kim idaṃ vastvadhiṣṭhānatvaṃ nāma | kiṃ pamparayāpi vastunaḥ sakāśād āgatatvam, atha vastuni kenacid ākāreṇa vyavahārakāraṇatvam, vastubhūtadharmipratibaddhatvaṃ vā |
children.translated_text: [Objection:] But this [reason] is not [valid], because it is a non-entity (<s>avastu</s>) — since the establishment of a valid means of knowledge requires a real entity as the basis of the property-locus (<s>dharmin</s>). [Reply:] What exactly is this 'real entity as basis'? Is it: having come from a real entity, even indirectly? Or: being a cause of convention regarding a real entity in some aspect? Or: being connected to a property-locus that is a real entity?

children.text: yady ādyaḥ pakṣas tadā kramākramasyārthakriyāyāś ca vyāptigrahaṇagocaravastupratibaddhatvam asyāpi na kṣīṇam |
children.translated_text: If the first alternative: then the connectedness of this [concept of sequence-and-non-sequence and causal efficacy] too with a real entity that is the object of the apprehension of pervasion is not diminished.

children.text: na dvitīye 'pi pakṣe doṣaḥ sambhavati, kṣaṇabhaṅgivastusādhanopāyatvād asya |
children.translated_text: Nor is there a fault in the second alternative, because this [concept] is a means of proving a real entity that is momentary.

children.text: na cāntimo 'pi vikalpaḥ kalpyate, tasyaiva nityavikalpasya vastuno dharmibhūtasya kramākramavad bāhyanityopādānaśūnyatvenārthakriyāvad bāhyanityopādānaśūnyatve prasādhanāt | paryudāsavṛttyā buddhisvabhāvabhūtākṣaṇikākāre vastubhūte dharmiṇi pratibaddhatvasambhavāt ||
children.translated_text: Nor is even the last alternative [to be] construed [against us], because the very eternality-concept — being the property-locus that is a real entity — is established as devoid of external-eternal-content, like sequence and non-sequence, just as [it is established as devoid of] causal efficacy, which [also] is devoid of external-eternal-content. Because a connection is possible with a property-locus that is a real entity — [namely,] the non-momentary aspect that is of the nature of cognition, being a real entity in the <s>paryudāsa</s> (nominally bound negation) sense.

children.text: ayam eva nyāyo na vaktā bandhyāsutaś caitanyābhāvād ityādau yojyaḥ | etena yathā vṛkṣābhāvādir antarbhāvayituṃ śakyate na tathāyam iti
children.translated_text: This very principle should be applied to [the reasoning] 'the speaker is not the son of a barren woman, because of the absence of consciousness' and the like. By this, <s>Trilocana</s>'s [argument]

children.text: trilocano
'pi nirastaḥ ||
children.translated_text: that 'just as the absence of a tree and the like can be subsumed [as a valid negation], this [case] cannot be [so subsumed]' — is also refuted.

children.text: na ca kramādyabhāvastrayīṃ doṣajātiṃ nātikrāmati, abhāvadharmatve 'pi āśrayāsiddhidoṣaparihārāt |
children.translated_text: And the absence of sequence and the like does not transgress the three classes of faults — even though it is a property of an absence — because the fault of the unestablished basis (<s>āśrayāsiddhi</s>) is avoided.

children.text: yat tv anena pramāṇāntarān nityānām asattvasiddhau kramādivirahasyābhāvadharmatā sidhyatīty uktam, tadbālasyāpi durabhidhānam | nityo hi dharmī | asattvaṃ sādhyam | kramikāryakāritvākramikāryakāritvaviraho hetuḥ | asya cābhāvadharmatvaṃ nāmāsattvalakṣaṇasvasādhyāvinābhāvitvam ucyate | tac ca kramākrameṇa sattvasya vyāptisiddhau sattvasya vyāpyasyābhāvena kramākramasya vyāpakasya viraho vyāptaḥ sidhyatīty abhāvadharmatvaṃ prāg eva vidhyor vyāptisādhanāt pratyakṣād anumānād ekasmād vā pramāṇāntarāt siddham iti netaretarāśrayadoṣaḥ |
children.translated_text: As for what he [the opponent] said — that 'the absence-property-status of the absence of sequence and the like is established by another means of valid knowledge [that proves] the non-existence of eternal things' — that is difficult to say even for a child. For the property-locus is 'the eternal'; the provable (<s>sādhya</s>) is 'non-existence' (<s>asattva</s>); the reason is 'the absence of the capacity to produce effects in sequence and non-sequence.' And its absence-property-status means its invariable concomitance with its own provable, viz., non-existence. And that is established: when the pervasion of existence (<s>sattva</s>) by sequence and non-sequence is established, the absence of sequence and non-sequence — being the absence of the pervaded [property, viz., existence] — is pervaded by the absence of the pervader — and so the absence-property-status is established prior to the demonstration of the pervasion of the two positive [properties], by perception, inference, or some other means of valid knowledge — so there is no fault of mutual dependence.

children.text: na ca sattāyām ivāsattāyām api tulyaḥ prasaṅgo bhinnanyāyatvāt | vastubhūtaṃ hi tatra sādhyaṃ sādhanaṃ ca | tayor dharmy api vastv eva yujyate |
children.translated_text: And the consequence does not equally apply to [the proof of] existence as it does to non-existence, because the reasoning is different. For there, both the provable and the proof are real entities (<s>vastu</s>). And for those, the property-locus too must be a real entity.

children.text: vastunas tu pratyakṣānumānābhyām eva siddhiḥ | tayor abhāve niyamenāśrayāsiddhir iti yuktam | asattāsādhane tv avastudharmo hetur avastuvikalpamātrasiddhe dharmiṇi nāśrayāsiddhidoṣeṇa dūṣayituṃ śakyaḥ | tathākṣaṇikasya kramayaugapadyābhyām arthakriyāvirodhaḥ sidhyaty eva |
children.translated_text: For a real entity is established only through perception and inference. In their absence, the basis is necessarily unestablished — this is justified. But in the proof of non-existence, the reason, which is a property of a non-entity, cannot be faulted with the defect of unestablished basis when the property-locus is established through conceptual construction alone. Similarly, the contradiction of the non-momentary with causal efficacy through sequence and simultaneity is certainly established.

children.text: tathā vikalpād evākṣaṇiko virodhī siddhaḥ | vikalpollikhitaś cāsya svabhāvo nāpara ity api vyavahartavyam | anyathā tadanuvādena kramākramādirahitatvādiniṣedhādikam ayuktam, tatsvarūpasyānullekhād anyasyollekhād ity akṣaṇikaśaśaviṣāṇādiśabdānuccāraṇaprasaṅgaḥ | asti ca | ato yathā pramāṇābhāve 'pi vikalpasiddhasya bandhyāsutādeḥ saundaryādiniṣedho 'nurūpas tathā vikalpopanītasyaivākṣaṇikarūpasya tata eva pratyanīkākāreṇa saha virodhavyavasthāyāṃ kīdṛśo doṣaḥ syāt | yadi cākṣaṇikānubhavābhāvād virodhapratiṣedhas tarhi bandhyāputrādyanubhavābhāvād eva saundaryādiniṣedho 'pi mā bhūt ||
children.translated_text: Likewise, the non-momentary — as a contradicting [entity] — is established from conceptual construction alone. And it should be maintained that its nature as delineated by conceptual construction is [precisely] this and nothing else. Otherwise, negation and the like — such as 'being devoid of sequence and non-sequence' — predicated of it [the eternal] by way of its [conceptual] description, would be unjustified, since its own nature is not delineated [and] something else is — and then there would be the absurd consequence of the non-utterance of words like 'non-momentary,' 'horn of a hare,' and the like. But they are [in fact] uttered. Therefore, just as the negation of beauty and the like of the son of a barren woman, established through conceptual construction even in the absence of a valid means of knowledge [for the referent], is appropriate — similarly, when the very non-momentary form, brought forth by conceptual construction alone, is established in contradiction with the form opposed to it through that very [conceptual construction] — what fault could there be? And if the absence of experience of the non-momentary [is used to block] the establishment of contradiction, then, by the very absence of experience of the son of a barren woman, the negation of his beauty and the like should also be [blocked]!

children.text: nanv evaṃ virodhasyāpāramārthikatvam | taddvāreṇa kṣaṇabhaṅgasiddhir apy apāramārthikī syād iti cet |
children.translated_text: [Objection:] If so, the contradiction would be non-ultimate (<s>apāramārthika</s>). And through that, the proof of momentariness too would be non-ultimate.

children.text: na hi virodho nāma vastvantaraṃ kiñcid ubhayakoṭidattapādasambandhābhidhānam iṣyate 'smābhir upapadyate vā yenaikasambandhino vastutvābhāve 'pāramārthikaṃ syāt | yathā tv iṣyate tathā pāramārthika eva | viruddhābhimatayor anyonyasvarūpaparihāramātraṃ virodhārthaḥ | sa ca bhāvābhāvayoḥ pāramārthika eva | na bhāvo 'bhāvarūpam āviśati, nāpy abhāvo bhāvarūpaṃ praviśatīti yo 'yam anayor asaṃkaraniyamaḥ sa eva pāramārthiko virodhaḥ | kālāntaraikarūpatayā hi nityatvam | kramākramau kṣaṇadvaye 'pi bhinnarūpatayā | tato nityatvakramākramikāryakāritvayor bhāvābhāvavad virodho 'sty eva ||
children.translated_text: [Reply:] No. For we do not accept or allow that contradiction is some other real entity with a relation established by having its feet in both relata — such that, in the absence of the reality of one relatum, it would be non-ultimate. Rather, as we accept it, it is entirely ultimate. The meaning of 'contradiction' is simply the mutual exclusion of each other's own-nature between the two that are considered contradictory. And that, between existence and non-existence, is entirely ultimate. Existence does not assume the form of non-existence, nor does non-existence assume the form of existence — this rule of their non-confusion is itself the ultimate contradiction. For eternality means having a single form even at another time. And sequence and non-sequence [mean having] different forms even at two moments. Therefore, between eternality and the capacity to produce effects in sequence and non-sequence, there is contradiction just as between existence and non-existence.

children.text: nanu nityatvaṃ kramayaugapadyavattvaṃ ca viruddhau dharmau vidhūya nāparo virodho nāma, kasya vāstavatvam iti cet |
children.translated_text: [Objection:] If the two contradictory properties — eternality and the possession of sequence-and-simultaneity — are set aside, there is no other [thing called] 'contradiction' — so what would be ultimately real?

children.text: na | na hi dharmāntarasya sambhavena virodhasya pāramārthikatvaṃ brūmaḥ | kiṃ tu viruddhayor dharmayoḥ sadbhāve | anyathā virodhanāmadharmāntarasambhave 'pi yadi na viruddhau dharmau kva pāramārthikavirodhasambhavaḥ | viruddhau ced dharmau tāvataiva tāttviko virodhavyavahāraḥ kim apareṇa pratijñāmātrasiddhena virodhanāmnā vastvantareṇa |
children.translated_text: [Reply:] No. For we do not assert the ultimate reality of contradiction by virtue of the existence of some other property [called 'contradiction']. Rather, [we assert it] by virtue of the existence of two contradictory properties. Otherwise, even if an additional property named 'contradiction' existed, if the two properties were not contradictory — where would the possibility of ultimate contradiction be? But if the two properties are contradictory, that alone suffices for the genuine convention of contradiction — what need is there for some other entity named 'contradiction,' established merely by assertion?

children.text:
tad ayaṃ pūrvapakṣasaṃkṣepaḥ
	gnityaṃ nāsti na vā pratītiviṣayas tenāśrayāsiddhatā hetoḥ svānubhavasya ca kṣatir ataḥ kṣiptaḥ sapakṣo 'pi ca |
	śūnyaś ca dvitayena sidhyati na cāsattā 'pi sattā yathā no nityena virodhasiddhir asatā śakyā kramāder api || J 89,16-19; cf. R 87,24-27 
	iti |
children.translated_text: This is the summary of the opponent's position: 'The eternal does not exist, nor is it an object of cognition — therefore [there is] the unestablished basis of the reason; one's own experience [of the eternal] is impaired; the positive example too is rejected; and [the reason] is devoid of both [positive and negative examples]; non-existence is not [established by the reason] just as existence is [not]; nor can the establishment of the contradiction of sequence and the like with the eternal be accomplished through a non-entity.'

children.text:
atra siddhāntasaṃkṣepaḥ 
	hdharmasya kasyacid avastuni mānasiddhā bādhāvidhivyavahṛtiḥ kim ihāsti no vā |
	kvāpy asti cet katham iyanti na dūṣaṇāni nāsty eva cet svavacanapratirodhasiddhiḥ ||  J 89,21-24; cf. R 88,4-7
children.translated_text: Here is the summary of the established conclusion: 'Is there or is there not, in a non-entity, an established-by-valid-cognition practice of invalidation, positive assertion, and convention regarding any property? If there is, at any point — then how [can you maintain] these many faults? And if there is not at all — then the establishment of contradiction with one's own words [is achieved]!'

children.text: tad evaṃ nityaṃ na kramikāryakāritvākramikāryakāritvayogīti paramārthaḥ | tataś ca sattāyuktam api naiveti paramārthaḥ | tataś ca kṣaṇikākṣaṇikaparihāreṇa rāśyantarābhāvād akṣaṇikān nivartamānam idaṃ sattvaṃ kṣaṇika eva viśrāmyat tena vyāptaṃ sidhyatīti sattvāt kṣaṇikatvasiddhir avirodhinī ||
children.translated_text: Thus, the ultimate [conclusion] is that the eternal does not possess the capacity to produce effects in sequence and non-sequence. And therefore the ultimate [conclusion] is that it does not possess existence (<s>sattā</s>) either. And therefore, since this [property of] existence — being excluded from the non-momentary — has no place in any other class [besides the momentary], being excluded from the non-momentary, it comes to rest only in the momentary, and being pervaded by that, it is proved. Thus, the proof of momentariness from existence is non-contradictory.

For here, what is associated in a single cognition (<s>ekajñānasaṃsargin</s>) is precisely what is to be conceptually constructed. And just as a horn observed on the head of a deer, being associated in a single cognition [with the deer], is negated [as existing] on the head of a hare precisely by the supposition that it would be associated in a single cognition with that [hare] — similarly, sequence and non-sequence, observed in association with one's own thesis-subject in the undetermined state of being eternal or non-eternal (as with blue and the like), if they belong to the eternal, should be apprehended in the cognition that grasps the eternal, together with the eternal thesis-subject itself — and it is by this very supposition that [their existence in the eternal] is negated through the door of association in a single cognition. [Objection:] But since there is ignorance as to whether [it is eternal] in this [instance], there is no shining forth of sequence and non-sequence — and yet we conceptualize the eternal as encompassing sequence and non-sequence. [Reply:] For precisely this reason the invalidator enters — because without the superimposition of the contrary, it would be pointless.

children.text: prakṛtiḥ sarvadharmāṇāṃ yad bodhān muktir iṣyate |
children.translated_text: 'The nature of all <s>dharmas</s> (phenomena), the realization of which is accepted as liberation —'

children.text: sa eva tīrthyanirmāthī kṣaṇabhaṅgaḥ prasādhitaḥ ||
children.translated_text: 'that very [momentariness], the destroyer of non-Buddhist [views], has been demonstrated as momentary destruction.'

children.text: iti kṛtir ayaṃ Ratnakīrteḥ ||

tad evaṃ pramāṇamātrāpratikṣepe pratyakṣaṃ
	tāvad ādau gaṇanīyam, tanmūlatvād aparapramāṇopapatteḥ | na ca cārvāko
	'py anumānam anavasthāpya sthātuṃ prabhavati, vyāpāratrayakaraṇāt |
children.translated_text: Thus, since means of knowledge in general are not rejected, perception should be counted first — because the coherence of other means of knowledge depends on its being the foundation. And even the <s>Cārvāka</s> is unable to remain without establishing inference — because he performs a threefold operation [of inference].

children.text:
tac chāstre hi
	pratyakṣetarasāmānyayoḥ pramāṇetaravidhānaṃ lakṣaṇapraṇayanato
	vidhātavyam | tac ca lakṣaṇaṃ pratyakṣe dharmiṇi lakṣye prāmāṇye
	pratyetavye svabhāvo hetuḥ | parabuddhipratipattau ca kāryādivyāpāraḥ
	kāryahetuḥ | paralokapratiṣedhe ca dṛśyānupalambho 'ṅgīkartavya iti
	katham anumānāpalāpaḥ | yad ācāryaḥ
children.translated_text: For in the [Buddhist] treatise, the establishment of [something] other [than perception] — in the general [domain of] perception-and-the-other [viz., inference] — is to be accomplished by the formulation of a definition, to establish the means of knowledge other [than perception]. And that definition [works as follows]: with respect to perception — the property-locus, the definiendum — in the provable, the validity to be cognized, the reason is own-nature (<s>svabhāva</s>). And for conveying [understanding] to another's intellect, the operation involving effect and the like [serves as] the effect-reason (<s>kāryahetu</s>). And in negating [the existence of] other worlds, the non-apprehension of what is fit to be apprehended (<s>dṛśyānupalambha</s>) must be accepted — so how can the rejection of inference [be maintained]? As the teacher (<s>Ācārya</s>) [says]:

children.text: pramāṇetarasāmānyasthiter anyadhiyo gateḥ |
children.translated_text: 'Because of the existence of [something] other [than perception] in the general [domain of] perception-and-the-other; because of the occurrence of another's cognition [through inference];

children.text: pramāṇāntarasadbhāvapratiṣedhāc ca kasyacit ||
children.translated_text: and because of the negation of some [other alleged] means of knowledge —'

children.text: pramāṇetarasāmānyasthiter anyadhiyo gateḥ /
pramāṇāntarasadbhāvaḥ pratiṣedhāc ca kasyacit //
(PVin I 2)
api ca
children.translated_text: Moreover:

children.text: arthasyāsambhave 'bhāvāt pratyakṣe 'pi pramāṇatā |

children.text: pratibaddhasvabhāvasya taddhetutve samaṃ dvayam ||
children.translated_text: For [an entity] whose own-nature is invariably connected [with another], when it is the reason for that [other] — both [perception and inference] are equal.'

Thus inference too is a means of knowledge. And its validity consists in its being the capacity to bring about [the attainment of]

	paramasaunārthād utpatteḥ, api tv arthadarśanād iti cet | kim idam

	draṣṭṛtvaṃ dṛśyatvaṃ ca na sambhavatīti kiṃ kenākṣipyatām | bhavatu vā
	prakārāntareṇāpi draṣṭṛdṛśyabhāvas tathāpi bhede saty avyabhicā
ra du
children.translated_text: the non-deviating

children.text:
tpattir eva prāptinimittam | sā ca prāpaṇaśaktiḥ
	pratyakṣānumānayor aviśiṣṭeti pramāṇe eva |
children.translated_text: origination alone is the ground of attainment. And that capacity for leading [to the object] is not different between perception (<s>pratyakṣa</s>) and inference (<s>anumāna</s>) — therefore, there are only [these] two means of valid knowledge.

children.text:
nanv anyad api śābdopamānādikaṃ pramāṇam
	asti | tathā hi śabdāc codanārūpād asannikṛṣṭe 'rthe svargādau yaj
	jñānam utpadyate tad api śābdaṃ jñānaṃ pramāṇam eva |
	pratyayitoditavākyaprasūtaṃ ca jñānaṃ pramāṇam | yad āha Kumārilaḥ
children.translated_text: Objection: There are also other means of valid knowledge (<s>pramāṇa</s>) such as verbal testimony (<s>śābda</s>), analogy (<s>upamāna</s>), etc. For from the Vedic injunction (<s>codanā</s>), regarding a non-proximate object such as heaven and the like, whatever cognition arises — that verbal cognition (<s>śābda jñāna</s>) is also indeed a valid means of knowledge. And cognition born from a statement uttered by a trustworthy person is also a valid means of knowledge. As <s>Kumārila</s> has said:

Objection: Let the capacity to lead to [its object] (<s>prāpaṇaśakti</s>) be the validity (<s>prāmāṇya</s>) [of a means of knowledge] — [this capacity arises] from the most excellent purpose (<s>paramasaunārthāt</s>), that is, from origination [in conformity with reality]. However, [we say it arises] from the apprehension of the object (<s>arthadarśana</s>). Reply: What is this 'apprehension of the object'? [Is it] the property of the object, namely visibility (<s>dṛśyatva</s>)? Or the property of cognition, namely the quality of being a seer (<s>draṣṭṛtva</s>)? On the first alternative, since visibility, like blueness, is also a universal property, an object that is the range of one [cognition] would become the range of all. For there is no difference among objects for each individual person, since that would entail the absurd consequence of selflessness (<s>nairātmya</s>) [of the objects]. On the second alternative, how could there be an expectation of an unrelated object when the quality of being a seer resides in another cognition-nature? Objection: The quality of being a seer, being impossible without visibility, implies the latter. Reply: But this establishment of the seer-visible relationship is precisely [based] on the conformity of origination (<s>utpattisārūpya</s>) between cognition and object. If [this conformity] is not accepted, neither the quality of being a seer nor visibility is possible — so what could imply what? Or even if the seer-visible relationship exists by some other means, nevertheless, when there is deviation,

children.text: tac cākartṛkato vākyād anyād vā pratyayito[?]ditāt |
children.translated_text: "That [verbal cognition arises] either from an authorless statement, or from [a statement] uttered by a trustworthy person" —

children.text: Find this! (Not in e-text of śv.)
iti |
children.translated_text: thus.

children.text: tatra yadā śabdasamutthaṃ jñānaṃ pramāṇaṃ tadopādānādibuddhiḥ phalam | yadā tu śabdas tadā tadālambanaṃ jñānaṃ phalam iti Naiyāyikasya punaḥ: āptopadeśaḥ śabdaḥ

, iti śabdapramāṇalakṣaṇasūtram | tatra śabda iti lakṣyapadam | āptopadeśa iti lakṣaṇapadam | asyāyaṃ saṃkṣepārthaḥ | āptopadiṣṭaḥ śabdaḥ pramāṇam iti | āptaś ca sākṣātkṛtaheyopādeyatattvo yathādṛṣṭasya cārthasyācikhyāsayā prayukta upadeṣṭā abhidhīyate | pramāṇaphalavyavasthā ca pūrvavad draṣṭavyeti |
children.translated_text: — this is the definitional <s>sūtra</s> of verbal testimony as a means of valid knowledge. Therein, '<s>śabda</s>' (word) is the term for the definiendum; '<s>āptopadeśa</s>' (instruction of a trustworthy person) is the definitional term. The summary meaning of this is: a word taught by a trustworthy person is a means of valid knowledge. And a trustworthy person (<s>āpta</s>) is one who has directly realized the truth about what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted, and who is motivated by the desire to communicate the object as it has been seen — [such a one] is called an instructor. The determination of the means of valid knowledge and its fruit should be understood as before.

In this regard: when the cognition produced from the word is the means of valid knowledge, then the cognition of taking up [an action] etc. is its fruit. But when the word [itself] is the means of valid knowledge, then the cognition that takes that [word] as its object is the fruit. Now for the <s>Naiyāyika</s> (logician), in turn: 'The instruction of a trustworthy person (<s>āpta</s>) is verbal testimony (<s>śabda</s>)'

children.text: tathā
Mīmāṃsakānām
children.translated_text: for the <s>Mīmāṃsakas</s>,

children.text: upamānaṃ pramāṇam | yad uktaṃ
children.translated_text: analogy (<s>upamāna</s>) is a means of valid knowledge. As stated

children.text: Śabarasvāminā
children.translated_text: by <s>Śabarasvāmin</s>:

children.text: upamānam api sādṛśyam
children.translated_text: "Analogy too is similarity (<s>sādṛśya</s>)"

children.text: asannikṛṣṭe 'rthe
children.translated_text: "regarding a non-proximate object"

children.text: 'rthe buddhim utpādayati | yathā gavayadarśanaṃ goḥ smaraṇasyeti |
children.translated_text: "it produces cognition. For example, the seeing of a <s>gavaya</s> (wild ox) produces the memory of a cow."

children.text: Cf.
: upamānam api sādṛśyam asaṃnikṛṣṭe 'rthe buddhim utpādayati, yathā gavayadarśanaṃ gosmaraṇasya.

children.translated_text: Likewise,

children.text: asyāyam arthaḥ | ekatra dṛśyamānaṃ sādṛśyaṃ kartṛ | pratiyogyantare dṛśyamānapratiyogisādṛśyaviśiṣṭatayaitatsādṛśyaviśiṣṭo 'sau ity asannikṛṣṭe 'rthe yāṃ buddhim utpādayati tadupamānaṃ pramāṇam iti yat tadoradhyāhāra iti |
tasmāt samaratīti smaraṇaṃ puruṣaḥ | tenāyam arthaḥ - yathā gavaye dṛśyamānaṃ sādṛśyaṃ gāṃ smarato manuṣyasya etatsādṛśyaviśiṣṭo 'sau gaur iti buddhim utpādayatīti |
children.translated_text: Therefore, '<s>smaraṇa</s>' (memory) means 'one who remembers (<s>samarati</s>),' i.e., the person. Thus the meaning is: just as the similarity perceived in a <s>gavaya</s> (wild ox), for the person who remembers the cow, produces the cognition 'that cow is qualified by this similarity' —

The meaning of this is: Similarity perceived in one [thing] is the agent. The cognition it produces regarding the non-proximate object — [cognition] of the form 'that one, qualified by the similarity to the counterpart seen in the other counterpart, is so qualified' — this [cognition produced by] analogy is the means of valid knowledge. That which is to be supplied [in the definition] is 'that [cognition].'

children.text: na cedam upamānaṃ smaraṇaṃ kartavyam, gavayasādṛśyaviśiṣṭasya gor goviśiṣṭasya ca sādṛśyasya prameyatvāt | gosādṛśyayor viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāvasyopamānapramāṇaviṣayasya gogrāhiṇā gavayagrāhiṇā vā pratyakṣeṇa kenacid agrahaṇāt | yad āha Bhaṭṭaḥ
children.translated_text: this analogy should not be reduced to mere memory, because the cow qualified by similarity to the <s>gavaya</s>, and the similarity qualified by the cow, are both objects of valid knowledge (<s>prameya</s>); and because the specific relation of qualifier and qualified between cow and similarity, which is the domain of the means of analogy, is not grasped by any perception — neither by that which grasps the cow, nor by that which grasps the <s>gavaya</s>. As <s>Bhaṭṭa</s> (<s>Kumārilabhaṭṭa</s>) has said:

children.text: pratyakṣe 'pi yathā deśe smaryamāṇe ca pāvake |
children.translated_text: "Even when the location is [known] through perception, and the fire through memory,

children.text: viśiṣṭasyānyataḥ siddher anumānapramāṇatā ||
children.translated_text: the qualified [whole], being established through something other [than either], has the character of inferential knowledge."

children.text: pratyakṣeṇāvabuddhe ca sādṛśye gavi ca smṛte |
children.translated_text: "Even when similarity is cognized through perception and the cow through memory,

children.text: viśiṣṭasyānyato 'siddher upamānapramāṇatā ||
children.translated_text: the qualified [whole], being not established through something other, has the character of analogical knowledge."

children.text: na ca grahaṇam antareṇa smaraṇam asti | tasmān nopamānaṃ smaraṇam ataḥ pramaṇam iti | Naiyāyikādīnāṃ tūpamānasūtram,
children.translated_text: And without apprehension, memory cannot occur. Therefore, analogy is not [reducible to] memory, and hence it is a [separate] means of valid knowledge. Now the <s>sūtra</s> of the <s>Naiyāyikas</s> and others on analogy [is]:

children.text: prasiddhasādharmyāt sādhyasādhanam upamānam iti |
children.translated_text: "Analogy is the means of establishing what is to be proved through the similarity of what is well-known."

children.text: asyāyam arthaḥ | prasiddhaṃ sādharmyaṃ yasya tasmād gavayādeḥ sādhyasya saṃjñāsaṃjñisambandhasya sādhanaṃ siddhis tadupamānaphalam | samākhyāsambandhapratipattihetur upamānam ity arthaḥ | ayam asya prapañcaḥ | yaḥ pratipattā gāṃ jānāti na gavayam, ādiṣṭaś ca svāminā gacchāraṇyaṃ gavayamānayāsmād iti, gavayaśabdavācyam artham ajānāno vanecaram anyaṃ vā tajjñaṃ pṛṣṭavān, bhrātaḥ kīdṛśo gavaya iti | tena cādiṣṭaṃ yathā gaus tathā gavaya iti | tasya śrutātideśavākyasya kasyāñcid araṇyānyām upagatasyātideśavākyārthsmaraṇasahakāri yad gavayasārūpyajñānaṃ tatprathamata evāsau gavayaśabdavācyo 'rtha iti pratipattiṃ prastuvānam upamānaṃ pramāṇam iti |
children.translated_text: The meaning of this is: from that which possesses well-known similarity — i.e., from the <s>gavaya</s> etc. — the establishment (<s>sādhana</s>) of the object to be proved, namely the relation between the name and the named (<s>saṃjñāsaṃjñisambandha</s>), is the fruit of analogy. In other words, analogy is the cause of the cognition of the relation of designation. The elaboration of this is as follows: A person who knows the cow but does not know the <s>gavaya</s>, who has been instructed by his master 'Go to the forest and bring the <s>gavaya</s>,' not knowing the object denoted by the word '<s>gavaya</s>,' asks a forest-dweller or another knower: 'Brother, what does a <s>gavaya</s> look like?' By him he is instructed: 'A <s>gavaya</s> is like a cow.' When that person, having heard this statement of extended comparison (<s>atideśa</s>), has gone to some forest, the cognition of similarity with the <s>gavaya</s>, in cooperation with the memory of the meaning of the comparative statement, first produces the cognition 'That object is the thing denoted by the word <s>gavaya</s>' — this, which initiates such cognition, is the means of valid knowledge called analogy.

children.text: tathārthāpattisaṃjñaṃ pramāṇaṃ mīmāṃsakasya | arthāpattir api dṛṣṭaḥ śruto vārtho 'nyathā nopadyamāno yad arthāntaraṃ parikalpayati sārthāpattiḥ | yathā jīvati devadatte gṛhābhāvadarśanena bahirbhāvasyārthasya parikalpanā | asyāyam arthaḥ | pratyakṣādibhiḥ ṣaḍbhiḥ pramāṇaiḥ prasiddho yo 'rthaḥ sa yena vinā na yujyate tasyārthasya kalpanam arthāpattir iti | sā ca ṣaṭpramāṇapūrvikā ṣaṭprakāraiveti ||
children.translated_text: Likewise, the means of valid knowledge designated <s>arthāpatti</s> (presumption) belongs to the <s>Mīmāṃsaka</s>. <s>Arthāpatti</s> is also [defined as follows]: when a seen or heard object cannot be otherwise [explained], the supposition of another fact — that is <s>arthāpatti</s>. For example, when <s>Devadatta</s> is alive, from the observation of his absence from the house, the supposition of the fact of his being outside. The meaning of this is: when an object established by the six means of valid knowledge (perception, etc.) cannot be consistent without something, the supposition of that something is <s>arthāpatti</s>. And since it is preceded by each of the six means of valid knowledge, it is itself sixfold.

children.text: pratyakṣānumānādipramāṇapañcakābhāvasvabhāvam abhāvākhyaṃ pramāṇam | prameyaṃ ghaṭādyabhāvaḥ | nāstīha ghaṭādīti jñānaṃ ghaṭādyabhāvālambanaṃ phalam | yadāha Kumārilaḥ
children.translated_text: The means of valid knowledge called <s>abhāva</s> (non-apprehension), whose nature is the absence of the five means of valid knowledge beginning with perception, inference, etc. The object of knowledge (<s>prameya</s>) is the absence of a pot, etc. The cognition 'There is no pot etc. here,' which takes as its object the absence of pot etc., is the fruit. As <s>Kumārila</s> has said:

children.text: pratyakṣāder anupattiḥ pramāṇābhāva ucyate |
children.translated_text: "The non-arising of perception and the rest is called the non-apprehension means of valid knowledge;

children.text: sātmano 'pariṇāmo vā vijñānaṃ vānyavastuni ||
children.translated_text: or it is the non-modification of self, or the cognition of another object."

children.text: pramāṇapañcakaṃ yatra vasturūpe na jāyate |
children.translated_text: "Where the five means of valid knowledge do not arise with respect to the form of a real entity,

children.text: vastusattāvabodhārthaṃ tatrābhāvapramāṇatā ||
children.translated_text: for the purpose of cognizing the existence of a real entity there, the means of valid knowledge is non-apprehension."

children.text: (ŚV XIII 11; 1)
iti |
children.translated_text: Thus.

children.text: etāni ṣaṭ pramāṇāni pratyakṣādīny asaṃkīrṇasvasvalakṣaṇayogitvād anyāpraviṣṭasvabhāvāni pratyetavyānīti ||
children.translated_text: These six means of valid knowledge beginning with perception — since each possesses its own unmixed definition — should be understood as having natures that do not enter into one another.

children.text: atrocyate | codanāyās tāvad bāhye 'rthe prati
bandhābhāvān na prāmāṇyam | prayogaḥ - yasya yatra
children.translated_text: it has no validity. The argument: That which has no invariable connection

children.text: pratibandho nāsti na
children.translated_text: with something does not

children.text: tasya tatra prāmāṇyam | yathā dahane 'pratibaddhasya rāsabhasya | apratibaddhāś ca bahirarthe vaidikāḥ
children.translated_text: have validity regarding it — like a donkey that has no invariable connection with fire. And the Vedic

children.text: śabdā iti
children.translated_text: words are without invariable connection

children.text: vyāpakānupalabdhiḥ | na tāvad ayam asiddho hetuḥ | śabdānāṃ vastutaḥ pratibandhābhāvāt | pratibaddhasvabhāvatā hi pratibandhaḥ | na ca sā nirnibandhanā, sarveṣāṃ sarvatra
children.translated_text: with external objects — this is a non-apprehension of the pervader (<s>vyāpakānupalabdhi</s>). Now, this reason is not unestablished, because words are in reality without invariable connection [with external objects]. For invariable connection is the state of having an invariably connected nature (<s>pratibaddhasvabhāvatā</s>). And that is not without a basis, since otherwise there would be the absurd consequence that everything would have an invariably connected nature with everything.

children.text: pratibaddha
children.translated_text: invariably connected

children.text: svabhāvatāprasaṅgāt |
children.translated_text: nature — that would be the absurd consequence.

children.text: nibandhanaṃ cāsyās tādātmyatadutpattibhyām anyan nopalabhyate, atatsvabhāvasyātadutpatteś ca tatrāpratibaddhasvabhāvatvāt | na hi śabdānāṃ bahirarthasvabhāvatāsti bhinnapratibhāsāvabodhaviṣayatvāt | nāpi śabdā bahirarthād upajāyante, artham antareṇāpi puruṣasyecchāpratibaddhavṛtteḥ śabdasyotpādadarśanāt |
children.translated_text: And the basis of this [invariable connection] is not found to be other than identity (<s>tādātmya</s>) and causal origination (<s>tadutpatti</s>), because that which does not have the nature of something and does not originate from it has no invariably connected nature with respect to it. For words do not have the nature of external objects, since they are objects of cognition with distinct appearances. Nor do words originate from external objects, since one observes the production of words from a person's effort-bound activity, even without any object.
To this we reply: First, as for the Vedic injunction (<s>codanā</s>), since there is no invariable connection (<s>pratibandha</s>) with external objects,

children.text: nanu yogyatayaiva kiñcit pratibaddhasvabhāvam upalabhyate | yathā cakṣur indriyaṃ rūpe | cakṣuḥ khalu vyāpāryamāṇaṃ rūpam evopalabhyati | tathaivaite vaidikāḥ śabdās tādātmyatadutpattiviyuktā api yogyatāmātreṇātīndriyam arthaṃ bodhayiṣyanti tat kathaṃ tādātmyatadutpattivirahamātreṇāpratibandho yenaivaṃ vyāpakānupalabdhiḥ sidhyatīti | naiṣa doṣaḥ | yataś cakṣur indriyam api rasādiparihāreṇa rūpa eva prakāśakatvena pratiniyataṃ tatkāryatvāt | rūpaṃ hi cakṣur upakaroti | na sattāmātreṇa cakṣū rūpaṃ prakāśayati, vyavahitasyāpi rūpopalabdhiprasaṅgāt | tasmād rūpād yogyadeśasannihitāt tajjñānajananayogyatām āsādya cakṣū rūpajñānam utpādayattatkāryam iti vyaktam avasīyate | anyathā tadupakārānapekṣasya tasyāpi tatprakāśananiyamo nopapadyate | na hy anupakāryatvāviśeṣe cakṣū rūpasyaiva prakāśakam, na rasāder iti ghaṭām upaiti niyamaḥ | ayam eva tarhi niyamaḥ kuto yad rūpeṇaiva cakṣur upakartavyam, na rasādineti | yadi vastuvaśād eva rūpam upakaroti na rasādikam, hanta tarhi yathopakāryatvaṃ prati niyamaś cakṣuṣo rūpeṇa, tathā śabdānām api svābhāvika evāstu bahirarthapratyāyananiyama iti |
children.translated_text: Objection: Something can be observed to have an invariably connected nature merely through fitness (<s>yogyatā</s>). For example, the visual sense-organ with respect to form. Indeed, the visual organ, when operative, perceives form alone. In the same way, even though these Vedic words are devoid of identity and causal origination [with respect to their objects], they will communicate supersensory objects through fitness alone. How then can non-invariable-connection be established merely from the absence of identity and causal origination, such that the non-apprehension of the pervader would succeed? Reply: This is no defect. For the visual sense-organ too is fixed in its capacity to illuminate form alone, to the exclusion of taste etc., because it is an effect of form. For form assists the eye. The eye does not illuminate form merely because it exists, since otherwise there would be the absurd consequence of perceiving even obstructed forms. Therefore, the eye, having obtained fitness to generate form-cognition from form present in a suitable location, produces form-cognition as its effect — this is clearly ascertained. Otherwise, the restriction that it illuminates only form, without depending on form's assistance, cannot be explained. For when there is no distinction in not being assisted, the restriction that the eye illuminates form alone and not taste etc. cannot hold. Then what is the source of the restriction that only form, not taste etc., assists the eye? If it is because, by the nature of things alone, form assists and not taste etc. — well then, just as the eye has its restriction regarding being assisted by form, so too let the words have a naturally inherent restriction regarding communicating external objects.

children.text:
atrocyate | na cakṣuṣaḥ svābhāviko rūpopakāryatāniyamaḥ,
	kasyacid vastunaḥ svābhāvikatvānupapatteḥ | tathā hi svābhāvikatvaṃ
	vastudharmasyānujānānaḥ praṣṭavyaḥ - kiṃ svābhāvika iti svato bhavati,
	āhosvit parataḥ, athāhetutaḥ | yadi svato bhavati, tad asaṅgatam,
	svātmani kriyāvirodhāt | athāhetutaḥ, tad ayuktam, ahetor
	deśādiniyamāyogāt | tasmān na svābhāviko rūpopakāryatāpratiniyamaś
	cakṣuṣaḥ | kiṃnibandhanas tarhi svahetupratibaddha iti, brūmaḥ -
	cakṣuḥ khalu svahetunā janyamānaṃ tādṛśam eva janitam
	yadrūpopakartavyam eva bhavati | rūpam api tādṛśam eva svahetunā
	janitaṃ yat tad upakārakasvabhāvam |
children.translated_text: To this we reply: There is no naturally inherent restriction of the eye regarding being assisted by form, because it is impossible for any property of any entity to be naturally inherent. For one who accepts 'natural inherence' as a property of a real entity should be asked: Does 'naturally inherent' mean arising from itself, or from another, or without a cause? If it arises from itself, that is incoherent, because of the contradiction of an action upon oneself. If without a cause, that is unreasonable, because a causeless thing cannot have restriction regarding location etc. Therefore, there is no naturally inherent restriction of the eye regarding being assisted by form. On what basis, then? We say: it is invariably connected with its own cause. For the eye, being produced by its own cause, is produced as precisely the sort [of thing] that must be assisted by form. And form too is produced by its own cause as precisely the sort [of thing] that has the nature of assisting [the eye].

children.text:
śabdānām api sa svabhāvaḥ svahetupratibaddho yenaite
	bāhyārthāvyabhicāriṇa iti cet | na śakyam evam abhidhātum,
	nityatvābhyupagamād vedavākyānām | athānityatvam abhyupagamyāyam
	ākṣepaḥ parihartum iṣyate, tad api duṣkaram, doṣāntaraprasaṅgāt | yadi
	svahetunaiva te niyamārthopadarśanaśaktimanto janitāḥ,
	tadāvyutpannasamayasyāpi svārtham avabodhayeyuḥ | yathā cakṣuḥ svaheto
	rūpaprakāśakam utpannaṃ sat prakāśayaty eva rūpam asaṅketavido 'pi, na
	ca śabdād uccaritāt prāgapratītasamayasyāpi viśeṣāvagamaḥ samasti |
	tasmān na svahetupratibaddhaś cakṣurāder iva śabdānām
	arthapratipādananiyama iti niścayaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Objection: Words too have that nature — invariably connected with their own cause — by which they are non-deviating from external objects. Reply: It is not possible to state this, because Vedic sentences are accepted as eternal [by the opponent]. If, on the other hand, one were to accept non-eternality and thereby seek to counter this objection, that too is difficult, because of the absurd consequence of another defect. For if they were produced by their own cause with the power to indicate the determinate object, then they would communicate their own meaning even to one who has not learned the convention (<s>samaya</s>). Just as the eye, produced by its own cause as an illuminator of form, illuminates form even for one who does not know any convention. But from a word that has been uttered, there is no apprehension of a specific [meaning] by one who has not previously learned the convention. Therefore, it is certain that words do not have a restriction regarding communicating objects that is invariably connected with their own cause, as the eye etc. do.

children.text: atha svahetubhir evāyam īdṛśas teṣāṃ svabhāvo datto yena te saṃketaviśeṣasahāyā eva kam apy artham avabodhayanti | na tarhi saṅketaparāvṛttau padārthāntaravṛttayo bhaveyuḥ | yadi hy ayam agnihotraśabdaḥ saṃketāpekṣo yāgaviśeṣapratipādakaḥ, kathaṃ saṅketānyatvenārthāntaraṃ pratipādayati | na hi kṣityādyapekṣeṇa bījena svahetor aṅkurajananasvabhāvenotpannena rāsabhaḥ śakyo janayitum, tathā śabdo 'pi yad arthapratipādananiyatas tam eva prakāśayet ||
children.translated_text: Objection: Perhaps it is precisely this nature that has been given to them by their own causes — that they communicate a certain object only with the assistance of a particular convention. Reply: Then, when the convention changes, they should not function with respect to a different meaning. For if this word '<s>agnihotra</s>' communicates a particular sacrifice depending on a convention, how can it communicate a different object through a different convention? For a sprout, produced by a seed — [whose] cause [gives it] the nature of generating a sprout in dependence on earth etc. — cannot be made to generate a donkey. Likewise, a word that has a fixed restriction regarding communicating [its] object should illuminate that very [object] alone.

children.text:
atha tattatsaṅketāpekṣas tattadarthapratyāyanayogya evāyaṃ
	jāta ity ucyate | tad api na prasutopayogi | na hy evam asya prāmāṇyam
	avatiṣṭhate | yadā hi saṅketenāpuruṣārthapratipādanam api sambhāvyata
	eva, tadā na śakyam upakalpayituṃ kim ayam abhimatasyaivārthasya
	dyotako na veti | tarhi vācyavācakalakṣaṇaḥ śabdārthayoḥ sambandho
	bhaviṣyati | tathā cāha
children.translated_text: Now, if it is said that [the word] is born capable of conveying particular meanings only in dependence on particular conventions — that too is of no use for the matter at hand. For its validity (<s>prāmāṇya</s>) does not stand thus. For when even the conveyance of what is not beneficial to a person is conceivable through convention, it cannot be determined whether this [word] indicates only the intended meaning or not. Then the relation between word and meaning will be of the nature of signified and signifier (<s>vācyavācaka</s>). And so it is said:

children.text: vācyavācakasambandhāḥ santi yady api vāstavāḥ |
children.translated_text: Even if the relations of signified and signifier are real,

children.text: saṅketair anabhivyaktā na te 'rthavyaktihetavaḥ ||
children.translated_text: without being manifested by conventions, they are not the causes of the manifestation of meaning.

children.text:
iti cet | nanu tasya vāstavatve 'saṅketavido 'py arthapratipattir
	  bhaved ity uktam, saṅketāpekṣāyāṃ cārthāntare na
	  pravartetetyādyabhihitam | ataḥ pūrvam evāyaṃ pratyākhyāto
	  vācyavācakalakṣaṇaḥ sambandhaḥ | tasmān na bahirarthe pratibandhaḥ
	śabdānām iti nirṇayaḥ ||
children.translated_text: [Objection:] But it has been said that if that [relation] were real, even one who does not know the convention would have cognition of the meaning; and that if convention is required, it would not operate regarding a different meaning, and so forth. Therefore, this relation characterized as signified-signifier has already been rejected. Hence, the conclusion is that words have no invariable connection (<s>pratibandha</s>) with external objects.

children.text: tataś ca nāsiddho hetuḥ ||
children.translated_text: Therefore, the reason is not unestablished.

children.text:
nāpy viruddhaḥ, viparyayavyāptyabhāvāt | tadabhāvaś ca
	sapakṣe vṛttyupadarśanāt | na hi viruddhasya sādharmyavati dharmiṇi
	sadbhāvo yuktaḥ, sādhyaviparyayasya tatrābhāvāt | na ca vyāpakam
	antareṇa vyāpyasya sambhavaḥ, tatpracyutiprasaṅgāt ||
children.translated_text: Nor is it contradictory (<s>viruddha</s>), because of the absence of pervasion with the contrary. And that absence [of pervasion with the contrary] is shown by demonstrating [the reason's] presence in the similar example (<s>sapakṣa</s>). For it is not proper for a contradictory [reason] to be present in a subject that possesses the similar property, because the contrary of the provable is absent there. And the pervaded cannot exist without the pervader, because there would follow the consequence of its deviation from that [pervader].

children.text: nāpy anaikāntiko hetuh, viparyaye bādhakapramāṇasambhavāt | prāmāṇyapratiṣedhe hi sādhye prāmāṇyam eva vipakṣaḥ | na ca tasmin pratibandhābhāvalakṣaṇo hetur asti, svaviruddhena pratibandhena vyāptatvāt | na khalv ayaṃ prādeśikaḥ pramāṇaśabdo jñāneṣu nirnibandhana eva, sarvajñāneṣu prāmāṇyavyapadeśaprasaṅgāt | nibandhanaṃ ca svaviṣayapratibandhād anyan nopapadyate | tasmāt pramāṇasya pramāṇavyapadeśaviṣayatvaṃ svaviṣayapratibandhena vyāptam | ataḥ pramāṇe dharmiṇi vipakṣe prāmāṇyasya viruddhavyāptasyopalambhena vipakṣe vyavacchedasiddher nānaikāntiko hetuḥ |
children.translated_text: Nor is the reason inconclusive (<s>anaikāntika</s>), because of the possibility of a counter-proof (<s>bādhaka pramāṇa</s>) regarding the contrary. For when the negation of validity (<s>prāmāṇya</s>) is the provable, validity itself is the dissimilar example (<s>vipakṣa</s>). And the reason characterized by the absence of invariable connection does not exist there [in the vipakṣa], because it is pervaded by an invariable connection that contradicts it. For this limited word 'valid cognition' (<s>pramāṇa</s>) is not applied to cognitions without any ground — otherwise there would be the consequence of calling all cognitions valid. And no ground other than invariable connection with its own object is tenable. Therefore, the designation 'valid cognition' for a valid cognition is pervaded by invariable connection with its own object. Hence, through the apprehension of validity — which is pervaded by the contradictory [property] — in the dissimilar example, the exclusion from the dissimilar example is established, and the reason is not inconclusive.

children.text: na cānyo doṣaḥ sambhavī | tasmān nirastāśeṣadoṣeṇa hetunā yat prasiddhaṃ tad upādeyam eva satām iti paṇḍitaśrījitāripādair eva vedāprāmāṇye darśitam |
children.translated_text: Nor is any other defect possible. Therefore, what is established by a reason from which all defects have been removed must be accepted by the wise — as has been demonstrated by the venerable <s>paṇḍita</s> <s>Jitāri</s> regarding the invalidity of the <s>Vedas</s>.

children.text: evaṃ ca vaidikaśabdānāṃ prāmāṇye niraste tadutthaṃ jñānam apy apramāṇam eva | āptapraṇītasya punar vacanasyārthāvyabhicāre tajjanmano jñānasyāvyabhicārasambhave 'pi na prāmāṇyam upagantuṃ śakyate, paracittavṛttīnām aśakyaniścayatvenāptatvāparijñānāt vacanasyāpi tatpraṇītatvāpratipatteḥ | prayogaś cātra -
children.translated_text: And thus, when the validity of Vedic words is removed, the cognition arising from them is also not valid. As for the statement of a trustworthy person (<s>āpta</s>), even if the non-deviation of the cognition born from it is possible when the statement does not deviate from the [true] meaning — still, its validity cannot be accepted, because the mental states of others cannot be ascertained with certainty, and hence the trustworthiness (<s>āptatva</s>) [of the speaker] is not known, and consequently the statement too is not recognized as composed by a trustworthy person. The formal argument here is:

children.text: yad yena rūpeṇa na niścitaṃ na tat tena rūpeṇa vyavahriyate | yathā rathyāpuruṣaḥ sarvajñatvena | na pratīyate cābhimatapuruṣa āptatveneti vyāpakānupalabdhiḥ ||
children.translated_text: Whatever is not ascertained in a certain form is not dealt with in that form — like a person in the street with respect to omniscience. And the person held [by you] to be [trustworthy] is not apprehended as trustworthy — this is a non-apprehension of the pervader (<s>vyāpakānupalabdhi</s>).

children.text: nāyam asiddhiḥ, āptābhimatasya tathātvāniścayāt | tathā hi paracittavṛttayo 'tīndriyatvān na pratyakṣasamadhigamyā iti kāyavāgvyavahārato 'numātavyāḥ | tau ca kāyavāgvyavahārau buddhir pūrvam anyathāpi kartuṃ śakyate | tatas tatpratibaddhatvenāniścayāt kathaṃ kāyavāgvyavahārato viśiṣṭaparacittavṛttyanumānam ||
children.translated_text: This [reason] is not unestablished, because of the non-ascertainment of the trustworthiness of the person held to be trustworthy. For thus: the mental states of others, being beyond the senses, cannot be ascertained through perception, and must therefore be inferred from bodily and verbal behavior. But both bodily and verbal behavior can be deliberately made otherwise by the mind beforehand. Therefore, since there is no certainty that [the mental states] are invariably connected with those [behaviors], how can the inference of specific mental states of others from bodily and verbal behavior [be valid]?

children.text: nāpi viruddhaḥ, sapakṣe sadbhāvasambhavāt ||
children.translated_text: Nor is it contradictory (<s>viruddha</s>), because of the possibility of its presence in the similar example.

children.text: nāpy anaikāntikaḥ, prāmāṇikatadrūpavyavahartavyatvaniścitatvayor vyāpyavyāpakabhūtayor vidhibhūtayor vṛkṣatvaśiṃśapātvayor iva pratyakṣānupalambhābhyāṃ sarvopasaṃhāreṇa vyāpteḥ siddhatvāt | tad ataḥ sādhanād doṣatrayarahitāt sādhyaṃ siddhyad avācyam eva | tad evam āptatvasya durbodhatvena tatpraṇītatvāniścayād ekaprahāranihatam āptavacasaḥ prāmāṇyam |
children.translated_text: Nor is it inconclusive (<s>anaikāntika</s>), because the pervasion is established through universal induction by perception and non-apprehension of the two [properties] — being a genuine [valid cognition] and being to be dealt with as having that form — which are pervaded and pervader, positive entities, like tree-hood and <s>śiṃśapā</s>-hood (being a particular kind of tree). Therefore, the provable, which is established by this proof free from the three defects, is simply undeniable. Thus, since trustworthiness (<s>āptatva</s>) is difficult to ascertain, and consequently the composition by a trustworthy person is uncertain, the validity of the trustworthy person's statement is demolished at a single stroke.

children.text: ato yad etasya prāmāṇyaprasiddhyarthaṃ vācaspatiprabhṛtīnāṃ valgitaṃ tadaprāptāvasaram eva | evaṃ pratyayoditam api bhaṭṭābhimataṃ śābdaṃ prāmāṇyaṃ vyastam iti boddhavyam | tasmāt sthitam etat na śābdaṃ bahirarthe pramāṇam astīti | buddhyākāre tu tatkāryaprasūtatvāt tadanumānam eveti |
children.translated_text: Therefore, the display by <s>Vācaspati</s> and others for the purpose of establishing its validity is simply out of place. Thus, the verbal validity maintained by <s>Bhaṭṭa</s> [i.e., <s>Kumārila</s>], which was raised as an objection, should be understood as refuted in detail. Therefore, this stands established: there is no verbal testimony (<s>śabda</s>) as a valid means of cognition regarding external objects. As for the mental image (<s>buddhyākāra</s>), since it arises as an effect of that [verbal cognition], it is merely an inference from that.

children.text:
mīmāṃsakoktaṃ tāvad upamānaṃ mānam eva na bhavati,
	nirviṣayatvād asya | ihāpi prayogaḥ - yasya na viṣayavattvaṃ na tasya
	prāmāṇyam | yathā keśoṇḍukajñānasya | na siddhaṃ ca viṣayavattvam
	upamānajñānasyeti vyāpakānupalambhaḥ |
children.translated_text: First, the comparison (<s>upamāna</s>) as maintained by the <s>Mīmāṃsakas</s> is simply not a valid means of cognition, because it has no object. Here too the formal argument is: Whatever lacks an object does not have validity — like the cognition of a ball of hair [by one with an eye disease]. And it is not established that the cognition from comparison has an object — this is a non-apprehension of the pervader.

children.text: nāyam asiddho hetuḥ, nirviṣayatvād upamānasya | tathā hi sādṛśyaviśiṣṭaḥ piṇḍaḥ piṇḍaviśiṣṭaṃ vā sādṛśyam upamānasya viṣayo varṇyate | na sadṛśavastuvyatiriktaṃ sādṛśyaṃ vyavasthāpayituṃ śakyate, pramāṇenāpratītatvāt |
nanu sādṛśyaṃ vastu durvāram eva | yadāha
children.translated_text: Objection: But similarity as a real entity is impossible to deny. As it is said:

This reason is not unestablished, because comparison is without an object. For thus: the object of comparison is described as either an individual qualified by similarity, or similarity qualified by the individual. But similarity as distinct from the similar thing cannot be established, because it is not apprehended by any means of valid cognition.

children.text: sādṛśyasya ca vastutvaṃ na śakyam apabādhitum |
children.translated_text: The reality of similarity cannot be refuted.

children.text: bhūyo 'vayavasāmānyayogo jātyantarasya tat ||
(ŚV XIII 18)

children.translated_text: It is the conjunction of a greater number of parts [in common] — that is another universal (<s>jāti</s>).

children.text: iti |
children.translated_text: Thus.

children.text: atrocyate | yadi sadṛśātiriktaṃ sādṛśyaṃ vastu dṛśyaṃ syāt, tadā dṛśyānupalambhagrastam eva, śāstrānāhitasaṃskāreṇāpi kenacit tasyādarśanāt | tasya cāstitve sarvaṃ sarvatrāstīty apravṛttinivṛttikaṃ jagadāpadyeta | athādṛśyaṃ tatsādṛśyam upeyate, tathāpi tatra prasiddhaliṅgābhāvād asiddham eva | siddhena ca tena viṣayavattopamānasya sidhyeta | sādṛśyapratyayas tu svahetos tathotpannena sadṛśavastunāpi kriyamāṇo ghaṭata eva iti na sādṛśyam upsthāpayituṃ prabhavati | upamānapramāṇabalād eva sādṛśyasiddhir iti cet | na | pramāṇāntarasiddhayor eva sādṛśyapiṇḍayor viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāvasyopamānaviṣayatvāt kathaṃ sādṛśyamātrasyopamānāt siddhiḥ | tataś ca sādṛśyasyāsiddher na tadviśiṣṭaḥ piṇḍaḥ piṇḍaviśiṣṭaṃ vā sādṛśyam upamānasya viṣayaḥ | tad evam upamānasya nirviṣayatvaṃ siddham iti nāsiddho hetuḥ | nāpi viruddhaḥ, sapakṣe bhāvāt |
children.translated_text: To this we reply: If similarity, as distinct from the similar things, were a visible real entity, then it would be consumed by the non-apprehension of the visible, since no one — even without dispositions cultivated by treatises — perceives it. And if it existed, everything would exist everywhere — the world would become one in which there is neither activity nor cessation. But if that similarity is held to be invisible, even so, due to the absence of a well-known inferential mark for it, it is simply unestablished. And if it were established, the comparison would thereby be established as having an object. But the cognition of similarity, being produced from a similar object by its own cause in the appropriate manner, is perfectly feasible — hence it cannot establish [the existence of] similarity [as a separate entity]. [Objection:] The establishment of similarity is from the very force of comparison as a means of valid cognition. [Reply:] No. Because the object of comparison is the qualifier-qualified relation between the similar thing and similarity, both of which are already established by other means of valid cognition — how then can mere similarity be established from comparison? Therefore, since similarity is not established, neither an individual qualified by similarity nor similarity qualified by an individual is the object of comparison. Thus, the objectlessness of comparison is established — hence the reason is not unestablished. Nor is it contradictory, because it is present in the similar example.

children.text: na cānaikāntikaḥ | tathā hi prāmāṇyānbhāve sādhye prāmāṇyam eva vipakṣaḥ | tac ca viṣayavattayā vyāptam, nirnimittatve sarvajñānaprāmāṇyaprasaṅgāt | tad yaṃ viruddhavyāptopalabdhyā vipakṣān nivartamāno viṣayavattvābhāvalakṣaṇo hetuḥ prāmāṇyābhāvalakṣaṇa eva viśrāmyatīti vyāptisiddhiḥ | ato nopamānaṃ pramāṇam iti |
children.translated_text: Nor is it inconclusive. For thus: when the absence of validity is the provable, validity itself is the dissimilar example. And that [validity] is pervaded by having an object, because otherwise there would be the consequence of calling all cognitions valid if [validity] had no ground. Therefore, this reason — characterized by the absence of having an object — which excludes itself from the dissimilar example through the apprehension of what is pervaded by the contradictory, comes to rest in the provable characterized by the absence of validity — thus the pervasion is established. Therefore, comparison is not a valid means of cognition.

children.text:
naiyāyikaparikalpitopamānanirākaraṇārtham apy ayam eva prayogo
	draṣṭavyaḥ, tasyāpi nirviṣayatvāt | tathā hi samākhyāsambandhas tasya
	viṣayo varṇyate | sa ca paramārthato nāsti | sa hi sambandhaḥ
	sambandhibhyāṃ bhinno 'bhinno vā | yadi bhinnas tadā tayor iti kutaḥ |
	na ca sambandhāntarād iti vaktavyam, tad api kathaṃ teṣām iti cintāyām
	anavasthāprasaṅgaḥ | na ca yathā pradīpaḥ prakāśāntaram antareṇa
	prakāśate tathā sambandho 'pi sambandhāntareṇa sambaddho bhaviṣyatīti
	vaktum ucitam | pramāṇasiddhe hi vasturūpe 'yam asya svabhāva iti
	varṇyate | yathā pradīpasyaiva | sambandhas tu na pramāṇapratītaḥ |
	tat ka evaṃ jānātv ayam asya svabhāva iti, yad vā nāsty evāyam iti |
	ayam anayoḥ sambandhaḥ sambaddhāv etāv iti tu buddhiḥ svahetubalāt
	sambaddhavastudvayād api sambhāvyamānā na sambandham ākṣeptuṃ
	prabhavati | tasmān na bhinnasambandhasiddhiḥ | athābhinnaḥ tadā
	sambandhināv eva kevalāv iti na samākhyāsambandho nāma, yaḥ kaścid
	upamānasya viṣayaḥ syāt | nanu sambandhabuddhijanakatvaṃ
	sambaddhapadārthād bhinnam abhinnaṃ vā | bhede ca sa eva sambandhaḥ
	nāmni paraṃ vivādaḥ | athābhinnam, tadā yathā sambaddhapadārthasya
	svabhāvaḥ sarvapadārthasādhāraṇas tathā tad api rūpaṃ tadavyatibhinnaṃ
	sarvapadārthasādhāraṇam iti sa padārtho 'bhimatapadārtheneva parair
	api padārthaiḥ saha sambaddhaḥ syāt |
children.translated_text: For the purpose of refuting the comparison as conceived by the <s>Naiyāyikas</s> too, this very same formal argument should be examined, because that too is without an object. For thus: the relation of name and named (<s>samākhyāsambandha</s>) is described as its object. But that does not exist ultimately. For that relation is either different from or identical with the relata. If different, then how is it 'theirs' [i.e., belonging to the relata]? And one should not say 'through another relation,' because in considering how that [further relation] too belongs to them, there follows an infinite regress. And it is not proper to say that just as a lamp illuminates without another illumination, so too a relation will be connected without another relation. For when a real nature established by a means of valid cognition [is in question], one describes 'this is its essential nature' — as in the case of the lamp itself. But a relation is not apprehended by a means of valid cognition. So who knows in this way 'this is its essential nature,' or indeed 'this does not exist at all'? But the cognition 'this is the relation of these two, these two are related' — being possible through the force of its own cause even from a pair of related things — cannot establish a [separate] relation. Therefore, there is no establishment of a relation as different [from the relata]. But if identical, then the relata alone exist by themselves — there is no such thing as a name-named relation that could be the object of comparison.

children.text: na caivam, tasmād bhinnaṃ tatsambandhabuddhijanakatvaṃ sambaddhapadārthād eṣṭavyam iti cet | nanv etad āśaṅkya Rājakulapādaiḥ parihṛtam eva | tathā hi
children.translated_text: [Objection:] The capacity to generate the cognition of relation, being either different or identical with the related entity — if identical, then just as the essential nature of the related entity is common to all entities, so too that form, being indistinct from it, would be common to all entities, and that entity would be related to all other entities as well as to the intended entity. And since this is not the case, that capacity to generate the cognition of relation must be sought as different from the related entity. [Reply:] But this objection has already been answered by the venerable <s>Rājakula</s> [i.e., <s>Jitāri</s>]. For thus:

children.text: sambaddhaṃ svayam eva cen nanu yathā taṃ tasya sambandhinaṃ pratyātmā jagatīm api prati tathā tat kena yogo 'sya na |
children.translated_text: If [the entity] is related by itself, then just as it is a relatum of that [intended correlate], so too it would be [a relatum] of the whole world — why would it not have connection with [everything]?

children.text: sambandhe parato 'pi tulyam akhilaṃ tenaiva cet saṃyamo hetuḥ kiṃ na niyāmakaḥ sa ca kathaṃ yogaḥ kvacin nāpare ||
children.translated_text: Even if [the connection comes] from another relation, everything is the same [problem]. If that very [relation] is the restraining [principle], why is that cause not determinative? And how is that connection in some [cases] and not in others?

children.text: iti | tasmāt sambandhābhāvāt pūrvoktena nyāyena sārūpyābhāvāc cāsiddhaṃ naiyāyikasyāpi nirviṣayam upamānaṃ pramāṇam ato 'nantareṇaiva vyāpakānupalambhena nirākṛtam |
children.translated_text: Therefore, because of the absence of relation, and because of the absence of similarity by the reasoning stated earlier, the comparison of the <s>Naiyāyikas</s> too is unestablished, without an object, and not a valid means of cognition — thus it is refuted by the very same non-apprehension of the pervader stated just before.

children.text: arthāpattir api | yad etat sāmānyalakṣaṇaṃ pratyakṣādipratīto yo 'rthaḥ sa yena vinā nopapadyate tasyārthasya parikalpanam athāpattir ity atra vicāryate | yasyārthasya darśanād yo 'rthaḥ parikalpyate tayor yadi pratibandho 'sti tadārthāpattir anumānam eva | athāpattir iti nāmāntarakaraṇe nāsmākaṃ kācid vipratipattiḥ | tathā hi pramāṇaparidṛṣṭo 'rthaḥ kenacid vinā nopapadyata iti kuto labhyate, yadi paridṛśyamānaparikalpyamānayoḥ kaścit sambandhaḥ syāt | anyathā tena vinā nopapadyata ity ahrīkād anyo na brūyāt, ghaṭapaṭavat | sa ca sambandhaḥ kvacit pūrvam avaśyaṃ pratyakṣānupalambhataḥ, kvacid adṛśyatve 'pi viparyayabādhakapramāṇabalād vā niścetavyaḥ | anyathā tena vinānupapattijñānasyaivānupapatteḥ | sati caivam, ekaṃ sambadhinaṃ dṛṣṭvā yatrasthena vinā tatrasthaṃ nopapadyate, tasya dvitīyasya sambandhinaḥ kalpanam anumānam eva | tatra svabhāvapratibandhe svabhāvahetujaiva sārthāpattiḥ | tadutpattipratibandhe kāryaliṅgajaiva | tad uktam: anyathānupapannatvam anvayavyatirekiṇy arthe bhavati yat, tasmān nārthāpattiḥ, pramāṇāntaram iti | tasmāt paridṛśyamānaparikalpyamānayoḥ sati pratibandhe nārthāpattiḥ pramāṇāntaram iti | atha tayor na pratibandhaḥ, tadārthāpattiḥ pramāṇam eva na bhavatīti mantavyam, sākṣāt pāramparyeṇa ca sambandhābhāvāt | yasya yatra pratibandho nāsti na tasya tatra prāmāṇyam ityādir vedanirākaraṇārthaṃ yaḥ pūrvam upanyastaḥ sa evāsyā api prāmāṇyanirākaraṇāya draṣṭavyaḥ | sāmānyenaivārthāpattau nirākṛtāyāṃ pratyakṣādir pūrvakatvalakṣaṇas tatprapañco nirasto bhavaty eveti tadarthaṃ na prabandho 'bhidhīyate, gavi nirākṛte śāvaleyanirākṛtivat | tasmān nārthāpattiḥ pramāṇāntaram iti |
children.translated_text: <s>Arthāpatti</s> (postulation) too [is examined]. The general definition is examined here: 'the supposition of that thing without which a thing cognized through perception and the like would be inexplicable is <s>arthāpatti</s>.' If there is a necessary connection (<s>pratibandha</s>) between the thing from the seeing of which another thing is supposed, then <s>arthāpatti</s> is simply inference (<s>anumāna</s>). We have no objection to its merely being given another name. For thus: from where is it obtained that an object ascertained by a valid cognition is inexplicable without something else, unless there is some relation between the observed and the supposed? Otherwise, no one but a shameless person would say 'it is inexplicable without that' — just as [one would not say so] with a pot and a cloth [which are unrelated]. And that relation must in some cases have been previously [established] through perception or non-apprehension, and in other cases, even when invisible, must be ascertained through the force of a counter-proof (<s>bādhaka</s>) that refutes the contrary. Otherwise, the very cognition of inexplicability-without-that would itself be inexplicable. And this being so, having seen one relatum, the supposition of the second relatum — without which, being located there, the first located there would be inexplicable — is simply inference. In the case of a natural connection (<s>svabhāvapratibandha</s>), that <s>arthāpatti</s> is essentially born of a natural reason (<s>svabhāvahetu</s>). In the case of a causal-origin connection (<s>tadutpattipratibandha</s>), it is essentially born of an effect-mark (<s>kāryaliṅga</s>). As stated: 'The fact of being otherwise-inexplicable pertains to a thing that has positive and negative concomitance; therefore <s>arthāpatti</s> is not a separate means of valid cognition.' Therefore, when there is a necessary connection between the observed and the supposed, <s>arthāpatti</s> is not a separate <s>pramāṇa</s>. But if there is no necessary connection between them, then <s>arthāpatti</s> must be regarded as not a <s>pramāṇa</s> at all, because of the absence of relation both directly and indirectly. The argument previously adduced for the refutation of the <s>Veda</s> — 'for that which has no necessary connection with something, there is no validity regarding it' and so on — should be applied here too for the refutation of its validity. Since <s>arthāpatti</s> is thus refuted in general, the elaboration of it that is characterized by perception and the like as prior [conditions] is also thereby refuted — hence no separate treatise is composed for that purpose, just as when a cow is refuted, the refutation of a dappled cow [follows automatically]. Therefore, <s>arthāpatti</s> is not a separate means of valid cognition.

children.text: tathā abhāvapramāṇasyāpi prāmāṇyaṃ nopapadyate, tasyāpi nirviṣayatvāt | tataś ca Mīmāṃsakopavalgitopamānanirākaraṇārtham upanyasto yo viṣayavattvābhāvalakṣaṇo 'nupalambhaḥ sa evāsyāpi nirāsārtham upanyasitavyaḥ | nanu cātrāsiddho hetuḥ |
children.translated_text: Likewise, the validity of the <s>pramāṇa</s> of <s>abhāva</s> (absence) is also untenable, because it too is without an object. Therefore, the non-apprehension characterized by the absence of objecthood (<s>viṣayavattvābhāva</s>), which was adduced for the refutation of the <s>upamāna</s> championed by the <s>Mīmāṃsakas</s>, should be adduced for the refutation of this [<s>abhāva-pramāṇa</s>] as well. [Objection:] But here the reason is unestablished.

children.text: tathā hi yadi ghaṭābhāvo vāstavaḥ prameyabhūto na syāt, tadā nāstīha ghaṭa iti pratyayaḥ katham utpadyata iti cet | kevalapradeśagrāhipratyakṣād iti brūmaḥ | nanu yadi kaivalyaṃ pradeśasvarūpaṃ tat tarhi saghaṭe 'pi pradeśe vidyata iti tatrāpi tasya pratyayasya sadbhāvaprasaṅgaḥ | athātiriktaḥ, mukhāntareṇābhāva evābhyupagato bhavatīti cet, na |
children.translated_text: For thus: if the absence of a pot were not a real thing and an object of valid cognition, then how would the cognition 'there is no pot here' arise? [Reply:] We say: from perception that apprehends the bare locus alone. [Objection:] But if it is merely the intrinsic nature of the locus in isolation, then that [nature] exists even in a locus that has a pot, and so the absurd consequence would follow that such a cognition exists there too. Or if [the nature of the locus without a pot] is something additional, then absence itself is accepted by another route. [Reply:] No.

children.text: kaivalyaṃ tadviviktatvam asaṅkīrṇatvam ityādibhiḥ padaiḥ pradeśasya ghaṭaṃ pratyanāpannādhārabhāvasya svahetuta utpannasya ghaṭapradeśād anya evātmābhidhīyate | sa eva cābhāvapratyayaṃ janayatīti kim apareṇābhāvena kartavyam |
children.translated_text: By the words 'isolation,' 'being separated from that,' 'being unmixed' and so on, what is denoted is precisely the distinct essential nature of the locus — which has not assumed the state of being a substratum for the pot, and which has arisen from its own cause — as different from the locus-with-a-pot. And it is that very [locus-nature] that generates the cognition of absence — so what need is there for a separate absence?

children.text: nanu ghaṭaṃ pratyanāpannādhārabhāvasya pradeśasyeti ghaṭābhāvayuktasya pradeśasyety uktaṃ bhavatīti cet | tarhi ghaṭābhāvo 'pi ghaṭaṃ pratyanāpannādhārabhāvaḥ kim abhāvāntareṇa svarūpeṇaiva vā | prathamapakṣe 'navasthā | atha tadabhāvarūpatvād abhāvāntaram antareṇaiva ghaṭābhāvo ghaṭaṃ pratyanāpannādhārabhāvaḥ | yady evam asahāyaḥ pradeśaviśeṣo 'pi paryudāsavṛttyā ghaṭābhāvarūpatvād abhāvaṃ vinaiva ghaṭaṃ pratyanāpannādhārabhāvo yukta iti kim akāṇḍam āhopuruṣikayā mithyāpralāpenābodhaviklavaṃ śiṣyapudgalam ākulayasi | tasmād bhūtalātiriktasyābhāvasyāsiddhatvān nāyaṃ viṣayavattābhāvalakṣaṇo hetur asiddhaḥ | pramāṇapañcakābhāvād eva tu prameyābhāvasiddhipratyāśāpi na yujyate, vipratipattiviṣayatvād asyānenaiva prameyābhāvasiddher ayogāt |
children.translated_text: [Objection:] But saying 'the locus that has not assumed the state of being a substratum for the pot' amounts to saying 'the locus that is conjoined with the absence of a pot.' [Reply:] Then, is the absence of the pot — which consists in not having assumed the state of being a substratum for the pot — [itself constituted] by yet another absence, or by its own intrinsic nature? In the first alternative, there is infinite regress. But if, because it has the nature of that absence, the absence of the pot is 'not having assumed the state of being a substratum for the pot' without requiring yet another absence — then if so, an unaccompanied particular locus too, by the exclusion-mode (<s>paryudāsa</s>), having the nature of the absence of the pot, is fit to be 'not having assumed the state of being a substratum for the pot' even without absence — so why do you pointlessly confuse your helpless pupil with false prattle and bravado? Therefore, since absence as something additional to the ground is unestablished, this reason characterized by the absence of objecthood is not unestablished. But since there is no establishment of the absence of a <s>prameya</s> (knowable) from the mere absence of the five <s>pramāṇas</s>, the hope for that is also unjustified, because this [absence of the knowable] is the very subject of dispute, and its establishment cannot properly come from this [mere absence of <s>pramāṇas</s>] alone.
