children.text: yad apy uktam | cittaśarīrayoḥ kiyatkālasthitinibandhanasya dṛṣṭasya nivṛttau cittasyāpi nivṛttiprasaṅgaḥ | maraṇavedanayā hi cittaṃ vikalam | tato 'vikalā cittāntarajananāvasthā na sambhavati | tasmād upasthite maraṇaduḥkhe sarvasaṃskāravirodhini cittam apy ucchidyeteti nāstikyam āyātam iti |
children.translated_text: As for the objection: 'Since the dependence of mind and body for a certain duration of stability has been observed, upon the cessation [of the body], there would be the consequence of the cessation of mind as well. For the mind is impaired by the sensation of death. From that, a condition for the birth of another mind that is not impaired is not possible. Therefore, when the suffering of death — which opposes all latent impressions — is at hand, the mind too would be annihilated' — thus nihilism (<s>nāstikya</s>) has arrived.

children.text: tad ayuktam | yato maraṇaduḥkhaṃ cittaviśeṣa eva, tasya cittāntarajananasāmarthyasvabhāvasya svabhāvād avāryaiva jñānotpattir iti |
children.translated_text: That is unjustified. Because the suffering of death is itself a particular mental state (<s>cittaviśeṣa</s>), and since its nature is the capacity to generate another mental state, the arising of cognition from its essential nature is simply unpreventable.

children.text: bandhān mokṣo 'pi saṃsāricittaprabandhād anāśravacittaprabandho yaḥ |
children.translated_text: Liberation (<s>mokṣa</s>) from bondage, too, is the stream of undefiled consciousness (<s>anāśravacittaprabandha</s>) [that arises] from the stream of <s>saṃsāric</s> consciousness.

children.text: śubhādimokṣayor api pravṛttir avāryā | yataḥ saty apy ātmany aham eva mukto bhaviṣyāmi sukhī cety ātmagrahalakṣaṇād adhyavasāyāt pravartate | na punar ātmanā galahastitaḥ | sa cānādyavidyāparamparāyātaḥ pūrvāparayor ekatvāropako mithyāsaṅkalpo bādhite 'py ātmany avyāhataprasara iti katham apravṛttiḥ |
children.translated_text: The engagement in virtuous [action] and liberation too is unpreventable. Because even when a self (<s>ātman</s>) exists, one engages [in action] from the determination characterized by self-apprehension: 'I myself shall be liberated, I shall be happy.' One is not dragged by the throat by the self. And this false conceptualization (<s>mithyāsaṅkalpa</s>), which superimposes unity upon the earlier and later [moments] and which has come down through a beginningless chain of ignorance (<s>avidyā</s>), continues unobstructed even when the self is refuted — so how can there be non-engagement?

children.text: nanu
children.translated_text: [Objection:] But

Similarly, memory, desire, the search for what one has previously deposited, the cessation of curiosity about what has been seen, the connection of action and result (<s>karmaphalasambandha</s>), and the determination preceded by doubt — all these are properly explained as being produced by the later experiences of objects, which are the effects (<s>upādeya</s>), bearing the impregnation of latent impressions (<s>saṃskāra</s>) contributed by the earlier experiences of objects that are the material causes (<s>upādāna</s>). What need is there for an additionally imagined self (<s>ātman</s>)?

children.text: nairātmyavādapakṣe [tu] pūrvam evāvabudhyate |
children.translated_text: in the position of the no-self doctrine (<s>nairātmyavāda</s>), one understands from the very beginning:

children.text: madvināśāt phalaṃ na syān matto 'nyasyāthavā bhaved ||
children.translated_text: 'From my destruction, the result will not exist; or it will belong to another, not to me.'

children.text: iti | apravṛttir evāstv iti cet |

astu ko doṣaḥ | yady ayam ātmagraho nirviṣayo 'pi pravṛttim anākṣipya kṣaṇam api sthātuṃ [na] prabhavati | yathā hi jātasyāvaśyaṃ mṛtyur iti jātavato 'py apratikriyaputrādimaraṇe sorastāḍam ākrando maraṇādau ca yatnaḥ śokodrekāt | evam avidyodrekād eva nairātmyaṃ jānann api pravartate | na sukham āsta iti kim atra kriyatām | avidyāyāḥ pravartanaśakter avāryatvāt |
children.translated_text: Let it be so — what fault is there? If this self-apprehension (<s>ātmagraha</s>), even though without a real object, is unable to remain even for a moment without impelling action — [consider:] Just as one who is born must inevitably die, yet even for one who knows this, at the unpreventable death of a child and the like, there is wailing and beating of the chest, and effort at [averting] death and so forth, due to the surge of grief — similarly, even one who knows the doctrine of no-self engages [in action] due to the very surge of ignorance (<s>avidyā</s>). One does not sit happily [doing nothing] — so what can be done about this? Because the power of ignorance to impel [action] is unpreventable.

children.text: pratyabhijñā ca pūrvam eva dhvastā | kāryakāraṇabhāvaniyatā paścādbhāvipūrvabhāvitā | sā ca kṣaṇike 'py aviruddhā | upādānopādeyatā ca kramisvasaṃvedanajñānadvayena sākṣātkṛta tatpṛṣṭhabhāvinā niścīyata iti,
children.translated_text: And recognition (<s>pratyabhijñā</s>) has already been refuted previously. The cause-effect relation is invariably [characterized by] the later being preceded by the earlier. And that is not incompatible even with momentariness. And the material-cause-and-effect relation is directly perceived through the two successive self-cognizing cognitions (<s>svasaṃvedanajñāna</s>) and is ascertained by the determination that follows upon them.

children.text: asaty apy ātmani pratisandhātari kāryakāraṇagrahaṇādaya upapadyamānā nātmānam upasthāpayituṃ prabhavanti | ato 'rthāpattir api na kṣameti bhāgyahīnamanorājyam iva sthirasiddhir viśīryata eva |
children.translated_text: Since memory, cause-effect apprehension, and the like are explicable even without a permanent self (<s>ātman</s>) as the connecting principle, they are unable to invoke the self. Therefore, <s>arthāpatti</s> (presumption) too is incapable [of proving the self] — and thus the proof of permanence crumbles like the castle-in-the-air of one devoid of merit.

children.text: tathā ca kṣaṇabhaṅgasandehe sattvādyanumānaṃ prāptāvasaram ||
children.translated_text: And accordingly, when there is doubt about momentary destruction, the inference from existence (<s>sattva</s>) and the like has found its occasion.
So let there be non-engagement. [Reply:]

children.text: Sthirasiddhidūṣaṇaṃ samāptam ||
children.translated_text: The <s>Sthirasiddhidūṣaṇa</s> (Refutation of the Proof of Permanence) is completed.

children.text: Citrādvaitaprakāśavādaḥ
children.translated_text: <s>Citrādvaitaprakāśavāda</s> (The Doctrine of Non-dual Variegated Consciousness)

children.text: || namas tārāyai ||
children.translated_text: Salutation to <s>Tārā</s>!

This direction, which is the means of establishing [the truth] against all opponents, one's own and others',

children.translated_text: and which dispels the mass of darkness [that is] the ignorance of the doctrine of non-dual variegated [consciousness].

iha khalu sakalajaḍapadārtharāśau

trātmake jagati vyavasthite

	tadā tāvad ākāracakraparikaritaṃ tadvijñānaṃ citrādvaitam iti
	sthitiḥ | tad evaṃ citram advaitaṃ vijñānam iti padatrayam iha
	pratyupasthitam ||
children.translated_text: is established — then for whomever, at whatever time, and to whatever extent a cognition flashes forth manifesting a wheel of forms, that person's cognition at that time and to that extent, adorned by that wheel of forms, is non-dual variegated [consciousness] (<s>citrādvaita</s>) — this is the thesis. Thus the three terms — 'variegated' (<s>citra</s>), 'non-dual' (<s>advaita</s>), and 'consciousness' (<s>vijñāna</s>) — are presented here.

Here, when the entire aggregate of inert entities has been rejected, and when the formless consciousness doctrine (<s>nirākāravijñānavāda</s>) has been refuted, and when the doctrine that the appearance is false while having [real] forms (<s>sākāravijñānālīkatvasamāropa</s>) has been properly uprooted, and when — like a dream — the world whose nature is mere consciousness manifesting unrefuted appearances of body, enjoyment, foundation and the like in each mental continuum,

children.text:
atra ca vipratipattir nāma kiṃ
	citratāyām advaite vijñānatve sarvatraiveti vikalpāḥ ||
children.translated_text: And here, the disagreement is: does it concern the variegated nature, the non-duality, the consciousness-nature, or all of these? — these are the alternatives.

children.text:
na tāvad asau citrasvarūpānusāriṇī
	bhavitum arhati, tanmātrasya
sarvajanānu

	anyathā śaśaviṣāṇādāv iva jaḍam idam alīkaṃ vijñānaṃ veti

children.translated_text: [continued] — otherwise, regarding inert [things] and false [things] like a hare's horn, there would be the absurd consequence of no scope for disputes such as 'Is this inert or false consciousness?'
To begin with, it cannot be directed at the variegated nature itself, because that alone

children.text: nāpi vijñānatve vivādaḥ kartum ucitaḥ,

— blue and the like have already been established as having the nature of consciousness with form (<s>sākāravijñāna</s>) by [the argument beginning with] this and similar [premises]. For this very reason, disagreement about everything [at once] is also unfounded, since the doctrine of non-dual variegated [consciousness] is introduced only upon the establishment of consciousness with form. Therefore, [the real dispute is:] 'Is this variegated nature contradictory to non-duality?' — from this confusion, the disagreement is precisely about

children.text: yat prakāśate tad ekam | yathā citrākāracakramadhyavartī nīlākāraḥ | prakāśate cedaṃ gauragāndhāramadhurasurabhisukumārasātetarādivicitrākārakadambakam iti svabhāvahetuḥ |

na tāvad asyāsiddhir abhidhātuṃ
	śakyate, pratyakṣapramāṇaprasiddhasadbhāve
	vijñānātmakanīlādyākāracakre dharmiṇi prakāśamānatāyāḥ
	pratyakṣasiddhatvāt | na cāsya
children.translated_text: To begin with, the unestablished-ness (<s>asiddhi</s>) of this [reason] cannot be asserted, because in the subject (<s>dharmin</s>) — the wheel of forms such as blue and the like, which has the nature of consciousness and whose existence is well-established through the valid means of perception — the property of being manifest is established by perception. Nor can the

children.text:
hetor
	viruddhatā sambhavati, vicitrākāramadhyavartini nīlākāre
	dṛṣṭāntadharmiṇi prakāśamānatālakṣaṇasya sādhanasya dṛṣṭatvāt | nanu
	caikatve sādhye yad aparam ekatvādhikaraṇaṃ tad iha dṛṣṭāntīkartum
	ucitam | na cāsya nīlākārasya ekatā vidyate,
	viruddhadharmādhyāsaprasiddhasyānekatvasya sambhavāt |
	deśakālākārabhedo hi viruddhadharmādhyāsaḥ | tataś ca yathā
	citratākāracakrasyākārabhedato bhedas tathā nīlākārasyāpi deśabhedato
	bhedaḥ | tad ayaṃ sādhyaśūnyo dṛṣṭānto hetuś ca vipakṣe paridṛśyamāno | yadi tatraiva niyatas tadā viruddhaḥ
children.translated_text: contradictoriness of this reason occur, because in the example-subject (<s>dṛṣṭāntadharmin</s>) — namely the blue form situated amidst variegated forms — the proving property characterized by being-manifest is observed. [Objection:] But when unity is to be proved, another locus of unity should be cited as the example. And this blue form does not possess unity, because non-unity is possible due to the well-known superimposition of contradictory properties. For the superimposition of contradictory properties consists in difference of place, time, and form. Therefore, just as the wheel of variegated forms has difference due to difference of form, so too the blue form has difference due to difference of place. Thus this is an example devoid of the property to be proved (<s>sādhya</s>), and the reason is observed in the counter-positive (<s>vipakṣa</s>). If it is restricted to that alone, then it is contradictory;

children.text: tatrāpi sambhave 'naikānta iti cet ||
children.translated_text: if it also occurs there, then it is inconclusive (<s>anaikāntika</s>).

Whatever manifests is one — like the blue form situated amidst a wheel of variegated forms. And this variegated assemblage (<s>kadambaka</s>) of forms — white, <s>gāndhāra</s> [musical tone], sweet, fragrant, soft, pleasant and otherwise — does manifest. This is the essential-nature reason (<s>svabhāvahetu</s>).

children.text:
atrocyate | yadi deśabhedato vijñānātmakasthūlanīlākārasya bhedas
	tadāsya pratiparamāṇudeśabhede bhedasambhavāt
	paramāṇupracayamātrātmako vijñānātmakasthūlanīlākāraḥ syāt | tathā ca
	sati sarveṣāṃ vijñānātmakanīlaparamāṇūnāṃ svasvarūpanimagnatvena
	saṃtamasanimagnānekapuruṣavad vyativedanābhāvāt
	sthūlanīlākhaṇḍalakapratibhāsābhāvaprasaṅgaḥ |
children.translated_text: To this we reply: If the gross blue form, which has the nature of consciousness, has difference due to difference of place, then — since it could have difference for each atomic location — the gross blue form having the nature of consciousness would be a mere aggregate of atoms. And in that case, since all the consciousness-natured blue atoms would be absorbed in their own form, like many persons immersed in pitch darkness, there would be no mutual awareness, and hence the absurd consequence of the absence of the appearance of an undivided gross blue [form].

children.text:
na ca svasvarūpanimagnatvenāpy anyenānyasya vedanaṃ yujyate, yena
	sthūlapratibhāsaḥ saṅgataḥ syāt, grāhyagrāhakalakṣaṇayoḥ purastād
	apakartavyatvāt |
children.translated_text: Nor is it possible that despite being absorbed in their own form, one is cognized by another — which would account for the gross appearance — because the subject-object relation (<s>grāhyagrāhakalakṣaṇa</s>) has been previously refuted.

children.text: na caivaṃ vaktavyam paramāṇūnāṃ
sva
children.translated_text: [are absorbed in]

children.text:
svarūpanimagnatve 'py
	ekopādānatayā puñjātmaiva sthūlaḥ sthūlam ātmanaṃ jñāsyatīti, saty apy
	ekopādānatve svasvarūpanimagnatvād eva sthūlavyavasthāpakasya
	bhinnasyātmano 'nyonyam vā grāhyagrāhakabhāvasyāyogāt | tādātmyena
	vyativedanasya cānabhyupagamāt |
children.translated_text: their own form, being of a single material cause (<s>ekopādāna</s>), [the consciousness] being of the nature of an aggregate will know itself as gross — because even when there is a single material cause, precisely due to being absorbed in their own form, the identity of the distinct [atoms] that would establish gross-ness, or the mutual subject-object relation, is impossible. And because mutual awareness through identity (<s>tādātmya</s>) is not accepted.

children.text: vargo vargaṃ veti
children.translated_text: 'One group cognizes another group'

children.text: ity asyānupadatvāt |
children.translated_text: — this is groundless.
Nor should it be said that even when the atoms

children.text: na ca

yathā
	bāhyārthavāde sthūlaikākārajñānapratibhāsa eva
	bāhyaparamāṇupracayapratibhāsavyavasthā gatyantarābhāvāt, tathā
	jñānaparamāṇuvyavasthā
children.translated_text: just as in the external realist doctrine (<s>bāhyārthavāda</s>) the arrangement of external atomic aggregates is [accounted for] precisely through the appearance of a gross unitary form in cognition — there being no other recourse — similarly, the arrangement of cognitive atoms

children.text: paka

children.text: nte

sthūlaikākārayogivijñānāntarasyānabhyupagamāt | abhyupagame vā tasyaiva dṛṣṭāntatvāt | tasmād yāvad yāvat
	pratibhāsas tāvat tāvat sthūlatayaiva vyāptaḥ | asthūle paramāṇau
	sthūlanivṛttimātre ca pratibhāsasya dṛśyānupalambhabādhitatvāt | yathā
	prasiddhānumāne sattvaṃ kṣaṇikatvena vyāptaṃ kramākramakāritvenāpi,
	kṣaṇikatvābhāvāc ca kramākramanivṛttau nivartamānaṃ kṣaṇikatve niyataṃ
	sidhyati, tathātrāpi prakāśamānatvaṃ sādhanam ekatvenāpi sthaulyenāpi,
	ekatvābhāvāc ca vipakṣāt paramāṇupuñjātmana ekatvanivṛttimātrātmanaś
	ca svaviruddhopalambhāt sthaulyasya vyāpakasya nivṛttau nivartamānam
children.translated_text: — because another consciousness that possesses a gross unitary form is not accepted [in this system]. Or if it were accepted, that very [consciousness] would serve as the example. Therefore, to whatever extent there is appearance, to precisely that extent it is pervaded by gross-ness alone. And in the non-gross atom and in the mere absence of gross-ness, the appearance is contradicted by the non-apprehension of the visible (<s>dṛśyānupalambha</s>). Just as in the well-known inference, existence (<s>sattva</s>) is pervaded by momentariness (<s>kṣaṇikatva</s>) as well as by being the producer of sequential and simultaneous [effects] (<s>kramākramakāritva</s>), and since from the absence of momentariness, [existence] — which ceases upon the cessation of sequential and simultaneous [production] — is established as restricted to momentariness, so too here, the proving property of being-manifest is [pervaded] by unity as well as by gross-ness, and since from the absence of unity — i.e., from the counter-positive, [namely] mere atomic aggregate and the mere absence of unity — gross-ness, the pervader, ceases due to the apprehension of what is incompatible with it, [the property of being-manifest,] ceasing upon the cessation of gross-ness,

children.text: ekatvaṃ
children.translated_text: is established as restricted to unity

children.text: ekatve
children.translated_text: [variant:] in unity

children.text:
niyataṃ sidhyati | tataś
	ca yathā bahirvyāptipakṣe ghaṭe dṛṣṭāntadharmiṇi
	viparyayabādhakapramāṇabalāt sattvaṃ kṣaṇikatvaniyatam
	avadhārya
children.translated_text: — this is established. And therefore, just as in the external-pervasion position, in the example-subject of a pot, by the force of the <s>viparyayabādhaka</s> (counter-factual defeater) proof, existence (<s>sattva</s>) is ascertained as restricted to momentariness,

children.text: dhārya
children.translated_text: [continued]

children.text:
sattvāt pakṣe
	kṣaṇikabhaṅgasiddhiḥ, tathātrāpi nīlākāre dṛṣṭāntadharmiṇi
	viparyayabādhakapramāṇabalād eva prakāśamānatvam ekatvaniyatam

	cānaikāntikatā ||
children.translated_text: and from existence, momentary destruction is established in the subject — so too here, in the example-subject of the blue form, by the very force of the counter-factual defeater proof, being-manifest is understood as restricted to unity, and from being-manifest, unity is established in the subject-to-be-proved, namely the wheel of variegated forms — thus the example is not devoid of the property to be proved. Nor is the reason contradictory. Nor is it inconclusive.
Nor [can it be said that]

children.text:
nanv ekatve sādhye tatpracyutir dvitvaṃ ca vipakṣaḥ, tasmāc
	ca vipakṣād dhetuvyatirekapratipattyavasare kiṃ vipakṣātmā prakāśate
	na vā | pratibhāsapakṣe prakāśamānatvasya hetoḥ sādhāraṇānaikāntikatā,
	vipakṣe 'pi dṛṣṭatvāt | atha na prakāśate tadā sandigdhavyatirekitvam,
	kuto vyatireka ity avadher evāprakāśamānaśarīratvāt katham ataḥ
	sādhyasiddhipratyāśā |
children.translated_text: [Objection:] But when unity is to be proved, the departure from it — namely duality — is the counter-positive (<s>vipakṣa</s>). And at the occasion of apprehending the exclusion of the reason from that counter-positive, does the counter-positive manifest or not? If it manifests, then the reason of being-manifest is an inconclusive common reason (<s>sādhāraṇānaikāntika</s>), since it is observed even in the counter-positive. But if it does not manifest, then [the reason] has doubtful negative concomitance (<s>sandigdhavyatirekin</s>) — whence the negative concomitance? Since the very body of the counter-positive does not manifest, how can the expectation of establishing the property to be proved [follow] from it?

children.text:
atrocyate | iha dvividho vijñānānāṃ
	viṣayaḥ grāhyo 'dhyavaseyaś ca | pratibhāsamāno grāhyaḥ | agṛhīto 'pi
	pravṛttiviṣayo 'dhyavaseyaḥ | tatrāsarvajñe 'numātari
	sakalavipakṣapratibhāsābhāvān na grāhyatayā vipakṣo viṣayo vaktavyaḥ,
	sarvānumānocchedaprasaṅgāt, sarvatra sakalavipakṣapratibhāsābhāvāt
	tato vyatirekāsiddheḥ | pratibhāse ca
	deśakālasvabhāvāntaritasakalavipakṣasākṣātkāre sādhyātmāpi virākaḥ
	sutarāṃ pratīyata ity anumānavaiyarthyam | tasmād apratibhāse 'py
	adhyavasāyasiddhād eva vipakṣād dhūmāder vyatireko niścitaḥ | tat kim
	artham atra vipakṣapratibhāsaḥ prārthyate | yadi punar asyādhyavasāyo
	'pi na syāt tadā vyatire
children.translated_text: [Reply:] It is said: Here, the objects of cognitions are of two kinds — the apprehended (<s>grāhya</s>) and the determined (<s>adhyavasāya</s>). What appears [directly in cognition] is the apprehended. What is not [directly] apprehended but is the object of [practical] activity is the determined. In that case, for an inferrer who is not omniscient, since there is no appearance of the totality of counter-examples, the counter-example cannot be said to be an object by way of being apprehended — because there would follow the consequence of the destruction of all inference, since the totality of counter-examples does not appear in any [inference]. And if there were [such] appearance — a direct perception of the totality of counter-examples separated by place, time, and nature — the provable itself would be manifested all the more clearly, and so inference would be pointless. Therefore, even without [direct] appearance, the exclusion of smoke and the like from the counter-example — [namely,] from what lacks fire — is ascertained precisely through determination. So for what purpose is the appearance of the counter-example demanded here? If, however, there were no determination of it either, then it would be correct [to say] that the negative concomitance is not ascertained, because there would be no restricted-object-based practical convention.

	niścīyata iti yuktam, pratiniyataviṣayavyavahārābhāvāt ||

children.text: nanv
asmin mate
children.translated_text: In this [your] doctrine,

children.text:
vastvavastvātmakasakalavipakṣapratipattisambhavāt tato hetuvyatirekaḥ
	saṃpratyetuṃ śakyata eva | na ca pratibhāsamātreṇa sattvaprasaṅgaḥ,
	arthakriyākāritvalakṣaṇatvāt sattvasya | tvanmate tu prakāśa eva
	vastutvam | ato vipakṣayor ekatvapracyu
children.translated_text: since apprehension of the totality of counter-examples — whether real or unreal in nature — is possible, the exclusion of the reason from that [totality] can indeed be understood. Nor does the consequence of existence [of what is unreal] follow from mere appearance, because existence has the defining characteristic of capacity for causal efficacy (<s>arthakriyākāritva</s>). But in your doctrine, manifestation (<s>prakāśa</s>) alone is reality. Therefore, when the two counter-examples — oneness and

children.text: tidvi
children.translated_text: duality —

children.text:
tvayoḥ pratibhāse prakāśamānatvasādhanasya
	vipakṣasādhāraṇatā | apratibhāse ca sandigdhavyatirekitvam iti codyaṃ
	duruddharam eveti cet | tad etad asaṅgatam | tathā hi dhūmādir
	avahnyāder vipakṣād vyāvṛtto vahnyādiniyataḥ sidhyati
children.translated_text: appear, the reason 'being manifest' becomes common to both the thesis-subject and the counter-examples. And if [they do] not appear, there is the doubt that the negative concomitance is uncertain — [so] the objection is irresistible. [Reply:] This is incoherent. For thus: smoke and the like, being excluded from the counter-example [i.e.,] what lacks fire, are established as restricted to what possesses fire and the like.

children.text:
tasya ca
	vastvavastvātmakasakalavipakṣapadārtharāśeḥ svarūpanirbhāsa iti kiṃ
	nirvikalpajñāne kalpanāyāṃ vā | nirvikalpe cet | pratibhāsa iti ca ko
	'rthaḥ | kiṃ nirākāre jñāne sakalavipakṣādisvarūpasya sākṣāt
	sphuraṇam, yadi vā tadarpitabuddhisvabhāvabhūtasadṛśākāraprakāśaḥ,
	atha samanantarapratyayabalāyātabuddhigatabāhyasadṛśākārapratibhāsaḥ,
	āhosvid buddher ātmabhūtavipakṣasadṛśālīkākāraparisphūrtiḥ |
children.translated_text: And [as for] the direct manifestation (<s>svarūpanirbhāsa</s>) of the entire mass of counter-example objects, whether real or unreal in nature — is this in non-conceptual cognition or in conceptual construction? If in non-conceptual [cognition]: then what is the meaning of 'appearance'? Is it the direct shining forth of the own-nature of the totality of counter-examples in a cognition that is without form (<s>nirākāra</s>)? Or is it the manifestation of a similar form (<s>sadṛśākāra</s>) that is of the nature of cognition and deposited [in the mind] by that [object]? Or is it the appearance of a form similar to the external [object] that is present in cognition and arrived at by the force of the immediately preceding condition (<s>samanantarapratyaya</s>)? Or else is it the shining forth of a false form (<s>alīkākāra</s>) resembling the counter-example that belongs to the very nature of cognition?

children.text: na tāvad ādyaḥ pakṣo yuktaḥ, deśakā
children.translated_text: To begin with, the first alternative is not tenable, because of the impossibility of the shining forth in a recent person and in a formless cognition of objects that are remote in place,

children.text:
lasvabhāvaviprakṛṣṭānāṃ padārthānām arvācīne
	jane nirākāre ca jñāne sphuraṇāyogād ity asyārthasya śāstre eva
	vistareṇa prasādhānāt | sphuraṇe
children.translated_text: time, and nature — since this point has been extensively demonstrated in the [Buddhist] treatise itself. And because it has been shown that if [all counter-examples were to] shine forth,

children.text: cā
children.translated_text: even

children.text: vā
children.translated_text: the provable too

children.text: vā
is not well distinguishable from
cā
in the script of
, and on
there is
sādhyātmāpi
, which one would also expect here.  Also,
vā
makes good sense, since this is an alternative to the non-appearance in the previous sentence. But
ca
in an adversative sense cannot be excluded.

sādhyasyāpi
	prakāśanaprasaṅge 'numānavaiyarthyasya pratipādanāt |
children.translated_text: would have the consequence of being manifest, and thus inference would be pointless.

children.text:
nāpi dvitīyaḥ pakṣaḥ, deśādiviprakṛṣṭatvād
	eva sākṣātsvākārasamarpaṇasāmarthyābhāvāt |
children.translated_text: Nor is the second alternative [tenable], because — precisely due to the remoteness in place and so forth — there is no capacity for the direct bestowal of one's own form.

children.text:
na ca tṛtīyaḥ saṅgataḥ, sādṛśyasambhave
	'pi samanantarabalād evāyātasya bāhyena saha pratyāsatter abhāvāt |
children.translated_text: Nor is the third [alternative] coherent, because — even if similarity were possible — what has arrived solely by the force of the immediately preceding [condition] has no proximity (<s>pratyāsatti</s>) with the external [object].

children.text:
na caturtho 'pi prakāraḥ
	sambhavati, asatprakāśayor virodhāt, sphurato 'līkatvāyogāt | tathā hy
	asatprakāśa iti kim asadīśvarādeḥ khyātiḥ, bhāsamāno vā ākāro 'san,
	san vā na kaścit khyātīti vivakṣitam | tatra yasya padārthasya
	svarūpaparinirbhāsaḥ sa katham asann iti prāṇadhāribhir abhidhātavyaḥ | sphurataḥ keśoṇḍukākārasya bāhyarūpatayā bādhyatve 'pi
	jñānarūpatayārthatvasya ācāryeṇa pratipāditatvāt
	grāhakābhimatanirākāraprakāśasyāpy asattvābhidhānaprasaṅgāt ||
children.translated_text: Nor is even the fourth mode possible, because of the contradiction between being unreal and being manifest — since what shines forth cannot be unreal. For thus: does 'the manifestation of the unreal' mean: the appearance of unreal [entities] such as <s>Īśvara</s> and the like? Or: the form that appears is unreal? Or: something real does not appear at all? — this is what is intended. In the first case, how can that object whose own-nature is fully manifest be said to be non-existent by any living being? Because even though the form of a hair-net (<s>keśoṇḍuka</s>) is sublated as having the nature of an external [object], the <s>Ācārya</s> has demonstrated that it has reality as a form of cognition. And there would follow the consequence of declaring even the formless manifestation accepted [by the opponent] as the apprehender to be non-existent.

children.text:
pratibhāse 'pi bādhanād asatyatvam iti cet | kiṃ tad bādhakam, pratyakṣam anumānaṃ vā | yady ekatra
	svarūpasā
children.translated_text: [Objection:] Even in the case of appearance, unreality [follows] because of sublation. [Reply:] What is that sublator — perception or inference? If — in one [case,] when perception directly apprehends the own-nature [of an object] —

children.text:
kṣātkāriṇi pratyakṣe 
	'viśvāsaḥ katham anyatra bādhake svarūpāntaraprakāśa eva nirvṛttis
	tatpūrvakam anumānaṃ ca sutarām aviśvāsabhājanam iti na bādhakavārtāpi | yad āhur guravaḥ
children.translated_text: there is no trust, how [can there be trust] in another [case where perception] is a sublator, [when] the accomplishment is merely the manifestation of a different own-nature? And inference, which is preceded by that [perception], is all the more unworthy of trust — so there is not even talk of a sublator. As our teachers say:
[Objection:]

children.text: yasya svarūpanirbhāsas tad evāsāt kathaṃ bhavet |
children.translated_text: 'How could that whose own-nature shines forth be non-existent?

children.text: bādhāto yadi sāpy ekā pratyakṣānumayor nanu ||
children.translated_text: If because of sublation — is not that [sublation] too one [instance] of perception and inference?

children.text: pratyakṣe yady aviśvāsa ekatrānyatra kā gatiḥ |
children.translated_text: If there is no trust in perception in one [instance], what recourse in another?

children.text: tatpūrvam anumānaṃ ca katham āśvāsagocaraḥ || iti |
children.translated_text: And how can inference, which is preceded by that [perception], be an object of confidence?' Thus.

children.text: nanu
children.translated_text: [Objection:]

children.text: dṛṣṭam eva dvicandrādipratibhāse 'pi bādhitam |
children.translated_text: 'It is well-known that even in the appearance of two moons and the like, [the appearance] is sublated.

children.text: na dṛṣṭe 'nupapannatvaṃ tajjñātam api bādhyate ||
children.translated_text: There is no impossibility in what is well-known — what is known through that [perception] is also sublated.'

children.text: iti cet | na | bādhyasyāpratibhāsanāt | pratibhāsinaś cābādhyatvāt | tathā hi
children.translated_text: [Reply:] No. Because what is sublated does not [actually] appear [as such]. And because what appears is not sublated. For thus:

children.text: buddhyākārasya nirbhāso bādhā bāhyasya vastunaḥ |
children.translated_text: 'The appearance of the mental form is [real]; the sublation is of the external object.

children.text: sphūrtāv apy aviśvāse kva viśvāsa iti kīrtitam ||
children.translated_text: If even in [direct] shining forth there is no trust — where then is trust?' — so it has been declared.

children.text:
etena bhāsamāno vākāro 'sann iti
	dvitīyo 'pi pakṣaḥ pratikṣiptaḥ, pratibhāsād eva sattāsiddher
	bādhakāvakāśābhāvāt |
children.translated_text: By this, the second alternative too — that 'the form that appears is unreal' — is also rejected, because existence is established from appearance itself, and there is no room for a sublator.

children.text:
tathā san vā kaścin na khyātīti
	tṛtīyasaṅkalpo 'pi vyākulaḥ, prakāśavyāptatvāt sattāyāḥ |
	aprakāśasyāsattayā grastatvāt ||
children.translated_text: Likewise, the third supposition too — that 'something real does not appear at all' — is also confounded, because existence is pervaded by manifestation. Because what is unmanifest is consumed by [its own] non-existence.

children.text:
nanu prakāśo nāma vastunaḥ
	sattāsādhakaṃ pramāṇam | na ca pramāṇanivṛttāv arthābhāvaḥ |
	arthakriyāśaktis tu sattvam | tac cāprakāśasyāpi na virudhyata iti
	cet | satyam etat | bahirarthavāde 'prakāśasyāpi
	sāmarthyābhyupagamāt | keśoṇḍukādipratibhāse
	'dhyavasitasyārthakriyāśaktiviyogād evābhāvasiddheḥ | sarvathā
	bahirabhāve tu jñānasya prakāśāvyabhicārāt tāvataiva sattve kim
	arthakriyayā |
children.translated_text: [Objection:] But manifestation is a means of valid knowledge that establishes the existence of a real entity. And the absence of a means of valid knowledge does not entail the absence of the object. Rather, capacity for causal efficacy (<s>arthakriyāśakti</s>) is existence. And that is not precluded even for what is unmanifest. [Reply:] This is true — in the externalist (realist) doctrine (<s>bahirarthavāda</s>), even what is unmanifest is admitted to have capacity. Because when the appearance of hair-nets and the like is followed by determination [of the object], non-existence is established precisely through the absence of capacity for causal efficacy. But when there is absolutely no external [object], since cognition does not deviate from manifestation, existence is [established] by that much alone — what need is there for causal efficacy?

children.text: katham anyahṛdaḥ sattvaṃ prakāśād eva nāsya cet |
children.translated_text: 'If the existence of another's mind [is established] from manifestation alone — then how not [the existence] of this [object]?

children.text: nārthakriyāpi sarvasmai kvacic ced bhāsanaṃ na kim ||
children.translated_text: If causal efficacy [were required] — it too is not [available] to everyone; and if something is [nonetheless] manifest somewhere, why not [accept its existence]?'

children.text:
iti | nirvikalpe tāvat svasaṃvedanasiddhasvākāram antareṇa vipakṣādayo
	  na parisphuranti | athāmī vikalpe pratibhāsanta iti dvitīyaḥ saṅkalpo
	  'bhyupagamyate, asminn api pakṣe pratibhāsamāna ākāro 'sādhāraṇo
	  'śabdasaṃsṛṣṭatayā svasaṃvedanatādātmye praviṣṭatvād vastusann eva |

adhyavseyatā vipakṣādayo gṛhyanta iti cet | tadāpi teṣāṃ
	  svarūpasya nirbhāso 'sti na vā | nirbhāse pratyakṣasiddhataiva,
	  nāsatkhyātiḥ | śāstre 'pi
children.translated_text: [Objection:] The counter-examples and the like are apprehended through determination (<s>adhyavasāya</s>). [Reply:] Even then, is the manifestation of their own-nature present or not? If there is manifestation, then it is established by perception alone — there is no appearance of the unreal (<s>asatkhyāti</s>). In the [Buddhist] treatise too,

Thus. In non-conceptual [cognition], apart from its own form established through self-awareness (<s>svasaṃvedana</s>), counter-examples and the like do not shine forth. Now if it is accepted as the second supposition — that these [counter-examples] appear in conceptual cognition (<s>vikalpa</s>) — even in this alternative, the form that appears is uncommon [to the object], and because of having entered into identity with self-awareness as being unsynthesized with words, it is in fact a real entity.

children.text: svarūpasākṣātkāritvam eva pratyakṣatvam
children.translated_text: 'being a direct apprehender of own-nature is precisely perceptual-ness'

children.text:
uktam | tasya cetarapratyakṣeṣv iva vikalpe 'pi svīkāre
	  viruddhavyāptopalambhena vikalpabhrāntatvayor dūram apāstatvād vikalpe
	  'pi tvanmate pratyakṣatvam akṣatam | tat kathaṃ tatsiddhasya
	  pratyakṣāntarānumānābhyāṃ bādhābhidhānam, tayor api
	  svarūpāntaraprakāśapauruṣatvāt ||

atha vikalpabhrāntatvayor vyāpakaviruddhayoḥ sambhavāt vikalpe
	  pratyakṣatvam evāsambhavi | nanv asya pratyakṣatvam a
children.translated_text: Now if [it is argued that] the erroneousness of conceptual cognition and [the presence of] the pervader of the contradictory are possible, [and so] perceptual-ness in conceptual cognition is simply impossible — [Reply:] But [to say] that perceptual-ness of this [conceptual cognition] is impossible

children.text:
sambhavīti
	  svarūpasākṣātkāritvam asambhavīty uktam | atha vipakṣādir artho 'smin
	  prakāśata iti vācā svarūpasākṣātkāritvaṃ kathitam iti mātā me
	  bandhyeti vṛttāntaḥ | iṣyate ca tvayā vipakṣādisvarūpasākṣātkāritvaṃ
	  vikalpasyeti pratyakṣatānatikramaḥ, apratyakṣatve
	  vastusvarūpasphuraṇāyogāt | tataś ca tatpratibhāsino 'pi rūpasya sata
	  eva khyātir nāsatkhyātiḥ | na ca tad eva vikalpe parisphuradrūpam
	  a
children.translated_text: is to say that being a direct apprehender of own-nature is impossible. Now if you say that the counter-example and the like appear in this [conceptual cognition] and yet claim by words that it has the nature of direct apprehension of own-nature — this is the case of 'My mother is barren.' And you yourself accept that conceptual cognition has the nature of direct apprehension of the own-nature of counter-examples and the like — so there is no escaping perceptual-ness, because in the absence of perceptual-ness, the shining forth of the own-nature of a real entity would be impossible. And consequently, even the form of what appears in it is the appearance of what is real, not the appearance of the unreal (<s>asatkhyāti</s>). Nor is that very form that shines forth in conceptual cognition

children.text:
satām īśvarādīnāṃ svarūpam, asattvasyaivābhāvaprasaṅgāt |
	  svarūpasphuraṇe 'py asattve 'nyatrāpi prakāśiny anāśvāsāt | tato yat
	  sākāravāde jalpitam
children.translated_text: the own-nature of non-existent [entities] such as <s>Īśvara</s> and the like — because there would follow the consequence of non-existence itself being absent. Even if the own-nature shines forth, if it is [declared] non-existent, there would be no confidence elsewhere either when [an entity] is manifest. Therefore, what has been asserted in the doctrine of cognition having form (<s>sākāravāda</s>) —

— has been stated. And if that [direct apprehension of own-nature] is accepted in conceptual cognition just as in other [forms of] perception — then since the apprehension of the pervader of the contradictory (<s>viruddhavyāptopalambha</s>) and the erroneousness of conceptual cognition are far removed [from being established], even in your doctrine perceptual-ness in conceptual cognition is unimpaired. So how can there be the assertion of sublation by another perception or inference of what is established through that [direct apprehension], since those too have their power only in manifesting a different own-nature?

children.text: nityādayaḥ santa eva syuḥ
children.translated_text: 'eternal [entities] and the like would be real' —

children.text: iti tadātmana eva patitam |

tato yat --- patitam
	  Ce'e JNA 392,15f. (has evāpatitam).
yad āhur
children.translated_text: As

children.text: guruvaḥ
children.translated_text: the teachers say:
that has fallen upon itself alone.

children.text: svarūpasākṣātkaraṇād adhyakṣatvaṃ na cāparam |
children.translated_text: 'Perceptual-ness is nothing other than the direct apprehension of own-nature.

children.text: vikalpabhramabhūmitvam ata eva hi bādhitam ||

Ce'
	  JNA 391,5f. For ab also cf. JNA 563,5.

children.translated_text: For this very reason, [its] being the ground of conceptual error is refuted.

children.text: yadi nādhyakṣatā tasya rūpanirbhāsa eva na |
children.translated_text: If it does not have perceptual-ness, then there is no manifestation of [its] form at all.

children.text: tatas tadasadīśādi pratibhātīty asaṅgatam ||
children.translated_text: Consequently, [the claim] that unreal <s>Īśvara</s> and the like appear [in it] is incoherent.

children.text: yadi tu pratibhāseta rūpam asya sad eva tat |
children.translated_text: But if a form does appear, that form of it is real indeed.

children.text: tad asat pratibhātīti tac ca bhāty asad eva vaḥ ||
children.translated_text: [And the claim] that what is unreal appears — that too, for you, means that what appears is unreal indeed.'

children.text:
athādhyavasāye
	'dhyavaseyasvarūpasya pratibhāso nāstīty ucyate | na tadā kasyacid
	adhyavasāyaḥ | katham ataḥ pratiniyatavastuvyavasthāsiddhiḥ | kiṃ ca
	ko 'yam adhyavasāyo nāma | kiṃ vyāvṛttibhedaparikalpitasya
	prakāśāṃśasya, svākārāṃśasya, alīkākārasya, bāhyavastuno 'vastuno vā
	sphuraṇam adhyavasāyārthaḥ | yadi vā svākāre bāhyāropaḥ, bāhye vā
	svākārāropaḥ, svākārabāhyayor yojanā, tayor ekīkaraṇam ekapratipattir
	abhedena pratipattiḥ, bhedāgraho 'dhyavasāyārtha iti vikalpāḥ |

tatra na tāvad ādimau pakṣau
	kalpanām arthaḥ | svarūpe sarvasyaiva sphuraṇasya nirvikalpatvād
	avasāyānupapattiḥ | itarathā nirvikalpakajñānābhāvaprasaṅgāt |
children.translated_text: To begin with, the first two alternatives are not the meaning of conceptual construction. Because any shining forth of own-nature is non-conceptual, [there would be] the impossibility of determination. Otherwise, there would follow the consequence of the absence of non-conceptual cognition.

children.text:
alīkasphuraṇaṃ tu prāk
	pratyākhyātam | saty api sphuraṇe 'sphuṭatvān nirvikalpakam etat |
	dvicandrādijñānavat | astu svagrāhye tannirvikalpakam, bāhye tu
	adhyavaseye adhyavasāya iti cet | na | tatsambandhābhāvāta,
	tadapratibhāsāc ca | anyathātiprasaṅgād ity uktaprāyam |
	bāhyavastusvarūpasphuraṇe tu pratyakṣapratipattir evāsāv iti ko
	'dhyavasāyaḥ | avastusphuraṇaṃ punas tridhā vikalpya prāg eva
	pratyākhyātam |
children.translated_text: The shining forth of the unreal, however, has been previously rejected. Even if there is shining forth, this is non-conceptual because of its indistinctness — like the cognition of two moons and the like. [Objection:] Let it be non-conceptual with respect to what it apprehends; but with respect to the external [object] that is determined, it is determination. [Reply:] No. Because there is no connection with that [external object], and because it does not appear [in cognition]. Otherwise there would be over-extension — as has been mostly stated. And the shining forth of the own-nature of an external real entity would be precisely perceptual apprehension — so what determination [would there be]? The shining forth of a non-entity, moreover, has been rejected above by being analyzed in three ways.

children.text:
svākāre tu bāhyāropo na sambhavaty
	eva | tathā hi jñānaṃ kenacid ākāreṇa satyenālīkena vopajātaṃ nāma |
	bāhyāropas tu tadākāre tatkṛto 'nyakṛto vā syāt | tatkṛtatve na tāvat
	tatkāla eva vyāpārāntaram anubhūyata iti kutas tadāropaḥ | kālāntare
	ca svayam evāsat kasya vyāpāraḥ syāt |
children.translated_text: As for the superimposition of the external upon one's own form — that is simply impossible. For thus: a cognition arises with some form, whether real or unreal. But the superimposition of the external upon that form would be produced either by that [cognition] itself or by something else. If produced by that [cognition] itself: to begin with, no other operation is experienced at that very moment [of cognition] — so whence that superimposition? And at another moment, [the cognition] itself, being non-existent, whose operation could it be?

Now if it is said that in determination (<s>adhyavasāya</s>) there is no appearance of the own-nature of what is determined — then there is no determination of anything. How then can the establishment of a convention regarding a specifically delimited real entity [be achieved]? Moreover, what is this determination? Is the meaning of determination: the shining forth of the manifestation-aspect delineated by differentiation of exclusion (<s>vyāvṛttibheda</s>)? Of the own-form-aspect? Of a false form? Of an external real entity? Or of a non-entity? Or is it the superimposition of the external upon one's own form, or the superimposition of one's own form upon the external, or the conjunction of one's own form and the external, or the unification of those two, or a single apprehension, or an apprehension without [recognizing] difference — [which of] these conceptual alternatives [is the meaning of determination]?

children.text:
dvitīyapakṣe jñānāntaram api
	nākārāroparāgasaṅginīm utpattim antareṇa vyāpārāntareṇa kvacit
	kiñcitkaraṃ nāma | tad etad arvācīnajñānasadṛśākāragocarīkaraṇe 'pi na
	bāhyāropavyāpāram aparaṃ spṛśati tadākāraleśānukāram apahāya | na ca
	śabdāmukhīkaraṇam atirikto vyāpāraḥ, śabdākārasyāpi svarūpa
	evāntarbhāvād iti nākārād anyo jñānavyāpāraḥ | āropyamāṇaś cāsāv artho
	bāhyaḥ | tatra buddhau yadi svarūpeṇa sphurati satyapratītir evāsau,
	ka āropaḥ | atha na parisphurati tathāpi ka āropaḥ | sphuraṇe
	vādhikaraṇabhūtasvākārātiriktasyāropyamāṇākārasyāpi
	pratibhāsaprasaṅgaḥ |
Parallel to

children.translated_text: In the second alternative [viz., produced by another cognition]: another cognition too, without an origination that is tainted by the imposition of a form, does not accomplish anything whatsoever through some other operation. And this [subsequent cognition], even in making the similar form of the preceding cognition its object, does not touch any other operation of external superimposition apart from imitating a trace of that [preceding cognition's] form. Nor is the act of being made the object of a word (<s>śabdāmukhīkaraṇa</s>) an additional operation, because even the form of a word is included in the own-nature itself — so there is no operation of cognition other than [its] form. And the object being superimposed is external. If it shines forth in cognition by its own-nature, that is simply a veridical apprehension — what superimposition [is there]? And if it does not shine forth, then too — what superimposition? And if it does shine forth, there would follow the consequence of the appearance of the superimposed form too, which is additional to the own-form that is the substrate.

children.text:
tadākārasphuraṇam eva tasya
	sphuraṇam iti cet | na | tasyāropaviṣayatvāt | na hi marīcisphuraṇam
	eva jalasphuraṇam iti na svākāre bāhyāropaḥ |
children.translated_text: [Objection:] The shining forth of that [cognition's] form is itself the shining forth of that [external object]. [Reply:] No. Because that [external object] is the object of superimposition. For it is not the case that the shining forth of a mirage is itself the shining forth of water — so there is no superimposition of the external upon one's own form.

children.text:
ata eva bāhye svākārāropo nāsti, āropaviṣayasya
	bāhyasyāsphuraṇāt |
children.translated_text: For this very reason, there is no superimposition of one's own form upon the external either, because the external — which is the object of superimposition — does not shine forth.

children.text:
tata eva svākārabāhyayor yojanāpy asambhavinī, yogyayor
	apratibhāsāt |
children.translated_text: For that very reason, the conjunction of one's own mental image and the external [object] is also impossible, because the two suitable [for conjunction] do not appear [together].

children.text:
na caikīkaraṇam adhyavasāyaḥ | ko 'yam ekīkaraṇārthaḥ | yady
	ekatāpatau prayojakatvaṃ tadāropyāropaviṣayayoḥ kadācid ekībhāvābhāvād
	asambhava eva | na hi śaśaviṣāṇe kāraṇaṃ kiñcit | na ca pūrvam anekam
	ekatām etīti kṣaṇikavādinaḥ sāṃpratam | arthāntarotpattimātraṃ tu
	syāt | na ca tadupalabdhigocaro 'nyatrāropaviṣayāt svākārāt | na ca
	tāvatāpy arthasya kiñcid iti katham ekīkaraṇam |
children.translated_text: Nor is determination (adhyavasaya) an identification [of the two]. What is meant by 'identification'? If it means causing unity, then since the superimposed and the object of superimposition never actually become one, it is simply impossible. For there is no cause whatsoever in a hare's horn. And for the proponent of momentariness, it is not the case that what was previously many now becomes one. There would be merely the production of another thing. And the domain of its apprehension is nowhere beyond the mental image, which is the object of superimposition. And even through that much, nothing [is gained] regarding the object — so how is there identification?

children.text:
athaikapratītir adhyavasāyaḥ | tathāpi na
	dvayor ekapratipattir adhyavaseyānubhavābhāvāt | na ca dvayoḥ pratītir
	ity evādhyavasāyaḥ nīlapītavat |
children.translated_text: If determination is a unitary cognition — even so, there is no unitary apprehension of two things, because there is no experience of the object to be determined. Nor is the [mere] cognition of two things determination — like [the simultaneous cognition of] blue and yellow.

children.text:
na cābhedena pratītir adhyavasāyaḥ | yataḥ paryudāsapakṣe
	aikyapratītir uktā bhavati | sā ca prayuktā, adhyavaseyapratyabhāvāt |
	bhedena pratītiniṣedhamātre 'pi na bāhyasya pratītir ukteti kutas
	tadadhyavasāyaḥ | yadi hi bāhyaṃ prakāśeta ekatvenānekatvena vā satā
	asatā vā pratītir iti yuktam |
children.translated_text: Nor is cognition as non-different determination. Because in the exclusion-alternative (<s>paryudasa</s>), a cognition of unity has been stated. And that [cognition of unity] has been applied [as an objection], because the object to be determined does not exist. Even in the mere negation of cognition as different, there is no stated cognition of the external [object] — so whence its determination? For if the external [object] appeared — whether as one or as many, as existent or as non-existent — then cognition would be justified.

children.text:
sarvākāratatsvarūpatiraskāreṇa sā
	pratītir ity ekapratītir iti cet | tatsvarūpatiraskāre tarhi
	tadapra

tibhāsanam eva | kasyacid aṃśasya pratibhāsanād iti
	cet | na | niraṃśatvād vastunaḥ sarvātmanā pratibhāso
	'pratibhāso veti śāstram evātra vistareṇa parīkṣyate |
children.translated_text: that is simply its non-appearance. [Objection:] Because some aspect of it appears. [Reply:] No. Because a real thing is without parts — it either appears in its entirety or does not appear at all — this is examined at length in the treatise itself.

children.text:
na ca bhedāgraho 'dhyavasāyo
	vaktavyaḥ | tathā hi kiṃ bāhye gṛhyamāṇe 'grahyamāṇe vā | na
	ca prathamaḥ pakṣaḥ, bāhyagrahaṇasya pratikṣiptatvāt | grahaṇe
	vādhyavasāyasya pratyakṣatāprasaṅgāt | agṛhyamāṇe tu bāhye
	pravṛttiniyamo na syā
children.translated_text: Nor should non-apprehension of difference be called determination. For thus: is it [non-apprehension] when the external [object] is apprehended, or when it is not? The first alternative is not [tenable], because the apprehension of the external has been rejected. Or, if there were apprehension, determination would have the consequence of being perception. But when the external is not apprehended, there would be no restriction of activity,

children.text:
t, anyeṣām api
	tadānīm agrahaṇād anyatrāpi pravṛttiprasaṅgāt |
children.translated_text: because even other [objects] are not apprehended at that time, and there would follow the consequence of activity even with respect to other things.
[Objection:] That cognition, by concealing its own form in every respect, is a unitary cognition. [Reply:] If its own form is concealed, then

children.text: trilocano
children.translated_text: <s>Trilocana</s>

children.text:
'pīttham adhyavasāyaṃ dūṣayati | ko 'yam adhyavasāyaḥ | kiṃ grahaṇam,
	ahosvit karaṇam, uta yojanā, atha samāropaḥ | tatra svābhāsam anartham
	arthaṃ kathaṃ gṛhṇīyāt, kuryād vā vikalpaḥ | na hi nīlaṃ pītaṃ śakyaṃ
	grahītuṃ kartuṃ vā śilpakuśalenāpi | nāpy agṛhītena svalakṣaṇena
	svākāraṃ yojayitum arhati vikalpaḥ | na ca svalakṣaṇaṃ
	vikalpagrahaṇagocaraḥ | na ca svākāram anartham artham āropayati | na
	tāvad agṛhītasvākāraḥ śakya āropayitum iti tadgrahaṇam eṣitavayam |
	tatra kiṃ gṛhītvā āropayati, atha yadaiva svākāraṃ gṛhṇati
	tadaivāropayati | nādyaḥ | na hi kṣaṇikaṃ vikalpavijñānaṃ kramavantau
	grahaṇasamāropau kartum arhati | uttarasmiṃs tu kalpe
	'vikalpasvasaṃvedanapratyakṣād vikalpākārād ahaṅkārāspadād
children.translated_text: too refutes determination thus: What is this determination? Is it apprehension, or making, or conjunction, or superimposition? Among these — how could conceptual cognition apprehend or make the non-object that is its own appearance into an [external] object? For even a skilled artisan cannot apprehend or make blue into yellow. Nor is conceptual cognition able to conjoin the <s>svalaksana</s> (particular), which is not apprehended, with its own image. And the <s>svalaksana</s> is not within the range of conceptual apprehension. Nor does it superimpose on its own image, a non-object, the [status of] an object. First, [the image] whose own form has not been apprehended cannot be superimposed — so its apprehension must be sought. In that case, does it apprehend [the image] first and then superimpose, or does it superimpose at the very moment it apprehends its own image? Not the first — for a momentary conceptual cognition is not able to perform the two acts of apprehension and superimposition in succession. But in the latter alternative, the [image] being superimposed by conceptual cognition — [being] from the self-awareness (<s>svasamvedana</s>) perception of conceptual cognition, from the conceptual image that is the locus of the sense of 'I' —

children.text: anahaṅkārāspadaḥ
children.translated_text: [while the external object is] not the locus of the sense of 'I,'

children.text:
samāropyamāṇo vikalpena
	svagocaro na śakyo 'bhinnaḥ pratipattum | nāpi bāhya
children.translated_text: being superimposed by conceptual cognition, cannot be apprehended as identical with [conceptual cognition's] own domain. Nor as identical with the external

children.text: svalakṣaṇaikatvena
children.translated_text: <s>svalaksana</s> (particular)

children.text:
śakyaḥ pratipattum,
	vikalpākāre svalakṣaṇasya bāhyasyāpratibhāsanād iti |
children.translated_text: can it be apprehended, because the external <s>svalaksana</s> does not appear in the conceptual image.

children.text: vācaspatir
children.translated_text: <s>Vacaspati</s>

children.text:
apy adhyavasāyaṃ
	pratikṣipati |
children.translated_text: too rejects determination.

children.text:
anarthaṃ
	svābhāsam artham adhyavasyatīti nirvacanīyam etat | nanv ayam
	āropayatīti kiṃ vikalpasya svarūpānubhava evāropaḥ, uta vyāpārāntaraṃ
	svarūpānubhavāt | na tāvat pūrvaḥ kalpaḥ, anubhavasamāropayor
	vikalpāvikalparūpatayā dravakaṭhinavat tādātmyānupapatteḥ |
	vyāpārāntaratve tu kramaḥ samānakālatā vā | na tāvat kramaḥ,
	kṣaṇikasya vijñānasya kramavadvyāpārāyogāt | akṣaṇikavādinām api
	buddhikarmaṇor viramya vyāpārānupapatteḥ na kramavadvyāpārasambhavaḥ |
	anubhavasamāropau samānakālāv iti cet | bhavatu samānakālatvaṃ
	kevalam | ātmā svabhāvasthita eva vedyaḥ, parabhāvena vedane
	svarūpavedanānupapatteḥ | tathā cātmā jñānasya grāhyagrāhakākāro
	'nubhūto 'rthaś ca samāropitaḥ | na tv ātmā vedyamānaḥ samāropito
	nārthaḥ samāropyamāṇaḥ pratyakṣavedyaḥ | sa ca samāropaḥ sato 'sato vā
	grahaṇam eva | na ca jñānātiriktasya grahaṇaṃ sambhavatīty
	upapāditam |
children.translated_text: 'It determines its own appearance, a non-object, as an object' — this needs to be explained. Now, [when it is said] 'it superimposes' — is the superimposition the very experience of the conceptual cognition's own form, or is it a different operation from the experience of its own form? The first alternative does not hold, because experience and superimposition, being of the nature of non-conceptual and conceptual respectively, cannot be identical — like liquid and solid. If it is a different operation, [is it] in succession or simultaneously? Not in succession, because a momentary cognition cannot have successive operations. Even for proponents of non-momentariness, since the operations of the mind cease [between acts], successive operations are not possible. [Objection:] Experience and superimposition are simultaneous. [Reply:] Let there be simultaneity. But the self must be known as it abides in its own nature, because when known through another's nature, knowledge of its own nature is impossible. And thus: the self of cognition — the image of apprehended and apprehender — is experienced, and the object is superimposed. But the self, being known, is not superimposed; and the object, being superimposed, is not known by perception. And that superimposition is the apprehension of what is either existent or non-existent. But it has been demonstrated that the apprehension of what is beyond cognition is impossible.

children.text:
svapratibhāsasya bāhyād bhedāgraho bāhyasamāropas tato
	bāhye vṛttir iti cet | sa kiṃ gṛhyamāṇe bāhye na vā | na tāvad
	gṛhyamāṇe | uktaṃ hy etan na
tadagrahaṇaṃ
children.translated_text: such non-apprehension [of difference]

children.text:
sambhavatīti | agṛhyamāṇe tu bhedāgrahe na pravṛttiniyamaḥ
	syāt, anyeṣām a
children.translated_text: is not possible. But when the external is not apprehended, there would be no restriction of activity from the non-apprehension of difference, because even other [things]

children.text:
pi tadānīm agrahād
	anyatrāpi pravṛttiprasaṅgād iti
children.translated_text: are not apprehended at that time, and there would follow the consequence of activity even toward other things.

children.text: to
is a quote from

tasmād yathā yathāyam adhyavasāyaś cintyate tathā tathā
	viśīryata eva | tathā vikalpāropābhimānagrahaniścayādayo 'py
	adhyavasāyavat svākāraparyavasitā eva sphuranto bāhyasya
	vārtāmātram api na
children.translated_text: Therefore, however this determination is examined, it simply crumbles. Likewise, conceptual cognition, superimposition, conceit, apprehension, ascertainment, and the like — appearing as confined to their own images, just like determination — do not even know the slightest bit about the external [object].

children.text:
jānantīty
	adhyavasāyasvabhāvā eva
children.translated_text: They are of the very nature of determination,

children.text: śabdapravṛttinimittabhede
children.translated_text: even when there is a difference in the ground for the operation of words,

children.text: 'pi, tat kathaṃ yuktyāgamābahirbhūto
children.translated_text: so how could [one say that what is] outside reasoning and scripture

children.text: Thakur
suggests an emendation to
yuktyāgamabahirbhūto

, but that seems
	unnecessary.
'nātmasphuraṇam ācakṣīta |
children.translated_text: declares the manifestation of what is not the self [i.e., of external objects]?

[Objection:] The non-apprehension of the difference of one's own appearance from the external [object] is the superimposition upon the external — hence activity toward the external. [Reply:] Is that [non-apprehension] when the external is apprehended or not? Not when it is apprehended — for it has been said that

children.text: nanv evaṃ
vikalpādīnām a
children.translated_text: even if conceptual cognition and the like

children.text: sambhave 'py
children.translated_text: are possible,

children.text:
anātmaprakāśakatvānabhyupagame
	sarvajanaprasiddhavidhipratiṣedhavyavahārocchedaprasaṅga iti
	lokavirodhaḥ | vikalpa ity adhyavasāya ity āropa ity abhimāna iti
	graha iti niścaya ityādikaṃ śāstre pratipadaṃ pratipāditam, tatsiddhaṃ
	ca bahirarthādikam abhyupagatam ity ācāryavirodhaḥ | nyāyavirodhaś ca |
children.translated_text: if it is not accepted that they reveal what is not the self, there would follow the consequence of the destruction of the universally acknowledged conventions of affirmation and negation — hence a contradiction with the world. [Furthermore,] 'conceptual cognition,' 'determination,' 'superimposition,' 'conceit,' 'apprehension,' 'ascertainment,' and so forth have been taught at every step in the treatise, and the external objects and the like established thereby have been accepted — hence a contradiction with the teacher (<s>acarya</s>). And there is a contradiction with reasoning.

children.text: tathā hi
children.translated_text: For thus:

children.text: sarvair eva prakāśair
children.translated_text: By all cognitions,

children.text: avipa
children.translated_text: since there is awareness of [their] own non-

children.text:
rītasvarūpasaṃvedanād bhrānter
	atyantam abhāvaḥ syāt | tataś ca sarvasattvāḥ sadaiva samyaksambuddhā
	bhaveyuḥ |
children.translated_text: inverted form, error would be absolutely absent. And then all sentient beings would always be perfectly enlightened (<s>samyaksambuddha</s>).
Objection: Thus,

children.text:
vikalpikā buddhir brāntiḥ,
	svapratibhāse 'narthe 'rthādhyavasāyād iti cet | katham
	avasīyamānas tayā so 'rtho na prakāśate | prakāśamāno vā
	katham asau tasyāṃ na prakāśate | atha prakāśata eva,
	tadārthasya tādātmyaprasaṅgaḥ | asati cārthe

sā
	na
children.translated_text: that [cognition]

children.text: syāt |
children.translated_text: would not exist [either].

children.text:
abhūn māndhātā, bhaviṣyati śaṅkho 'styātmā, nityaḥ śabda iti
	sarvātmanā ca niścayaḥ syāt | gaur iti spaṣṭena ca svena
	lakṣaṇena prakāśeta | svalakṣaṇe ca
children.translated_text: [If the object appeared in conceptual cognition,] then there would be complete certainty regarding [such propositions as] '<s>Mandhata</s> existed,' 'there will be [a king named] <s>Sankha</s>,' 'the self exists,' 'sound is permanent.' And a cow would appear with its own distinct particular characteristic (<s>svalaksana</s>) through the word 'cow.' And since convention (<s>sanketa</s>) is inapplicable to a <s>svalaksana</s>,

children.text: saṅketāyogād vikalpikaiva
children.translated_text: that cognition would not be conceptual at all.

children.text:
sā buddhir na syāt | tasmād aśeṣagovyaktisādhāraṇena gotvena
	gobuddhir alīkena sābhilāpena viplavāt prakhyātīti tathā
	prakāśanam asyā gavārthāvasā
children.translated_text: Therefore, cow-cognition — which is erroneous, accompanied by verbal expression (<s>sabhilapa</s>), and manifests through the false [universal of] <s>gotva</s> (cowness) common to all cow-individuals — its illumination of a cow-object should be understood as determination (<s>adhyavasaya</s>).

children.text:
ya
	ity eṣṭavyam | evaṃ hy ete doṣā na syuḥ, apratibhāsamānasyāpi
	svalakṣaṇasya bhrāntyāvasāyād iti ||
children.translated_text: For in this way, these defects would not arise — because the <s>svalaksana</s>, even though it does not appear, is determined through error.

[Objection:] Conceptual cognition is error, because it determines its own appearance, a non-object, as an object. [Reply:] How can that object, being determined by it, not appear? And if it does appear, how does it not appear in that [cognition]? But if it does appear, then there would follow the consequence of the object being identical [with the cognition]. And if the object does not exist,

children.text:
atrābhidhīyate | na tāval
	lokaśāstraviro

dhau, agṛhīte 'pi
	bāhye pravṛttinivṛttyādisamarthanāt
	svaparavādiduratikramādhyavasāyasvarūpanirvacanāt |
children.translated_text: because activity and cessation and the like are justified even when the external is not apprehended, and because the essential nature of determination — which is impossible to transcend for both one's own and the opponent's school — has been defined.
To this we reply: To begin with, there is no contradiction with the world or with the treatise,

children.text: nyāyavirodhasya tu gandho 'pi nāsti |

tathā hi kā punar ayaṃ bhrāntir
	asatkhyātir atasmiṃs tadgraho vā
children.translated_text: For thus: What is this error — is it the cognition of the non-existent (<s>asatkhyati</s>), or the apprehension of that [which is not] in that [which is]?

children.text: yadabhāvād idānīm eva muktir āsajyate |
children.translated_text: From the absence of which, liberation would follow right now.

children.text:
na tāvad ādyaḥ pakṣaḥ, asatkhyāteḥ
	pratyākhyānāt | yad āhur
children.translated_text: Not the first alternative, because the cognition of the non-existent has been rejected. As the

children.text: guruvaḥ
children.translated_text: teachers

children.text: yasya svarūpanirbhāso bādhakād yadi tan na sat |
children.translated_text: say: 'If that whose own form appears is non-existent because of a sublating cognition, then',

children.text: bādhake 'pi ka āśvāsaḥ svarūpāntarabhāsini ||
children.translated_text: 'what confidence is there even in the sublating cognition, which manifests [yet] another form?'

children.text: anyasvarūpopanayāt tatsvarūpanivāraṇam |
children.translated_text: 'The negation of its own form [comes about] through the introduction of another form;'

children.text: tatrāpi saṃśayo jātaḥ pūrvabādhopalabdhitaḥ ||
children.translated_text: 'doubt has arisen even about that [other form], from the observation of previous sublation.'

children.text: iyam evāgrahe bādhā
nādyajasyāparā
children.translated_text: 'of the first — [there is] no other [sublation]'

children.text: yadi |
children.translated_text: 'if [you say so].'
'This non-apprehension is itself the sublation'

children.text: asyāḥ pūrvaiva
children.translated_text: 'Of this [sublation], the prior one'

children.text: bhavatu rūpanirbhāsanaṃ samam ||
children.translated_text: 'let the manifestation of form be equal [i.e., equally doubtful].'

children.text: nānyā ca bhāvinīty atra pramāṇaṃ kiñcid asti vaḥ |
children.translated_text: 'And you have no evidence that another [sublation] will not [occur].'

children.text: api svarūpanirbhāse yadā
bādhakasambhavaḥ
children.translated_text: 'there is the possibility of sublation,'
'Moreover, when even regarding the appearance of own form,'

children.text: anirbhāse svarūpasya hetuśodhanaviplave |
children.translated_text: 'when there is no appearance of own form, and the examination of the reason collapses — if even then, when the mere suspicion of sublation does not appear, there is [said to be a] collapse, the collapse would be great indeed.'

children.text: bādhaśaṅkāvinirbhāse 'py evaṃ ced viplavo mahān ||
iti ||
children.translated_text: Thus.

children.text: Cf.

children.translated_text: And there is not even the slightest contradiction with reasoning.

children.text:
śāstre ca atasmiṃs tadgrahāt
      svapratibhāse 'narthe 'rthādhyavasāyād dṛśyavikalpyayor ekīkaraṇād
      bhrāntir uktā | tām ayaṃ samarthayitum asamarthaḥ
      svātantryeṇālīkasphuraṇaṃ bhrāntir iti kāvyaṃ viracayya vistārayati |
children.translated_text: And in the treatise, error is stated as the identification of the seen and the conceptualized (<s>drsya</s> and <s>vikalpya</s>), from the apprehension of that [which is not] in that [which is], from the determination of a non-object — one's own appearance — as an object. This [opponent], unable to justify that [definition], independently composes poetry, proclaiming that the autonomous manifestation of what is false is error.

children.text:
nanv atasmiṃs tadgraho 'pi bhramaḥ
      svā
children.translated_text: Objection: But even the apprehension of that [which is not] in that [which is] as error, [being] beyond cognition confined to its own

children.text:
kāraparyavasitajñānād atirikto bahubhir
      bahudhā vicārya pratyākhyātaḥ | tat kathaṃ tasminn api pakṣe na
      bhrāntikṣatir yenedānīm eva muktiprasaṅgo na syād iti cet | tad etad
      bhagavato
children.translated_text: image, has been rejected in many ways by many [thinkers] upon thorough examination. So how, in that alternative too, is there no destruction of error, such that the consequence of immediate liberation would not follow? [Reply:] That is the cry of one whose mind is bewildered by the poison of hostility toward the view of the blessed

children.text: bhāṣyakārasya
children.translated_text: <s>Bhasyakara</s> [i.e., <s>Dharmakirti</s>],

children.text: matavidveṣaviṣavyākulavikrośitam atikātarayati kṛpāparavaśadhiyaḥ |
children.translated_text: and it exceedingly pains [us] whose minds are overcome by compassion.

children.text: tathā hi samanantarapratyayabalāyātasvapratibhāsa
children.translated_text: For thus: from the mere awareness of a specific appearance that has arrived through the force of the immediately preceding condition (<s>samanantarapratyaya</s>),

children.text:
viśeṣavedanamātrād
      agṛhīte 'pi paratra pravṛttyākṣepo 'dhyavasāyaḥ | na cāsau
      pūrvoktavāgjālaiḥ pratihantuṃ śakyaḥ, sarvaprāṇabhṛtāṃ
      pratyātmaviditatvāt, kaiścid apy anudbhinnatvāt | ayam eva ca saṃsāras
      tatkṣayo mokṣa iti kvedānīm eva tadvārtāpi | tathā hi
      vicitrānādivāsanāvaśāt prabodhakapratyayaviśeṣāpekṣayā vikalpaḥ
      kena
children.translated_text: even when the external is not apprehended, the prompting of activity toward the other [i.e., the external] is determination. And that cannot be struck down by the previously stated verbal nets, because it is known to every living being from within, and has never been contradicted by anyone. And this [determination] itself is <s>samsara</s> (the cycle of existence), and its cessation is <s>moksa</s> (liberation) — so where is there even talk of [liberation] right now? For thus: through the force of manifold beginningless latent impressions (<s>vasana</s>), and in dependence on specific awakening conditions, conceptual cognition,

children.text:

In that [process], the capacity for activity in both ways [toward and away] — which has arrived through the force of its own cause — this very [capacity] is the superimposition of being the object of activity, also called determination (<s>adhyavasaya</s>). Just as the operation of apprehension of cognition of the moon and the like — whether erroneous or non-erroneous — is simply the generation of the conviction and determination of seeing that [object].

Likewise, for conceptual cognition too — arising with an image such as 'fire is here' — the prompting of activity is what is called 'terminating in the external.' And just as the very form of the image of non-conceptual [cognition of] two moons and the like is the instrument of determination, so too, for determination itself, it is precisely such a form of the image that is the instrument of activity directed away from other objects.

children.translated_text: No — or rather, even when a hare's horn and the like do not appear, the obstruction to [their] establishment cannot be averted even by <s>Brahmā</s>. For the convention regarding objects is of two kinds: through appearance (<s>pratibhāsa</s>) and through determination (<s>adhyavasāya</s>). So here, even in the absence of appearance, objecthood is stated through mere determination of the particular (<s>svalakṣaṇa</s>) and the like that are excluded from the contrary — because if [cognition] were entirely without an object, the absurd consequence would follow that all conventions such as engagement and withdrawal would be destroyed. And therefore, that [object] is conveyed by that [cognition], yet in the cognition there is no

children.text:
tatprakāśa iti saṅgatir asty
      eva, prakāśyaprakāśakabhāvābhāve 'py

children.translated_text: and the determiner — because the object-possessor relation is tenable [even through determination alone].

Objection: But that [external object] is conveyed by that [cognition], and yet it does not appear in that cognition — even by oath, this cannot be believed. [Reply:] This is incoherent. For from determination, since there is the intervention of a sublating cognition regarding the external thing such as cloth and the like, and since the

children.text:
nanu yadi nādhyavaseyapratītis
      tadāgṛhīte 'pi svalakṣaṇādau pravṛttir iti sarvatrāviśeṣeṇa
      prasajyeta, sarvatrāgṛhītatvena viśeṣābhāvāt | tataś ca prāptir
      api nābhimatasya niyamenety anumānam api viplutam |

atra
      brūmaḥ | yady adhyavaseyam agṛhītaṃ viśvam apy agṛhītam, tathāpi

      asadutpattivat | sarvatrāsattve 'pi hi bījād
      aṅkurasyaivotpattiḥ,
children.translated_text: To this we reply: Even if the determinable is ungrasped, and indeed everything is ungrasped, still engagement is directed only toward a fixed object and not everywhere, because the conceptual cognition has a fixed capacity due to its having a determinate form brought about by the force of the immediately preceding condition (<s>samanantarapratyaya</s>) of that kind. For entities with fixed capacities have their essential nature established by valid cognition and are not subject to the charge of confusion of capacities — just like origination from a non-existent [cause being impossible]. For even though [the cause] is non-existent everywhere, from a seed only a sprout arises,

children.text:
tatraiva tasya śakteḥ pramāṇena nirūpaṇāt |
      tathehāpi hutavahākārasya vikalpasya dāhapākādyarthakriyārthinas
      tatsmaraṇavato hutavahaviṣayāyām eva pravṛttau sāmarthyaṃ
      pramāṇapratītaṃ katham atiprasaṅgabhāgi | pratyāsatticintāyāṃ ca
      tāttvikasyāpi vahner jvaladbhāsvarākā
children.translated_text: because the capacity for that is ascertained in that [seed] alone by valid cognition. Likewise here too, the capacity of the conceptual cognition having the form of fire — for one who remembers it and desires the causal efficacy (<s>arthakriyā</s>) of burning, cooking, and the like — to engage only with respect to fire as its object is established by valid cognition. How can it be subject to over-extension? And in the analysis of proximate relation, even real fire has the nature of blazing luminous

children.text:
ratvaṃ vikalpollikhitasyāpīti,
      tāvatā tatraiva pravartanaśaktir jvalanavi
children.translated_text: color, and so does [fire] as delineated by conceptual cognition — and to that extent, the capacity of the conceptual cognition of fire to prompt engagement is [confined] there alone and not in water and the like.

children.text: kalpasya na jalādau ||

children.translated_text: [Objection:] If there is no cognition of the determinable, then engagement would absurdly follow even with respect to a particular (<s>svalakṣaṇa</s>) that has not been grasped, and this would apply everywhere without distinction, because there is no distinction since [the particular] is ungrasped everywhere. And therefore, the attainment [of the desired object] would not invariably be of the intended [object] — so inference too would be vitiated.

children.text:

children.translated_text: and constitutes <s>saṃsāra</s> (the cycle of existence). As the treatise [states]:

[Objection:] Now, with the superimposition by way of resemblance, is it the superimposition of one's own form upon the external, or of the external upon one's own form? In both cases there is incoherence, because it is impossible to grasp both — one's own form and the external — which are the superimposed and the locus of superimposition. [Reply:] We do not assert that engagement is through superimposition. Rather, that cognition, arising by the force of the maturation of its own latent impressions (<s>vāsanā</s>), even without seeing the external, extends engagement toward the external — and thus it is deluded

children.text: na jñāne tulyam utpattito dhiyaḥ |
children.translated_text: There is nothing equal to cognition in the origin of [conceptual] thought.

children.text: tathāvidhāyāḥ

By this, the objection 'that [external object] is not cognized, and yet through that [cognition] there is the appearance of non-difference' is shown to be untenable,

Therefore, the apprehension of identity in what is not [identical], which is charming [only] without investigation, is precisely error, also called superimposition (<s>āropa</s>); and its cessation is liberation (<s>mokṣa</s>)

children.text: iti yuktam |
children.translated_text: — this is fitting.

Therefore, engagement is not through superimposition as in the case of silver [on mother-of-pearl], but rather because of the restriction of capacity bound to the arising of a specific form. And it is not the case that one who investigates would not engage due to the certainty of not seeing a real entity. For even in [direct] seeing, engagement is due to the desire for causal efficacy (<s>arthakriyā</s>). And the attainment of causal efficacy depends on the restriction to the existence of real entities. And that restriction, just as it is produced through seeing by the connection with a real entity, so too

And so, as long as investigation has not arisen, this is existence (<s>bhava</s>); its cessation

the thorough understanding of existence itself

children.translated_text: and that there is no conjunction of words with the self, and therefore conceptual cognition simply does not exist, so whose is this analysis of conceptual cognition? — to this we reply: Here, the determination 'there is fire here,' just as

children.text:
kāyikīṃ vṛttiṃ prasūte tathāgnir mayā
      pratīyata iti vācikīm api prasūte, etadākārānuvyavasāyarūpāṃ mānasīm

      chabdākārasyāpi sphuraṇāt | tasmād arthagrahābhimānavān mānavastāvad
      abhidhānasaṃyuktagrahaṇā
children.translated_text: it produces bodily activity, so too it produces verbal activity [such as] 'fire is cognized by me,' and it also produces mental [activity] in the form of a reflective determination of that same form. And this being so, just as there is the certainty 'this object was grasped by conceptual cognition,' so too [there is the certainty] 'it was grasped in conjunction with a word' — because the form of the word also flashes forth, just like a trace of the object's form. Therefore, a human being who has the notion of grasping the object also has the notion of grasping

children.text:
bhimānavān apīty avasāyānurodhād eva
      vikalpavyavasthā na tattvataḥ | yad āhur guravaḥ
children.translated_text: [the object] in conjunction with expression — and the establishment of conceptual cognition is merely in conformity with determination, not in reality. As the teachers say:

	vākṣarākārākīrṇaḥ sphurati punar arthākṛtilavaḥ |
children.translated_text: There is no connection with words anywhere; nor externally. But in the mind, pervaded by the form of syllables and letters, there flashes forth a trace of the form of the object.

children.text:
ubhāv apy ākārau yad api dhiya evādhyavasitir vidhatte tau bāhye
	vacasi ca vikalpasthitir ataḥ ||
JNA 227,6ff.

children.translated_text: Both forms — though they belong to cognition alone — determination projects them onto the external [object] and [external] speech; hence conceptual cognition has this [conventional] status.

īdṛśaḥ

through the distinction of dependent origination (<s>pratītyutpāda</s>), this is merely a conventional arrangement

From non-conceptual [perception], when conceptual cognition arises,

children.translated_text: and from the speech of one who makes conventions, regarding the cognitive image that is qualified —
